10.1007/s11065-023-09592-5.printed_title: Assessing Inhibitory Control Deficits in Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Stop-signal Task

sentences.s1: REVIEW Assessing Inhibitory Control Deficits in Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta‑analysis of the Stop‑signal Task Daniel Senkowski1 · Theresa Ziegler1 · Mervyn Singh2 · Andreas Heinz1 · Jason He3 · Tim Silk2 · Robert C.
sentences.s2: Lorenz4 Received: 12 July 2022 / Accepted: 21 March 2023 / Published online: 10 June 2023 © The Author(s) 2023 Abstract In recent years, there has been an increasing quest in improving our understanding of the neurocognitive deficits underlying adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
sentences.s3: Current statistical manuals of psychiatric disorders emphasize inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, but empirical studies have also shown consistent alterations in inhibitory control.
sentences.s4: To date, there is no established neuropsychological test to assess inhibitory control deficits in adult ADHD.
sentences.s5: A common paradigm for assessing response inhibition is the stop-signal task (SST).
sentences.s6: Following PRISMA-selection criteria, our systematic review and meta-analysis integrated the findings of 26 publications with 27 studies examining the SST in adult ADHD.
sentences.s7: The meta-analysis, which included 883 patients with adult ADHD and 916 control participants, revealed reliable inhibitory con- trol deficits, as expressed in prolonged SST response times, with a moderate effect size g = 0.51 (95% CI: 0.376–0.644,p < 0.0001).
sentences.s8: The deficits were not moderated by study quality, sample characteristics or clinical parameters, suggesting that they may be a phenotype in this disorder.
sentences.s9: The analyses of secondary outcome measures revealed greater SST omission errors and reduced go accuracy in patients, indicative of altered sustained attention.
sentences.s10: However, only few (N < 10) studies were available for these measures.
sentences.s11: Our meta-analysis suggests that the SST, in conjunction with other tests and questionnaires, could become a valuable tool for assessing inhibitory control deficits in adult ADHD.
sentences.s12: Keywords Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder · Impulsivity · Cognition · Attention · Cognitive deficits · Neuropsychology Introduction Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that emerges during child- hood or young adulthood and is characterized by symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity (Adler et al., 2017; Asherson et al., 2016).
sentences.s13: Adults with ADHD have a global prevalence of 2.58% (persistent disorder) and 6.76% (symptomatic disorder) (Song et al., 2021).
sentences.s14: In clinical prac- tice, adult ADHD is assessed using questionnaires, interviews with relatives and inspection of school certificates.
sentences.s15: Although neurocognitive deficits are inherent to ADHD, there is still no established test or test battery that is commonly used in the assessment of this disorder (Fried et al., 2021; Nikolas et al., 2019).
sentences.s16: Nevertheless, neuropsychological tests should be used in patients with presumed cognitive deficits to objectify these deficits during the diagnostic process.
sentences.s17: To date, there is an emerging quest to establish neurocognitive paradigms as complementary tools in the assessment of adult ADHD.
sentences.s18: Early research on ADHD has suggested that deficits in inhibitory control are a primary phenotype in this disorder (Barkley, 1997).
sentences.s19: Support for the inhibition deficit model has come from studies showing altered executive functions in adult ADHD (Hadas et al., 2021; Linhartová et al., 2021; Nigg et al., 2002; Silverstein et al., 2020).
sentences.s20: An important aspect of executive functions is inhibitory control, which has often been investigated with the stop-signal task (SST; Verbruggen * Daniel Senkowski daniel.senkowski@charite.de 1 Department of Psychiatry and Neurosciences, Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and Humboldt Universität Zu Berlin, Charité Campus Mitte (CCM), Charitéplatz 1, 10117 Berlin, Germany 2 Centre for Social and Early Emotional Development (SEED) and School of Psychology, Deakin University, Geelong, Victoria, Australia 3 King’s College London, London WC2R 2LS, UK 4 Lise Meitner Group for Environmental Neuroscience, Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Lentzeallee 94, 14195 Berlin, Germany & Logan, 2008), but also with other paradigms such as the go/ no-go task (Fisher et al., 2011).
sentences.s21: However, there are substantial differences between the two tasks.
sentences.s22: For instance, the go/no-go task does not include a measure of individual response inhibi- tion speed, which is explicitly obtained in the SST.
sentences.s23: Moreover, it has been shown that different neural mechanisms under- lie stimulus processing in the two tasks (Raud et al., 2020).
sentences.s24: Hence, the go/no-go task and the SST likely capture different facets of response inhibition and therefore, they should be examined independently.
sentences.s25: In the current review and meta- analysis, we focused on the SST in adult ADHD (for a meta- analysis on the go/no-go task in combined children, and adult studies, see Wright et al., 2014).
sentences.s26: In the SST, participants are instructed to make a forced- choice response following a ‘go-signal’, e.g., an arrow point- ing to the left or right, and to respond with a left or right button press, respectively.
sentences.s27: Crucially, in a small proportion of trials, an auditory or visual ‘stop-signal’ is presented after the go-signal and participants are required to withhold the behavioral response.
sentences.s28: In most studies an adaptive approach is used to obtain the delay interval between the go-signal and the stop-signal for which the response inhibition rates are around 50% at the individual subject level.
sentences.s29: Based on this delay interval and the response times to go-trials, the stop- signal reaction time (SSRT) is calculated, which has become an established measure of response inhibition (Logan et al., 2014).
sentences.s30: A previous meta-analysis of the SSRT, which involved studies in children and adults diagnosed with ADHD, has revealed deficits of moderate effect sizes (g) = 0.62 across age groups (Lipszyc & Schachar, 2010).
sentences.s31: This meta-analysis included 68 studies with children but only 10 studies with adult ADHD.
sentences.s32: Therefore, the validity of this analysis regard- ing adult ADHD was limited and the degree of SSRT deficits in adult ADHD remains to be investigated.
sentences.s33: Here, we performed a review and meta-analysis that con- formed to current PRISMA guidelines focusing on response inhibition deficits, as measured by the SSRT, in adult ADHD.
sentences.s34: Our analysis included 26 publications with 27 studies, which allowed for a reliable estimation of response inhibition defi- cits in patients.
sentences.s35: We performed a quality assessment of the SST following a recent consensus paper (Verbruggen et al., 2019) and estimated the risk of bias (RoB) for each study.
sentences.s36: We thoroughly examined whether the study quality as well as participant-related and clinical factors influence response inhibition deficits in adult ADHD.
sentences.s37: Methods The protocol of this systematic review and meta-analysis has been pre-registered in the PROSPERO database (PROS- PERO ID: CRD42021266709).
sentences.s38: Study Selection The following study selection criteria were applied: 1.
sentences.s39: Patient population: Studies contained at least one group of adult par- ticipants (18 +) with a current diagnosis of ADHD in accord- ance with the DSM criteria (5 or earlier) or Hyperkinetic Disorder according to the ICD (10 or earlier) criteria.
sentences.s40: Stud- ies investigating populations with only subclinical ADHD symptoms were not included. 2.
sentences.s41: Control group: Studies must include at least one healthy control group. 3.
sentences.s42: Experimental task: Response inhibition performance had to be assessed using the SST or the Stop-Change Task, which is a modified version of the SST in which individuals swith to a secondary response after they have inhibited an ongoing response (Ver- bruggen & Logan, 2009).
sentences.s43: Studies using atypical SST para- digms such as dual tasks or the selective SST were excluded.
sentences.s44: Also excluded were studies in which participants received feedback on stop-signal performance, as feedback and reward influence response inhibition (Lipszyc & Schachar, 2010; Slusarek et al., 2001). 4.
sentences.s45: Outcome measure: Sufficient test statistics for the stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) must be provided to calculate standardized mean differences (Hedge’s g). 5.
sentences.s46: Other criteria: Empirical articles written in English or German language and published or accepted for publication in peer-reviewed journals during the period 2000–2022.
sentences.s47: Search Strategy To identify relevant articles, an electronic search was con- ducted up to April 14, 2022 in two major publication data- bases: Medline and PsycInfo (accessed from EBSCOhost).
sentences.s48: The following syntax, adapted from Lipszyc and Schachar (2010), was used: [(attention deficit hyperactivity disorder OR ADHD) AND Adult* AND (stop task OR stop signal OR response inhibition OR executive function)].
sentences.s49: Limiters were set so that only articles published in peer-reviewed journals in English or German since the 1st of January 2000 were included.
sentences.s50: Furthermore, reference lists of the identified empirical articles, previous meta-analyses and systematic reviews were scanned to ensure that all relevant articles were captured.
sentences.s51: Study Selection The study selection process was conducted by two authors (TZ and DS) and included two stages: 1.
sentences.s52: Initial screening of titles and abstracts using the inclusion and exclusion cri- teria described above. 2.
sentences.s53: For the resulting set of studies full texts were obtained and reviewed in detail for eligibility.
sentences.s54: Screening of eligible articles was performed in Endnote.
sentences.s55: In case of disagreement between authors regarding the eligibil- ity of studies, studies were screened by other team members and disagreements during the first or the second screening process were discussed until consensus was reached.
sentences.s56: Data Extraction and Outcomes Data were extracted independently by two authors (TZ and MS).
sentences.s57: When statistical values were insufficiently reported for the meta-analysis, the authors of the articles were contacted and asked to provide the missing information.
sentences.s58: The following measures of the SST were extracted from the articles, sepa- rately for patients and controls: SSRT as primary outcome; stop commission errors (responding on a stop trial); go dis- crimination errors (e.g., responding with the left arrow key, even though a rightwards pointing arrow was presented); go omission errors (not responding on a go trial); and go accuracy (percentage of correct go trials) as secondary out- comes.
sentences.s59: In addition, important variables that might influ- ence behavioral performance in the planned analysis were extracted and tabulated for each study: Age; IQ; percentage of males; ADHD subtype; years of education; comorbidities; medication status; patient recruitment setting.
sentences.s60: Assessments of the SST Validity and Risk of Bias The validity of the SST and the risk of bias (RoB) in each study are important factors that could influence group dif- ferences between patients and controls.
sentences.s61: Therefore, they were explicitly examined in the current analysis.
sentences.s62: Both SST validity and RoB were assessed by two independent raters (TZ and MS).
sentences.s63: In case of disagreement between the authors, a con- sensus was reached by discussion with other team members.
sentences.s64: To increase inter-rater reliability, a calibration session was conducted in which the assessments were applied to two arti- cles not included in this review.
sentences.s65: This allowed the two raters to identify possible sources of disagreement and to decide on rules for the assessment of ambiguous cases (Supplementary Text 1).
sentences.s66: Across studies selected for this meta-analysis, there is considerable variability in the administration of the SST, and the analytic procedures used to derive outcome measures.
sentences.s67: To determine the validity of the SST, we used the recent con- sensus guide developed by Verbruggen et al. (2019), which provides 12 ‘best practice’ recommendations for the design, implementation and analysis of the SST.
sentences.s68: We selected four main criteria from this consensus guide and rephrased them into four dichotomous items, i.e., item fulfilled or not, for the critical appraisal (Supplementary Text 2).
sentences.s69: In case of missing information, the criterion was rated as not fulfilled.
sentences.s70: The overall validity of the SST was then rated as fol- lows: < 3 criteria fulfilled = low validity; 3 criteria ful- filled = moderate validity; 4 criteria fulfilled = high validity.
sentences.s71: Cohen’s unweighted kappa for nominal data were calculated for each item.
sentences.s72: In case of a bias or a prevalence problem, Byrt’s bias and prevalence adjusted kappa were additionally reported (Byrt et al., 1993; Hallgren, 2012).
sentences.s73: For the RoB assessment, we applied the adapted Hombrados and Waddington criteria that have been recently used for studies with ADHD patients (Hulsbosch et al., 2021): (1) Equivalent group sizes; (2) Use of a diagnostic interview or questionnaires to determine ADHD diagnosis; (3) Sufficient sample sizes; (4) All sta- tistical outcomes are reported; (5) Transparent reporting of the data analysis; (6) Reporting of missing/excluded data.
sentences.s74: Each item was rated as “good/low RoB”, “satisfactory/mod- erate RoB”, or “poor/high RoB”.
sentences.s75: In accordance with the rat- ing system described in the Cochrane Handbook, an overall quality rating of low, moderate or high was assigned to each study based on the following criteria: If at least one of the categories was rated as having a moderate RoB, the overall RoB could only be rated as moderate as well, even if all other categories were rated as having a low RoB.
sentences.s76: The same prin- ciple applied if at least one category was rated as having a high RoB.
sentences.s77: Cohen’s weighted Kappa was calculated for each individual domain (Cohen, 1968; Hallgren, 2012).
sentences.s78: After all studies were rated for SST validity and RoB, a overall study quality variable was created combining the RoB ratings and SST validity.
sentences.s79: Studies with high RoB and low SST validity were rated as having low overall quality, and studies with moderate or low RoB AND moderate or high SST validity were rated as having moderate to high overall quality.
sentences.s80: Stud- ies characterized by the remaining combinations of RoB and SST validity (low RoB and low SST validity; moderate RoB and low SST validity; high RoB and moderate SST validity; high RoB and high SST validity) were assigned to the cat- egory moderate to low overall quality.
sentences.s81: This categorization was used for subgroup analyses (see below).
sentences.s82: Meta‑Analysis The meta-analysis was carried out in R (version 4.0.3; R Core Team, 2020) and the metafor package (version 3.0.2; Viechtbauer, 2010).
sentences.s83: Hedges’ g was calculated for each indi- vidual study and each outcome (primary outcome SSRT and secondary outcomes) displaying the effect size of the group difference.
sentences.s84: Given that various sources could account for dif- ferences in findings between studies, e.g., examination of different patient samples or use of different SST paradigms, a random-effects model was fitted to the data.
sentences.s85: Instead of the usual large-sample approximation, the sampling variance was adjusted by taking the sample-size weighted average of the Hedges' g values into the equation, as this approach has been shown to be less biased (Lin & Aloe, 2021).
sentences.s86: For computing confidence intervals, the method introduced by Knapp and Hartung (2003) was chosen.
sentences.s87: To assess for hetero- geneity, (1) 휏2 was estimated using the restricted maximum- likelihood estimator (Viechtbauer, 2005), (2) the Q-test for heterogeneity and (3) the I2 statistics (Higgins & Thompson, 2002) are reported.
sentences.s88: If heterogeneity between studies is pre- sent, i.e., 𝜏2 > 0 , regardless of whether the Q-test reaches significance, a prediction interval for the true outcomes is provided (Riley et al., 2011).
sentences.s89: The results will be visual- ized using forest plots.
sentences.s90: Furthermore, the model is assessed regarding (1) potential outliers, i.e. studies with studentized residuals larger than the 100 × (1 −0.05∕(2 × k))th percen- tile of a standard normal distribution, considering a Bon- ferroni correction with 훼= 0.05 (two-sided) for k included studies as well as (2) potentially overinfluential studies, i.e. with a Cook’s distance larger than the median plus 6 times the interquartile range of the Cook’s distances (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010).
sentences.s91: If outliers were detected, leave-one-out diagnostics for sensitivity analysis were conducted.
sentences.s92: Assessment of Publication Bias Evidence of publication bias was assessed using a combina- tion of visual and statistical approaches.
sentences.s93: First, the funnel plot (Copas & Chi, 2000) of standardized mean difference (SMD) against the inverse square root of the sample size was visu- ally inspected for asymmetries (Zwetsloot et al., 2017).
sentences.s94: In the absense of bias, the funnel plot should be symmetrical and narrow down at the top, where studies with larger sample sizes are located and the effect estimate is more precise.
sentences.s95: How- ever, determining of publication bias using visual inspection methods (such as funnel plots) is often subjective and prone to judgment errors (Wang & Bushman, 1998).
sentences.s96: Therefore, it is recommended to additionally compute a quantile–quantile plot (Q-Q plot) to aid in the assessment of publication bias.
sentences.s97: Next, Egger’s regression test was computed using the inverse of the square root sample size as a predictor to statistically test for asymmetry of the funnel plot (Zwetsloot et al., 2017).
sentences.s98: Meta‑Regression and Subgroup Analysis To assess whether the pre-specified extracted demographic and clinical variables as well as study quality influenced the meta-analytic outcome and to explore the source of potential heterogeneity, a meta-regression analysis was performed for continuous (age, sex, IQ) and a subgroup analysis for categorical covariates (RoB, SST validity and overall study quality, comorbidities, patient setting and medication status).
sentences.s99: Mixed-effects models were fitted to the data for the meta-regression analysis.
sentences.s100: If sufficient data were avail- able across studies, the extracted variables were included in a multivariate regression model.
sentences.s101: Otherwise, univari- ate models were fitted.
sentences.s102: The parameter 휏2 , which indicates the residual heterogeneity not explained by the included moderators (Viechtbauer, 2010), was estimated using the REML-estimator (Viechtbauer, 2005).
sentences.s103: Tests and confidence intervals were calculated by the Knapp and Hartung (2003) method.
sentences.s104: The mean values for age, IQ, and percentage of males of the study samples were computed for inclusion in a regression model.
sentences.s105: For this purpose, the reported means of the patients and the means of the controls were averaged.
sentences.s106: When sample sizes of ADHD participants and healthy con- trols differed substantially, a sample-size weighted mean was calculated.
sentences.s107: When IQ scores were reported separately for ver- bal and non-verbal IQ in a study, the mean of these scores was calculated.
sentences.s108: IQ was centered before taken into a uni- variate regression model.
sentences.s109: Age and gender were standardized before taken into a multivariate regression model.
sentences.s110: The following variables were considered for subgroup analysis: (1) RoB with the levels low RoB vs. moderate RoB vs. high RoB; (2) SST validity with the levels low validity vs. moderate validity vs. high validity; (3) overall study quality with the levels low overall quality vs. low to moderate overall quality vs. moderate to high overall qual- ity; (4) psychiatric comorbidities in patients with the levels comorbidities allowed vs. comorbidities not allowed; (5) psychiatric comorbidities in control participants with the levels comorbidities allowed vs. comorbidities not allowed; (6) patient setting with the levels subgroups recruited from a clinical-setting vs. recruited from a non-clinical setting vs. recruited from both (mixed); (7) medication status with the levels subgroups medicated vs. unmedicated.
sentences.s111: Separate random-effects models were fitted for each of these vari- ables.
sentences.s112: Then, a fixed-effects regression including a moderator with the effect estimates of the subgroups was calculated to test whether it significantly moderated SSRT.
sentences.s113: Finally, for both meta-regressions and subgroup analyses an omnibus test of moderators was conducted, testing all coefficients excluding the intercept against 0.
sentences.s114: If the omnibus test reaches significance, it may indicate that some of the heterogeneity could be explained by the predictors included in the model (Viechtbauer, 2010).
sentences.s115: Secondary Outcome Measures of the SST In addition to the SSRT, the SST identifies other outcome measures that are recommended to be reported (Verbruggen et al., 2019).
sentences.s116: For the current meta-analysis, we examined stop commission errors, go discrimination errors, go omis- sion errors and go accuracy.
sentences.s117: All studies that reported these parameters were included in the meta-analyses.
sentences.s118: When errors were reported in numbers (i.e., means, standard deviations), then the percentage of errors was calculated.
sentences.s119: The analytical procedures were the same as for the SSRT, except that no meta-regression or subgroup analyses were conducted, due to the smaller number of available studies.
sentences.s120: Results Study Selection The electronic search resulted in 1186 articles in MED- LINE and 1353 in PsycInfo (Fig. 1).
sentences.s121: Limiters described in the Methods section excluded 215 of these articles.
sentences.s122: Search results were exported to EndNote, where EBSCOhost auto- matically removed 662 duplicates, resulting in 1662 studies.
sentences.s123: After removing the remaining duplicates using EndNote’s automatic deduplication tool (n = 177) and manual inspec- tion (n = 36), 1449 articles remained.
sentences.s124: Screening of titles and abstracts for eligibility resulted in the exclusion of 1288 studies.
sentences.s125: Full texts of the remaining 161 studies were obtained and checked thoroughly checked for eligibility.
sentences.s126: Of the 161 studies, 116 were excluded because they did not include a healthy control group (n = 1), assessed only sub- clinical symptomatology (n = 2), included ADHD only as comorbid disorder (n = 1), or did not use an SST paradigm (n = 112).
sentences.s127: Another 4 studies were excluded because they had substantially modified the SST paradigm and another 8 studies were excluded because their samples included both children and adults.
sentences.s128: Six studies reported insufficient statistical values for the meta-analysis and authors were contacted.
sentences.s129: We received data from four studies, which were then included in the final sample.
sentences.s130: It is important to note that Bekker et al. (2005a, b) and van Dongen-Boomsma et al. (2010) reported identical SSRTs, i.e., for the same experimental session and the same sample of participants.
sentences.s131: The same accounted for Nigg et al. (2005), Stavro et al. (2007) and Martel et al. (2017) as well as for Linhartová et al. (2020) and Linhartová et al. (2021).
sentences.s132: For these groups of articles, the reported SSRT value was extracted and counted as a single sample in the meta-analysis.
sentences.s133: Finally, Szekely et al. (2017) conducted two SST experiments, one implemented for fMRI and one for MEG.
sentences.s134: Although the samples for these two experiments partially overlapped (63 completed the SST during MEG and fMRI, 85 during fMRI only, and 33 during MEG only), they were treated as single observations in the analysis.
sentences.s135: Screening of reference lists did not revealed any additional articles.
sentences.s136: Thus, in total, 26 publi- cations with 27 studies were included in the meta-analysis (1799 participants; ADHD = 883; controls = 916).

sentences.s138: Twenty-four out of 27 studies prohibited stimulant medi- cation on the day of testing, two studies did not report this information and one study allowed medication (Linhartová et al., 2021).

sentences.s225: Discussion In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we integrated the data from 27 studies that examined the stop-signal task in adult ADHD.
sentences.s226: The analysis revealed inhibitory control deficits, as expressed in prolonged SSRTs, with a moderate effect size g = 0.51.
sentences.s227: These deficits were not significantly moderated by the study quality, sample characteristics, or clinical parameters.
sentences.s228: In addition, the analyses of secondary outcome measures revealed greater SST omission errors and reduced go accuracy in patients, although only few stud- ies (n < 10) were available for these measures.
sentences.s229: Behavioral Inhibition Deficits in Stop‑Signal Response Times The main finding of our meta-analysis is that patients with adult ADHD reliably show moderate deficits in the SSRT.
sentences.s230: The magnitude of the deficits is consistent with the results of a previous meta-analysis, which included a much smaller number of studies in adult ADHD (Lipszyc & Schachar, 2010).
sentences.s231: Our meta-analysis of 27 studies establishes the SSRT as a reliable measure for assessing inhibitory control deficits in adult ADHD.
sentences.s232: Extending previous work, we evaluated the quality of the SST using the recommendations of a recent consensus paper (Verbruggen et al., 2019) and estimated the risk of bias for each study.
sentences.s233: The large number of obser- vations allowed us to examine whether study quality, taking into account RoB and the validity of the SST, demograph- ics (age and gender), IQ or clinical parameters (comorbidi- ties and setting) influence SSRT deficits in patients.
sentences.s234: To this end, we computed meta-regression and subgroup analyses including all studies that reported the respective variables.

sentences.s236: This suggests that the prolonged SSRT in patients can be observed in experimental settings even when the study quality and other parameters are not optimal.
sentences.s237: The finding that there were no variables which significantly moderated SSRT deficits sug- gests that deficits in inhibitory control may be a phenotype in adult ADHD.
sentences.s238: Another important question is how SSRT deficits relate to clinical symptoms in adult ADHD.
sentences.s239: In a large-scale study, Kamradt et al. (2014) examined correlations between SSRTs and ratings of current inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive symptoms and executive functions in patients.
sentences.s240: The study revealed significant moderate relationships between SSRTs and all symptom domains (r = 0.23 to 0.30).
sentences.s241: Using a hier- archical linear regression model that included other neu- ropsychological paradigms and demographic covariates, the authors found that only the SSRT and the continuous performance test predicted total symptom scores for inat- tention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.
sentences.s242: Similarly, Stavro, Nigg and colleagues (Nigg et al., 2005; Stavro et al., 2007) also found moderate (r = 0.29) relationships between SSRT deficits and executive functions, as expressed in inattentive- disorganized and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms.
sentences.s243: Thus, inhibitory control deficits, although frequently reported in empirical studies, are not well reflected in the diagnostic criteria for adult ADHD.
sentences.s244: For this reason, it could be that these deficits are often neglected during the diagnostic pro- cess and therefore also not treated, e.g., in the framework of neurocognitive training.
sentences.s245: It is important to note that SSRT deficits are found not only in ADHD but also in other psychiatric disorders such as obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), addiction or schizophrenia (Lipszyc & Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014).
sentences.s246: For example, Lipszyc and Schachar (2010) observed SSRT deficits with effect sizes g = 0.77 and g = 0.69 in OCD and schizophrenia, respectively.

sentences.s253: In conclusion, the finding of reliable moderate deficits in the SSRT suggests that the SST may become a valuable tool for the neuropsychological assessment of inhibitory control deficits in adult ADHD.

sentences.s280: Third, meta- regression analyses based on study-level-averages, such as the mean age of the total study sample carry the risk of an ecological bias.
sentences.s281: For example, age may be correlated with the outcome within sudies (e.g., Congdon et al., 2014), but not across studies, or vice versa (Higgins & Thompson, 2002).
sentences.s282: For this reason, the possibility that demographic or clinical variables might influence the results of the SST at the individual study level cannot be completely excluded.
sentences.s283: Fourth, the validy assessment of the SST revealed that most studies did not use cut-offs in order to identify invalid task behavior.
sentences.s284: It has been shown that adults with ADHD often failed performance validity measures, i.e., some partici- pants in the studies might have intentionally performed the task incorrectly to mimic cognitive deficits (Marshall et al., 2010, 2016).
sentences.s285: Therefore, the results of the SSRT meta-analysis results may be biased to some extent.
sentences.s286: Finally, the quality of most of the studies included in our meta-analysis was not optimal.
sentences.s287: Therefore, we suggest that future studies should fol- low recently published best practice recommendations for the design, implementation, analysis and reporting of the SST (Verbruggen et al., 2019) and apply the adapted Hombrados and Waddington criteria to ensure that a representative clini- cal sample is assessed (Hulsbosch et al., 2021).
sentences.s288: Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis revealed reliable moderate deficits in inhibitory control, as reflected in the SST, in adult ADHD.
sentences.s289: Our meta-regression and subgroup analyses further demonstrated no significant contribution of demographic and study quality variables on the observed group differences in SSRTs.
sentences.s290: This suggests that inhibitory control deficits can be considered a phenotype in adult ADHD.
sentences.s291: Our review and meta-analysis suggest that the SST in conjunction with other neurocognitive tests and clini- cal questionnaires, could become an important tool for the assessment of inhibitory control deficits in adult ADHD.

Asmundson Anxiety and Illness Behaviours Laboratory, University of Regina, Regina, SK, Canada S4S0A2 Received 13 October 2006; received in revised form 26 February 2007; accepted 18 April 2007 Abstract Fears related to anxiety sensitivity (AS)—illness/injury sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation, and fear of pain—may have important theoretical associations with intolerance of uncertainty (IU).
sentences.s3: In separate investigations, AS and IU have been independently related to the same anxiety-related psychopathology.
sentences.s4: AS and IU seem to share a basis in fearing unknown, potentially harmful consequences; however, their inter-relationship remains uncertain.
sentences.s5: IU regarding a speciﬁc stimulus, a physical sensation for example, may result in a variety of interpretations and responses, including the catastrophic appraisals that characterize AS.
sentences.s6: The association between AS and IU was examined in a sample of 293 undergraduates.
sentences.s7: Results of conﬁrmatory factor and correlation analyses suggest the two constructs are related, but nonetheless independent.
sentences.s8: It appears that IU may be a required component of catastrophic misappraisals while being an important construct related to fear and anxiety in its own right.
sentences.s9: Future research directions and potential applications are discussed. r 2007 Elsevier Ltd.
sentences.s10: Keywords: Intolerance of uncertainty; Anxiety sensitivity; Fear of the unknown; Fundamental fears Introduction Fear is a basic, adaptive, protective response to a current, identiﬁable threat (e.g., being attacked), accompanied by a strong physiological reaction enabling a ﬁght or ﬂight response (Barlow, 2002).
sentences.s11: In contrast, anxiety is a more complex preparatory response comprising worry regarding a potential threat as yet unidentiﬁed or unrealized (e.g., a possible attack, somewhere, sometime) accompanied by a similar—but attenuated—version of the physiological reaction to fear (Asmundson, Taylor, Bovell, & Collimore, 2006; Barlow, 2002).
sentences.s12: The degree of uncertainty regarding threat is the primary cognitive difference between these two constructs.
sentences.s13: Unlike fear associated with an objectiﬁable threat, anxiety involves a varying degree of uncertainty because the threat has not yet been realized.
sentences.s14: Moreover, uncertainty itself can be considered threatening (Epstein, 1972), therein promoting or maintaining anxiety and exacerbating the perception of threat (e.g., Hadjistavropoulos, Craig, & Hadjistavropoulos, 1998; Heydayati, Dugas, Buhr, & Francis, 2003; Hock & Krohne, 2004). www.elsevier.com/locate/brat 0005-7967/$ - see front matter r 2007 Elsevier Ltd.
sentences.s16: E-mail address: carletor@uregina.ca (R.
sentences.s17: The differences in certainty of threat that help to distinguish fear and anxiety converge within the anxiety sensitivity (AS) construct.
sentences.s18: AS is a person’s propensity to appraise the anxiety-related physiological sensations (e.g., increased heart rate, palpitations, trembling), cognitive changes (e.g., difﬁculty concentrating, racing thoughts), and social consequences (e.g., humiliation, rejection) based on the belief that these symptoms have harmful consequences (Taylor, 1999).
sentences.s19: Originally derived from the expectancy model of fear (Reiss & McNally, 1985), AS has been conceptualized as one of several fundamental fears.
sentences.s20: Other fundamental fears include illness/injury sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation (Reiss, 1991; Taylor, 1993), and fear of pain (Asmundson & Carleton, 2005).
sentences.s21: AS is categorized as a fundamental fear because the construct focuses on identiﬁable stimuli rather than an ambiguous cognitive appraisal lacking an objective focus (i.e., as in anxiety).
sentences.s22: The catastrophic misappraisal of the stimuli associated with AS requires a physiological sensation, cognitive change, or publicly observable event accompanied by uncertainty regarding the subsequent consequences of the sensation, change, or event (Reiss, Peterson, Gursky, & McNally, 1986).
sentences.s23: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—the tendency for an individual to consider the possibility of a negative event occurring as unacceptable and threatening irrespective of the probability of its occurrence—has become a popular construct for explaining anxiety (e.g., Holaway, Heimberg, & Coles, 2006).
sentences.s24: Individual differences in the ability to tolerate uncertainty impact levels of anxiety (Greco & Roger, 2001, 2003).
sentences.s25: For persons who are intolerant of uncertainty, engaging in situations with uncertain outcomes is likely to induce and per- petuate a heightened level of anxiety (Dugas, Gosselin, & Ladouceur, 2001).
sentences.s26: Moreover, people with high IU interpret ambiguous information as threatening (Heydayati et al., 2003), contributing to increased arousal (e.g., increased heart rate and blood pressure; Greco & Roger, 2001, 2003).
sentences.s27: AS and IU seem to share a basis in fear or anxiety related to unknown, potentially harmful consequences; however, their relationship with each other has yet to be established.
sentences.s28: IU regarding a speciﬁc stimulus, a physical sensation for example, may result in a variety of interpretations and responses (Greco & Roger, 2001, 2003; Lazarus, 1991), including the type of catastrophic appraisal that deﬁnes AS (Starcevic & Berle, 2006).
sentences.s29: In separate investigations, AS and IU have been independently related to the same anxiety-related psychopathology.
sentences.s30: For example, measures of AS and IU have been correlated respectively with measures of panic disorder (Apfeldorf, Shear, Leon, & Portera, 1994; Dugas et al., 2001), generalized anxiety disorder (Holaway et al., 2006; Keller, 2002; Starcevic & Berle, 2006), and pathological worry (Buhr & Dugas, 2002; Dugas, Gosselin, & Ladoucer, 2001; Taylor, Koch, McNally, & Crockett, 1992).
sentences.s31: Several studies (see Taylor, 1999 for a review) have explored the relationship between measures of AS and measures of each of the other fundamental fears (i.e., illness/injury sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation, fear of pain), how AS and the fears relate, and the relationships between AS and complex disorders like chronic musculoskeletal pain (Carleton, Asmundson, Collimore, & Ellwanger, 2006) and social phobia (Carleton, Collimore, & Asmundson, 2007).
sentences.s32: In contrast, there is a paucity of research investigating relationships between IU and each of the fundamental fears despite correlational evidence suggesting such relationships exist (e.g., Asmundson & Carleton, 2005).
sentences.s33: The lack of research investigating the relationships between IU and fundamental fears can be attributed to the relatively recent appearance of the IU construct (Freeston, Rhe´ aume, Letarte, Dugas, & Ladouceur, 1994).
sentences.s34: Assessing the relationship between AS and IU is important both for theoretical and clinical reasons.
sentences.s35: If AS and IU are highly associated and load on a single higher-order factor (i.e., together they represent different aspects of one construct), it might suggest that IU is merely a latent component of AS (i.e., catastrophic interpretation of symptoms of arousal).
sentences.s36: In such a case, investigating IU independent of AS is unnecessary, being intolerant of uncertainty would be a manifestation of fear related to the uncertain meaning behind anxiety-related responses brought on by the uncertainty.
sentences.s37: Conversely, if the two constructs are unrelated and load onto independent higher-order factors, generalized IU and AS-speciﬁc uncertainty may require different therapeutic interventions.
sentences.s38: In this case, it would become critical to know whether a person with anxiety is generally intolerant of any uncertainty, or fearful of the uncertain meaning of the physiology symptoms related to their anxiety.
sentences.s39: If elements of the two constructs are moderately associated and load onto correlated higher-order factors, IU and AS may be mutually maintaining constructs.
sentences.s40: From a therapeutic perspective, given that both are dependent on IU, addressing the IU may serve to alleviate the AS, as well as other fears.
sentences.s41: In any case, it is important to know the nature of that relationship.
sentences.s42: Such information would provide direction for R.
sentences.s43: Nicholas Carleton et al. / Behaviour Research and Therapy 45 (2007) 2307–2316 2308 future studies to explore the comparative utility of therapies focused either on a general reduction of IU (e.g., unpredictable events are not inherently threatening) or on reducing fear of non-speciﬁc correlates of anxiety (e.g., a racing heart).
sentences.s44: Thus, the present investigation had two primary goals.
sentences.s45: The ﬁrst goal was to evaluate the relationship between IU and AS for inter- or independence.
sentences.s46: Based on the theoretical deﬁnitions for IU and AS introduced above, we believe the two are indeed related, with AS being IU regarding anxiety-related sensations.
sentences.s47: Therefore, we hypothesize the relationship to be one of moderate association between two independent, but related and possibly mutually maintaining constructs.
sentences.s48: The second goal was to assess the relationship of IU to the other fundamental fears (Taylor, 1993)—illness/injury sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation, and fear of pain.
sentences.s49: Each fundamental fear is moderately related to AS; we expect a moderate association between AS and IU.
sentences.s50: Therefore, we hypothesize that IU and AS will be comparably related to each of the other fundamental fears.
sentences.s51: Method Participants Participants for this study were 293 undergraduate students (70 men, aged 18–33 years (M ¼ 21.2; SD ¼ 3.5) and 223 women, aged 17–50 years (M ¼ 21.4; SD ¼ 5.3)) from the University of Regina who participated in a large questionnaire-based study approved by the University Research Ethics Board.
sentences.s52: There was no statistically signiﬁcant difference between men and women on age, t(290) ¼ .31, p 4 .10, or years of education, t(290) ¼ .84, p 4.10.
sentences.s53: The majority of participants self-declared as Caucasian (90%), First Nations (4%), or Asian (3%).
sentences.s54: Participants were recruited through brief in-class presentations and poster advertisements that directed them to a secure website for web-based completion of the questionnaire package.
sentences.s55: Web-based data collection has been demonstrated to be a valid approach for questionnaire-based research (Gosling, Vazire, Srivastava, & John, 2004).
sentences.s56: Participants received course credit for participation.
sentences.s57: Measures Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale Short Form (IUS-12; Carleton, Norton, & Asmundson, 2007) This 12-item scale is a short-form of the original 27-item IU Scale (Freeston et al., 1994) that measures reactions to uncertainty, ambiguous situations, and the future (e.g., unforeseen events upset me greatly).
sentences.s58: Items are scored on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all characteristic of me) to 5 (entirely characteristic of me).
sentences.s59: The IUS-12 has a strong correlation with the original scale, r ¼ .96, and has been shown to have two factors, Prospective Anxiety (7 items; e.g., I can’t stand being taken by surprise) and Inhibitory Anxiety (5 items; e.g., When it’s time to act, uncertainty paralyses me), both with identically high internal consistencies, a ¼ .85 (Carleton, Norton et al., 2007).
sentences.s60: AS Index (Peterson & Reiss, 1992) The AS index (ASI) is a 16-item measure assessing the tendency to fear symptoms of anxiety based on the belief that they may have harmful consequences (e.g., It scares me when I feel faint).
sentences.s61: Items are rated on a 5- point Likert scale ranging from 0 (very little) to 4 (very much).
sentences.s62: Factor analytic investigations indicate the ASI comprises three internally consistent lower-order factors (i.e., fear of somatic sensations (e.g., It scares me when my heart beats rapidly), fear of cognitive dyscontrol (e.g., When I cannot keep my mind on a task, I worry that I may be going crazy), and fear of socially observable anxiety reactions (e.g., It is important to me not to appear nervous)) that load on to a single higher-order factor (Taylor, Koch, Woody, & McLean, 1996; Zinbarg, Barlow, & Brown, 1997).
sentences.s63: The validity and reliability of using the ASI total or subscale scores have been well-documented (see Peterson & Plehn, 1999; Taylor, 1999).
sentences.s64: Illness/Injury Sensitivity Index-Revised (Carleton, Park, & Asmundson, 2006) The Illness/Injury Sensitivity Index-Revised (ISI-R) is 9-item revision of the original Illness/Injury Sensitivity Index (Taylor, 1993) designed to measure fears of illness and injury (e.g., I worry about my physical health).
sentences.s65: Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (agree very little) to 4 (agree very R.
sentences.s66: Nicholas Carleton et al. / Behaviour Research and Therapy 45 (2007) 2307–2316 2309 much).
sentences.s67: Two factors, Fear of Illness (e.g., I worry about becoming physically ill) and Fear of Injury (e.g., I am frightened of being injured), are represented within the ISI-R (Carleton, Asmundson, & Taylor, 2005); however, the total summed score is used in most analyses.
sentences.s68: The ISI-R has been shown to have excellent internal consistency (a ¼ .86), convergent validity with other measures related to injury and illness (r4.65), and correlates highly with the original index, r ¼ .96 (Carleton, Asmundson et al., 2006).
sentences.s69: Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation scale, version 2 (Carleton, McCreary, Norton, & Asmundson, 2006) The Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation scale, version 2 (BFNE-II) is a revised version of the Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation scale (BFNE; Leary, 1983) used for measuring social anxiety (Stopa & Clark, 2001).
sentences.s70: Revisions to the BFNE were made in accordance with Taylor’s (1993) suggested changes to remove a methodological issue stemming from four reverse-worded items (Carleton, McCreary et al., 2006; Weeks et al., 2005).
sentences.s71: The BFNE-II consists of 8 items (e.g., I am afraid that others will not approve of me) each rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all characteristic of me) to 4 (extremely characteristic of me), has been shown to have excellent internal consistency (a ¼ .95), and correlates highly with the original scale, r ¼ .99 (Carleton, McCreary et al., 2006; Carleton, Collimore et al., 2007).
sentences.s72: Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale—Short Form (McCracken & Dhingra, 2002) The Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale—Short Form (PASS-20) is a short form of the original Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale (PASS; McCracken, Zayfert, & Gross, 1992) used to measure pain-related anxiety.
sentences.s73: Each of the 20 items (e.g., When I feel pain I am afraid that something terrible will happen) are rated on a 6-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (never) to 5 (always).
sentences.s74: Each of four, 5-item subscales (i.e., Cognitive (e.g., I can’t think straight when in pain), Fear (e.g., Pain sensations are terrifying), Escape/Avoidance (e.g., I will stop any activity as soon as I sense pain coming on), Physiological (e.g., Pain makes me nauseous)) provides a score that can be considered separately or, when summed, as a general measure of pain-related anxiety.
sentences.s75: Factorial validity for both the total and subscale scores has been demonstrated for clinical (Coons, Hadjistavropoulos, & Asmundson, 2004) and non-clinical samples (Abrams, Carleton, Stapleton, & Asmundson, 2006).
sentences.s76: Analyses First, descriptive data were calculated for each measure using the entire sample, including internal consistency for each measure.
sentences.s77: A series of independent t-tests were conducted to check for any substantial sex differences within the ASI, BFNE-II, ISI-R, IUS, or PASS-20.
sentences.s78: Thereafter, a correlation analysis was used to check for an effect of age on any of the measures.
sentences.s79: Second, conﬁrmatory factor analyses (CFA) were conducted to assess the independence of the ASI and IUS.
sentences.s80: CFAs provide goodness-of-ﬁt indices that can be used for comparing the ﬁt of predeﬁned model factor structures to an available data set (Hu & Bentler, 1999).
sentences.s81: In this way, the goodness-of-ﬁt indices can provide comparative measures of whether the ASI and IUS items load better onto one or two latent factors, and the strength of the relationship between those latent factors, while still maintaining the factors established for each measure.
sentences.s82: A model (Model 1) with all item parcels from both the ASI and the IUS loading on one latent factor was compared against a second model (Model 2) with two correlated latent factors—AS and IU—each with item parcels loading on precedent factors.
sentences.s83: Item parcels were created to serve as observed variables.
sentences.s84: Item parcels reduce the number of indicators per latent variable, have a stronger relationship to the latent variables than individual items, and serve to restrain the model degrees of freedom (Bandalos, 2002; Little, Cunningham, Shahar, & Widaman, 2002).
sentences.s85: The analyses were performed using AMOS 5.0 (Arbuckle, 2003) with the raw data as input and the maximum likelihood estimation procedure.
sentences.s86: Models were evaluated using several goodness of ﬁt indices and following recommendations by Hu and Bentler (1999): (1) w2 (values should not be statistically signiﬁcant); (2) w2/df ratio (values should be o2.0); (3) Comparative Fit Index (CFI; values should be close to .95); (4) Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA; values should be p.06); (5) the Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR; values should be p.08); and (6) the Expected Cross Validation Index (ECVI; for comparing non-nested models).
sentences.s87: The latter ﬁve ﬁt indices are emphasized because w2 statistics are inﬂated in larger samples (Hu & Bentler, 1999).
sentences.s88: Nicholas Carleton et al. / Behaviour Research and Therapy 45 (2007) 2307–2316 2310 Third, Pearson correlational analyses were performed to assess the relationships between the full and subscale scores for the ASI, IUS, BFNE-II, ISI-R, IUS, and PASS-20.

sentences.s90: Unlike a multiple regression analysis that is limited to the evaluation of multiple predictor variables against only one outcome variable, canonical correlation permits the analysis of multiple predictor and multiple outcome variables simultaneously.
sentences.s91: A combination of predictor variables is derived that has the highest correlation with a combination of the outcome variables (see Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001).

sentences.s127: Discussion The present investigation had two goals.
sentences.s128: The ﬁrst goal was to evaluate the inter- or independence of the IU and AS constructs.
sentences.s129: We hypothesized the relationship between IU and AS would be one of moderate association between two independent, but related and possibly mutually maintaining, constructs.
sentences.s130: The CFA analyses did not support elements of IU and AS loading onto a single higher order factor; further, the moderate correlations between the higher order factors and the elements of each construct preclude the possibility of construct independence.
sentences.s131: Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the IU and AS constructs are moderately correlated, but because neither subsumes the other, they are independent.
sentences.s132: This independence suggests that while IU and AS are related, IU is more than a latent component of AS.
sentences.s133: The second goal of this investigation was to evaluate the IU–AS inter-relationship by assessing their relationships with other fundamental fears (Taylor, 1993), speciﬁcally illness/injury sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation, and fear of pain.
sentences.s134: We hypothesized that IU and AS would be comparably related to each of the other fundamental fears.
sentences.s135: Each of these fears also shares overlapping variance with IU, implying a potentially important theoretical and applied role for IU in all anxiety-related psychopathology.
sentences.s136: Correlation analysis revealed moderate, comparable, positive correlations between both the IUS and the ASI and each of the remaining fundamental fears.
sentences.s137: The IU–AS independence supported by the CFA suggested canonical correlation analysis might reveal differential patterns associating IU and AS with each of the other constructs.
sentences.s138: The canonical correlation analysis supported the associations between the IUS and the ASI with each of the other measures of fear.
sentences.s139: Furthermore, the directional implications from both canonical roots were theoretically sound (Carleton, McCreary et al., 2006; Carleton, Collimore et al., 2007).
sentences.s140: The ﬁrst root indicated a strong relationship between the IU and AS, as well as correlations with each of the other fears.
sentences.s141: The second root indicated a high score on the ASI fear of somatic sensations subscale and a low score on the ASI fear of socially observable anxiety reactions subscale correlated with a high score on both the PASS-20 fear subscale and the ISI as well as a low score on the BFNE-II.
sentences.s142: This suggests that fears of somatic sensations, pain, and illness are all associated, as are fears of socially observable anxiety reactions and fears of negative evaluation.
sentences.s143: So, while IU is related to AS and each of the other fundamental fears, the fears of somatic sensations and socially observable anxiety reactions are more highly correlated with fears of pain, illness, and negative evaluation, respectively, than with IU.
sentences.s144: This is reasonable given the somatically based nature of pain and illness (Hadjistavropoulos & Craig, 2004), as well as the speciﬁc relationship between social fears and fear of negative evaluation.
sentences.s145: Nicholas Carleton et al. / Behaviour Research and Therapy 45 (2007) 2307–2316 2313 Overall, the results of this investigation support a highly correlated, but nonetheless independent relationship between IU and AS.
sentences.s146: The overlap may be explained, in part, by the fact that high levels of AS are characterized by a degree of uncertainty regarding the consequences of arousal-related sensations (e.g., heart palpitations may or may not signal a pending heart attack).
sentences.s147: Increasing inability to tolerate the uncertainty surrounding such sensations is likely to result in heightened anxiety and catastrophic thinking.
sentences.s148: Conversely, being highly tolerant of the uncertainty is likely to ameliorate anxiety and catastrophic thinking.
sentences.s149: It may be that IU and AS respectively represent the most basic fears.
sentences.s150: Indeed, if heightened IU is a requisite component of the fundamental fears—independent of AS levels—then IU itself may represent the most basic component of pathological anxiety; however, this speculation requires additional research.
sentences.s151: There are some limitations to this study that warrant consideration and provide directions for future research.
sentences.s152: First, only one self-report measure was used to evaluate each of the fear constructs, making cross- validation impossible, risking artiﬁcial inﬂation of correlations due to method invariance between measures, and artiﬁcial inﬂation of internal consistency and within the measures.
sentences.s153: In other words, only self-report measures were used and the items were grouped into their original questionnaires; future studies should vary presentation format (e.g., common item presentation but in random order) to evaluate the robustness of these results.
sentences.s154: Subsequent investigations of these relationships should include multiple measures.
sentences.s155: Second, the original 16-item ASI was used, rather than the 36-item revision (ASI-R; Taylor & Cox, 1998), for the sake of brevity; however, future studies might further examine whether IU and the fundamental fears overlap differentially with speciﬁc aspects of AS (e.g., fears of respiratory symptoms, fears of cognitive symptoms), but not others (e.g., fears of socially observable symptoms).
sentences.s156: Third, a larger, more diverse sample size would have been ideal for evaluating the effects of high and low ASI/IUS combinations.
sentences.s157: High levels of either AS or IU alone may be insufﬁcient to exacerbate other fears and therein enable anxiety-related psychopathology.
sentences.s158: The development of anxiety-related disorders may require both high AS (see, e.g., Taylor, Koch, & McNally, 1992) and high IU.
sentences.s159: If correct, low IU may act as a resiliency factor against the development of anxiety-related psychopathology.
sentences.s160: Further, the sample size was insufﬁcient for a comprehensive path analysis of hierarchical fear structures including IU and fear of pain.
sentences.s161: Fourth, the inter-relations between fears may be different when evaluated with other samples (e.g., primarily male samples, other age groups, other socioeconomic status levels, and other ethnicities).
sentences.s162: Until these other groups have been assessed, the generalizability of these results, though enticing, is restricted.
sentences.s163: Evaluation with clinical samples is particularly critical because of the potentially poignant possibilities for treatment.
sentences.s164: If the relationships between the fear constructs investigated here are pervasive in clinical populations, it might prove efﬁcacious for some patient populations to have therapeutic interventions that focus on reducing IU in general.
sentences.s165: These same interventions might also serve to reduce AS and other related fears, comprehensively reducing the impact of anxiety-related suffering and disability.
sentences.s166: Based on the literature and data reviewed here, it is reasonable to suggest that IU may be a fundamental component of all anxiety disorders.
sentences.s167: This is particularly important for many cognitive-behavioral models, which depend on catastrophic misinterpretations and ruminations (see for review, Barlow, 2001).
sentences.s168: For example, persons tolerant of uncertainty are unlikely to be concerned with the ambiguity associated with some physical sensations (e.g., rapid heart rate); therefore, they should be less likely to catastrophically ruminate about those sensations, avoiding spiraling cycles of anxiety.
sentences.s169: Similarly, such tolerant persons are unlikely to catastrophize about the unknown consequences associated with social situations/behaviors, intrusive thoughts, or uncontrollable eventualities.
sentences.s170: Conversely, people with high IU may be very likely to engage in catastrophic rumination, given that some uncertainty exists in most situations.
sentences.s171: Moreover, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (American Psychiatric Association, 2000) may be categorically dividing people’s mechanisms for coping with IU—cognitive and behavioral symptom presentations— associated with various uncertain situations into each of the current anxiety disorders.
sentences.s172: This is not to suggest that diagnostic differentiation is not useful; rather, it suggests that most anxiety disorders have a shared basis in fearing unknown and potentially dangerous consequences associated with a myriad of stimuli and behavior.
sentences.s173: Future research must explore whether treating IU (and/or AS), regardless of the speciﬁc anxiety disorder diagnosis, can be effective in alleviating symptoms.
sentences.s174: This would be in line with recent suggestions for transdiagnostic approaches for treating anxiety (e.g., Harvey, Watkins, Mansell, & Shafran, 2004; Norton, R.

10.1016/j.cpr.2004.11.001.printed_title: The impact of reinforcement contingencies on AD/HD: A review and theoretical appraisal

sentences.s1: The impact of reinforcement contingencies on AD/HD: A review and theoretical appraisal Marjolein Luman*, Jaap Oosterlaan, Joseph A.
sentences.s2: Sergeant Department of Neuropsychology, PI Research, Rijksstraatweg 145, P.O. Box 366, 1115 ZG Duivendrecht, The Netherlands Department of Clinical Neuropsychology, Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, The Netherlands Received 7 June 2004; received in revised form 10 September 2004; accepted 8 November 2004 Abstract One of the core deficits in attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (AD/HD) is thought to be an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement, such as reward and response cost.
sentences.s3: Twenty-two studies (N=1181 children) employing AD/HD and reinforcement contingencies are reviewed from vantage points: task performance, motivation, and psychophysiology.
sentences.s4: Results indicate that reinforcement contingencies have a positive impact on task performance and levels of motivation for both children with AD/HD and normal controls.
sentences.s5: There is evidence that the effect related to task performance is somewhat more prominent in AD/HD.
sentences.s6: There is some evidence that a high intensity of reinforcement is highly effective in AD/HD.
sentences.s7: Children with AD/HD prefer immediate over delayed reward.
sentences.s8: From a psychophysiological point of view, children with AD/HD seem less sensitive to reinforcement compared to controls.
sentences.s9: While comorbid disorders are suggested to be confounders of the dependent variables, many studies do not examine the effect of oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) and conduct disorder (CD).
sentences.s10: We discuss the implications of the findings for five theoretical frameworks, including the model by Haenlein and Caul (1987), Douglas (1999), the cognitive-energetic model (CEM) (Sergeant et al., 1999), the dual-pathway model (Sonuga- Barke, 2003) and the BIS/BAS model (Quay, 1988a,b,c).
sentences.s11: Results show a discrepancy between the theoretical models and the behavioural findings.

sentences.s15: Introduction Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (AD/HD) is one of the most prevalent psychiatric disorders in children and adolescents, characterized by inattentive, hyperactive, and impulsive behavior (American Psychiatric Association, 1994).
sentences.s16: In several theoretical explanations, AD/HD is thought to be associated with an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement, including reward, punishment, and reinforcement schedules (e.g., manipulation of reinforcement frequency and delays in reinforcement administration) (Douglas, 1989; Haenlein & Caul, 1987; Quay, 1988a, 1988b, 1988c; Sagvolden, Johansen, Aase, & Russell, in press; Sagvolden & Sergeant, 1998; Sergeant, Oosterlaan, & Van der Meere, 1999; Sonuga-Barke, 2002; Wender, 1972).
sentences.s17: Since reinforcement is highly associated with motivation, research suggests that an unusually low level of effort or intrinsic motivation accounts for the performance deficits in children with AD/HD (August, 1987; Barber, Milich, & Welsch, 1996; Borcherding et al., 1998; Sergeant & Van der Meere, 1990; Van der Meere, Hughes, Bo¨rger, & Sallee, 1995; Wilkison, Kircher, McMahon, & Sloane, 1995).
sentences.s18: For example, without supervision or when tasks are extremely boring, the attention span of children with AD/ HD is very limited (Van der Meere, Shalev, Bo¨rger, & Gross-Tsur, 1995).
sentences.s19: Haenlein and Caul (1987) suggested that children with AD/HD have an elevated reward threshold and, therefore, require higher rates of reinforcement compared to normal children.
sentences.s20: They hypothesized that children with AD/HD, compared to normal children, perform poorer under partial and delayed reinforcement, since the intensity of reward in these conditions is lower compared to conditions of continuous and immediate reinforcement.
sentences.s21: Johansen, Aase, Meyer, and Sagvolden (2002), Sagvolgen, Aase, Zeiner, and Berger (1998), Sagvolden and Sergeant (1998), and Sagvolden et al. (in press) claimed that the main symptoms of AD/ HD are caused by a deficit in reinforcement processes, in part, due to a hypoefficient central nervous dopaminergic system.
sentences.s22: According to Sagvolden et al. (in press), children with AD/HD have a shorter and steeper delay-of-reinforcement gradient.
sentences.s23: The delay gradient describes the time interval between the response and reinforcer and its relation to the impact of a reinforcer.
sentences.s24: The reinforcing effect is largest, when the reinforcer is delivered immediately after the response.
sentences.s25: In children with AD/HD, unlike normally developing peers, only responses in close proximity to a reinforcer will be conditioned.
sentences.s26: In addition, relatively few correct responses between the delivery of two consecutive reinforcers will be maintained.
sentences.s27: As a result, the association between response and reinforcer will be less consistent and dsustained attentionT will be impaired.
sentences.s28: When reinforcers are powerful and frequent, however, the differences in behavior between children with AD/HD and controls are expected to be minimal.
sentences.s29: Douglas (1989, 1999) and Douglas and Parry (1994) suggested that children with AD/HD are unusually sensitive to reward and suffer from a heightened frustration level in response to the loss of anticipated rewards.
sentences.s30: Because of the heightened frustration level, performance of children with AD/HD is predicted to deteriorate under conditions of partial compared to continuous reward.
sentences.s31: Another theoretical position was offered by Quay (1988a, 1988b, 1988c, 1997) who tried to explain AD/HD symptoms in terms of Gray’s (1982, 1987) psychobiological theory of learning and emotion.
sentences.s32: Gray developed a theory in which three collaborative brain systems modulate behavior.
sentences.s33: The two most relevant here are the behavioral activation system (BAS), which involves the dopaminergic pathway, nucleus accumbens, and ventral striatum, and the behavioral inhibition system (BIS), which is located in the septo-hippocampal system.
sentences.s34: The BAS, according to Gray, is activated by conditions of reward, and initiates approach behavior and active avoidance.
sentences.s35: The BIS is activated by conditions of punishment and nonreward, and interrupts ongoing or anticipated motor behavior.
sentences.s36: A third system, called the nonspecific M.
sentences.s37: Luman et al. / Clinical Psychology Review 25 (2005) 183–213 184 arousal system (NAS), is activated by both the BIS and the BAS, and acts to increase the intensity (speed/force) of behavior.
sentences.s38: According to Quay (1988a, 1988b, 1988c), in normal children, the BIS and the BAS cooperate with one another to meet situational demands.
sentences.s39: For example, when response inhibition is required, the BIS is activated and temporarily predominates over the BAS.
sentences.s40: Quay argued that children with AD/HD have difficulty in inhibiting ongoing and anticipated motor behavior because of an underactive BIS.
sentences.s41: Furthermore, Quay argued that children with AD/HD are less responsive to signals of punishment and nonreward.
sentences.s42: Fowles (1987) reviewed psychophysiological experiments that provide evidence of two independent psychophysiological measures supporting Gray’s psychobiological theory of learning and emotion.
sentences.s43: Fowles (1980, 1987) noted evidence for increased heart rate in normal adults in the face of appetitive stimuli and signals of reward.
sentences.s44: On the basis of these findings, Fowles proposed that heart rate reflects activity in the BAS.
sentences.s45: In contrast, skin conductance responses increase in the face of aversive stimuli and signals of punishment, and are unaffected by appetitive or rewarding stimuli.
sentences.s46: The changes in skin conductance were suggested to reflect activity in the BIS.
sentences.s47: The role of reinforcement has been examined by Sonuga-Barke (2002), who proposed a dual-pathway model of AD/HD in which he recognized two distinct subtypes of the disorder.
sentences.s48: One subtype is associated with diminished inhibitory control.
sentences.s49: The other subtype is characterized by a motivational style, in which children with AD/HD show aversion to delayed reinforcement, associated with fundamental alternations in reward mechanisms.
sentences.s50: Children with AD/HD were hypothesized to rate immediate rewards as more and future rewards as less valuable compared to control children.
sentences.s51: Sonuga-Barke acknowledged Sagvolden et al.’s (1998) theory concerning a steeper and shorter delay-of-reinforcement gradient in AD/HD, as evidence of delay aversion.
sentences.s52: In contrast, Sergeant et al. (1999) hypothesized that children with AD/HD suffer from a nonoptimal energetic state explained in terms of the cognitive–energetic model (CEM).
sentences.s53: This model is based on the assumption that information processing is influenced by both computational (process) factors and state factors such as effort, arousal, and activation (Sanders, 1983; Sergeant, 2000; Sergeant & Scholten, 1985; Sergeant & Van der Meere, 1990; Sergeant et al., 1999).
sentences.s54: The effort pool controls the state of the lower layers of the model, namely, the arousal and activation pool.
sentences.s55: Effort (which is related to motivation) is conceived as the energy necessary to meet the demands of the task.
sentences.s56: Reinforcement contingencies are presumed to have their influence on this pool.
sentences.s57: The highest level of the CEM is a monitoring system, which is sensitive to dknowledge of results.T According to the CEM, if children with AD/HD suffer from a deficit in the effort pool, performance may be poor due to a nonoptimal energetic state.
sentences.s58: Since reinforcement is expected to activate the effort pool, reinforcement will induce the necessary energy to meet the task demands.
sentences.s59: As a result, performance on cognitive tasks improves.
sentences.s60: In addition, from a clinical perspective, children with AD/HD are described as benefiting from reinforcement contingencies.
sentences.s61: In several behavioral modification programs, reinforcement has proven to be highly effective in the treatment of AD/HD (Barkley, 2002).
sentences.s62: Reinforcement contingencies are found to normalize behavior that characterizes AD/HD in school, sports, and home settings, and to improve academic functioning (Hupp, Reitman, Northup, O’Callaghan, & LeBlanc, 2002; Kelly & McCain, 1995; Pelham et al., 1993; Pelham & Hinshaw, 1992; Rapport, Murphy, & Bailey, 1982).
sentences.s63: These findings further emphasize the role of reinforcement contingencies in AD/HD.
sentences.s64: Given the heterogeneous findings related to AD/HD and reinforcement contingencies, on one hand, and, on the other hand, the emphasis on reinforcement in several accounts, there is a clear call for a review of the literature related to the impact of reinforcement on AD/HD.
sentences.s65: The aim of this paper is to M.
sentences.s66: Luman et al. / Clinical Psychology Review 25 (2005) 183–213 185 review the literature regarding sensitivity of children with AD/HD to environmental contingencies, such as reward, punishment, and reinforcement schedules.
sentences.s67: First, we will provide an extensive overview of the studies that have focused on task performance, motivation level, and psychophysiology of children with AD/HD under reinforcement contingencies.
sentences.s68: Since the publication of the hallmark article by Douglas and Peters (1979), such an attempt has not been made.
sentences.s69: Secondly, we wish to investigate whether the findings fit into the models encompassing reinforcement contingencies as a central aspect for the theoretical explanations of AD/HD; we will focus on possible shortcomings within this field of research. 1.1.
sentences.s70: Organization of this review We will compare the performance of children with AD/HD and normal controls on different tasks that measure cognitive processing (e.g., inhibition) and response output (e.g., reward choice behavior) under various reinforcement conditions.
sentences.s71: Next, since motivation and reinforcement are thought to be highly associated (e.g., Sergeant et al., 1999), we will specify the role of motivation.
sentences.s72: We review psychophysiological measures of heart rate (interbeat interval) and skin conductance (skin conductance level and response) under different reinforcement conditions.
sentences.s73: These measures may provide us with evidence whether children with AD/HD suffer from diminished BIS activity as suggested by Quay (1988a, 1988b, 1988c).
sentences.s74: Given the heterogeneous findings in the literature concerning AD/HD and reinforcement contingencies, it seems important to acknowledge possible confounding variables that can influence the results.
sentences.s75: AD/HD is highly associated with oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) and conduct disorder (CD) (Angold, Costello, & Erkanli, 1999), and the impact of the possible confounding effects of ODD and CD on the findings are reviewed.
sentences.s76: ODD and CD were combined because ODD is frequently found to be a developmental antecedent of CD, and because ODD is generally considered a milder form of CD (APA, 1994).
sentences.s77: Another important potential confounder may be reinforcement allocation policy.
sentences.s78: This policy concerns whether reinforcement allocation is based on task performance or whether it is based on task participation (irrespective of response accuracy).
sentences.s79: The expectancy related to reinforcement occurrence may differ between the two policies, which, according to Schultz (2000), may influence the rate of reinforcement learning and task performance.
sentences.s80: Important possible confounders are the specific characteristics of the reinforcer that differ between studies reviewed here.
sentences.s81: It is acknowledged that neurons in the amygdala seem to be involved in processing the intensity of reinforcement (Schultz, 2000).
sentences.s82: Neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex, in contrast, can discriminate between different forms of reinforcement, such as liquid or solid reward (Schultz, 2000, 2002).
sentences.s83: Since AD/HD is associated with a deficiency in the orbitofrontal area (Barkley, 1997) and the mesolimbic system (Quay, 1988a, 1988b, 1988c; Sonuga-Barke, 2002, 2003), children with AD/HD may be differentially affected by different intensities and forms (e.g., money, tokens, and presents) of reinforcement.
sentences.s84: Finally, the impact of AD/HD subtypes, gender, age, and IQ is discussed. 2.
sentences.s85: Qualitative overview of studies concerning AD/HD, task performance, and reinforcement contingencies This review covers 22 studies published between 1986 and February 2003, which includes 1181 children.
sentences.s86: The studies were located in PubMed (Medline), PsycINFO, and ISI Web of Knowledge M.
sentences.s87: Luman et al. / Clinical Psychology Review 25 (2005) 183–213 186 databases.
sentences.s88: We searched for empirical studies that investigated primarily the effect of reinforcement contingencies on task performance of children with AD/HD.
sentences.s89: We searched for studies that investigated the effects of reinforcement contingencies on measures of motivation and psychophysiology.
sentences.s90: We combined search terms related to AD/HD (such as AD/HD, hyperactive, and attention) with search term related to reinforcement (such as reward, punishment, response cost, reinforcement, feedback, and contingencies).
sentences.s91: The reference lists of published articles were used to locate additional relevant studies.
sentences.s92: Dissertations, abstracts, as well as clinical studies were not included.
sentences.s93: In addition, studies that included less than 10 subjects in one of the groups of interest were excluded from this review.
sentences.s94: Furthermore, studies conducted before 1986 were excluded because of changes in the diagnostic criteria for AD/HD, related to the emergence of the third revised edition of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM III-R).
sentences.s95: Finally, studies that focused on the perception of reward and response cost and imaging studies that did not report performance data were excluded.
sentences.s96: The main features of the 22 studies are summarized in Table 1.
sentences.s97: Twenty studies in this review compared an AD/HD group with a group of normally developing children (control group) without a psychiatric or learning disorder.
sentences.s98: Two studies did not include a control group, but compared the performance of children with AD/HD on and off medication (Pelham, Milich, & Walker, 1986; Wilkison et al., 1995).
sentences.s99: In three studies included in this review (Daugherty & Quay, 1991; Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1998; Sonuga-Barke, Taylor, Sembi, & Smith, 1992), the children in the psychiatric groups were not diagnosed according to DSM III, DSM III-R, or DSM IV criteria, in contrast with the remaining 19 studies.
sentences.s100: Although all the studies discussed in this review investigated the effects of reinforcement contingencies in AD/HD, the authors adopted five different approaches to study the effects (see Table 1).
sentences.s101: A first approach was to compare reward with nonreward conditions; to compare reward with response cost conditions; to compare reward, response cost, and nonreward conditions; and also to compare mixed reward and response cost with feedback-only conditions.
sentences.s102: In a second approach, continuous reward schedules were compared to partial reward schedules.
sentences.s103: In a third approach, reward delay was manipulated.
sentences.s104: A fourth approach was to study an altered response to reward by manipulating the reward ratio.
sentences.s105: Changes in the intensity of reward were studied in a fifth approach.
sentences.s106: A variety of tasks that study cognitive processing and tasks that study response output were used (e.g., Arithmetic Task, Continuous Performance Task, Choice-Delay Task, Paired Associate Memory Task, Repetitive Motor Task, and a Stop Signal Task).
sentences.s107: These tasks capture different aspects of cognitive functioning, such as vigilance, working memory, inhibition, perseveration, abstract reasoning, and stimulus detection.
sentences.s108: Other tasks focus more on aspects of response output such as reward choice behavior.
sentences.s109: To overcome the problem of heterogeneity in task performance, we focus exclusively on the absolute change in task performance reflected by different dependent measures.
sentences.s110: This measurement is independent of specific cognitive functions or reward choice studied in this review. 3.
