sentences.s377: AD/HD versus normal controls under immediate and delayed reward Three studies compared task performance under immediate and delayed reward.
sentences.s378: When children were required to make a choice between an immediate and a delayed reward, children with AD/HD chose more often for an immediate reward compared to controls (Rapport et al., 1986; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992; Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s379: They chose more often for the immediate reward, even though the delayed reward was larger (Rapport et al., 1986).
sentences.s380: In contrast, normal controls chose more often for the larger delayed reward (Rapport et al., 1986), or showed a smaller response bias for the immediate reward (Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s381: In addition, reward choice on earlier trials did not change the preference for an immediate reward for children with AD/HD (Rapport et al., 1986; Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s382: Normal controls, however, seemed to incorporate recently gained reward into their reward choice: When previous reward was small (Rapport et al., 1986) or immediate (Tripp & Alsop, 2001), the preference for an immediate (small) reward in the consecutive trial diminished.
sentences.s383: When a maximum amount of reward was predetermined or when the maximum amount of time to complete the task was set, the response pattern of children with AD/HD did not differ from normal controls (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992).
sentences.s384: Both groups responded in a pattern that maximized the amount of reward.
sentences.s385: However, when the number of trials was predetermined, which implied a maximum number of responses, the AD/HD group chose more often for the reward that minimized time-on-task.
sentences.s386: The normal control group maximized their total amount of reward (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992).
sentences.s387: Moreover, when overall delay was similar, by adding a postreward delay, Sonuga-Barke et al. (1992) observed that both children with AD/HD and normal controls chose for the large delayed reward.
sentences.s388: The result led Sonuga- Barke to conclude that children with AD/HD are extremely sensitive to delay and are delay-averse rather M.

sentences.s412: Summary task performance Firstly, a majority of studies described in this section indicate that reward and response cost have a positive effect on task performance of both children with AD/HD and controls.
sentences.s413: Additionally, in terms of the number of studies showing improvement in performance, the improvement is somewhat more prominent for children with AD/HD than in normal controls (Carlson et al., 2000; Carlson & Tamm, 2000; Iaboni et al., 1997; Konrad et al., 2000; McInerny & Kerns, 2003; Scheres et al., 2001; Solanto, 1990).
sentences.s414: Six studies that compared reward with response cost conditions found that reinforcement condition did not differentiate performance of children with AD/HD from controls.
sentences.s415: Luman et al. / Clinical Psychology Review 25 (2005) 183–213 200 Secondly, one of three studies showed that performance of children with AD/HD deteriorated under partial compared to continuous reward (Douglas & Parry, 1994).
sentences.s416: When children were required to perform a task under partial and nonreward conditions, no differences were found in three studies that compared children with AD/HD (Barber et al., 1996; Douglas & Parry, 1994) or children with ADD (Pelham et al., 1986) and controls.
sentences.s417: Third, compared to controls, children with AD/HD seem to choose more often an immediate reward than a delayed reward, irrespective of the previous reward trial and whether the delayed reward was large (Rapport et al., 1986; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992; Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s418: Fourth, when reward schedules are manipulated in such a way that the chances of receiving reward diminished over time, no differences in response rate were observed between children with AD/HD and controls (Daugherty & Quay, 1991).
sentences.s419: Children with CD, however, showed a high response rate irrespective of diminishing chance on receiving reward, which turned out to be a less profitable response strategy.
sentences.s420: Fifth, when reward conditions were compared to a condition of response cost or nonreward, the authors failed to find any differential effects on task performance in studies where children with ODD/ CD were compared to children with AD/HD (Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1998; Scheres et al., 2001).
sentences.s421: There are some limitations related to the findings described above that need to be highlighted.
sentences.s422: The main concern is heterogeneity in the dependent variables employed in the empirical studies.
sentences.s423: Also, the confounding variables that have been taken into account differ between studies.
sentences.s424: Furthermore, form, amount, and delivery of reinforcement vary, and not all studies make sure that the total amount of reinforcement is similar for all groups.
sentences.s425: A limitation of a different caliber is that the findings in this review are based on a small number of studies.
sentences.s426: Finally, a possible ceiling effect of performance in the control group may confound the findings related to task performance. 4.

sentences.s528: General discussion The goal of this review was twofold.
sentences.s529: On one hand, we have charted the behavioral findings regarding the role of reinforcement contingencies in AD/HD—an attempt that has not been made for some time (Douglas & Peters, 1979).
sentences.s530: On the other hand, we wished to study the implications of the behavioral findings for the theoretical frameworks related to this body of research.
sentences.s531: We first summarize the results of the studies in this review: We found clear evidence that reward and response cost have a positive effect on performance and on levels of motivation of both children with AD/HD and normal controls.
sentences.s532: Additionally, a performance improvement was reported more often for the AD/HD group than for controls (Carlson et al., 2000; Carlson & Tamm, 2000; Konrad et al., 2000; McInerny & Kerns, 2003).
sentences.s533: With respect to the levels of motivation, no significant interactions were found between group and reinforcement condition.
sentences.s534: Another evident finding is that compared to controls, children with AD/HD seem to choose more often for an immediate reward irrespective of the previous reinforcement trial or whether the delayed reward was large (Rapport et al., 1986; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992; Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s535: Less clear is the role of partial reward.
sentences.s536: In one of three studies, performance of children with AD/HD diminished under partial compared to continuous reward, while performance of controls remained the same (Douglas & Parry, 1994).
sentences.s537: Furthermore, children with AD/HD and normal controls responded in a similar pattern, when response perseveration was measured in a task where the chance on receiving reward diminished (Daugherty & Quay, 1991).
sentences.s538: When heart rate and skin conductance measures are investigated, children with AD/HD seem to be psychophysiologically less sensitive to reinforcement contingencies (Crone et al., 2003; Iaboni et al., 1997).
sentences.s539: The decreased sensitivity for reinforcement at a psychophysiological level seems to contrast with the findings related to performance: At a performance level, in some studies, reinforcement contingencies are more beneficial for children with AD/HD than for controls (Carlson et al., 2000; Carlson & Tamm, 2000; Konrad et al., 2000; McInerny & Kerns, 2003).
sentences.s540: We now discuss the implications of the findings in terms of five models described in the Introduction.

sentences.s542: A more prominent improvement in performance of children with AD/HD under reward conditions supports this hypothesis (Carlson & Tamm, 2000; Konrad et al., 2000; McInerny & Kerns, 2003).
sentences.s543: Partial reward was suggested to result in diminished task performance.
sentences.s544: The findings, however, only partly support this suggestion, since only one of three studies revealed clear evidence on this issue (Douglas & Parry, 1994).
sentences.s545: When the chance of receiving reward diminished (Daugherty & Quay, 1991), children with AD/HD showed a similar response pattern compared to controls, in contrast to the ideas of Haenlein and Caul.
sentences.s546: In addition, Haenlein and Caul argued that that medication would lower the reward threshold.
sentences.s547: When confronted with a diminishing chance of receiving reward, children with AD/HD on medication showed a more optimal performance compared to children with AD/HD receiving placebo (Wilkison et al., 1995).
sentences.s548: The psychophysiological findings concerning a diminished sensitivity to reinforcement are in line with the suggestion of an elevated reward threshold.
sentences.s549: The preference for immediate reward of children with AD/ HD supports Haenlein and Caul’s model, since they suggested that the impact of a reward is larger when M.

10.1016/j.cpr.2017.08.007.printed_title: Associations between rejection sensitivity and mental health outcomes: A meta-analytic review

sentences.s1: Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Clinical Psychology Review journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/clinpsychrev Review Associations between rejection sensitivity and mental health outcomes: A meta-analytic review Shuling Gaoa,b, Mark Assinkc, Andrea Ciprianid, Kangguang Lina,b,⁎ a Department of Aﬀective Disorders, The Aﬃliated Brain Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou Huiai Hospital, Guangzhou, China b Laboratory of Emotion and Cognition, The Aﬃliated Brain Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou Huiai Hospital, Guangzhou, China c Research Institute of Child Development and Education, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands d Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford, Oxford OX3 7JX, UK H I G H L I G H T S • This is the ﬁrst meta-analysis examining rejection sensitivity and mental health. • Rejection sensitivity is moderately associated with several mental health problems. • The associations were similar for clinical and non-clinical samples. • The association between rejection sensitivity and anxiety seems stronger for males. • Paying attention to rejection sensitivity in clinical practice is recommended.
sentences.s2: A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Rejection sensitivity Depression Anxiety Borderline personality disorder Body dysmorphic disorder Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Rejection sensitivity is a personality disposition characterized by oversensitivity to social rejection.
sentences.s3: Using a three-level meta-analytic model, 75 studies were reviewed that examined associations between rejection sen- sitivity and ﬁve mental health outcomes: depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline personality disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder.
sentences.s4: The results showed signiﬁcant and moderate associations between rejection sensi- tivity and depression (pooled r = 0.332; p < 0.001), anxiety (pooled r = 0.407; p < 0.001), loneliness (pooled r = 0.386; p < 0.001), borderline personality disorder (pooled r = 0.413; p < 0.001), and body dysmorphic disorder (pooled r = 0.428; p < 0.001).
sentences.s5: The associations between rejection sensitivity and de- pression, anxiety, and borderline personality disorder varied by type of sample, but the associations were similar for clinical and non-clinical (i.e., community) samples.
sentences.s6: The association between rejection sensitivity and anxiety was negatively moderated by percentage of females in samples.
sentences.s7: The association between rejection sensitivity and depression was negatively moderated by length of follow-up.
sentences.s8: The longitudinal associations between rejection sensitivity and depression, anxiety, and loneliness were stable over time.
sentences.s9: Implications of the ﬁndings for both risk assessment and prevention and intervention strategies in mental health practice are discussed. 1.
sentences.s10: Introduction Numerous studies have reported that early interpersonal trauma (e.g., childhood maltreatment) has long-term eﬀects on later psycho- pathology (see for instance, Kim & Cicchetti, 2010; Lansford et al., 2002; Wolfe, Wekerle, Scott, Straatman, & Grasley, 2004).
sentences.s11: However, the ﬁeld has made little progress in identifying the mechanisms of these behavioral eﬀects.
sentences.s12: Rejection sensitivity has been identiﬁed as a po- tential mechanism linking early interpersonal trauma to its sequelae (Downey, Khouri, & Feldman, 1997).
sentences.s13: Extensive research has shown that rejection sensitivity is associated with a range of mental health pro- blems (e.g., Chango, McElhaney, Allen, Schad, & Marston, 2012; Chesin, Fertuck, Goodman, Lichenstein, & Stanley, 2015; Rowe, Gembeck, Rudolph, & Nesdale, 2015; Webb et al., 2015).
sentences.s14: However, there are discrepancies in the magnitude of reported associations.
sentences.s15: Therefore, synthesizing empirical evidence is important for a better understanding of how rejection sensitivity is connected to diﬀerent mental health problems.
sentences.s16: Until now, a systematic review statistically summarizing associations between rejection sensitivity and mental health problems was not available.
sentences.s17: To remedy this deﬁciency, the aim http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2017.08.007 Received 2 April 2017; Received in revised form 12 August 2017; Accepted 14 August 2017 ⁎ Corresponding author at: Department of Aﬀective Disorders, The Aﬃliated Brain Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, 36 Mingxin Road, Guangzhou, Guangdong Province 510370, China.

sentences.s20: MARK of the present study was to statistically summarize associations between rejection sensitivity and a number of diﬀerent mental health problems by conducting a series of meta-analyses. 1.1.
sentences.s21: Conceptualization and measurement of rejection sensitivity Rejection sensitivity is thought to develop as a result of an in- dividual's early experience of rejection, neglect, or abuse (Ayduk & Gyurak, 2008).
sentences.s22: More broadly, it is thought to arise as a result of an individual's exposure to situations in which the physical or emotional acts of others, either overt or covert, and active or passive, communicate rejection (Romero-Canyas, Downey, Berenson, Ayduk, & Kang, 2010).
sentences.s23: Rejection sensitivity can be deﬁned as a per- sonality disposition characterized by oversensitivity to social rejection.
sentences.s24: In particular, Downey and colleagues deﬁned rejection sensitivity as a cognitive-aﬀective processing disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and overreact (emotionally or behaviorally) to rejection (Downey et al., 1997; Downey & Feldman, 1996).
sentences.s25: Boyce and Parker (1989) proposed the construct interpersonal sensitivity, which is a si- milar concept to rejection sensitivity, and which they deﬁned as an undue and excessive awareness of, and sensitivity to, the behavior and feelings of others.
sentences.s26: Individuals with high interpersonal sensitivity are particularly preoccupied with perceived or actual situations of criticism or rejection, vigilant to the behavior and moods of others, and overly sensitive to problems in any interpersonal interaction (Boyce & Parker, 1989).
sentences.s27: Research has evidenced that individuals with high rejection sensi- tivity show greater responsivity to social rejection than individuals with low rejection sensitivity, implying that social rejection can be empiri- cally diﬀerentiated from a broader sensitivity to threats.
sentences.s28: Speciﬁcally, this can be derived from the work of Burklund, Eisenberger, and Lieberman (2007), who examined neural responses to threatening facial expressions depicting disapproval, anger, and disgust, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
sentences.s29: They found that individuals who scored higher on a measure of rejection sensitivity exhibited greater dorsal anterior cingulate cortex activity in response to disapproving facial expressions, but not in response to facial expressions of anger or disgust.
sentences.s30: This suggests that, at the neural level, individuals high in re- jection sensitivity may be more sensitive to facial expressions signaling potential rejection, but not to threatening facial expressions in general.
sentences.s31: This implies that rejection sensitivity may be qualitatively diﬀerent from a general sensitivity to threats.
sentences.s32: Similar evidence can also be found in other research (e.g., Olsson, Carmona, Downey, Bolger, & Ochsner, 2013).
sentences.s33: In the empirical literature, rejection sensitivity has been measured predominantly by diﬀerent versions of the Rejection Sensitivity Questionnaire (RSQ) (Downey & Feldman, 1996) and the Interpersonal Sensitivity Measure (IPSM) (Boyce & Parker, 1989).
sentences.s34: The RSQ was coined by Downey and colleagues who viewed defensive expectations of rejection to be the core component of rejection sensitivity (Downey et al., 1997).
sentences.s35: They operationalized rejection sensitivity as anxious or angry expectations of rejection in situations where rejection is possible.
sentences.s36: Based on this concept, Downey and Feldman (1996) developed an in- strument for measuring rejection sensitivity (the RSQ-Personal), which measures two components: concern or anxiety and expectations.
sentences.s37: Re- searchers have argued that rejection sensitivity is learned through ex- perience (Romero-Canyas et al., 2010) and that the learned nature of feeling rejected implies that rejection sensitivity may be situation-spe- ciﬁc (Levy, Ayduk, & Downey, 2001).
sentences.s38: Consequently, researchers have recently developed various instruments for measuring rejection sensi- tivity for diﬀerent populations, including the Children's RSQ (Downey, Lebolt, Rincon, & Freitas, 1998), the adult RSQ (Berenson et al., 2009), the appearance-based RSQ (Park, 2007), the weight-based RSQ (McClure Brenchley & Quinn, 2016), the gender-based RSQ (London, Downey, Romero-Canyas, Rattan, & Tyson, 2012), the race-based RSQ (Mendoza-Denton, Downey, Purdie, Davis, & Pietrzak, 2002), the age- based RSQ (Kang & Chasteen, 2009), the gay-related rejection scale (Pachankis, Goldfried, & Ramrattan, 2008), the sexual minority women rejection sensitivity scale (Dyar, Feinstein, Eaton, & London, 2016), and the status-based rejection sensitivity questionnaire for Asian Americans (Chan & Mendoza-Denton, 2008).
sentences.s39: In parallel with the RSQ and its diﬀerent versions, the IPSM (Boyce & Parker, 1989) has also attracted growing interest from re- searchers and has been validated recently in Italy (Masillo et al., 2014) and Korea (Lee et al., 2013).
sentences.s40: The 36-item IPSM encompasses ﬁve fac- tors: interpersonal awareness, the need for approval, separation an- xiety, timidity, and a fragile inner-self (Boyce & Parker, 1989).
sentences.s41: Unlike the RSQ, which is based on traditional theories (i.e., a cognitive-aﬀec- tive framework and a defensive motivational system), the IPSM was developed out of clinical experience.
sentences.s42: The RSQ tends to consider rejec- tion sensitivity as a personality disposition, whereas rejection sensi- tivity is regarded as a personality trait in the IPSM.
sentences.s43: Appendix A presents an overview of available instruments measuring rejection sensitivity. 1.2.
sentences.s44: Rejection sensitivity and mental health The cognitive-aﬀective processing systems (CAPS) framework (Mischel, 1973; Mischel & Shoda, 1995) can be used to account for possible associations between rejection sensitivity and mental health problems.
sentences.s45: The CAPS theory (Mischel & Shoda, 1995) explains why and how people's behavior varies stably across situations.
sentences.s46: It explains how personality processes emerge in speciﬁc Person × Situation interac- tions (Romero-Canyas et al., 2010).
sentences.s47: Speciﬁcally, this theory stresses the presence of ‘if … then…’ patterns in the assiciation between rejection sensitivity and behavior (Ayduk & Gyurak, 2008) – that is, if situation X occurs, an individual does A; but if situation Y occurs, the individual does B.
sentences.s48: For example, Jane does not see herself as a pretty girl, but she does get good grades in school.
sentences.s49: If her peers are discussing school per- formance, she feels conﬁdent, but as soon as her peers start discussing appearance, she is prone to feelings of depression.
sentences.s50: These situation-be- havior relations reﬂect the presence of a stable network of distinctive personality processing dynamics that is activated.
sentences.s51: These dynamics link fears and expectations of rejection, perceptions or attributions of re- jection, and aﬀective or behavioral overreactions to perceived rejection (Ayduk & Gyurak, 2008).
sentences.s52: The relation between psychological features of situations and behavior is assumed to be mediated by ﬁve types of person variables (Mischel, 1973): encoding and construction compe- tencies, expectations and beliefs, feelings and emotions, goals and va- lues, and self-regulatory abilities.
sentences.s53: Individuals with high levels of re- jection sensitivity tend to fear or anxiously expect rejection of others (Ayduk & Gyurak, 2008; Romero-Canyas et al., 2010).
sentences.s54: This anticipation may lead to a self-fulﬁlling prophecy in which individuals behave out of fear, thereby creating a situation that elicits rejection from others and in which the previous fears are conﬁrmed (Downey, Freitas, Michaelis, & Khouri, 1998).
sentences.s55: Rejection sensitivity can also be explained as a state of a defensive motivational system (Downey, Mougios, Ayduk, London, & Shoda, 2004; Romero-Canyas et al., 2010).
sentences.s56: Rejection sensitivity results from previous experiences of social rejection and the rejection sensitivity system is intended to protect the self against future rejection by trig- gering rapid defensive responses when social threats exist (Romero- Canyas et al., 2010).
sentences.s57: When rejection is the threat, activation of the rejection sensitivity system prepares individuals to detect signs of social threat, and to be ready for immediate action in order to avert the danger by being self-defensive (Downey et al., 2004).
sentences.s58: Compared to individuals with low rejection sensitivity, individuals with high rejec- tion sensitivity show heightened physiological activity (Downey et al., 2004), are on alert for rejection-related cues, automatically process rejection-related content (Berenson et al., 2009), show a lower threshold for detecting social threats, see cues of rejection as more negative (Olsson, Carmona, Downey, Bolger, & Ochsner, 2008), and are prone to personalize ambiguous cues of rejection (Downey & Feldman, 1996).
sentences.s59: The defensive motivational system disposes the individual to- ward active avoidance and ﬁght-or-ﬂight behavior (Gray, 1987; Lang, Davis, & Öhman, 2000), which may lead to increased internalizing symptoms or disorders such as depression, anxiety, and personality disorders (Bijttebier, Beck, Claes, & Vandereycken, 2009).
sentences.s60: In the present study, associations between rejection sensitivity and diﬀerent mental health problems will be further examined using a meta-analytic design.
sentences.s61: This study is relevant for several reasons.
sentences.s62: First, new knowledge of the associations between rejection sensitivity and diﬀerent mental health problems is generated.
sentences.s63: According to the DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association, 1994), rejection sensitivity is an atypical feature of major depressive disorder.
sentences.s64: Additionally, individuals with a social anxiety disorder or a borderline personality disorder are very sensitive to being negatively evaluated and to social rejection (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
sentences.s65: However, based on the DSM- 5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), we do not know whether rejection sensitivity is also related to other types of negative mental health outcomes such as loneliness and body dysmorphic disorder.
sentences.s66: Second, examining the magnitude of these associations advances our fundamental knowledge of the degree to which rejection sensitivity contributes to negative mental health outcomes.
sentences.s67: Third, further insight into the associations between rejection sensitivity and negative mental health outcomes may improve current clinical assessment practices.
sentences.s68: After all, if rejection sensitivity is related to negative mental health outcomes, it becomes relevant to measure rejection sensitivity in the identiﬁcation of both mental health problems and care needs.
sentences.s69: Fourth, the results of the present study may foster the development and im- provement of programs aimed at the prevention or treatment of mental health problems.
sentences.s70: Taken together, the primary aim of this meta-analytic review is to estimate overall associations between rejection sensitivity and diﬀerent mental health problems.
sentences.s71: The secondary aim is to investigate whether and how each overall association between rejection sensitivity and a mental health problem is moderated by sample characteristics, research design characteristics, and other characteristics. 2.
sentences.s72: Methods The present review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaﬀ, & Altman, 2009). 2.1.
sentences.s73: Protocol and registration To minimize the risk of bias in this systematic review, the research protocol was registered on the International Prospective Register for Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), registration number CRD42016053389, available from http://www.crd.york.ac.uk/ PROSPERO/display_record.asp?ID=CRD42016053186. 2.2.
sentences.s74: Study selection We were interested in the associations between rejection sensitivity and the broadest possible range of mental health problems.
sentences.s75: Therefore, at the initial stage of study selection, the ﬁrst author merely used the keyword “rejection sensitivity” to search for primary studies published between January 1, 1990 and December 31, 2016 in six electronic databases: PsycINFO, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar.
sentences.s76: After the ﬁrst author screened all the primary studies on rejection sensitivity and mental health problems, we set two inclusion criteria: ﬁrst, we included only those primary studies reporting on at least one association between rejection sensitivity and a speciﬁc mental health problem; and second, we only focused on those mental health problems for which suﬃcient primary studies were available.
sentences.s77: In this review, the minimum number of studies for examining a separate mental health outcome was set to ﬁve.
sentences.s78: We chose for this minimum because of statistical power and reliability considerations (see, for instance, Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009).
sentences.s79: Thus, we decided not to focus on mental health problems for which less than ﬁve studies were available.
sentences.s80: As a result, we focused on the fol- lowing ﬁve mental health problems in the present review: depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline personality disorder, and body dys- morphic disorder.
sentences.s81: Next, a three-step literature search was adopted to identify relevant literature on the ﬁve mental health outcomes (i.e., depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline personality disorder, and body dysmorphic dis- order).
sentences.s82: First, we searched in the following six electronic databases for primary studies published between January 1, 1990 and December 31, 2016: PsycINFO, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar.
sentences.s83: No restrictions were set in terms of study char- acteristics (i.e., participants and research design characteristics) or publication status.
sentences.s84: Second, reference lists of eligible studies and re- levant review articles (i.e., Marin & Miller, 2013; Premkumar, 2012; Romero-Canyas et al., 2010) were searched manually to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant studies.
sentences.s85: Third, prominent researchers in the ﬁeld were identiﬁed and all their publications were evaluated for inclusion.
sentences.s86: The literature search was independently performed by two authors of the current study (SG and KL) in the above-mentioned databases.
sentences.s87: The following combination of two syntax components were used in the electronic search: (“rejection sensitivity”) AND (“depression” OR “de- pressive symptoms” OR “depressed mood” OR “anxiety” OR “anxious symptoms” OR “loneliness” OR “borderline personality disorder” OR “borderline personality features” OR “borderline personality symp- toms” OR “body dysmorphic disorder” OR “body dysmorphic symp- toms” OR “mental health” OR “psychopathology” OR “internalizing problems” OR “psychological well-being” OR “adjustment” OR “nega- tive aﬀect” OR “psychological stress” OR “negative feelings” OR “gen- eral distress” OR “total diﬃculties”).
sentences.s88: Using these components, we conducted advanced searches in the keywords, title, and abstract ﬁelds of each database to retrieve relevant literature.
sentences.s89: Results from all in- formation resources were combined and duplicates were subsequently removed.
sentences.s90: Each unique search result was reviewed independently by two authors (SG and KL) to determine eligibility.
sentences.s91: First, the title and abstract of each potentially relevant primary study were screened to ascertain whether the study met the inclusion criteria.
sentences.s92: In cases where the eligibility of the study could not be ruled out based on the title and abstract, the full article text was also examined.
sentences.s93: Primary studies were included in this review if they fulﬁlled the following criteria. 1) The study design was quantitative and empirical in nature; thus review papers, qualitative studies, and case studies were discarded. 2) The study was written in English. 3) Studies had a cross- sectional, longitudinal, or experimental design. 4) The study examined at least one association between rejection sensitivity and one or more of the following mental health problems: depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline personality disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder.
sentences.s94: Studies not examining a speciﬁc mental health problem but examining con- structs or symptoms that are only broadly related to mental health (e.g., general mental health, psychological stress, negative aﬀect, negative feelings, total diﬃculties, internalizing problems, general distress, or adjustment) were excluded.
sentences.s95: Studies combining anxiety and depression disorders into a single outcome (e.g., depressive and anxious symp- toms) were also excluded, because including such outcomes would undermine our conclusions regarding the association between rejection sensitivity and the speciﬁc outcome of depression or anxiety. 5) The study reported on statistical information that is required to obtain or calculate at least one bivariate eﬀect size (i.e., Pearson's r).
sentences.s96: When it was unclear whether a study should be included or not, the disagreement was handled by consulting an expert in rejection sensi- tivity to determine whether the primary study should be included.
sentences.s97: If a study appeared eligible on the basis of the inclusion criteria, but not all required information could be coded, we contacted the study's authors and requested the required information.
sentences.s98: In total, six authors were contacted in an attempt to obtain missing information.
sentences.s99: Each author was informed of the purpose of the current study and was provided with a list of variables that were necessary for the meta-analysis (e.g., corre- lations between rejection sensitivity and one of the ﬁve mental health problems), but were not reported on in their studies.
sentences.s100: Four authors re- plied and provided the requested information.
sentences.s101: As for the mental health problems in the present meta-analysis, we deﬁned the following ﬁve domains: (a) depression; (b) anxiety; (c) loneliness; (d) borderline personality disorder; and (e) body dys- morphic disorder.
sentences.s102: These problems (except loneliness) can be deﬁned using the criteria as described in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM 5th ed.; American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
sentences.s103: In short, depression is a state of sad, empty, or irritable mood, accompanied by somatic and cognitive changes that aﬀect the in- dividual's capacity to function.
sentences.s104: Anxiety is an emotion characterized by expectations of future threat associated with muscle tension and vigi- lance in preparation for future danger and cautious or avoidant beha- viors.
sentences.s105: Loneliness is a subjective feeling of social isolation associated with the absence of certain social relationships, feelings of emptiness or abandonment (De Jong-Gierveld, 1987).
sentences.s106: Borderline personality dis- order is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in inter- personal relationships, self-image, and aﬀects, together with marked impulsivity that is present in a variety of contexts.
sentences.s107: Body dysmorphic disorder is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or ﬂaws in one's physical appearance, which are viewed as unattractive, abnormal or deformed.
sentences.s108: In this study, it is important to note that the above mentioned problems were regarded as either “symptoms” or “diagnoses.” When regarded as “diagnoses,” we fol- lowed the guidelines of DSM-5 to deﬁne the criteria of depressive dis- orders and anxiety disorders.
sentences.s109: The instruments that were used in pri- mary studies to measure the ﬁve mental health problems are summarized in Appendix B1. 2.3.
sentences.s110: Coding of studies If inclusion criteria were met, the full-text of each article was re- trieved and coded using a standardized extraction sheet and codebook in accordance with the guidelines of Lipsey and Wilson (2001).
sentences.s111: To meaningfully synthesize results, each study was coded and evaluated based on the following characteristics: (a) authors and year of pub- lication; (b) study design (i.e., cross-sectional, longitudinal, or experi- mental); (c) continent in which the primary study was conducted (grouped into four continents: North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia); (d) sample type (sample was coded as “clinical” when partici- pants were recruited from clinical settings, “community” when parti- cipants were recruited from general community settings, and “mixed” when participants were recruited in both clinical and community set- tings); (e) sample size; (f) gender (i.e., percentage of females); (g) mean age (in years); (h) age group (samples were coded as “younger than 18 years” or “18 years or older”); (i) measure of rejection sensitivity (i.e., RSQ and versions thereof, IPSM, and others); (j) type of mental health outcome (i.e., depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline per- sonality disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder); (k) type of measure- ment for the outcome variables (e.g., Beck Depression Inventory, Children's Depression Inventory); (l) eﬀect size (i.e., correlation coef- ﬁcients).
sentences.s112: Whenever possible, unadjusted eﬀect sizes (i.e., study results did not control for variables such as gender, age, or other variables) were extracted.
sentences.s113: For longitudinal studies, we extracted both cross-sec- tional associations (i.e., baseline correlations and correlations at mul- tiple time points) and longitudinal associations (i.e., correlations be- tween baseline rejection sensitivity and depression at all follow-ups). (m) type of eﬀect size (i.e., associations were coded as baseline or follow-up); and (n) length of follow-up (time duration between asso- ciations measured at diﬀerent time points, usually in months).
sentences.s114: Ap- pendix B2 presents an overview of the coded variables.
sentences.s115: If studies reported on results of more than one sample, eﬀect sizes for each sample were included in the meta-analysis, where possible.
sentences.s116: If studies reported eﬀect sizes for both a total sample and subgroups (for instance, males and females), only eﬀect sizes reported for the sub- groups were included.
sentences.s117: This reduced the problem of redundancy and enabled analyses for subgroups.
sentences.s118: If studies analyzed males and females separately, the male and female samples were considered unique samples.
sentences.s119: If studies reported on multiple measures for the same con- struct (such as two diﬀerent measures of rejection sensitivity or an- xiety), multiple eﬀect sizes were coded.
sentences.s120: When studies reported on multiple outcomes (such as depression and anxiety and loneliness), multiple eﬀect sizes were also coded.
sentences.s121: If studies reported on duplicate samples (for instance, two articles used the same sample and reported similar results), only one study was included and coded.
sentences.s122: We coded several sample descriptors, research design descriptors, and other descriptors that may moderate overall associations.
sentences.s123: First, the gender of the sample was coded (i.e., the percentage of females) since previous research reported mixed ﬁndings on rejection sensitivity for males and females (e.g., Calogero, Park, Rahemtulla, & Williams, 2010; Park, Calogero, Young, & Diraddo, 2010; Webb et al., 2015).
sentences.s124: Second, we coded the age of participants since several researchers reported mixed ﬁndings on how rejection sensitivity varies with age (e.g., De Panﬁlis, Meehan, Cain, & Clarkin, 2015; Rowe et al., 2015; Zimmer- Gembeck, Trevaskis, Nesdale, & Downey, 2014).
sentences.s125: We coded age both as a continuous variable (i.e., mean age of the sample) and a categorical variable (i.e., “18 years or older” versus “younger than 18 years”).
sentences.s126: Third, we coded type of sample (clinical, community, and mixed sample) since prior research found diﬀerences in associations between rejection sensitivity and mental health problems between populations (e.g., Staebler, Helbing, Rosenbach, & Renneberg, 2011).
sentences.s127: As for research design descriptors, we coded the type of measure- ment of both rejection sensitivity and the ﬁve mental health problems to examine whether the type of instruments used by primary re- searchers moderates the overall associations between rejection sensi- tivity and the mental health problems.
sentences.s128: We also coded type of eﬀect size (baseline or follow-up) and length of follow-up (in months).
sentences.s129: Lastly, we coded publication year and continent (i.e., North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia) in which the study was performed.
sentences.s130: Two authors (SG and KL) coded independently all primary studies that were included in this meta-analysis.
sentences.s131: Inter-rater reliability was as- sessed by calculating intraclass correlation coeﬃcients (ICC) for con- tinuous variables and by calculating kappa coeﬃcients (k) for catego- rical variables.
sentences.s132: In cases where discrepancies between coders were identiﬁed, both coders independently reviewed the study again, after which errors were identiﬁed and corrected.
sentences.s133: To minimize possible bias in individual studies, the National Institutes of Health's Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies (National Institutes of Health, 2014) was used to assess the quality of the included studies.
sentences.s134: Each study was as- sessed using 14 criteria and was rated using a three-point scale (good, fair, and poor).
sentences.s135: The speciﬁc list of criteria used in the present study and results of the quality assessment is available from the authors upon request.
sentences.s136: Quality assessment was independently conducted by two au- thors (SG and KL), and disagreements were resolved via discussion between these two raters. 2.4.
sentences.s137: Statistical analyses The correlation coeﬃcient was chosen as the primary index of eﬀect size in the present meta-analysis.
sentences.s138: We computed Pearson's r for each eﬀect size that could be extracted from each primary study.
sentences.s139: Prior to conducting the meta-analyses, all correlations were converted to the Fisher's transformation of r (Zr), since the sampling distribution of r is negatively skewed (Card, 2012; Hedges & Olkin, 1985).
sentences.s140: After con- ducting all analyses, the Fisher's z values were re-transformed into Pearson's r for interpretability.
sentences.s141: If studies did not report on the Pearson's correlation coeﬃcient r, it was calculated whenever possible using the available data reported in the primary study (e.g., by using t-statistics).
sentences.s142: It was not possible to convert betas from multiple regression models into correlation coeﬃcients as we were interested in calculating a bi- variate association (see also the inclusion criteria described above).
sentences.s143: A positive r value indicates that a high level of rejection sensitivity is associated with a high level of a speciﬁc mental health problem (i.e., depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline personality disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder).
sentences.s144: Conversely, a negative r value indicates that a high level of rejection sensitivity is associated with a low level of a speciﬁc mental health problem.
sentences.s145: The formulae of Hedges and Olkin (1985), Borenstein et al. (2009), Card (2012), and Cheung (2014) were used for calculating (and transforming) the Pearson's correlation coef- ﬁcient and Fisher's z values (see Appendix D).
sentences.s146: To reduce the disproportionate inﬂuence of extreme eﬀect sizes on the results of the statistical analyses, we checked for outliers by searching for eﬀect sizes with very large standardized z scores (i.e., in excess of ± 3.29) (Tabachnik & Fidell, 2013).
sentences.s147: One eﬀect size in the depression domain was identiﬁed with a z value larger than 3.29.
sentences.s148: To reduce the impact of this outlier, the raw r value of the outlier was replaced by a new r value that equaled the highest eﬀect falling within the normal range.
sentences.s149: Most primary studies included in the present meta-analysis reported on multiple eﬀect sizes that could be extracted, because many studies reported on multiple outcome variables, or used multiple instruments to assess the same construct.
sentences.s150: In addition, many studies reported on results using diﬀerent types of reporters, or diﬀerent study samples and/or subsamples.
sentences.s151: As eﬀect sizes obtained from the same study are more likely to be related than eﬀect sizes obtained from diﬀerent stu- dies, the assumption of independence of eﬀect sizes in traditional meta- analytic approaches is violated (see, for instance, Lipsey & Wilson, 2001).
sentences.s152: Therefore, a traditional two-level meta-analytic approach would not be appropriate in the present review.
sentences.s153: To deal with the inter- dependency of eﬀect sizes, we used a multilevel approach to meta- analysis (Assink & Wibbelink, 2016), which is a strong method for dealing with dependency of eﬀect sizes, as it accounts for the hier- archical structure of the data in which eﬀect sizes are nested within studies (Van Den Noortgate & Onghena, 2003).
sentences.s154: In the present study, a three-level meta-analytic model was used to synthesize eﬀect sizes and to conduct moderator analyses.
sentences.s155: The three- level random eﬀects model examined three sources of variance: sam- pling variance of the observed eﬀect sizes (Level 1); variance between eﬀect sizes from the same study (Level 2); and variance between studies (Level 3) (Cheung, 2014; Van den Noortgate, López-López, Marín- Martínez, & Sánchez-Meca, 2013, 2015).
sentences.s156: Using this three-level meta- analytic model, all relevant eﬀect sizes can be extracted from one pri- mary study, so that all information can be preserved and maximum statistical power can be achieved (Assink et al., 2015).
sentences.s157: In contrast, in studies using more traditional two-level meta-analytic models, eﬀect sizes extracted from the same primary study are often averaged into a single eﬀect or discarded, meaning loss of information and lower sta- tistical power in the analyses.
sentences.s158: All analyses were conducted in R version 3.3.2 (R Core Team, 2016), using the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010).
sentences.s159: The R syntax was written following Assink and Wibbelink's (2016) tutorial.
sentences.s160: We es- timated the sampling variance of observed eﬀect sizes (Level 1) using the formula of Cheung (2014).
sentences.s161: In each meta-analysis, we performed two separate one-tailed log-likelihood-ratio-tests to examine whether the variance between eﬀect sizes extracted from the same study (Level 2) and the variance between studies (Level 3) were signiﬁcant.
sentences.s162: These tests were performed one-sided, since variance components can only deviate from zero in a positive direction (Assink & Wibbelink, 2016).
sentences.s163: All other tests were conducted two-tailed, and a p value smaller than 0.05 was considered statistically signiﬁcant.
sentences.s164: Before variables were tested as moderators, each continuous variable was centered around its mean, and dichotomous dummy variables were created for each category of a discrete variable.
sentences.s165: All model parameters were estimated using the re- stricted maximum likelihood method (REML) (Viechtbauer, 2005).
sentences.s166: In performing the statistical analyses, we ﬁrst estimated an overall association between rejection sensitivity and each of the ﬁve mental health outcomes (i.e., depression, anxiety, loneliness, borderline per- sonality disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder) by building ﬁve se- parate meta-analytic intercept-only models.
sentences.s167: In interpreting these overall associations, we followed Cohen's (1992) guidelines in which r of at least 0.1 is a small eﬀect; r of at least 0.3 is a medium eﬀect, and r of at least 0.5 is a large eﬀect.
sentences.s168: Second, using mixed-eﬀect models we conducted bivariate moderator analyses in which potential moderators of the associations between rejection sensitivity and one of the ﬁve mental health problems were examined.
sentences.s169: In a mixed-eﬀects model, the eﬀect sizes (i.e., correlation coeﬃcients) are considered as a random- eﬀect, whereas the potential moderator is considered a ﬁxed-eﬀect.
sentences.s170: Publication bias is a common concern in conducting meta-analytic research.
sentences.s171: That is, studies reporting on nonsigniﬁcant ﬁndings are less likely to be published than studies reporting on signiﬁcant ﬁndings.
sentences.s172: Consequently, the results of meta-analytic research may be biased.
sentences.s173: To evaluate the extent to which the results of the present meta-analytic review were biased because of publication bias or any other form of bias, we visually inspected funnel plots of the eﬀect sizes, and we conducted Duval and Tweedie's trim-and-ﬁll analysis (Duval & Tweedie, 2000).
sentences.s174: A funnel plot was created for each mental health outcome, in which the eﬀect sizes were plotted against their standard errors.
sentences.s175: If ef- fect sizes are symmetrically distributed around the mean eﬀect, it is assumed that the results are not aﬀected by a form of bias.
sentences.s176: However, an asymmetric distribution of eﬀect sizes may indicate that bias is present in a meta-analysis (Borenstein et al., 2009).
sentences.s177: Duval and Tweedie's trim- and-ﬁll analysis generates estimates of eﬀect sizes that seem to be missing based on the asymmetry of a funnel plot.
sentences.s178: Next, these estimated missing eﬀect sizes can be added to the original dataset, after which an adjusted overall eﬀect can be estimated.
sentences.s179: If the initial and adjusted overall eﬀect sizes diﬀer, this indicates that publication bias may be present in the results of the meta-analysis.
sentences.s180: Following a similar procedure as outlined above, we also performed a number of meta-analyses on the association between rejection sensi- tivity and mental health problems using only longitudinal associations that could be extracted from the included primary studies.
sentences.s181: For the purpose of these analyses, we deﬁned longitudinal associations as correlations that were measured at diﬀerent points in time (e.g., re- jection sensitivity measured at baseline and depression measured in a follow-up one year later).
sentences.s182: These longitudinal associations diﬀer from cross-sectional associations in the sense that the latter were deﬁned as (bivariate) correlations between rejection sensitivity and one of the mental health problems that were simultaneously measured at a single point in time. 3.
sentences.s183: Description of included studies The results of the literature search strategy are presented in Appendix C.
sentences.s184: Seventy-ﬁve studies (44 on depression, 31 on anxiety, 9 on loneliness, 19 on borderline personality disorder, and 5 on body dys- morphic disorder), from which a total of 245 correlations (212 cross- sectional and 33 longitudinal correlations) could be extracted, met the inclusion criteria and were thus included in the present meta-analytic study.
sentences.s185: Because multiple correlations could be extracted from many single primary studies, there were more correlations than studies.
sentences.s186: All associations included in the present meta-analysis were unadjusted estimates except the association that was extracted from the study of Kawamoto, Ura, and Hiraki (2017), which was controlled for age and sex.
sentences.s187: As for the inter-rater agreement between the two raters, it was excellent for all coded variables (the ICCs ranged from 0.90 to1.00 and the kappa values ranged from 0.95 to1.00).
sentences.s188: All disagreements were subsequently resolved and, in the end, 100% consensus was reached.
sentences.s189: The included studies and some their characteristics are presented in Appendix B1.
sentences.s190: Of the 75 studies included in this review, 68.0% (n = 51) used a cross-sectional design, 24.0% (n = 18) used a longitudinal de- sign, and 8.0% (n = 6) used an experimental design. 6.7% (n = 5) of the studies used a clinical or high-risk sample, 82.7% (n = 62) used a community sample, and 10.7% (n = 8) used a mixed sample. 60.0% (n = 45) of the studies were conducted in North America, 18.7% (n = 14) of the studies took place in Europe, and only 13.3% (n = 10) and 8.0% (n = 6) of the studies were conducted in Australia and Asia, respectively.
sentences.s191: The total sample size was 21,008 and the mean age of all the participants was 24.058 years (SD = 11.520).

sentences.s1: Investigating the construct validity of intolerance of uncertainty and its unique relationship with worry Kristin Buhr, Michel J.
sentences.s2: Dugas * Department of Psychology (PY-170), Concordia University, 7141 Sherbrooke Street West, Montreal, Que., Canada H4B 1R6 Received 19 April 2004; received in revised form 15 September 2004; accepted 22 December 2004 Abstract Although recent ﬁndings suggest that intolerance of uncertainty is a fundamental construct involved in excessive worry, additional research is required to further establish the construct validity of intolerance of uncertainty and demonstrate its unique contribution to the understanding of worry.
sentences.s3: The present study examined the relationships among measures of worry, intolerance of uncertainty, intolerance of ambiguity, perfectionism, and perceived control in a sample of 197 university students.
sentences.s4: The ﬁndings indicated that intolerance of uncertainty moderately overlaps with earlier conceptualizations of intoler- ance of ambiguity; however, worry was more highly related to intolerance of uncertainty than to intolerance of ambiguity.
sentences.s5: Intolerance of uncertainty also emerged as the most salient predictor of worry compared to other cognitive processes such as perfectionism and perceived control.
sentences.s6: Worry and intolerance of uncertainty continued to be signiﬁcantly related after controlling for intolerance of ambiguity, perfectionism, and perceived control, which implies that intolerance of uncertainty shares a unique association with worry that is not accounted for by these other cognitive factors.
sentences.s7: Overall, the ﬁndings provide evidence of construct validity and underscore the role of intolerance of uncertainty in the conceptua- lization of worry. # 2005 Elsevier Inc.
sentences.s8: Keywords: Intolerance of uncertainty; Construct validity; Worry; Intolerance of ambiguity; Perfectionism; Perceived control Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 * Corresponding author.
sentences.s10: E-mail address: Michel.Dugas@concordia.ca (M.J. Dugas).
sentences.s11: Research advances in the area of worry have led to development of a number of conceptual models that identify constructs that may be involved in the etiology of excessive worry (e.g., Dugas, Gagnon, Ladouceur, & Freeston, 1998; Tallis & Eysenck, 1994; Wells, 1999).
sentences.s12: Although numerous constructs have been linked to worry, recent ﬁndings suggest that intolerance of uncertainty may play a fundamental role in the development and subsequent continuation of problematic worry (Dugas, Freeston, & Ladouceur, 1997; Dugas et al., 1998; Freeston, Rhe´aume, Letarte, Dugas, & Ladouceur, 1994).
sentences.s13: Intolerance of uncertainty can be deﬁned as the tendency to react negatively on an emotional, cognitive, and behavioral level to uncertain situations and events (Dugas, Buhr, & Ladouceur, 2004).
sentences.s14: More speciﬁcally, individuals who are intolerant of uncertainty ﬁnd ambiguity stressful and upsetting, believe uncertainty is negative and should be avoided, and have difﬁculty functioning in uncertain situations.
sentences.s15: Unfortunately, individuals who are intolerant of uncertainty may ﬁnd many situations unbearable, given that some level of ambiguity is present in everyday life, and the tendency to react negatively to uncertainty is likely to lead to heightened distress and worry.
sentences.s16: Research has demonstrated a strong relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and worry, which cannot be explained by other factors associated with worry, such as anxiety and depression (Buhr & Dugas, 2002; Dugas et al., 1997; Freeston et al., 1994).
sentences.s17: Intolerance of uncertainty has also emerged as the most salient predictor of worry, beyond other constructs believed to be involved in the development of excessive worry, such as positive beliefs about the function of worry, negative orientation towards problem situations, and cognitive avoidance (Lachance, Ladouceur, & Dugas, 1999; Laugesen, Dugas, & Bukowski, 2003; Robichaud, Dugas, & Conway, 2003).
sentences.s18: Recent efforts to develop efﬁcacious treatments for excessive worry have shown that including strategies aimed at facilitating clients’ tolerance towards uncertainty leads to a reduction in levels of worry and anxiety (Dugas & Ladouceur, 2000; Dugas et al., 2003; Ladouceur, Dugas et al., 2000).
sentences.s19: More importantly, changes in level of tolerance towards uncertainty generally precede changes in level of worry, over the course of treatment, which implies that intolerance of uncertainty may be a casual risk factor for excessive worry.
sentences.s20: This idea is further supported by research investigations that have demonstrated that the experimental manipulation of intolerance of uncertainty leads to changes in worry level with increased intolerance of uncertainty leading to heightened levels of worry (Ladouceur, Gosselin, & Dugas, 2000).
sentences.s21: Although the research thus far suggests that intolerance of uncertainty is a fundamental construct involved in excessive worry, additional research is required to further establish the construct validity of intolerance of uncertainty and demonstrate its unique contribution to the understanding of worry above and beyond other cognitive processes associated with worry, such as perfectionism and perceived control.
sentences.s22: Intolerance of uncertainty, as described in the present paper, is a relatively new construct having ﬁrst appeared in the worry literature in 1994 (see Freeston et al., K.
sentences.s23: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 223 1994) and subsequently used in the examination of anxiety disorders, in particular generalized anxiety disorder or GAD (e.g., Dugas et al., 1998; Ladouceur et al., 1999).
sentences.s24: Conversely, the concept of intolerance towards ambiguity emerged in the literature as early as the 1940s and originally was utilized to study authoritarian personality styles (see Frenkel-Brunswick, 1948, 1949) and later used to investigate religious beliefs, general attitudes, and career choices (Budner, 1962; Furnham, 1994).
sentences.s25: This early construct was deﬁned as ‘‘the tendency to perceive ambiguous situations as sources of threat’’ in which ambiguous situations were thought to represent novel, complex, or insoluble situations (Budner, 1962, p. 29).
sentences.s26: Individuals deemed intolerant of ambiguity were believed to have negative perceptions, evaluations, and feelings towards ambiguity, which would consequently impact their behavior.
sentences.s27: Initial examination of this deﬁnition suggests that it is synonymous with the description of intolerance of uncertainty, which involves the tendency to react negatively on an emotional, cognitive, and behavioral level to uncertain situations and events.
sentences.s28: Although conceptually the constructs appear similar, a closer examination of the relevant literature suggests that they have distinct elements.
sentences.s29: For instance, the most commonly used measures of intolerance of ambiguity have underlying factors that include conservative points of view, adventurousness, predictability, clarity, variety, originality, regularity, and anxiety related to ambiguity (see Furnham, 1994 for a review).
sentences.s30: In contrast, intolerance of uncertainty, as measured by the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS; Freeston et al., 1994), has been shown to have a four-factor structure, which includes the idea that uncertainty is stressful and upsetting, uncertainty leads to the inability to act, uncertain events are negative and should be avoided, and being uncertain is unfair (Buhr & Dugas, 2002).
sentences.s31: Despite similarities in the negative emotional reactions to uncertain stimuli and a preference towards predictability, the underlying structure of these constructs contains some unique dimensions.
sentences.s32: However, the differences between intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of ambiguity have yet to be established empirically.
sentences.s33: Various dimensions of perfectionism have been signiﬁcantly linked to anxiety and worry (Flett, Hewitt, & Dyck, 1989; Flett, Hewitt, Endler, & Tassone, 1995; Hewitt & Flett, 1991; Kawamura, Hunt, Frost, & DiBartolo, 2001; Sto¨ber & Joormann, 2001).
sentences.s34: Frost, Martin, Lahart, and Rosenblate (1990) have postulated that perfectionism involves setting excessively high personal standards, the tendency to be overly critical or doubtful of one’s abilities and actions, the expression of concern over mistakes, and the belief that others place high expectation on them, in particular parental ﬁgures.
sentences.s35: Hewitt and Flett (1991) propose an alternative model of perfectionism that includes three main dimensions: self-oriented perfectionism, which concerns unreasonably high personal standards; socially-prescribed perfectionism, which taps the belief that others have set excessively high standards and will be disappointed if those standards are not met; and other-oriented perfectionism, which is concerned with the tendency to set unreasonable expectations for others.
sentences.s36: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 224 Self-oriented and socially-prescribed perfectionism have been shown to correlate highly with measures of anxiety (Hewitt & Flett, 1991), while concern over mistakes, doubts about one’s abilities and actions, parental criticisms and expectations, and socially-prescribed perfectionism, have been shown to be highly related to worry (Flett et al., 1995; Kawamura et al., 2001; Sto¨ber & Joormann, 2001).
sentences.s37: Perfectionists may experience increased levels of worry and emotional distress as a result of an elevated fear of failure and the pursuit of unrealistic goals (Flett, Madorsky, Hewitt, & Heisel, 2002; Norman, Davies, Nicholson, Cortese, & Malla, 1998).
sentences.s38: The connection between perfectionism and worry is further supported by research that has shown that worriers display elevated evidence requirements (Pratt, Tallis, & Eysenck, 1997; Tallis, Eysenck, & Mathews, 1991).
sentences.s39: According to Pratt et al. (1997), the need for additional information before arriving at a decision may be indicative of unreasonably high personal standards that involve excessive concern about making mistakes and doubts about one’s abilities.
sentences.s40: Worriers may need to feel that they are making the ‘‘perfect’’ decision before responding.
sentences.s41: Perceived control, which relates to one’s perceived ability to affect the outcome of situations and events, has been linked to anxious responding with low levels of control being related to high levels of anxiety (Endler, Macrodimitris, & Kocovask, 2000).
sentences.s42: In addition, experimentally increasing people’s perceptions of control appears to lead to reductions in levels of anxiety and panic symptoms (Sanderson, Rapee, & Barlow, 1989; Zvolensky, Lejuez, & Eifert, 1998).
sentences.s43: Perceived control has also been shown to share a negative relationship with worry and this association is stronger than the link between perceived control and somatic anxiety (Zebb & Beck, 1998).
sentences.s44: A greater sense of control may serve to decrease the ambiguous or threatening elements of various situations making them more manageable, while a lack of perceived control may lead to heightened levels of worry, given that individuals may feel that they have little control over the outcome of situations.
sentences.s45: The goals of the present study are to further establish the construct validity of intolerance of uncertainty and to continue assessing the relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and worry in a nonclinical sample.
sentences.s46: Speciﬁcally, the current study will examine the relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of ambiguity, and contrast the association between each of these constructs and worry.
sentences.s47: Furthermore, the study will assess the relationship between worry and intolerance of uncertainty, perfectionism, and control, in order to ascertain whether intolerance of uncertainty shares a unique association with worry that is not better explained by these other cognitive factors.
sentences.s48: The ﬁndings from the present study will further establish the validity and importance of intolerance of uncertainty in the conceptualization of worry.
sentences.s49: Research has demonstrated that similar processes are involved in both clinical and nonclinical worry (see Dugas & Ladouceur, 1998, for a review), thus the study of nonclinical worry provides an opportunity to gain a greater understanding of worry in both clinical and nonclinical populations.
sentences.s50: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 225 The study has three main hypotheses.
sentences.s51: First, based on the examination of the literature, it is proposed that intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of ambiguity will be moderately related, but that intolerance of uncertainty will emerge as a distinct construct in relation to worry.
sentences.s52: Second, based on the ﬁndings suggesting a strong correlation between intolerance of uncertainty and worry, it is predicted that worry will share a stronger relationship with intolerance of uncertainty than with perfectionism and control.
sentences.s53: Finally, it is expected that intolerance of uncertainty and worry will share a unique association that will not be accounted for by intolerance of ambiguity, perfectionism, or control. 1.
sentences.s54: Participants One hundred and ninety-seven (N = 197) participants were recruited through various undergraduate courses at Concordia University.
sentences.s55: There were 152 (77.2%) female and 45 (22.8%) male participants with a mean age of 22.56 (S.D. = 5.5) years.
sentences.s56: Concerning the ethnicity of the sample, 69.6% of participants identiﬁed themselves as Caucasian, 6.8% as African American, 6.3% as Asian, 2.1% as Hispanic, and 15.2% as other ethnic origins.
sentences.s57: The majority of the sample (54.8%) was enrolled in their ﬁrst year of university, 21.3% in their second year, 14.7% in their third year, and 9.2% of participants indicated that they were in their fourth year or greater.
sentences.s58: In addition, 81.9% of participants indicated that their ﬁeld of study was the social sciences, 15% the pure or applied sciences, 2.1% the humanities, and 1% ﬁne arts.
sentences.s59: Students were invited to participate at the start of a regular undergraduate course and participation was voluntary. 1.2.
sentences.s60: Instruments The Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS; original French version: Freeston et al., 1994; English translation: Buhr & Dugas, 2002) includes 27 items relating to the idea that uncertainty is stressful and upsetting, uncertainty leads to the inability to act, uncertain events are negative and should be avoided, and being uncertain is unfair.
sentences.s61: Participants rate items on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = ‘‘not at all characteristic of me’’ to 5 = ‘‘entirely characteristic of me.’’ Examples of items include ‘‘Uncertainty makes me uneasy, anxious, or stressed’’ and ‘‘My mind can’t be relaxed if I don’t know what will happen tomorrow.’’ The IUS has excellent internal consistency (a = .94), and good test–retest reliability over a 5-week period (r = .74; Buhr & Dugas, 2002).
sentences.s62: Moreover, the convergent and divergent validity of the IUS has been supported by research assessing its relation to symptom measures of worry, depression, and anxiety (Buhr & Dugas, 2002; see Dugas et al., 2004, for a detailed review of the psychometric properties of the IUS).
sentences.s63: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 226 The Scale of Tolerance–Intolerance of Ambiguity (TIA; Budner, 1962) is one of the most common and widely used instruments for assessing intolerance of ambiguity (Furnham, 1994).
sentences.s64: The scale examines the tendency to perceive ambiguous situations as a source of threat and items refer to three features of ambiguity: novelty, complexity, and insolubility.
sentences.s65: Participants are asked to rate 16 items on a 6-point Likert scale ranging from 0 = ‘‘strongly disagree’’ to 5 = ‘‘strongly agree.’’ Examples of items include ‘‘A good job is one where what is to be done and how it is to be done are always clear’’ and ‘‘What we are used to is always preferable to what is unfamiliar.’’ The scale has good test–retest reliability over a 2-month period (r = .85), but only moderate internal consistency (a = .49–.59; Budner, 1962; Furnham, 1994).
sentences.s66: However, research suggests that the measure shows sufﬁcient evidence of validity, correlating with other measures of intolerance of ambiguity (r = .44–.57; Furnham, 1994) as well as measures of conventionality and authoritarianism (Budner, 1962).
sentences.s67: The Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ; Meyer, Miller, Metzger, & Borkovec, 1990) is the most widely used instrument for assessing the tendency to engage in excessive, uncontrollable, and generalized worry.
sentences.s68: Participants rate items on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = ‘‘not at all typical of me’’ to 5 = ‘‘very typical of me.’’ Examples of items include ‘‘My worries overwhelm me’’ and ‘‘Once I start worrying, I can’t stop.’’ Research has demonstrated that the PSWQ is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing trait worry (Brown, Antony, & Barlow, 1992; Davey, 1993; Meyer et al., 1990).
sentences.s69: More speciﬁcally, the PSWQ is a unifactorial measure with excellent internal consistency (a = .86–.95) and test–retest reliability (r = .74–.93; Molina & Borkovec, 1994).
sentences.s70: The questionnaire has been shown to have substantial convergent and divergent validity demonstrating greater correlations with measures of worry than with measures of anxiety and depression (Molina & Borkovec, 1994; see Turk, Heimberg, & Mennin, 2004, for a detailed review of the psychometric properties of the PSWQ).
sentences.s71: The Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (MPS; Hewitt & Flett, 1991) is a 45- item measure of personal characteristics and traits associated with perfectionism.
sentences.s72: Thiswidelyusedinstrumenthasthreesubscales:self-orientedperfectionism(SOP), which examines self-directed perfectionism; socially-prescribed perfectionism (SPP), which assesses the need to meet the expectations of others; and other- oriented perfectionism (OOP), which taps expectations about the capabilities of others.
sentences.s73: Participants rate items on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = ‘‘strongly disagree’’ to 7 = ‘‘strongly agree.’’ Items assessing self-oriented perfectionism include ‘‘When I work on something, I cannot relax until it is perfect.’’ Items examining socially-prescribed perfectionism include ‘‘The people around me expect me to succeed at everything I do.’’ Finally, other-oriented perfectionism is assessed through items such as ‘‘If I ask someone to do something, I expect it to be done ﬂawlessly.’’ The MPS has excellent internal consistency in a student sample (SOP: a = .89; SPP: a = .86; OOP: a = .79; Hewitt & Flett, 1991) and research supports the convergent and divergent validity of the MPS subscales (Hewitt & Flett, 1991; Hewitt, Flett, Turnbull-Donovan, & Mikail, 1991).
sentences.s74: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 227 The Sense of Control Scale (SC; Lachman & Weaver, 1998) is a 12-item questionnaire assessing an individual’s perceived sense of control.
sentences.s75: The SC has two subscales: personal mastery (PM), which reﬂects one’s personal sense of efﬁcacy in reaching goals; and perceived constraints (PC), which assesses one’s belief in obstacles beyond one’s control that may interfere with achieving goals.
sentences.s76: Participants rate each item on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = ‘‘disagree strongly’’ to 7 = ‘‘agree strongly.’’ Examples of items assessing personal mastery include ‘‘I can do just about anything I really set my mind to’’ and ‘‘What happens to me in the future mostly depends on me.’’ High scores are indicative of greater personal mastery.
sentences.s77: Items assessing perceived constraints include ‘‘Other people determine most of what I can do and cannot do’’ and ‘‘What happens in my life is often beyond my control.’’ High scores reﬂect greater perceived constraints.
sentences.s78: Factor analysis supports the two dimensions and the measure has high internal consistency (PM: a = .70; PC: a = .86; Lachman & Weaver, 1998).
sentences.s79: Moreover, perceived constraints have been shown to positively correlate with depressive symptoms and negatively correlate with measures of life satisfaction and perceived health, while the reverse is true for personal mastery (Lachman & Weaver, 1998). 1.3.
sentences.s80: Procedure Participants were asked to provide demographic information and complete the ﬁve questionnaires, which were randomly ordered.
sentences.s81: Testing was completed during one 30-min period and groups of approximately 60 participants were run on several separate occasions.
sentences.s82: Participants were informed that the purpose of the study was to assess the relationship between worry and constructs related to worry. 2.
sentences.s83: Preliminary data analyses Prior to carrying out the main statistical analyses, the data were screened to determine whether statistical assumptions were met and to ascertain whether the data were appropriate for further analyses (see Tabachnick & Fidell, 1996, for a review of data screening procedures).
sentences.s84: The assumption of normality, linearity, homogeneity of variance, as well as multicollinearity and singularity were met for all measures. 2.2.
