sentences.s110: Discussion As expected, intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of ambiguity were moderately associated with each other and signiﬁcantly related to worry.
sentences.s111: However, the relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and worry was signiﬁcantly stronger than the association between intolerance of ambiguity and worry, and this latter relationship became nonsigniﬁcant once intolerance of uncertainty was statistically controlled.
sentences.s112: This pattern of ﬁndings may be due to the underlying dimensions of these constructs.
sentences.s113: Speciﬁcally, the instruments used in the current study to measure intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of ambiguity (IUS: Freeston et al., 1994; TIA: Budner, 1962, respectively) share underlying factors that tap a general preference for predictability and certainty.
sentences.s114: These shared elements may explain the signiﬁcant relationship between these constructs and may also account for the signiﬁcant correlation between both of these constructs and worry.
sentences.s115: Conversely, the unique aspects of these constructs may be responsible for their differential relation to worry and their only moderate, albeit signiﬁcant, correlation with each other.
sentences.s116: In addition to a general preference for predictability, tolerance towards ambiguity also includes elements of variety, originality, clarity, and regularity (Budner, 1962; Furnham, 1994), which may be unrelated to worry.
sentences.s117: In contrast, the underlying dimensions of intolerance of uncertainty, which include negative emotional responses to uncertainty, the tendency for uncertainty to interfere with functioning, and the general belief that being uncertain is unfair (see Buhr & Dugas, 2002), may play a greater role in worry.
sentences.s118: These ﬁndings indicate that intolerance of uncertainty is a distinct construct in relation to intolerance of ambiguity and that intolerance of uncertainty is a more relevant construct in the understanding in worry.
sentences.s119: Despite signiﬁcant associations between worry and self-oriented and socially- prescribed perfectionism, the correlations were only modest, and worry K.
sentences.s120: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 231 maintained a signiﬁcantly stronger relationship with intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s121: These ﬁndings may stem from the underlying aspects of perfectionism.
sentences.s122: Hamachek (1978) postulated that perfectionism is composed of both adaptive and maladaptive components.
sentences.s123: Adaptive perfectionism can be differentiated from maladaptive perfectionism by the ability to derive pleasure from one’s efforts.
sentences.s124: Individuals with adaptive perfectionistic tendencies are more likely to be successful achievers who gain a sense of pleasure from reaching their goals, while individuals with maladaptive perfectionism are likely to be engaged in efforts to attain unrealistic goals and believe that the optimal level of perfectionism has not yet been met.
sentences.s125: These individuals may experience distress and concern regarding their attempts at unattainable perfectionism.
sentences.s126: Frost, Heimberg, Holt, Mattia, and Neubauer (1993) proposed that socially- prescribed perfectionism is a maladaptive or negative form of perfectionism, while self-oriented and other-oriented perfectionism appear to represent more positive or adaptive aspects of perfectionism.
sentences.s127: However, self-oriented perfection- ism is signiﬁcantly associated with other aspects of perfectionism, such as concern over mistakes, parental expectations, and doubts about one’s actions, which are considered to constitute the maladaptive form of perfectionism (Frost et al., 1993) and have been shown to be related to high levels worry (Sto¨ber & Joormann, 2001).
sentences.s128: In addition, socially-prescribed perfectionism has been shown to be signiﬁcantly related to personal standards, which is considered a positive form of perfectionism (Frost et al., 1993).
sentences.s129: It may be that the negative aspects of perfectionism are associated with high levels of worry, whereas the positive elements of perfectionism are not.
sentences.s130: Thus, the combined effects of the positive and negative aspects of self-oriented and socially-prescribed perfectionism may account for: (1) the limited, albeit signiﬁcant, correlations between these constructs and worry; and (2) the weaker association between these aspects of perfectionism and worry relative to the association between intolerance of uncertainty and worry.
sentences.s131: In contrast to perfectionism, intolerance of uncertainty is not adaptive and most aspects of it can be considered negative.
sentences.s132: By deﬁnition, individuals who are intolerant of uncertainty react in a negative manner to uncertain situations and events; furthermore, intolerance of uncertainty has consistently been linked to negative mood (e.g., Buhr & Dugas, 2002; Dugas, Gosselin, & Ladouceur, 2001; Freeston et al., 1994; Sexton, Norton, Walker, & Norton, 2003), which suggests that it is not an adaptive way of responding to one’s environment.
sentences.s133: In the present study, the relationship between worry and dimensions of perfectionism decreased substantially when the variance explained by intolerance of uncertainty was removed, which implies that intolerance of uncertainty may be accounting for a large part of the relationship between worry and perfectionism.
sentences.s134: Worriers may experience heightened levels of distress in situations in which there is no clear answer or ‘‘perfect’’solution as a function of the uncertain nature of the situation, rather than a desire for perfectionism, and they may worry regardless of whether things are perfect now because there is K.
sentences.s135: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 232 uncertainty about how things will be tomorrow and that uncertainty is likely to lead to distress.
sentences.s136: Although worry was also signiﬁcantly linked to perceived constraints, a dimension of perceived control, this relationship was substantially smaller than the association between intolerance of uncertainty and worry.
sentences.s137: People’s general attitudes about control may help explain the ﬁndings.
sentences.s138: For instance, individuals who perceive themselves as having minimal control over a situation may feel that their lack of control resolves them of responsibility for the outcome and consequently they feel little distress or concern about the resolution of the situation.
sentences.s139: Moreover, perceived control may be situation-speciﬁc to the extent that some individuals, in a particular situation, may feel a heightened sense of control and believe that they have the necessary skills and abilities to successfully impact their environment and as a result experience little or no anxiety or distress.
sentences.s140: Conversely, in a different situation, the same individuals may feel that they lack control and subsequently experience a heightened level of concern.
sentences.s141: Variations in level of perceived control, as a function of attitude or situation, may be responsible for the weaker correlation between control and worry compared to intolerance of uncertainty and worry.
sentences.s142: In contrast, the greater connection between intolerance of uncertainty and worry may be due to the fact that uncertainty is pervasive in everyday life.
sentences.s143: Most situations are not straightforward and contain some level of uncertainty; thus, someone who is intolerant of uncertainty will likely have negative reactions to uncertainty on a frequent basis.
sentences.s144: To a large extent, intolerance of uncertainty may also be accounting for the relationship between worry and perceived control as evidenced by the ﬁnding that when the contribution of intolerance of uncertainty was statistically removed, the association between perceived control and worry was no longer signiﬁcant.
sentences.s145: Thus, a lack of control may be related to worry in situations in which there is an elevated level of uncertainty.
sentences.s146: Finally, intolerance of uncertainty was uniquely related to worry, i.e., their relationship remained signiﬁcant when shared variance with intolerance of ambiguity, perfectionism, and perceived control was statistically removed.
sentences.s147: This last ﬁnding suggests that although intolerance of uncertainty overlaps to some extent with the other processes assessed in this study (in terms of their respective relationships with worry), it also offers something unique to our understanding of worry, which is not captured by constructs that have long been recognized to be related to worrying behavior.
sentences.s148: Together, these ﬁndings add to a growing body of literature suggesting that intolerance of uncertainty may play an important role in the etiology of worry.
sentences.s149: Although interesting ﬁndings have emerged from the present study, it is not without limitations.
sentences.s150: First, the majority of participants were female and previous research has shown that women tend to report higher levels of worry (see Stavosky & Borkovec, 1987).
sentences.s151: Results from the current study revealed signiﬁcant gender differences on measures of worry and self-oriented perfectionism.
sentences.s152: Although gender was statistically controlled, the discrepancy in the number of K.
sentences.s153: Buhr, M.J. Dugas / Anxiety Disorders 20 (2006) 222–236 233 male and female participants may have affected the results and should be considered when interpreting the ﬁndings.
sentences.s154: In addition, participants were composed of undergraduate students potentially limiting the generalizability of the ﬁndings.
sentences.s155: Future studies should strive to include a sample that incorporates an equal distribution of males and females from alternative populations.
sentences.s156: In addition, the choice of instruments may have impacted the results and the inclusion of alternative measures may have altered the ﬁndings.
sentences.s157: For example, there are numerous instruments available for assessing tolerance towards ambiguity and including a measure more closely resembling intolerance of uncertainty may have led to different ﬁndings.
sentences.s158: However, Furnham (1994) evaluated the most widely used measures of tolerance towards ambiguity and suggested that these alternative measures contain only a limited number of factors consistent with the underlying dimensions of intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s159: Similarly, the current study focused speciﬁcally on a self-report measure of perceived control, rather than on other processes and behaviors related to control.
sentences.s160: Individuals may engage in speciﬁc behaviors aimed at exerting control over the environment, despite reporting low levels of personal control.
sentences.s161: Thus, perceived control may not be an ideal indicator of actual control; however, perceptions of control, regardless of actual control or control related-behaviors, are more likely to be related to worry.
sentences.s162: In summary, the ﬁndings provide further evidence of the construct validity of intolerance of uncertainty and suggest that it makes a unique contribution to the understanding of worry.
sentences.s163: Future research should focus on understanding the exact mechanisms underlying intolerance of uncertainty and endeavor to delineate its speciﬁc role in the etiology of excessive worry and GAD.

sentences.s1: Norton b, Gordon J.G. Asmundson a a Anxiety and Illness Behaviours Laboratory, University of Regina, Regina, Sask., Canada S4S 0A2 b Department of Psychology, University of Houston, Houston, TX, United States Received 6 October 2005; received in revised form 9 March 2006; accepted 27 March 2006 Abstract Intolerance of uncertainty is the tendency of an individual to consider the possibility of a negative event occurring unacceptable, irrespective of the probability of occurrence.
sentences.s2: It is a key component of worry, state anxiety, and related anxiety pathologies.
sentences.s3: The 27-item Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS) was developed to measure intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s4: Previous psychometric analyses of the IUS have suggested both four- and ﬁve-factor models.
sentences.s5: High inter-item correlations, factor instability, and previous theoretical research support the development of a reduced measure.
sentences.s6: The present study used two undergraduate samples and evaluated a psychometrically stable 12-item two-factor version of the IUS.
sentences.s7: The reduced measure (IUS-12) retained exemplary internal consistency, while correlating extremely well with the original IUS and related measures of anxiety and worry.
sentences.s8: The IUS-12 also demonstrated a stable two-factor structure, representing both anxious and avoidance components of intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s9: Keywords: Intolerance of uncertainty; IUS; Anxiety; Avoidance; Worry 1.
sentences.s10: Introduction Fear is a protective response to a current, identiﬁable threat (e.g., being attacked by a harmful animal) and is typically accompanied by a ﬁght or ﬂight response having a strong physiological reaction (e.g., blood pressure increase, muscle tension, startle response) (Barlow, 2002; McNeil & Vowles, 2004).
sentences.s11: In contrast, anxiety is a response to a potential threat that may or may not occur at some point in the future (e.g., a harmful animal might attack, somewhere, sometime) and is Journal of Anxiety Disorders 21 (2007) 105–117 * Corresponding author.
sentences.s13: Worrying can be interpreted as ruminating about the possibility of a negative occurrence (e.g., another attack), thereby maintaining a heightened level of anxiety (Dugas, Gosselin, & Ladoucer, 2001).
sentences.s14: These ruminations are validated and supported because the possibility of re-exposure to the fearful stimulus is not zero (e.g., the harmful animal, or similar ones, continue to exist in the same environment as the worrier) (Dugas et al., 2001).
sentences.s15: Therefore, how tolerant a person is of uncertainty surrounding the possibility of re-exposure will impact how often they worry (Laugesen, Dugas, & Bukowski, 2003) and therein their anxiety (Greco & Roger, 2001, 2003).
sentences.s16: Intolerance of uncertainty has been identiﬁed as a discriminating individual difference characteristic involved in excessive worry (Laugesen et al., 2003), state anxiety (Greco & Roger, 2001), and to have strong positive associations with anxiety pathologies such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD), and Panic Disorder (Dugas, Gagnon, Ladouceur, & Freeston, 1998; Dugas et al., 2001; Tolin, Abramowitz, Brigidi, & Foa, 2003).
sentences.s17: It is intolerance of the notion that negative events may occur and there is no deﬁnitive way of predicting such events.
sentences.s18: Indeed, people who are intolerant of uncertainty are likely to interpret all ambiguous information as threatening (Heydayati, Dugas, Buhr, & Francis, 2003), contributing to signiﬁcant somatic stress reactions (e.g., increased heart rate and blood pressure; Greco & Roger, 2001, 2003).
sentences.s19: Furthermore, high intolerance of uncertainty may impair problem- solving skills, leading to inaction and avoidance of ambiguous situations (Dugas, Freeston, & Ladoucer, 1997).
sentences.s20: The Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS; Freeston, Rhe´aume, Letarte, Dugas, & Ladouceur, 1994) is one of several scales developed to measure intolerance of uncertainty, which is conceptually linked to ambiguity (Greco & Roger, 2001).
sentences.s21: Popular alterative measures are either longer than the IUS (e.g., Uncertainty Response Scale, Greco & Roger, 2001) or suffer from poor internal reliability and convergent validity (e.g., Intolerance of Ambiguity Scale, Budner, 1962; Tolerance of Ambiguity Scale, Kirton, 1981).
sentences.s22: The original IUS was developed (in French) to assess reactions to ambiguous situations, uncertainty, and future events (Freeston et al., 1994).
sentences.s23: The items were derived from a larger list of statements that had irrelevant or redundant items removed using rational relatedness followed by discriminant and correlational validations.
sentences.s24: Assuming the possibility that intolerance of uncertainty might be a multidimensional construct, an exploratory factor analysis was performed with an unspeciﬁed rotation and Cattell’s (1966) scree test to determine the number of factors to retain.
sentences.s25: The ﬁnal scale consisted of 27 items representing ﬁve different factors; however, one item of the 27 was hyperplanar (i.e., did not load signiﬁcantly on any factor) and four items cross- loaded (i.e., loaded onto more than one factor).
sentences.s26: The ﬁve factors were the Unacceptability and Avoidance of Uncertainty (nine items), Negative Social Evaluation Caused by Uncertainty (nine items), Uncertainty-Related Frustration (three items), Uncertainty Causes Stress (four items), and Uncertainty Preventing Action (two items; Freeston et al., 1994).1 Each item was rated on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all characteristic of me) to 5 (entirely characteristic of me).

sentences.s89: Measures The Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI; Beck et al., 1961, 1988).
sentences.s90: The BAI is a 21-item self-report measure designed as a general measure of anxiety symptom severity (Beck et al., 1988).
sentences.s91: The psychometric properties of BAI for non-clinical populations have been well established (see Creamer, Foran, & Bell, 1995).

sentences.s93: The BDI-II is a 21-item measure intended to assess the somatic, cognitive and affective domains of depression.
sentences.s94: The BDI-II has well-established reliability and validity (Dozois, Dobson, & Ahnberg, 1998).
sentences.s95: The Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (Buhr & Dugas, 2002; Freeston et al., 1994).
sentences.s96: This 27- item scale assesses reactions to uncertainty, ambiguous situations, and the future.
sentences.s97: Items are scored on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all characteristic of me) to 5 (entirely characteristic of me), yielding possible scores from 27 to 135.
sentences.s98: Despite the reported multifactor structures, the IUS is most commonly summed as a total scale score (Antony, Orsillo, & Roemer, 2001).

sentences.s102: Sensitivity, speciﬁcity, reliability, and both convergent and discriminant validity of the GADQ-IV has been established (Newman et al., 2002).

sentences.s110: Conﬁrmatory factor analysis Conﬁrmatory factor analyses were conducted to assess the degree to which unitary, four-, and ﬁve-factor structures of the IUS ﬁt the Regina data set.
sentences.s111: These analyses were performed using R.N. Carleton et al. / Journal of Anxiety Disorders 21 (2007) 105–117 109 LISREL 8.3 (Jo¨reskog & So¨rbom, 1999), and followed the procedures outlined by Jo¨reskog and So¨rbom (1996).
sentences.s112: The raw data were used as input, along with a maximum likelihood estimation procedure with the covariance matrix.
sentences.s113: Item loadings for the four- and ﬁve-factor structures were based on the recommendations from Buhr and Dugas (2002) and Freeston et al. (1994), respectively.
sentences.s114: Following recommendations by Hu and Bentler (1999), model ﬁt was determined using several indices: (1) x2/df ratio (values should be <2.0), (2) Comparative Fit Index (CFI; values should be >0.95), (3) Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA; values should be <0.06), (4) the Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR; values should be <0.08) (see also Browne & Cudeck, 1993; Marsh, Balla, & McDonald, 1988), and (5) Expected Cross- Validation Index (ECVI; lower values indicate increasingly better ﬁt; Browne & Cudeck, 1989, 1993).
sentences.s115: Because x2 statistics are inﬂated in larger samples, emphasis is placed on the latter ﬁt indices (Hu & Bentler, 1999).
sentences.s116: The initial CFA results of the tested structures (i.e., unitary, four, and ﬁve factors) with the Regina sample did not indicate adequate ﬁt with the data.
sentences.s117: Further, comparisons of the three structures were inconclusive because of similarity between the ﬁt indices of the solutions (see Table 2).
sentences.s118: However, the unitary solution presented the worst ﬁt, suggesting it to be least likely.
sentences.s119: All factor loadings, residual terms, and latent factor variances were statistically signiﬁcant (P <.01).
sentences.s120: High numbers of cross-loading items in the four- and ﬁve-factor solutions (six in the four-factor solutions, nine in the ﬁve-factor solutions), along with a high Cronbach’s a (a = .96), supported Buhr and Dugas’ (2002) suggestion that ﬁve factors may be inappropriate and Norton’s (2005) suggestion that a more efﬁcient version that still meets minimum criteria for reliability is possible.
sentences.s121: Interestingly, both the Buhr and Dugas (2002; four-factor) model and the Freeston et al. (1994; ﬁve-factor) model had one factor for which the loaded items were shared between all but one of the factors in the other model.

sentences.s168: Discussion This study had two main goals.
sentences.s169: The ﬁrst goal was to perform the ﬁrst CFA of the English version of the IUS, comparing the unitary, four-, and ﬁve-factor models.
sentences.s170: The results of the CFA indicated that none of these models appropriately ﬁt the data.
sentences.s171: Furthermore, the comparison did not result in any one model being superior.
sentences.s172: This pattern of ﬁndings did, however, lend support to the notion of revising the measure as recommended by Norton (2005), which was the second goal of this study.
sentences.s173: Using one factor from each of the earlier multi-factorial models a 17-item reduced scale was created.

sentences.s187: The reduced scale (IUS-12) maintained exemplary internal consistency, was highly correlated with the 27-item version, and based on principle of parsimony was accepted over the 17-item version.
sentences.s188: Following the reduction process, a CFA using an independent sample for replication and cross-validation of the postulated 12-item, two-factor structure of the IUS-12 was conducted.
sentences.s189: The results supported the postulated model, and the two factors were named Prospective Anxiety and Inhibitory Anxiety.
sentences.s190: The internal consistency of each of the factors was acceptable and the two remained moderately correlated, as expected when measuring two aspects of one latent variable.
sentences.s191: Collectively these ﬁndings provide convincing support for use of the IUS-12 as an efﬁcient, psychometrically-sound tool for measuring intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s192: This shorter IUS should also encourage a broader evaluation of intolerance of uncertainty in both clinical and non-clinical populations.
sentences.s193: Intolerance of uncertainty, being fundamental to worry (Laugesen et al., 2003), state anxiety (Greco & Roger, 2001), and related anxiety pathologies (Tolin et al., 2003), may play an as-of-yet unexplored but substantial role in several anxiety disorders.
sentences.s194: The clinical and theoretical utility of the statistically signiﬁcant variance beyond depression and anxiety accounted for by the IUS-12 in the measures of worry remains to be assessed.
sentences.s195: Although the additional variance was small, future models of anxiety constructs can test whether intolerance of uncertainty is a core component of anxiety disorders in general, similar to the growing research investigating various fears as vulnerability factors in diathesis-stress models of psychopathology.
sentences.s196: For example, recent research has suggested that a variety of cognitive vulnerability factors contribute to the development of pathologies such as PTSD and chronic pain (e.g., Asmundson, 1999; Asmundson, Coons, Taylor, & Katz, 2002; Keane & Barlow, 2002).
sentences.s197: Anxiety sensitivity – the tendency to catastrophically misinterpret physical sensations related to anxiety (e.g., rapid heart rate, shaky hands) as being threatening (Peterson & Reiss, 1992) – is a cognitive vulnerability that may have a signiﬁcant relationship with intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s198: Ambiguity or uncertainty itself can be considered threatening (Epstein, 1972), provoking anxiety, and further enhancing the perceived threat of a stimulus or situation (e.g., Hadjistavropoulos, Craig, & Hadjistavropoulos, 1997; Heydayati et al., 2003; Hock & Krohne, 2004; Mogg et al., 1994).
sentences.s199: Uncertainty regarding a stimulus opens a person to a variety of potential interpretations and responses (Lazarus, 1991), including catastrophic appraisal.
sentences.s200: A person with high anxiety sensitivity may be uncertain whether a heart palpitation is a nondescript anomaly or a precursor to a heart attack.
sentences.s201: If the person was certain the palpitation was not threatening, that certainty might alleviate or completely ameliorate associated anxiety and fear.
sentences.s202: Therefore, intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety sensitivity may have a hierarchical or mediational relationship; however, this remains to be explored.
sentences.s203: The IUS-12 facilitates such explorations by eliminating difﬁculties with the length and unstable psychometric properties of the original IUS (Buhr & Dugas, 2002; Freeston et al., 1994; Norton, 2005).
sentences.s204: In spite of the positive implications this work has for anxiety research, there are some limitations that provide avenues for future evaluation of the IUS-12.
sentences.s205: First, it could be argued that the positive keying of all items in both the IUS and the IUS-12 precludes the opportunity to provide scales that are balanced in their keying direction.
sentences.s206: However, with fewer items there is less opportunity for an unintentional response bias that could be corrected by negatively keying some items.
sentences.s207: Regarding intentional response biases, it was thought premature to suggest both item reduction and re-keying simultaneously, particularly given the evidence that reverse-wording can R.N. Carleton et al. / Journal of Anxiety Disorders 21 (2007) 105–117 114 create undesirable methodological factors (see Marsh, 1996; Rodebaugh et al., 2004; Spector, Van Katwyk, Brannick, & Chen, 1997).
sentences.s208: Second, the persistent use of undergraduate samples in the design and revision of the IUS makes establishing psychometric validity for clinical populations an important next step for research into intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s209: Until then, the use of the IUS-12 in clinical populations warrants caution.
sentences.s210: Third, discriminant and clinical validity of the IUS-12 remain to be tested, as do psychometric properties for different racial groups and languages for which it might be translated.
sentences.s211: Future research should include additional measures of anxiety disorders and anxiety-related constructs (e.g., GAD, OCD, panic disorder).
sentences.s212: Dugas et al. (2001) began such work by associating panic sensations and anxiety sensitivity with intolerance of uncertainty using the original IUS.
sentences.s213: Given the reasonable prospect that intolerance of uncertainty may have overlap with anxiety sensitivity, it may also overlap with other related fears such as illness/injury sensitivity and fear of negative evaluation (Carleton, Asmundson, & Taylor, 2005; Taylor, 1993), which could be included in future investigations.
sentences.s214: The theoretical association between an inability to cope with ambiguity or uncertainty and the development or maintenance of an anxiety disorder may be demonstrable with the IUS-12.
sentences.s215: This is an avenue of future investigation that may result in further delineation of fundamental dimensions and underlying mechanisms of the anxiety disorders; thereby improving assessment and treatment efforts for these potentially chronic and debilitating conditions.

sentences.s2: Nicholas Carleton ∗ University of Regina, Regina, Saskatchewan, Canada a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 17 September 2015 Received in revised form 12 February 2016 Accepted 16 February 2016 Available online 27 February 2016 Keywords: Fear of the unknown Intolerance of uncertainty Anxiety Neuroticism Temperament Emotion a b s t r a c t The current review and synthesis serves to deﬁne and contextualize fear of the unknown relative to related constructs, such as intolerance of uncertainty, and contemporary models of emotion, attachment, and neuroticism.

10.1016/j.janxdis.2016.03.011.printed_title: Fear of the unknown: One fear to rule them all?

sentences.s1: Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Anxiety Disorders Fear of the unknown: One fear to rule them all?
sentences.s2: Nicholas Carleton Anxiety and Illness Behaviours Laboratory, Department of Psychology, University of Regina, Regina, SK, Canada a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 17 February 2016 Received in revised form 26 March 2016 Accepted 26 March 2016 Available online 29 March 2016 Keywords: Fear of the unknown Intolerance of uncertainty Anxiety Neuroticism Fundamental fears a b s t r a c t The current review and synthesis was designed to provocatively develop and evaluate the proposition that “fear of the unknown may be a, or possibly the, fundamental fear” (Carleton, 2016) underlying anxiety and therein neuroticism.
sentences.s3: Identifying fundamental transdiagnostic elements is a priority for clinical theory and practice.
sentences.s4: Historical criteria for identifying fundamental components of anxiety are described and revised criteria are offered.
sentences.s5: The revised criteria are based on logical rhetorical arguments using a constituent reductionist postpositivist approach supported by the available empirical data.
sentences.s6: The revised criteria are then used to assess several fears posited as fundamental, including fear of the unknown.
sentences.s7: The review and synthesis concludes with brief recommendations for future theoretical discourse as well as clinical and non-clinical research. © 2016 The Author.

sentences.s10: Introduction One fear to rule them all, one fear to ﬁnd them, one fear to bring them all and in the black box bind them.
sentences.s11: The pastiche of Tolkien’s text (1954) represents an ideal place to begin a review and synthe- sis designed to provocatively develop and evaluate the proposition that “fear of the unknown may be a, or possibly the, fundamental fear” underlying anxiety and therein neuroticism (Carleton, 2016; p. 39).
sentences.s12: Fear of the unknown (FOTU) will be deﬁned herein as, “an individual’s propensity to experience fear caused by the perceived absence of information at any level of consciousness or point of pro- cessing”; relatedly, intolerance of uncertainty (IU) will be deﬁned as, “an individual’s dispositional incapacity to endure the aver- sive response triggered by the perceived absence of salient, key, or sufﬁcient information, and sustained by the associated percep- tion of uncertainty.” (Carleton, 2016; p. 31).
sentences.s13: The paper begins with a brief historical overview of anxiety determinants and hierarchical models for anxiety and fear.
sentences.s14: The original criteria for fundamental fears are presented as foundations for contemporary revisions.
sentences.s15: The revised criteria are then used to assess several fears posited as fun- damental, including fear of the unknown.
sentences.s16: The paper concludes with brief recommendations for future theoretical discourse as well as clinical and non-clinical research.

sentences.s18: Determining anxiety Psychologists have sought fundamental determinants of cog- nitions, behaviours, personalities, and pathologies since Wundt.
sentences.s19: Contemporary textbooks describe psychology as a science dedi- cated to understanding the multiple determinants of cognitions, behaviours, and emotions (e.g., Gerrig, Zimbardo, Desmarais, & Ivanco, 2011; Lilienfeld et al., 2015).
sentences.s20: Many psychologists rely on a constituent reductionist postpositivist philosophy of science in such efforts; oversimpliﬁed, the approach identiﬁes increasingly fundamental components of a construct (i.e., constituent reduc- tionism), without ignoring the emergent properties, and while accepting an underlying reality that can be measured or understood by progressive but imperfect approximations (i.e., postpositivism).
sentences.s21: Identifying fundamental components has broadly beneﬁted many scientiﬁc ﬁelds (e.g., chemistry, biology, physics).
sentences.s22: Such practices ﬁt well with structuralism and functionalism (Munger, 2003), and Gestalt researchers acknowledge progressive reductionism as ben- eﬁcial, caveating costs to understanding complex whole systems (Humphrey, 1924a, 1924b).
sentences.s23: Accordingly, many psychologists have applied similar practices to understanding and modifying cogni- tions, emotions, and behaviours.
sentences.s24: Theorists from Freud (Breuer & Freud, 1974; Freud, 1924), to Spielberger (1975), to Barlow (2000, 2002), have suggested individ- ual differences make some people more likely to experience fear or anxiety.
sentences.s25: The tendency to respond with fear or to experience perva- sive anxiety was called neuroticism by Freud and trait anxiety by Spielberger.
sentences.s26: Spielberger (1972) described anxiety as “psychobio- logical” (p.489) and “extremely complex and involve[ing] a number of different measurable components” (Spielberger, 1975; p. 139). http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.janxdis.2016.03.011 0887-6185/© 2016 The Author.

sentences.s29: He posited an interaction between exposure to stressors, appraisals of stressors (in line with Scherer, 2009), and a recursive interac- tivity between experiences of state and trait anxiety (in line with Scherer & Brosch, 2009).
sentences.s30: Spielberger (1975) further suggested com- ponents of anxiety “should be independently conceptualized and operationally measured as critical variables in a state-trait theory of anxiety” (p. 139).
sentences.s31: In other words, anxiety was not fundamental1 unto itself, and Spielberger underscored the differentiation of state and trait anxiety was only the beginning of understanding anxiety.
sentences.s32: Theorists have since supported a constituent reductionist post- positivist approach to understanding trait anxiety (Barlow, Ellard, Sauer-Zavala, Bullis, & Carl, 2014; Barlow, Sauer-Zavala, Carl, Bullis, & Ellard, 2014; Brown & Barlow, 2009; Cuijpers et al., 2010; Lahey, 2009), particularly when used synonymously with constructs like neuroticism (Ormel, Rosmalen, & Farmer, 2004).
sentences.s33: Such synonymous usage has led prominent theorists to argue the functional equiva- lency of several constructs related to trait anxiety.
sentences.s34: For example, Kagan and Snidman (2004) clarify that inhibited and uninhibited to the unfamiliar temperament categories refer to introverted and extraverted, respectively.
sentences.s35: Barlow and colleagues (Barlow, Sauer- Zavala et al., 2014) argue the same two categories respectively refer to trait anxiety and negative affect, as well as positive affect.
sentences.s36: Clark and Beck (2010) argued trait anxiety is “. . .so closely related to negative emotionality (i.e., Neuroticism or Negative Affect) that the two are considered almost synonymous” (p.104).
sentences.s37: If (1) neu- roticism by any name is a higher-order biopsychosocial construct that is facilitated by fear of potentially recurring aversive experi- ences (Barlow, 2000); (2) fear is distinguished from anxiety by being present-oriented and relatively certain, rather than future-oriented and relatively uncertain (Barlow, 2000); (3) proliﬁc anxiety deﬁnes neuroticism (Barlow, Sauer-Zavala et al., 2014); and (4) fear “is the basic cognitive process underlying all anxiety disorders” (Clark & Beck, 2010, p. 29), then a hierarchical structure identifying increas- ingly fundamental fears offers several potential advantages; for example, informing and being informed by psychological theories of evolution, emotion, cognition, development, personality, and decision-making. 2.
sentences.s38: Hierarchical models of fears Initial hierarchical models for neuroticism, fears, and phobias were based on evidence from researching learning.
sentences.s39: That evidence underscored neuroticism as learned and, therein, governed by the laws of learning (Eysenck, 1966).
sentences.s40: Following that premise, Rachman (1977) posited a fear acquisition model that implicated conditioning, vicarious exposure (i.e., observational learning), and information transmission (i.e., didactics), which accumulated sig- niﬁcant support (e.g., Muris, Merckelbach, de Jong, & Ollendick, 2002; Rachman, 1991).
sentences.s41: Contemporary fear acquisition models (see for review, Armﬁeld, 2006; Coelho & Purkis, 2009; Mallan, Lipp, & Cochrane, 2013) assume cognitive or emotional factors underlie fear responses (Coelho & Purkis, 2009); however, interactions between naturally selected predispositions and environmental variables remain crit- ical for fear acquisition (Coelho & Purkis, 2009; p. 343).
sentences.s42: In line with contemporary appraisal models of emotion (Moors, 2009), there may be evolutionarily-supported fears prepared or inherited (i.e., requiring little or no learning) based on biological substrates.
sentences.s43: Those fears, in conjunction with environmental inﬂuences (e.g., direct or indirect learning), might explain all fear acquisition and, therein, neuroticism.
sentences.s44: That said, arguments for cohesive sets of stim- uli as biologically prepared (e.g., snakes, spiders) are supported by 1 “serving as, or being an essential part of, a foundation or basis; basic; underlying” (“fundamental,” n.d.). some evidence (e.g., Cook & Mineka, 1989; Ohman & Mineka, 2001; Poulton & Menzies, 2002b; Waters, Lipp, & Randhawa, 2011), but confounded by others.
sentences.s45: Certain fears, such as the fear of spiders, are frequently referred to as “biologically prepared.” However, only approximately 200 species of spiders worldwide can cause severe human envenom- ing, out of the more than 30,000 species of spiders (Diaz, 2004).
sentences.s46: The contrary is true of mushrooms, which are usually viewed as not biologically relevant to fear.
sentences.s47: Nevertheless, some mush- rooms, such as the Amanita phalloides, are one of the toxic agents most responsible for fatal cases in Poland (Kotwica & Czerczak, 2007), and unintentional poisoning with plants is common in small children (Eddleston & Persson, 2003).

(Coelho & Purkis, 2009, p. 342) The challenge may be partially resolved by considering whether the cohesive stimuli sets are biologically prepared, or the elements therein.
sentences.s49: Fear of snakes has been argued as innate for primates (e.g., Hebb, 1949); however, 6-month-old infants show no fear of snakes because the fear has not yet been learned (Kagan & Snidman, 2004); in contrast, 4-month-old infants broadly demonstrate fear responses to unfamiliar stimuli (Kagan & Snidman, 2004).
sentences.s50: Snakes may become more likely to produce fear because, relative to other more frequently encountered stimuli, snakes have unfamiliar skin, body shape, and movement patterns (Kagan & Snidman, 2004), all of which speaks more to a biological preparedness for unknowns (Carleton, 2016), or other elements of the stimulus, than to the cohesive stimulus itself.
sentences.s51: There are also more unknowns associ- ated with encountering a snake than a mushroom, not the least of which being the snake moves quickly whereas the mushroom does not–a potentially critical element underscored in looming models (Riskind, 1997).
sentences.s52: Recent research comparing responses to snakes and ﬂowers demonstrated that novelty (i.e., the unknown; Carleton, 2016) was the key element for activation of the amygdala, with no evi- dence of a novelty by stimulus interaction (Balderston, Schultz, & Helmstetter, 2013); however, neurological responses subsequent to the amygdala (e.g., hippocampal responses) did evidence per- ception of the snake as more threatening.
sentences.s53: As such, appraisals of associated cues–knowns and unknowns–can dramatically inﬂu- ence fear (Carleton, 2016).
sentences.s54: For example, a planned encounter with a snake secured behind glass might be less fear provoking than being told your meal contains mushrooms of ambiguous origin.
sentences.s55: Similarly, as recently synthesized by Carleton (2016), theorists have argued that appraised elements, context, and the relative number of unknowns, may be the critical determinants of an emotional response.
sentences.s56: For example, what is it that water phobic individuals react to?
sentences.s57: Clearly it is not water per se as they likely seek water to drink, to bathe in, and to nourish their plants.
sentences.s58: If so, how deep is deep enough?
sentences.s59: Or is it water in which they might drown, or in which they might not be able to negotiate their way to safety?
sentences.s60: These later two possibilities sound rather like cognitive processes at work.
sentences.s61: At least for adults, it appears that such reac- tions are somehow bound up with perception and cognition of certain stimulus elements. (Kleinknecht, 2002; p. 162) Contemporary fear acquisition models argue fear and anxiety involves context, appraisal, learning, scaffolding, or generalization of stimuli and responses (Coelho & Purkis, 2009); nevertheless, since Spielberger (1972) and Rachman (1977), fears described as effectively unconditioned have been posited and referred to as basic, evolutionarily-supported, fundamental, inherent, innate, non-associative, predisposed, or prepared.
sentences.s62: There is evidence sup- porting such fears (Poulton & Menzies, 2002b) as congruent with learning models (Poulton & Menzies, 2002a).
sentences.s63: There are theorists who argue that unequivocal and deﬁnitive evidence for any fear as unlearned is impossible (e.g., Muris et al., 2002; Rachman, 1991); however, others argue for nearly innate fears (e.g., Mineka & Ohman, 2002), and still others argue that models of emotion and anxiety explicitly posit at least one category of stimuli, the unknown, as innately facilitating a fear response (see for review, Carleton, 2016). 3.
sentences.s64: The original fundamental fears In 1991, Reiss explicated a logical, constituent reductionist, post positivist method for identifying key cognitive elements of anxiety, which he called fundamental fears.
sentences.s65: Reiss (1991) used a variant of the downward arrow technique to argue: Fundamental fears provide reasons for fearing a wide range of stimuli, whereas ordinary fears do not have this characteristic.
sentences.s66: For example, consider the rational relationships among three different fears: (a) the fear of snakes; (b) the fear of heights; and (c) the fear of anxiety.
sentences.s67: Fears of snakes and heights are ratio- nally unrelated to one another in the sense that having one of the fears is not a reason for having the other fear.
sentences.s68: It makes no sense for a person to say, “I am afraid of heights because I am afraid of snakes.” On the other hand, the fear of anxiety is ratio- nally related to the fear of snakes and heights.
sentences.s69: A rational person might say, “I am afraid of snakes and heights because I am afraid I would have a panic attack if I encountered those stimuli.” A person who is unusually afraid of (or sensitive to) the possibil- ity of a panic attack holds a reason for potentially fearing snakes, heights, or any other situation that might be expected to lead to panic. (Reiss, 1991, p. 147) Reiss’ revised theor (Reiss, 1997) posited a hierarchical structure that placed anxiety sensitivity (AS), the fear of negative evaluation (FNE), and the fear of injury – later labelled illness/injury sensitivity (IIS; Taylor, 1993) – as fundamental2 elements underlying all fears and therein neuroticism.
sentences.s70: AS, the propensity to catastrophically appraise the symptoms or sensations related to anxiety (e.g., palpitations, trembling), describes fearing potential consequences associated with anxiety sensations (Taylor, 1999), and several symptom proﬁle mod- els incorporate AS as critical (Olatunji, Broman-Fulks, Bergman, Green, & Zlomke, 2010).
sentences.s71: FNE describes fearing negative evalua- tions (Heimberg, Brozovich, & Rapee, 2010; Leary, 1983) and is a hallmark of social anxiety (Heimberg et al., 2010).
sentences.s72: IIS describes fearing physical harm and the associated consequences (Carleton, Asmundson, & Taylor, 2005; Reiss, Peterson, Gursky, & McNally, 1986; Taylor, 1993).
sentences.s73: IIS relates to speciﬁc phobias (e.g., spiders; Page, 1994), pain-related anxiety (Vancleef, Peters, Roelofs, & Asmundson, 2006), chronic pain (Thibodeau, Fetzner, Carleton, Kachur, & Asmundson, 2013; Verbunt et al., 2003), and disability (Carleton, Abrams, Kachur, & Asmundson, 2009, Carleton, Abrams, Kachur, & Asmundson, 2010).
sentences.s74: Reiss’ (1991) approach to identifying fundamental fears was summarized by Taylor (1993): “Reiss (1991), and personal com- munication, June 1991) used two criteria to deﬁne these fears as fundamental; (1) they are fears of inherently noxious [aversive] 2 Paralleling Spielberger’s (1972) use of the term fundamental. stimuli, and (2) other, ‘common’ fears can be logically reduced to them” (p. 289).
sentences.s75: Taylor implied fundamental fears cannot require a priori learning (i.e., an unconditioned stimulus and an uncon- ditioned response), should underlie more “common” fears and anxieties, and should not be rationally related to other fears (Taylor, 1993).
sentences.s76: Neither inherent3 nor noxious4 were deﬁned by Reiss (1991) or Taylor (1993), implying the dictionary deﬁnitions, and Reiss (1991) argued AS, FNE, and IIS were inherent.
sentences.s77: Accordingly, neuroti- cism would result from learned fears facilitated by inherent AS, FNE, and IIS.
sentences.s78: The supposition accords with notions that “neuroticism is not an explanatory concept in the aetiology of psychopathology, since it measures a person’s characteristic level of distress over a protracted period of time” (Ormel et al., 2004; p. 906), as well as Clark and Beck’s (2010) notions that “fear, then, is the basic cognitive process underlying all anxiety disorders” (p. 29).
sentences.s79: Each of AS, FNE, and IIS appears at least partially distinct from each other (e.g., Carleton, Thibodeau, Osborne, Taylor, & Asmundson, 2014; Taylor, 1993) and neuroticism (e.g., Cornwell, Johnson, Berardi, & Grillon, 2006; Muris, Vlaeyen, & Meesters, 2001; Thibodeau, Carleton, Collimore, & Asmundson, 2012; Vancleef et al., 2006); however, the intercorrelations range from 0.24 to 0.76, indi- cating important shared variance (e.g., Carleton, Thibodeau et al., 2014; Thibodeau et al., 2012).
sentences.s80: Each has also demonstrated theo- retical and predictive utility beyond neuroticism for common fears (Heimberg et al., 2010; Olatunji et al., 2010; Thibodeau, Fetzner et al., 2013).
sentences.s81: More importantly, reductions in one (e.g., AS), can reduce common fears (Boswell, Thompson-Hollands, Farchione, & Barlow, 2013), even when related more to another fundamen- tal fear.
sentences.s82: For example, interoceptive exposure reduces AS, but also social anxiety (Collimore & Asmundson, 2014; Dixon, Kemp, Farrell, Blakey, & Deacon, 2015), which appears more related to FNE (Heimberg et al., 2010). 4.
sentences.s83: Revisiting the criteria for fundamental fears The criteria introduced by Reiss (1991) and Taylor (1993) pro- vide a solid foundation for identifying fundamental fears that can be expanded in at least two ways.
sentences.s84: First, by integrating requirements from contemporary emotion theories (Mulligan & Scherer, 2012).
sentences.s85: Second, by integrating subsequent criteria proffered for identify- ing fundamental fears or elements in psychological constructs as identiﬁed from a brief literature review.
sentences.s86: The review was not intended to be exhaustive and comprehen- sive.
sentences.s87: Instead, English articles in Thomson Reuters’ Web of Science Core Collection database that referenced Taylor (1993), 55 in total, were reviewed for critiques or revisions to the criteria; however, none were identiﬁed.
sentences.s88: The same database was searched for English psychology or psychiatry articles titled with the phrase innate fear or non-associated fear, which have also been used to describe fundamental fears.
sentences.s89: The result was 35 articles, one of which ref- erenced Poulton and Menzies (2002a,b) criteria for such fears.
sentences.s90: Poulton and Menzies’ article had been cited 20 times, none of which proffered revisions to their criteria.
sentences.s91: The same database was searched for the term “fundamental” as a title in English psy- chology or psychiatry review articles published since 1993.
sentences.s92: Among those, one article provided a set of criteria for identifying fundamental elements of a psychological construct (i.e., Anderson, Hildreth, & Howland, 2015), which was based on a second article from the same result set (Baumeister &Leary, 1995).
