sentences.s96: Accord- ingly, increasingly fundamental (i.e., lower-order) fears should be as follows, with examples of supporting evidence in Table 1. 4.1.
sentences.s97: Criterion One Fundamental fears should be emotions.
sentences.s98: Following Mulligan and Scherer’s (2012) deﬁnition, a fundamental fear is (1) time limited, (2) triggered by at least one appraisal, (3) guided by at least one appraisal, (4) contains bodily changes (e.g., arousal) that are felt, and (5) involves a perceptual or intellectual episode.
sentences.s99: A percept in and of itself is not an emotion; therefore, sensations (e.g., noci- ception) and reﬂexes (e.g., startle) are not emotions (Leventhal & Scherer, 1987; Moors, 2009); however, a stimulus (perceived pre- consciously or consciously), sensation, or reﬂex that results in an inherent appraisal that triggers an emotion of fear (Mulligan & Scherer, 2012) would meet Criterion One.
sentences.s100: Emotions are experi- enced on continua of intensities (e.g., Fox, 2008; Lang, 1995; Lang, Bradley, & Cuthbert, 1998a, Lang, Bradley, & Cuthbert, 1998b; Lang, Bradley, Fitzsimmons et al., 1998; Scherer, 2005); as such, per Carleton (2016), fear will refer to a continuum ranging from low (e.g., dislike, bother) to moderate (e.g., fearful) to high (e.g., terror). 4.2.
sentences.s101: Criterion Two Fundamental fears should be responses to stimuli inherently appraised as aversive.
sentences.s102: The stimulus should (nearly) automati- cally activate the Behavioural Inhibition System (BIS; Gray & McNaughton, 2003; Gray, 1976) or analogue thereof because the stimulus is inherently appraised as aversive; herein, inherent describes responses requiring little or no a priori learning (i.e., con- ditioning or observation) and aversive describes “an actually or potentially tissue-damaging event” (Loeser & Treede, 2008; p. 475). 4.3.
sentences.s103: Criterion Three Fundamental fears should be evolutionarily supported such that the fear produced by the stimulus would have a logically- defensible selection bias.
sentences.s104: An evolutionary selection bias dovetails with Criterion Two.
sentences.s105: Normative phenotypic levels should provide logically supported evolutionary individual and group level advan- tages, with extreme phenotypic levels advantaging the group.
sentences.s106: For example, normative IIS would be evolutionarily supported at the individual level.
sentences.s107: Extremely high IIS for a group subset might mit- igate group risk; in contrast, extremely low IIS for a group subset might facilitate protection from predators. 4.4.
sentences.s108: Criterion four Fundamental fears should be continuously and normally dis- tributed in the population.
sentences.s109: An inherent fear would be biologically supported with an underlying genetic basis (i.e., Criteria Two and Three).
sentences.s110: The fear should be present at some level in most healthy individuals, with pathology and/or group-speciﬁc advan- tages rather than individual advantages occurring at extremes (i.e., the tails of the distribution). 4.5.
sentences.s111: Criterion Five A fundamental fear should be a logical reduction of higher-order constructs (e.g., “common” fear- and anxiety-related constructs; personality constructs, such as trait anxiety, neuroticism, neurotic temperament, negative affectivity; disorder-related symptoms).
sentences.s112: For example, high neuroticism > fearing unemployment > fears of insufﬁcient resources > fears of starvation > fears of physical harm; fearing unemployment (relatively higher-order) would contribute to heightened neuroticism, but be driven by fear of physical harm (relatively lower-order fear; increasingly fundamental).
sentences.s113: Fearing unemployment logically requires substantial a priori learning, the elements of which can then be logically reduced to include a relationship between employment, access to food, and avoiding physical harm. 4.6.
sentences.s114: Criterion Six Fundamental fears should be non-derivative (i.e., logically irreducible).
sentences.s115: As fears become increasingly fundamental (i.e., lower- order; non-derivative), fewer a priori determinants should be required.
sentences.s116: For example, “What is fear-inducing about being unem- ployed?” might be followed by, “What is fear-inducing about not being paid?” At some point the iterative downward arrow logical reduction process should produce a logical tautologically expressed rhetorically as, “I fear it because I fear it”.
sentences.s117: Criteria Two, Three, Five, and Six are related because higher-order constructs would necessarily be learned derivations of lower-order fears, whereas a non-derivative fear should be inherent and tautological.
sentences.s118: Fears that are part of an irreducible cyclical tautology (e.g., I fear X because of Y, and I fear Y because of X, but neither X nor Y are feared because of an irreducible Z) could also be argued as non-derivative and therein potentially fundamental. 4.7.
sentences.s119: Criterion Seven Fundamental fears should be able to account for variance in higher-order constructs; as such, fundamental fears should be increasingly correlated with increasingly proximal higher-order constructs (i.e., requiring fewer downward arrow iterations).
sentences.s120: For example, if public performance fears can be readily reduced to FNE, the constructs should be highly correlated.
sentences.s121: Other variables might still be important (e.g., fear of being injured by an angry mob), but would have lower correlations.
sentences.s122: The fear should also be correlated with increasingly distal higher-order constructs (e.g., neuroticism); however, the relationship should become smaller as contributions from other lower-order elements are included or accounted for.
sentences.s123: Changes to lower-order constructs should also produce diffuse changes in related higher-order constructs.
sentences.s124: For example, rather than targeting public speaking, giving a perfor- mance, or blushing, therapists could target FNE, broadly reducing all related higher-order fears (Barlow, Ellard et al., 2011; Barlow, Farchione et al., 2011); that said, FNE might be targeted using expo- sures involving those higher-order fears (Heimberg & Becker, 2002; Heimberg, Becker, Goldﬁnger, & Vermilyea, 1985; Heimberg et al., 2010; Hofmann, 2007). 4.8.
sentences.s125: Criterion Eight A fundamental fear should be factorially distinct.
sentences.s126: Paralleling Criterion Seven, Criterion Eight provides more than logical or rhetorical evidence of Criteria Five and Six. 5.
sentences.s127: Reassessing the original fundamental fears AS, FNE, and IIS appear important, inﬂuential, and lower-order constructs that contribute to higher-order constructs (e.g., neuroti- cism; psychopathological symptoms); however, whether they are fundamental remains debatable.
sentences.s128: Since Reiss’ (1991) publication at least three additional fears have been posited as potentially funda- mental: fear of death (Iverach, Menzies, & Menzies, 2014), fear of pain (Carleton, Abrams, Asmundson, Antony, & McCabe, 2009), and FOTU (Carleton, 2012, 2016).
sentences.s129: What follows is neither an exhaustive discussion of each fear, nor intended to discount the importance of any fear.
sentences.s130: Instead, the discourse is intended to provocatively argue the relative fundamentality of FOTU.
sentences.s131: There appears to be initial evidence that AS, FNE, and IIS meet criteria One, Four, Five, Seven, and Eight.
sentences.s132: Each appears to be an emo- tion.
sentences.s133: Moreover, moderately intense AS, FNE, and IIS, would facilitate self-care, mitigate inappropriate risk-taking, and support the devel- opment of social networks (Buss, 1990); however, too much would be paralyzing and too little would be self-destructive.
sentences.s134: Having a group subset with higher than average fears might facilitate appropriate group-level safety behaviours (e.g., avoiding danger- ous locations) and group cohesion (e.g., encouraging pro-social behaviours).
sentences.s135: In contrast, having a group subset with lower than average fears might facilitate protection from predators (e.g., mem- bers willing and able to risk individual harm to protect the group).
sentences.s136: Each appears to be a logical reduction of higher-order constructs.
sentences.s137: AS appears to be a logical reduction of anxiety and, therein, most if not all anxiety disorders (Taylor, 1999).
sentences.s138: AS accounts for variance in higher-order constructs (Naragon-Gainey, 2010; Olatunji et al., 2010; Smits, Berry, Tart, & Powers, 2008; Taylor, 1999), including neuroticism (Calkins et al., 2009; Olatunji & Wolitzky-Taylor, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2010; Schmidt & Mallott, 2006; Taylor, 1999), and has dimensions that appear continuously distributed in the popu- lation (Asmundson, Weeks, Carleton, Thibodeau, & Fetzner, 2011; Bernstein, Zvolensky, Norton et al., 2007; Bernstein, Zvolensky, Stewart, & Comeau, 2007).
sentences.s139: FNE is the hallmark logical reduction of social anxiety and accounts for variance in the higher-order con- struct (e.g., Heimberg et al., 2010); furthermore, the latent structure of FNE and social anxiety appears continuous (Weeks, Carleton, Asmundson, McCabe, & Antony, 2010; Weeks, Norton, & Heimberg, 2009).
sentences.s140: IIS appears to be a logical reduction of harm-related phobias (e.g., health anxiety) and accounts for variance in related higher- order constructs (Asmundson, Abramowitz, Richter, & Whedon, 2010; Thibodeau, Fetzner et al., 2013); the latent structure of IIS remains to be assessed.
sentences.s141: Each appears at least partially factorially distinct (Carleton, Thibodeau et al., 2014; Taylor, 1993).
sentences.s142: Despite Reiss’ (1991) original contention, AS, FNE, and IIS do not appear to meet Criterion Two or Criterion Six.
sentences.s143: None appear to be fearful emotional responses to stimuli that are necessarily inher- ently appraised as aversive.
sentences.s144: Individuals may yet be predisposed to or prepared for such fears, but each appears to require a priori learn- ing.
sentences.s145: In addition, none appear to be necessarily non-derivative (i.e., logically irreducible) because they can be logically reduced to one or more other component fears, or appear to be dependent on a moderator (e.g., another fear). 5.1.
sentences.s146: Not necessarily inherent AS appears to require a priori learning about potential con- sequences for the sensations (Taylor, 1993, 1999).
sentences.s147: For example, elevated heart rate, palpitations, and shortness of breath are not inherently aversive; instead, some people actively seek such sen- sations by engaging in higher-risk behaviours for entertainment (e.g., movies, sky diving; Allison et al., 2012; Rooney, Benson, & Hennessy, 2012) or due to problematic behaviours (e.g., sub- stance use, gambling; Comeau, Stewart, & Loba, 2001; Hittner & Swickert, 2006; Schmidt, Mussel, & Hewig, 2013).
sentences.s148: The sensations do not become aversive, facilitating AS, without (1) an anticipated consequential threat that would have required learning (i.e., not inherent); (2) fear of some potential consequential threat (e.g., heart palpitations may precede a heart attack; Carleton, 2012; Carleton, Norton, & Asmundson, 2007; Fergus & Bardeen, 2013; Taylor, 1999); or (3) fear because of insufﬁcient certainty of safety (Carleton, 2012, 2016).
sentences.s149: The stimuli would not be appraised as threatening without a priori learning that such stimuli can precede aversive consequences, FOTU acting as a moderator, or FOTU acti- vating the BIS (Carleton, 2016).
sentences.s150: An evolutionary argument for AS preparedness could be made (e.g., mitigating injury and illness); however, effective interventions (e.g., pharmaceuticals to mitigate heart attacks) supporting the beneﬁts for early reactions to such sensations (e.g., racing heart) are relatively recent.
sentences.s151: FNE may also require a priori learning.
sentences.s152: For example, the complex rules associated with even relatively simple and common social interactions are not universal (e.g., eye contact; Akechi et al., 2013).
sentences.s153: Rules for conversations and overt behaviours are even more com- plex.
sentences.s154: Learning the social rules alone is not sufﬁcient to produce FNE.
sentences.s155: The consequences for violating those social rules (i.e., garner- ing negative evaluation) must also be learned, directly or indirectly; however, FNE could be moderated by FOTU.
sentences.s156: That said, an evolution- ary argument for FNE preparedness may be particularly defensible.
sentences.s157: Cooperative group membership would offer a substantial evolu- tionary advantages (e.g., Ackerman, Huang, & Bargh, 2012) and FNE may have reduced the risk of critical group membership breaches (Baumeister & Leary, 1995; Haselton & Nettle, 2006).
sentences.s158: IIS also appears to require a priori learning.
sentences.s159: For example, a person could be born having not experienced (i.e., exposure), witnessed (i.e., vicarious exposure), or understood (i.e., didactic exposure; e.g., taught about Type I diabetes) injury or illness.
sentences.s160: Until such learn- ing occurred there would be no way to know that injury or illness existed, much less that they can be aversive and should be feared; however, IIS could be moderated by FOTU.
sentences.s161: Again, an evolutionary argument for IIS preparedness could be made (e.g., reducing the probability of death before sexual maturity); however, such general fears become conﬂated with mechanisms (e.g., predators), intensi- ties (e.g., a laceration vs. a bruise; a common cold vs. tuberculosis), or nociception.
sentences.s162: Fearing illness as inherent on the basis of an evo- lutionary argument would be particularly challenging.
sentences.s163: Our ability to identify illness with our primary senses (e.g., visual assessment) is relatively poor except for advanced stages of some illnesses (e.g., small pox) and our understanding of illness as typically induced by other agents (e.g., bacteria, virus, genetics) is very recent.
sentences.s164: Despite their importance, the evidence does not appear to support AS, FNE, or IIS as being deﬁnitively inherent.
sentences.s165: All three appear to require another fear or substantial learning contingent on expectations of aversive consequences–speciﬁc, non-speciﬁc, or unknown–which then become the focus of fear, rather than the AS sensations, the negative evaluation, the actual illness or injury. 5.2.
sentences.s166: Arguably derivative (i.e., not necessarily logically irreducible) AS subsumes fearful responses to somatic, cognitive, and social categories of interoceptive stimuli “based on the belief that the sensations have adverse consequences such as death, insanity, or social rejection (Reiss & McNally, 1985)” (Taylor et al., 2007; p. 177).
sentences.s167: Example descriptions can be drawn from the Anxiety Sen- sitivity Index 3 (Taylor et al., 2007): “When I feel pain in my chest, I worry that I’m going to have a heart attack” (Somatic); “When my thoughts seem to speed up, I worry that I might be going crazy” (Cognitive); “When I begin to sweat in a social situation, I fear peo- ple will think negatively of me (Social)”.
sentences.s168: The description of AS and the exemplar items appears to suggest the fear is logically reducible to at least one other fear (e.g., heart attack; psychopathology; negative evaluation).
sentences.s169: Furthermore, insufﬁcient certainty regard- ing the pending consequences appears critical (Carleton, Sharpe, & Asmundson, 2007).
sentences.s170: FNE refers to “apprehension about others’ evaluations, distress over their negative evaluations, avoidance of evaluative situations, and the expectation that others would evaluate oneself negatively” (Watson & Friend, 1969; p. 449).
sentences.s171: Example descriptions can be drawn from the Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale (Rodebaugh et al., 2004; Weeks et al., 2005): “I am frequently afraid of other peo- ple noticing my shortcomings”; “I am afraid that other people will ﬁnd fault with me”.
sentences.s172: Negative evaluation could well lead to physi- cal harm in modern or historical societies (Ackerman et al., 2012) through being physically attacked or ostracized.
sentences.s173: Social dimensions of AS (e.g., fearing blushing or sweating), are related to social anxiety (Carleton, Collimore, & Asmundson, 2010; Rector, Szacun- Shimizu, & Leybman, 2007; Taylor et al., 2007), possibly because they can compromise status (Seyfarth & Cheney, 2012).
sentences.s174: A related construct, fear of positive evaluation (FPE; Weeks, Heimberg, Rodebaugh, & Norton, 2008), also appears important and distinct (Weeks, Jakatdar, & Heimberg, 2010; Whiting et al., 2014).
sentences.s175: Exam- ple descriptions can be drawn from the Fear of Positive Evaluation Scale (Weeks, Heimberg, & Rodebaugh, 2008): “I am uncomfort- able exhibiting my talents to others, even when I think my talents will impress them”.
sentences.s176: FPE has not been posited as fundamental, but therein appears to have strengths and limitations similar to FNE.
sentences.s177: IIS subsumes fearful responses to becoming ill or injured (Carleton et al., 2005).
sentences.s178: Example descriptions can be drawn from the Illness/Injury Sensitivity Index-Revised (Carleton, Park, & Asmundson, 2006): “I am frightened of being injured” (Injury); “The thought of physical illness scares me” (Illness).
sentences.s179: The breadth may be problematic because objective indications of tissue damage (e.g., unexplained bruises) may be dismissed as non-threatening; similarly, evidence of infection (e.g., a virus screen) may be asso- ciated with no threatening symptoms.
sentences.s180: Conversely, persons can report experiencing substantial symptoms indicating tissue dam- age or infection, with no objective indications of either (Asmundson & Carleton, 2008).
sentences.s181: There would also be considerable difﬁculty in disentangling IIS from fears of the causal mechanism (e.g., preda- tion) and aversive sensations (e.g., dizziness, pain).
sentences.s182: Accordingly, IIS may be logically reducible to AS, fear of pain (Carleton, Abrams, Asmundson et al., 2009), FNE (Carleton & Asmundson, 2012), or FOTU (Carleton, 2012, 2016).
sentences.s183: Each of AS, FNE, and IIS appears well-supported as lower-order relative to common fears, higher-order factors, and psychopatholo- gies; however, sensations (e.g., chest pain), negative evaluations (e.g., by a competitor with insufﬁcient agency for retribution), or injuries and illnesses (e.g., a trivial scratch) sufﬁciently known to be inconsequential are unlikely to be feared; instead, sufﬁcient certainty of safety can make anxiety-related sensations appeti- tive, rather than aversive, negative evaluations empowering, and soreness from minor post-workout injuries invigorating.
sentences.s184: By con- trast, pending sufﬁcient certainty of aversive consequences, the fear could refer to a consequence and only tangentially to AS, FNE, or IIS (Carleton, 2012; Carleton, Sharpe et al., 2007).
sentences.s185: In the absence of sufﬁcient certainty, responses appear to depend signiﬁcantly on individual responses to unknowns (Carleton, 2012, 2016).
sentences.s186: In any case, AS, FNE, and IIS, appear reﬂexively related and reducible to fears of death, pain, or unknowns; therefore, despite being lower- order and critical, none appear deﬁnitively fundamental. 5.3.
sentences.s187: Fear of death as fundamental Benjamin Franklin is often referenced as saying nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
sentences.s188: Death is the conclu- sion of the process that is dying.
sentences.s189: Fearing death is not evidenced by reﬂexes to preserve life (e.g., breathing, Moro5), because reﬂexes are not emotions (Leventhal & Scherer, 1987; Moors, 2009; Moors, Ellsworth, Scherer, & Frijda, 2013).
sentences.s190: Reﬂexes could be appraised per- cepts causally associated with fear pending appropriate learning (Mulligan & Scherer, 2012); however, reﬂexes would not evidence 5 An infant reﬂex of adduction and then ﬂexion of the arms, triggered by a per- ception of falling (Zafeiriou, 2004). fear of death as inherent any more than salivation evidences fear of starvation as inherent.
sentences.s191: For example, Moro following a sudden drop could cause fear of vestibular motor sensations associated with falling or fear of pain after impact; conversely, it could cause joy if caught repeatedly being caught by a parent was perceived as certain.
sentences.s192: A person who fears death may not fear death, per se, instead fear- ing (1) the process of dying, which is reducible to other fears (e.g., AS, FNE, IIS, fear of pain); (2) that death will be unpleasant (e.g., the afterlife may be painful); (3) unknowns about death (e.g., death may or may not involve an afterlife), making the unknown the object of fear; or (4) the concept of oblivion, an unequivocal unknown, which requires substantial a priori learning.
sentences.s193: Neither dying nor death are inherent concepts; both must be learned (Balk, 2010). “Absence of fear of death among children under ten [years of age] is in keeping with Anthony’s study reported in The Child’s Discovery of Death (Anthony, 1940)” (Bowlby, 1973, p.117).
sentences.s194: As detailed in Car- leton’s review (Carleton, 2016), children fear unknowns, darkness, and snakes–among other things–long before demonstrating under- standing or fear of death (Bowlby, 1973; Kagan & Snidman, 2004).
sentences.s195: Furthermore, death is not necessarily aversive or avoided.
sentences.s196: Many religions posit death as involving a fantastic and appetitive after- life (Segal, 2010).
sentences.s197: Where the afterlife is potentially appetitive, any associated fear must result from (1) insufﬁcient certainty in the promise of that appetitive afterlife or (2) the process of dying as a transition to that afterlife.
sentences.s198: Notional development of an appetitive afterlife may have been to cope with unknowns related to death. “For this fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being the appearance of knowing the unknown; since no one knows whether death, which they in their fear apprehend to be the greatest evil, may not be the greatest good” (Socrates, 399 BC).
sentences.s199: In any case, fear of death, while arguably pervasive and poignant, does not appear fundamental. 5.4.
sentences.s200: Fear of pain as fundamental Haruki Murakami claimed “Pain is inevitable.
sentences.s201: Suffering is optional” (Murakami, 2009; p.vii); relatedly, fear of pain may be fundamental (Carleton, 2012; Carleton, Abrams, Asmundson et al., 2009).
sentences.s202: Pain is a sensory and emotional experience associated with perceived or potential tissue damage (Loeser & Treede, 2008; p. 475).
sentences.s203: Nociception is the neuronal processing of noxious stimuli, beginning with the activation of nociceptors (Loeser & Treede, 2008; p. 475).
sentences.s204: Nociception is inherently aversive (Pear, 2014; Rolls, 2013), but evolutionarily derivative for mitigating injury and death (Broom, 2001; Fields, 2006) and not necessarily fear provoking (Asmundson & Carleton, 2008; Carleton & Asmundson, 2012).
sentences.s205: Noci- ception is neither an emotion (Leventhal & Scherer, 1987; Moors, 2009) nor synonymous with the subjective and complex experi- ence of pain, which involves nociception, appraisals, attributions of meaning (Asmundson, Norton, & Norton, 1999; International Association for the Study of Pain, 1986; Loeser & Treede, 2008; Melzack & Katz, 2004).
sentences.s206: The distinction complicates assessing fear of pain as fundamental because fear of pain typically refers to the experience of pain rather than nociception (Asmundson & Carleton, 2008; Carleton & Asmundson, 2012).
sentences.s207: Nociception evokes appraisals that may produce the experience of pain (Asmundson & Wright, 2004) and is not required to experi- ence pain (e.g., phantom limb pain; Diers, Christmann, Koeppe, Ruf, & Flor, 2010; Melzack, 1990).

10.1016/j.janxdis.2016.04.011.printed_title: Intolerance of uncertainty, anxiety sensitivity, health anxiety, and anxiety disorder symptoms in youth

sentences.s1: Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Anxiety Disorders Intolerance of uncertainty, anxiety sensitivity, health anxiety, and anxiety disorder symptoms in youth Kristi D.
sentences.s2: Wright a,∗, Megan A.N. Adams Lebell b, R.
sentences.s3: Nicholas Carleton a a Department of Psychology, University of Regina, 3737 Wascana Parkway, Regina, SK, Canada b Department of Educational Psychology and Special Education, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, SK, Canada a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 27 October 2015 Received in revised form 19 April 2016 Accepted 22 April 2016 Available online 27 May 2016 a b s t r a c t Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) – difﬁculty coping with uncertainty and its implications – is tradition- ally studied in adult populations, but more recently has been explored in children and adolescents.
sentences.s4: To date, the association between IU and health anxiety has not been explored in a child or adolescent sam- ple.
sentences.s5: Further, it is unknown whether the relationship between IU and health anxiety may be mediated by anxiety sensitivity (i.e., fear of anxiety-related sensations) in this population.
sentences.s6: We sought to extend the existing research and expand our understanding of IU as a transdiagnostic construct by exploring the association between IU and health anxiety, anxiety sensitivity, and DSM-IV anxiety disorder symp- tom categories in 128 youth (M age = 12.7 years, SD = 0.82, range 11–17 years).
sentences.s7: Participants completed measures of IU, health anxiety, anxiety sensitivity, and anxiety disorder symptom categories.
sentences.s8: Results demonstrated signiﬁcant positive associations between IU and all measures.
sentences.s9: Mediation analyses sup- ported the direct and indirect importance of each IU subscale on health anxiety.
sentences.s10: Future directions and implications are discussed. © 2016 Published by Elsevier Ltd. 1.
sentences.s11: Introduction Intolerance of uncertainty (IU), “an individual’s dispositional incapacity to endure the aversive response triggered by the per- ceived absence of salient, key, or sufﬁcient information, and sustained by the associated perception of uncertainty” (Carleton, 2016a; p. 31), has been, for the most part, studied in adult samples.
sentences.s12: As such, much of what we understand about the transdiagnos- tic nature of IU (Carleton et al., 2012) and its relationship to anxiety disorders and related constructs such as health anxiety (Carleton, 2016a), has been demonstrated and replicated within adult samples [i.e., with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD; e.g., Dugas, Gagnon, Ladouceur, & Freeston, 1998); social anxiety disor- der (SAD; e.g., Carleton, Collimore, & Asmundson, 2010); obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD; e.g., Gentes & Ruscio, 2011); and health anxiety (e.g., Boelen & Carleton, 2012; Fergus & Valentiner, 2011)].
sentences.s13: Researchers eventually included IU in cognitive behavioral mod- els for several anxiety disorders, most notably GAD, as a critical cognitive risk factor underlying symptom development and main- tenance (e.g., Dugas & Koerner, 2005).
sentences.s14: Below, we provide a brief overview of existing research ﬁndings in the areas of IU and children ∗Corresponding author.
sentences.s15: E-mail address: kristi.wright@uregina.ca (K.D. Wright). and adolescents, the association between IU and health anxiety, and health anxiety in children and adolescents. 1.1.
sentences.s16: IU in children and adolescents The notion that difﬁculty tolerating uncertainty plays a criti- cal role in the etiology of GAD and chronic worry has been widely accepted for some time (Dugas, Buhr, & Ladouceur, 2004); how- ever, only recently have researchers extended examinations of IU and its associations with particular types of psychopathology to include children and adolescents (i.e., Barahmand, 2008; Comer et al., 2009; Dugas, Laugesen, & Bukowski, 2012; Fialko, Bolten, & Perrin, 2012; Krain et al., 2006, 2008; Laugesen, Dugas, & Bukowski, 2003; Read, Comer, & Kendall, 2013).
sentences.s17: Research to-date has pro- duced ﬁndings that are consistent, and in some cases inconsistent, with those observed in the adult literature.
sentences.s18: For example, IU has demonstrated strong associations with worry, beyond positive beliefs about worry, negative problem orientation, and cognitive avoidance, and demonstrated utility in discriminating between moderate and high worriers (Laugesen et al., 2003) as well as between those with and without an anxiety disorder diagnosis (i.e., GAD, social phobia, separation anxiety disorder, OCD, or panic dis- order; Comer et al., 2009).
sentences.s19: IU was the best predictor of a primary GAD diagnosis and a signiﬁcant predictor of child-reported anxiety severity (Read et al., 2013). http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.janxdis.2016.04.011 0887-6185/© 2016 Published by Elsevier Ltd.
sentences.s20: The aforementioned results appear generally in line with research from adult samples, but there are also divergent results.
sentences.s21: For example, the adult cognitive behavioral model of excessive worry and anxiety proposed by Dugas et al. (1998) that included IU, cognitive avoidance, and positive beliefs, was assessed with a child and adolescent sample (aged 7–19 years; Fialko et al., 2012).
sentences.s22: The results replicated signiﬁcant associations between IU, cognitive avoidance, positive beliefs about worry, worry, and anxiety across the age range akin to what we see in adult samples; however, the best ﬁtting model was different for children (aged 7–12 years) and adolescents (aged 13–19 years).
sentences.s23: Speciﬁcally, positive beliefs about worry had to be removed from the child model.
sentences.s24: In turn, cognitive avoidance was associated with anxiety via worry in children, while a direct path was observed from IU to worry and anxiety in both age groups.
sentences.s25: These latter ﬁndings highlight the potential impact of age on the association between IU and worry, albeit Fialko et al. note that this relationship is not easily understood and requires further examination.
sentences.s26: A 5-year, ten wave longitudinal study of adolescents exploring the temporal relation between IU and fear of anxiety and worry dur- ing adolescence indicated a bi-directional mediation between IU and worry (Dugas et al., 2012).
sentences.s27: The results suggested IU and worry impact each other uniformly over time, which contrasts results from adult samples that suggested that change in IU leads to change in worry (i.e., Grenier & Ladouceur, 2004; Ladouceur, Gosselin, & Dugas, 2000).
sentences.s28: Lastly, converging evidence from neuroimaging stud- ies of decision-making in adult clinical populations characterized by IU has identiﬁed speciﬁc brain regions that may be impacted by IU [e.g., anterior cingulate cortex (ACC); Sachdev & Malhi, 2005].
sentences.s29: Initial fMRI research with adolescents has similarly highlighted activity in the ACC during completion of decision-making tasks.
sentences.s30: Adolescents, but not adults, demonstrated robust linear increases in ACC activity and differences in activation patterns across incorrect trials relative to correct trials (Krain et al., 2006).
sentences.s31: Krain et al. note that although adults demonstrated higher IU scores, they did not show the latter relationship between IU and ACC activity suggest- ing “mature brain circuits may develop compensatory mechanisms so that ACC activity, while still related to task-based uncertainty, is no longer associated with IU” (p. 1028).
sentences.s32: Collectively, the extant research with child and adolescent sam- ples has established an association between IU and anxiety, worry, and anxiety disorders; however, child and adolescent results have occasionally diverged from adult sample results (i.e., Dugas et al., 2012; Fialko et al., 2012; Krain et al., 2006).
sentences.s33: Research with adult samples has also established an association between IU and the associated construct of health anxiety (e.g., Boelen & Carleton, 2012; Fergus & Bardeen, 2013; Norton, Sexton, Walker, & Norton, 2005; Sexton, Norton, Walker, & Norton, 2003), an association that has yet to be explored in children and adolescents. 1.2.
sentences.s34: IU and health anxiety Health anxiety represents an umbrella construct for several somatic-related disorders that have diagnostic similarities with anxiety disorders (Asmundson, Taylor, Sevgur, & Cox, 2001).
sentences.s35: Generally, health anxiety refers to apprehension and fear that changes in bodily sensations may be indicative of a serious illness (Asmundson, Abramowitz, Richter, & Whedon, 2010).
sentences.s36: A diagno- sis may be warranted when health anxiety becomes excessive and impacts day-to-day functioning.
sentences.s37: Classiﬁcations of clinical levels of health anxiety fall within the somatic symptom and related disorders section of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5; APA, 2013).
sentences.s38: Hypochondriasis has been elimi- nated as a disorder and replaced with somatic symptom disorder (i.e., for those with signiﬁcant somatic symptoms and health anxiety) and illness anxiety disorder (i.e., for those with high health anxiety without somatic symptoms) (APA, 2013).
sentences.s39: The relationship between IU and health anxiety in adult sam- ples has a far less established research history when considering the present knowledge base amassed regarding the association between IU and excessive worry and anxiety.
sentences.s40: Collectively, the results have been mixed.
sentences.s41: Sexton et al. (2003) identiﬁed signiﬁcant associations between IU and health anxiety in an undergrad- uate sample; however, the association became non-signiﬁcant when controlling for anxiety sensitivity (AS; i.e., a variable iden- tiﬁed as a cognitive risk factor for anxiety and refers to the fear of anxiety-related sensations and their potential harmful conse- quences; Taylor et al., 2007).
sentences.s42: Sexton et al.’s results were replicated by the same research group with an adult outpatient sample (Norton et al., 2005) and extended to illness/injury sensitivity in an undergraduate sample by Carleton, Sharpe, & Asmundson (2007).
sentences.s43: In contrast, Boelen and Carleton (2012) failed to replicate the results in a sample of bereaved adults, ﬁnding neither AS nor IU to be signiﬁ- cantly related with health anxiety after controlling for neuroticism.
sentences.s44: In 2013, Fergus and Bardeen examined the incremental speci- ﬁcity of AS and IU in relation to health anxiety in a large community sample of adults.
sentences.s45: Results demonstrated that both AS and IU incre- mentally contributed to the concurrent prediction of health anxiety beyond both negative affect and one another; nevertheless, the physical concerns component of AS and inhibitory IU were the only components of AS and IU that shared unique relations with health anxiety.
sentences.s46: Fergus and Bardeen noted their results suggested AS may play a more crucial role in etiology of health anxiety than IU.
sentences.s47: Current theory implicates IU as a core component of AS (Carleton, Sharpe et al., 2007) that directly and indirectly through AS impacts anxi- ety and related symptoms such as health anxiety (Carleton et al., 2012); accordingly, mediation analyses may be particularly bene- ﬁcial for evaluating the relationship between IU (i.e., IU subscales), AS, and health anxiety.
sentences.s48: To-date the association between IU, AS, and health anxiety in a child and/or adolescent population has not been explored. 1.3.
sentences.s49: Health anxiety in children and adolescents Health anxiety research with children and adolescents is nascent, in part because health anxiety was thought to originate during the adult years; in contrast, burgeoning research has sug- gested that this is likely not true (e.g., Eminson et al., 1996; Delparte et al., 2015; Koteles, Freyler, Kokonyei, & Bardos, 2014; Marshall, Jones, Ramchandani, Stein, & Bass, 2007; Rask, Elberling, Skovgaard, Thomsen, & Fink, 2012; Wright & Asmundson, 2003, 2005; Wright, Reiser, & Delparte, 2015).
sentences.s50: Overall, the results from research using self-reports (i.e., Eminson et al., 1996; Koteles et al., 2014; Marshall et al., 2007; Wright et al., 2015; Wright & Asmundson, 2003, 2005) and parent reports (Rask et al., 2012) suggest children and adoles- cents do worry about their health and the health of their signiﬁcant others.
sentences.s51: Parents appear to play a key role in the development of health anxiety in this population (Marshall et al., 2007; Koteles et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2015), as does the AS levels of children and adolescents (i.e., Delparte et al., 2015; Wright & Asmundson, 2003; Wright et al., 2015).
sentences.s52: That said, little else is known about child and adolescent health anxiety.
sentences.s53: Accordingly, additional research with child and adolescent samples is required to thoroughly understand the developmental trajectory of health anxiety and the complex relationship with IU and AS.
sentences.s54: The results would further inform the transdiagnostic nature of IU, support the development of interven- tions tailored for youth, and further inform our understanding of adult health anxiety.
sentences.s55: The current study examined the relationship between IU and health anxiety, and for comparison purposes, explored the relation- ship between IU and DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom categories, allowing us to evaluate the transdiagnostic nature of IU in a youth sample (11–17 years).
sentences.s56: AS was also assessed for mediation of the relationship between both prospective and inhibitory IU and health anxiety individually.
sentences.s57: Based on existing research, we hypothesized that IU would be associated with measures of health anxiety and DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom categories.
sentences.s58: Further, we hypothesized that AS would mediate the relationship between both prospective and inhibitory IU and health anxiety. 2.
sentences.s59: Participants Participants were 128 youth [63 female and 65 male].
sentences.s60: The youth were 11–17 years, with a mean age of 12.72 years (SD = 0.85).
sentences.s61: The majority participants self-identiﬁed as Caucasian (i.e., 95%) and for the most part resided in a rural setting (i.e., 95%). 2.2.
sentences.s62: Procedure The current study was approved by the University Research Ethics Board.
sentences.s63: Participants were recruited from a local rural school system and community activities such as basketball camps.
sentences.s64: Infor- mation letters as well as consent and assent forms were sent home to parents/guardians.
sentences.s65: Both assent and parent consent were required for participation in the study.
sentences.s66: Youth who provided assent and whose parents provided consent completed measures in a group setting.
sentences.s67: Research assistants provided assistance to youth to facilitate completion of measures when needed.
sentences.s68: Youth were entered into a draw for one of ten $20 movie gift cards as thanks for their participation. 2.3.
sentences.s69: Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-Revised The Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-R (IUS-R; Walker, Birrell, Rogers, Leekam, & Freeston, 2010) is a 12-item questionnaire assessing IU across the lifespan.
sentences.s70: The IUS-R was adapted from the 12-item version of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12; Carleton, Norton, & Asmundson, 2007).
sentences.s71: Items are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (Not at all like me) to 5 (Entirely like me).
sentences.s72: Total scores range from 12 to 60 with higher scores reﬂecting higher levels of intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s73: The IUS-R has two subscales, tapping Prospective IU (seven items; e.g., “I can’t stand being taken by surprise”) and Inhibitory IU (ﬁve items; e.g., “When it’s time to act, uncertainty paralyses me”).
sentences.s74: For the current study, the IUS-R total score had good internal consistency ( = 0.87) and the IUS-R subscales (i.e., Prospective IU and Inhibitory IU) demonstrated good to fair internal consistency ( = 0.81 & = 0.79, respectively). 2.3.2.
sentences.s75: Childhood Illness Attitude Scales The Childhood Illness Attitude Scales (CIAS; Wright & Asmundson, 2003) is a 35-item self-report measure designed to measure fears, beliefs and attitudes associated with health anxi- ety and illness behavior in school-age children (8–15 years of age).
sentences.s76: Items are rated on a 3-point scale (1 = none of the time, 2 = sometimes, 3 = a lot of the time), with the exception of items 29 through 31 (assess frequency of treatment experiences) which are rated on a 3-point frequency scale (1 = 0 times, 2 = 1–2 times, 3 = 3 or more times), and items 28 and 32 which are open-ended questions pro- viding supplementary information and not included in scoring.
sentences.s77: As suggested by Wright and Asmundson (2005), items 8, 11, 15, and 25 were excluded from scoring resulting in 29 items used in the total score.
sentences.s78: Total scores may range from 29 to 87 with higher scores reﬂecting higher levels of health anxiety and illness behavior.
sentences.s79: The CIAS is comprised of four subscales (i.e., fears, help seeking, symptom effects, and treatment experiences; Wright & Asmundson, 2005).
sentences.s80: The CIAS total (29 items) has demonstrated excellent internal consistency ( = 0.89), good construct validity, and high test-retest (10–14 days) reliability (Wright & Asmundson, 2003).
sentences.s81: For the current study, the CIAS total score had good internal consistency ( = 0.83).
sentences.s82: The internal consistency for the CIAS sub- scale scores were all acceptable with coefﬁcient s of 0.78 (fears), 0.75 (help seeking), 0.71 (symptom effects), and 0.65 (treatment experiences). 2.3.3.
sentences.s83: Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale The Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale (SCAS; Spence, 1997) is a 44-item self-report measure designed to measure a broad spec- trum of anxiety symptoms.
sentences.s84: SCAS items are consistent with speciﬁc Diagnostic and Statistical Manual for Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV; American Psychiatric Association, 2000) anxiety dis- orders (i.e., obsessive-compulsive symptoms, separation anxiety, social phobia, panic/agoraphobia, generalized anxiety/overanxious symptoms).
sentences.s85: Each item is rated on a 4-point (never = 0, some- times = 1, often = 2, always = 3) Likert scale.
sentences.s86: Of the 44 items, 38 items are related to anxiety symptoms and 6 items are ﬁller items.
sentences.s87: Total scores range from 0 to 84 with higher scores reﬂecting higher levels of anxiety.
sentences.s88: SCAS test-retest reliability was found to be acceptable and the SCAS is said to possess good construct validity (Spence, 1998).
sentences.s89: For the current study, the SCAS total score had excellent internal consistency ( = 0.91).
sentences.s90: The internal consistency for the SCAS subscale scores were all acceptable with coefﬁcient s of 0.77 (panic-agoraphobia), 0.72 (social phobia), 0.72 (generalized anxiety), 0.71 (obsessive-compulsive problems), and 0.68 for (sep- aration anxiety), with the exception of the physical injury fears subscale (i.e., = 0.47).
sentences.s91: The aforementioned values are fairly con- sistent with Spence (1998), albeit the internal consistency for the physical illness fears in the current study was lower than observed by Spence (i.e., = 0.60). 2.3.4.
sentences.s92: Childhood Anxiety Sensitivity Index The Childhood Anxiety Sensitivity Index (CASI; Silverman, Fleisig, Rabian, & Peterson, 1991) is an 18-item self-report measure designed to measure fear of anxiety-related symptoms.
sentences.s93: Each item is rated on a 3-point Likert scale (1 = none; 2 = some; 3 = a lot).
sentences.s94: CASI total scores can range from 18 to 54 with higher scores reﬂecting higher levels of anxiety sensitivity.
sentences.s95: Silverman et al. (1991) reported good internal consistency ( = 0.87) and two-week test-retest reli- abilities of 0.76 and 0.79 for nonclinical and clinical samples, respectively.
sentences.s96: Conﬁrmatory factor analytic research has established that CASI is comprised of three lower-order factors (i.e., physical, social, and psychological concerns; McLaughlin, Stewart, & Taylor, 2007; Wright et al., 2010).
sentences.s97: For the current study, the CASI total score had good internal consistency ( = 0.80).
sentences.s98: The internal consistency for the CASI physical subscale was acceptable with coefﬁcient of 0.75; however, the social and psychological concerns subscales demonstrated poor internal consistency (i.e., = 0.45 & = 0.31, respectively). 2.4.

sentences.s102: Second, independent sample t-tests were computed to examine potential gender differences across all mea- sure total and subscale scores.
sentences.s103: Third, bivariate correlations were computed between IUS-R total and subscale scores and other mea- sure total and subscale scores.

sentences.s107: Hayes’ (2013) PROCESS macros were completed to assess whether AS mediates the relationship between the IU subscales and health anxiety.
sentences.s108: PROCESS uses an ordinary least squares regression to estimate direct and indirect coefﬁcients for moderation and mediation mod- els, as well as effect sizes, using bootstrapping and Monte Carlo conﬁdence intervals (Hayes, 2013).
sentences.s109: Assumptions for PROCESS map on to assumptions for regression and include linearity, normal- ity, homoscedasticity, and independence; however, Hayes focuses on the importance of linearity and normality, underscoring that violations are common and require caveats rather than alterna- tive analyses (Hayes, 2013).
sentences.s110: PROCESS assumes complete data and excludes cases from analyses that are missing on any of the included variables.
sentences.s111: The current model of interest was based on prior research and theory suggesting IU represents a lower order factor for AS speciﬁcally (e.g., Carleton, Sharpe et al., 2007), as well as health anxiety and anxiety more generally (e.g., Carleton, 2016a).
sentences.s112: There is no empirical or theoretical rationale for exploring alternative mod- els; as such, no atheoretical alternatives were tested in the current analyses.
sentences.s113: The analyses placed either prospective IU or inhibitory IU as the underlying independent “X” variable, the CASI total score as the mediating “Mi” variable, and the CIAS total score as the dependent “Y” variable.
sentences.s114: The conﬁdence intervals were based on 2000 bootstrapped samples.
sentences.s115: PROCESS was used to test a media- tion model, recognizing that strictly speaking mediation analyses require longitudinal rather than cross-sectional datasets; accord- ingly, the current test assesses the strength of a priori theoretically posited directional network between IU, AS, and HA, as indexed by the self-report measures and the sample. 3.

sentences.s146: Discussion A small existing research base has provided initial insights into IU as it pertains to worry and anxiety in children and adolescents (i.e., Barahmand, 2008; Comer et al., 2009; Dugas et al., 2012; Fialko Fig. 1.
sentences.s147: AS as mediator of the relationship between prospective IU and health anxiety. Fig. 2.
sentences.s148: AS as mediator of the relationship between inhibitory IU and health anxiety. et al., 2012; Krain et al., 2006, 2008; Laugesen et al., 2003; Read et al., 2013).
sentences.s149: Speciﬁcally, signiﬁcant associations between IU and worry, anxiety disorders, and speciﬁc brain structures have been observed demonstrating similarities (and some differences) with ﬁndings in adults.
sentences.s150: However, unlike the expansion of knowledge surrounding the transdiagnostic nature of IU in adults (Carleton, 2016a), exploration of the construct had not extended past worry and anxiety for children and adolescents.
sentences.s151: The overall purpose of the current study was to explore the transdiagnostic nature of IU in a youth sample.
sentences.s152: We had two speciﬁc purposes: (1) explore the relationship between IU and health anxiety, and for comparison purposes, examine the relationship between IU and DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom categories, and (2) examine AS as a mediator of the relationship between both prospective and inhibitory IU and health anxiety.
sentences.s153: The primary ﬁndings are discussed below.
sentences.s154: The current study is the ﬁrst to explore the association between IU and self-reported DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom cate- gories (i.e., panic/agoraphobia, social phobia, separation anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and generalized anxiety) as mea- sured by the SCAS in a youth sample.
sentences.s155: As recommended in the adult literature (i.e., Boelen & Carleton, 2012), we employed multiple indices of IU (i.e., IUS-R total, prospective IU, and inhibitory IU sub- scale scores) in order to better understand the relationship between IU and the speciﬁc anxiety disorder symptom categories.
sentences.s156: We hypothesized that IU would be associated with the self-reported DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom categories based upon the lim- ited existing child and adolescent ﬁndings (i.e., Comer et al., 2009; Read et al., 2013) and related adult literature (e.g., Carleton et al., 2010; Dugas et al., 1998; Gentes & Ruscio, 2011).
sentences.s157: Overall, our data supported our hypothesis as we observed signiﬁcant associations between all indices of IU and self-reported DSM-IV anxiety symp- tom categories; nevertheless, a few associations were no longer signiﬁcant when we accounted for the multiple correlations (i.e., with the physical illness fears symptom category).
sentences.s158: Moderate correlations were demonstrated between both prospective and inhibitory IU and all symptom categories (with the exception of the physical illness fears symptom category).
sentences.s159: Prospective IU refers to worry about uncertain future events and inhibitory IU refers to uncertainty that thwarts action and behav- ior (Boelen & Carleton, 2012).
sentences.s160: In contrast, in adult samples the IU dimensions have demonstrated differential associations.
sentences.s161: Speciﬁ- cally, prospective IU was related more with GAD and OCD, while inhibitory IU was related more with panic disorder, social anxiety, and depression (Carleton et al., 2010; McEvoy & Mahoney, 2011).
sentences.s162: These contrasting ﬁndings are less likely to be true differences but may be explained by methodology.
sentences.s163: The current study examined the association between IU and DSM-IV anxiety disorder symptom cat- egories based upon a continuous score yielded for each symptom category rather than exploring IU by anxiety disorder grouping.
sentences.s164: In order to further evaluate the transdiagnostic nature of IU in youth, IU should be explored in various diagnostic groups as determined by structured clinical interviews with both parent/guardian and Table 3 All partial correlation values.

sentences.s166: In terms of the most novel contribution of the current study to the literature, we are the ﬁrst to explore the association between IU and health anxiety in a youth sample.
sentences.s167: We hypothesized that IU would be associated with health anxiety based upon existing adult literature (i.e., Boelen & Carleton, 2012; Fergus & Bardeen, 2013; Norton et al., 2005; Sexton et al., 2003).
sentences.s168: Overall, we observed signiﬁ- cant associations between IU and health anxiety as measured by the CIAS total score and individual subscales; however, the treatment experiences subscale was no longer signiﬁcant when we accounted for the multiple correlations.
sentences.s169: Both prospective and inhibitory IU was signiﬁcantly associated with CIAS total and subscale scores (with the exception of the treatment experiences subscale).
sentences.s170: These correlational results provide initial support for the transdiagnostic nature of IU as it relates to health anxiety in a youth sample.
sentences.s171: We speculate that having a reduced tolerance for uncertainty sets the stage for escalation of anxiety and worry when exposed to uncer- tain (i.e., ambiguous) somatic stimuli (i.e., increased heart rate, lump) or illness-related information (e.g., via television, Internet, friends) and/or with an uncertain outcome, resulting in conviction of having or heightened risk of contracting a future illness.
sentences.s172: We further extended our examination of the transdiagnostic nature of IU by assessing AS as a mediator of the relationship between IU and health anxiety.
sentences.s173: Research has previously demon- strated an association between AS and health anxiety in children and adolescents (i.e., Delparte et al., 2015; Wright & Asmundson, 2003; Wright et al., 2015), but no studies existed that concurrently considered the association of IU and AS with health anxiety.
sentences.s174: In adults, mixed ﬁndings have been reported (i.e., Boelen & Carleton, 2012; Fergus & Bardeen, 2013; Norton et al., 2005; Sexton et al., 2003); albeit it appears that AS remains implicated within the relationship between IU and health anxiety in some way.
sentences.s175: In turn, Carleton, Sharpe et al. (2007), Carleton et al. (2012) and Carleton (2016b) have suggested that IU is a core component of AS.
sentences.s176: Based on aforementioned adult ﬁndings, we hypothesized that AS would mediate the relationship between IU and health anxiety.
sentences.s177: Our hypothesis was supported.
sentences.s178: However, our results provided evi- dence of both direct and indirect effects for both prospective and inhibitory IU on health anxiety through AS.
sentences.s179: A similar relationship has been observed between IU, AS, and panic disorder symptoms (Carleton et al., 2014).
sentences.s180: For example, we speculate that uncertainty about future health problems may also increase AS, facilitating attention towards physical symptoms (e.g., heart rate), worry, and maladaptive avoidance behaviours, all of which facilitate health anxiety.
sentences.s181: It could also be the case that other factors (not exam- ined within the current study) present in Dugas model of IU (Dugas et al., 2007) such as cognitive avoidance (i.e., strategies employed to avoid exposure to threatening outcomes and unpleasant emotions) and negative problem orientation (i.e., negative approach to prob- lems, problem solving, and outcomes of problem-solving) might operate alongside AS to mediate the relationship between IU and health anxiety.
sentences.s182: Future research may wish to explore the role these factors play in the relationship between IU, AS and health anxiety.
sentences.s183: Related research with adults has also demonstrated a relation- ship between AS and health anxiety (Olatunji et al., 2009; Stewart, Sherry, Watt, Grant, & Hadjistavropoulos, 2008), although the latter research examined the relationship between the speciﬁc AS dimen- sions and health anxiety as opposed to AS as whole as we did in the current study. 4.1.
sentences.s184: Limitations There are several limitations that require consideration.
sentences.s185: First, although our sample size was similar to or larger than those employed in some of the existing related research (i.e., Comer et al., 2009; Read et al., 2013), it was small (i.e., 128 youth participants).
sentences.s186: Future studies should seek out a larger sample size in order to ensure the study is not under powered and increase the likeli- hood of study ﬁndings being generalizable.
sentences.s187: Second, age was not evenly distributed across the sample.
sentences.s188: Speciﬁcally, youth ranged in age from 11 to 17 years, however the majority of participants were 12–13 years.
sentences.s189: An even age distribution would allow for examina- tion of potential age-related differences in the relationship between IU and health anxiety.
sentences.s190: Third, we employed self-report measures in the present study.
sentences.s191: This method of inquiry is valid, however employing structured clinical interviews utilizing DSM-5 criteria would allow examination of IU as it pertains to speciﬁc disorder groups and would strengthen the overall methodology of future studies.
sentences.s192: Fourth, related to the latter limitation, we employed the SCAS subscales as a proxy for anxiety disorder symptom categories; rather than employing structured clinical interviews to establish true diagnostic groups.
sentences.s193: We observed large and signiﬁcant corre- lations between the SCAS subscales.
sentences.s194: We also observed relatively similar sized correlations between IU and the majority of the SCAS subscales.
sentences.s195: Given the correlations between IU and SCAS subscales are similar, it may be possible that our ﬁndings demonstrate a lack of discriminant validity of the SCAS subscales as opposed to sub- stantiating the transdiagnostic effects of IU.
sentences.s196: As noted above, further exploration of the possible transdiagnostic nature of IU in youth and extension of these preliminary ﬁndings requires examination within a sample of youth with established DSM-5 diagnoses.
sentences.s197: Fifth, we utilized a cross-sectional design, negating our ability to deﬁni- tively assess the direction of effects and limiting the mediation results to informing the a priori theoretically posited directional network between IU, AS, and HA.
sentences.s198: Future studies should consider employing a longitudinal or experimental design to more deﬁnitely assess the direction of the relationships. 4.2.
sentences.s199: Summary These preliminary ﬁndings extend our understanding of IU as a transdiagnostic construct to include an association with health anxiety in youth.
sentences.s200: Correlational analyses demonstrated signiﬁcant relationships between IU and all constructs of interest (i.e., health anxiety, AS, anxiety disorder symptom categories).
sentences.s201: Mediation anal- yses further supported the direct and indirect importance of each IU subscale on health anxiety.
sentences.s202: Subsequent research is required to further understand the relationship between IU and health anxiety in youth.
sentences.s203: It would be advantageous for researchers to explore IU in groups of youth who meet criteria for speciﬁc disorders that ﬁt under the health anxiety umbrella, such as somatic symptom dis- order or anxiety illness disorder (APA, 2013).
sentences.s204: If future research continues to substantiate the observed relationship between IU, AS, and health anxiety, this information can be utilized to inform the development and/or modiﬁcation of existing intervention and pre- vention programs for children and adolescents with health anxiety whereby IU and/or AS may be directly targeted.
