10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2012.09.036.printed_title: Timing deficits in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): Evidence from neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies

sentences.s1: Timing deﬁcits in attention-deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): Evidence from neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies Valdas Noreika a,b,c,n, Christine M.
sentences.s2: Falter d,a, Katya Rubia e a Oxford Centre for Human Brain Activity, Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford, Warneford Hospital, Oxford OX3 7JX, United Kingdom b Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience, Department of Psychology, University of Turku, Assistentinkatu 7, Turku 20014, Finland c Medical Research Council Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, 15 Chaucer Road, Cambridge CB2 7EF, United Kingdom d Clinical and Developmental Neuropsychology, Faculty of Behavioural and Social Sciences, University of Groningen, Grote Kruisstraat 2/1, 9712 TS Groningen, The Netherlands e Department of Child Psychiatry/SGDP, Institute of Psychiatry, P046, King’s College London, De Crepigny Park, London SE5 8AF, United Kingdom a r t i c l e i n f o Available online 28 September 2012 Keywords: ADHD Motor timing Perceptual timing Temporal foresight fMRI Neural mechanisms Executive functions Inferior frontal cortex Prefrontal cortex Supplementary motor area Cerebellum Parietal lobe a b s t r a c t Relatively recently, neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies have indicated that individuals with attention-deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may have deﬁcits in a range of timing functions and their underlying neural networks.
sentences.s3: Despite this evidence, timing deﬁcits in ADHD are still somewhat neglected in the literature and mostly omitted from reviews on ADHD.
sentences.s4: There is therefore a lack of integrative reviews on the up-to-date evidence on neurocognitive and neurofunctional deﬁcits of timing in ADHD and their signiﬁcance with respect to other behavioural and cognitive deﬁcits.
sentences.s5: The present review provides a synthetic overview of the evidence for neurocognitive and neurofunctional deﬁcits in ADHD in timing functions, and integrates this evidence with the cognitive neuroscience literature of the neural substrates of timing.
sentences.s6: The review demonstrates that ADHD patients are consistently impaired in three major timing domains, in motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight, comprising several timeframes spanning milliseconds, seconds, minutes and longer intervals up to years.
sentences.s7: The most consistent impairments in ADHD are found in sensorimotor synchronisation, duration discrimination, reproduction and delay discounting.
sentences.s8: These neurocognitive ﬁndings of timing deﬁcits in ADHD are furthermore supported by functional neuroimaging studies that show dysfunctions in the key inferior fronto-striato-cerebellar and fronto-parietal networks that mediate the timing functions.
sentences.s9: Although there is evidence that these timing functions are inter-correlated with other executive functions that are well established to be impaired in the disorder, in particular working memory, attention, and to a lesser degree inhibitory control, the key timing deﬁcits appear to survive when these functions are controlled for, suggesting independent cognitive deﬁcits in the temporal domain.
sentences.s10: There is furthermore strong evidence for an association between timing deﬁcits and behavioural measures of impulsiveness and inattention, suggesting that timing problems are key to the clinical behavioural proﬁle of ADHD.
sentences.s11: Emerging evidence shows that the most common treatment of ADHD with the dopamine agonist and psychostimulant Methylphenidate attenuates most timing deﬁcits in ADHD and normalises the abnormally blunted recruitment of the underlying fronto-striato-cerebellar networks.
sentences.s12: Timing function deﬁcits in ADHD, therefore, next to executive function deﬁcits, form an independent impairment domain, and should receive more attention in neuropsychological, neuroimaging, and pharmacological basic research as well as in translational research aimed to develop pharmacological or non-pharmacological treatment of abnormal timing behaviour and cognition in ADHD. & 2012 Elsevier Ltd.
sentences.s13: Introduction Timing refers to the ability to deal with the temporal domain in behaviour, such as the adjustment of behaviour to speciﬁc timeframes, the ability to perceive and estimate time intervals, and the ability to consider future consequences of behaviour in order to make use of temporal foresight for inter-temporal choices.
sentences.s14: Timing functions are therefore commonly subcategorised into motor timing (i.e., adjustment of behaviour or motor responses to exter- nally or internally deﬁned timeframes, typically measured in the range of milliseconds and seconds), perceptual timing (i.e., time estimation and discrimination, also measured in intervals of milli- seconds and seconds), and temporal foresight or inter-temporal bridging (considering future outcomes to make present choices, typically comprising longer intervals of days to years) (Rubia, 2006; Contents lists available at SciVerse ScienceDirect journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/neuropsychologia Neuropsychologia 0028-3932/$ - see front matter & 2012 Elsevier Ltd.
sentences.s15: Currently at: Medical Research Council Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, 15 Chaucer Road, Cambridge CB2 7EF, United Kingdom.
sentences.s17: E-mail addresses: valdas.noreika@mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk, valnoreika@gmail.com (V.
sentences.s18: Noreika), c.m.falter@rug.nl (C.M. Falter), katya.rubia@kcl.ac.uk (K.
sentences.s19: For instance, accurate motor timing is needed to execute action at an optimal moment, such as hitting a tennis ball when it is not too close or too far.
sentences.s20: Perceptual timing is required to estimate the duration of events, such as whether you have enough time to reach a drop-shot ball.
sentences.s21: Temporal foresight is needed to estimate future implications of immediate actions, such as playing too hard might result in a back pain next morning.
sentences.s22: Despite obvious differences, all three timing functions are closely intertwined in order to provide the most adaptive behaviour, and they might even share the same underlying neural mechanisms (Rubia, 2006; Wiener, Turkeltaub, & Coslett, 2010).
sentences.s23: Due to evidence for differences in neural networks involved based on the duration of processed intervals, in particular differences between timing processes that occur within milliseconds and longer durations of seconds and more, another common subcategorisation has been made between sub-second and supra-second timing functions (Lewis & Miall, 2003a, 2003b; Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s24: This differentiation takes also into account that sub-second timing processes typically rely less on other cognitive functions that are necessary for longer interval timing functions, such as attention to time, working memory and cognitive control functions.
sentences.s25: For this review, we will use the ﬁrst subcategorisation, i.e., the distinction between motor timing, perceptual timing, and temporal foresight (for a more detailed description of different timing functions and tasks, see Section 2), but throughout the review we will point out the temporal domains that are being discussed.
sentences.s26: Timing functions are associated with diverse functions such as perception of phoneme duration (Liberman et al., 1961), verbal skills (Stanford & Barratt, 1996), expressive performance of music (Repp, 1995), time perspective and future planning (Teuscher & Mitchell, 2011), gross and ﬁne motor skills (Bartscherer & Dole, 2005), and emotional intelligence (Stolarski, Bitner, & Zimbardo, 2011).
sentences.s27: There are several basic cognitive functions that are closely interlinked with timing functions, in particular attention and working memory (Pouthas & Perbal, 2004).
sentences.s28: Attention to time is crucial to estimate time or to adjust motor responses to externally determined time intervals (Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010), whereas working memory is necessary to hold temporal informa- tion online, which is particularly relevant for the temporal reproduction of time intervals or for inter-temporal decision making (Dutke, 2005; Hinson, Jameson, & Whitney, 2003).
sentences.s29: Developmental research shows that some perceptual timing tasks such as temporal bisection can be carried out already at a very early stage of life, possibly relying on implicit sensory learning.
sentences.s30: For instance, infants as young as 4 month old were able to be trained to discriminate whether intervals between standard durations of 0.5 s and 1.5 s were closer to the shorter or the longer standard (Provasi et al., 2011), demonstrating that neurocognitive capabilities for making comparative judgements regarding varying duration of sensory stimuli are present in the infant brain.
sentences.s31: However, their temporal performance was marked by a large number of random responses.
sentences.s32: In general, however, children have a limited abstract sense of time until late childhood, e.g., they tend to confuse time with distance (Siegler & Richards, 1979), and there is consistent evidence that the timing functions, i.e., motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight, continue to develop until adolescence and even mid-adulthood (Christakou, Brammer, & Rubia, 2011; Drake, Jones, & Baruch, 2000; Droit-Volet & Wearden, 2001; Fischer & Hartnegg, 2004; McAuley, Riess-Jones, Holub, Johnston, & Miller, 2006; Rozek, Wessman, & Gorman, 1977; Smith et al., 2011; Steinberg et al., 2009; for a recent review, see Allman, Pelphrey and Meck (2012)).
sentences.s33: For example, performance of motor tapping in the milliseconds range was shown to improve throughout the life-span in 305 participants between 4 and 95 years, e.g., the average free tapping tempo decreased progressively from the age of 4 until the age of 75 and later (McAuley et al., 2006).
sentences.s34: Regarding perceptual timing tasks in the milliseconds range, discrimination of auditory tempo improves from the age of 4 to 10 and further (Drake et al., 2000) and detection of brief temporal gaps of silence changes signiﬁcantly from 7 to 19 years of age (Fischer & Hartnegg, 2004).
sentences.s35: A similar improvement in the accuracy of perceptual timing from childhood to adolescence and adulthood has been reported in a number of studies that probed perception of longer supra-second durations (for a review, see Block, Zakay, & Hancock, 1999).
sentences.s36: Droit-Volet and Wearden (2001) tested 3, 5 and 8 year old children and found an age-dependent improvement of performance in a temporal bisection task within a range of several seconds, while Rozek et al. (1977) found a similar improvement in a task requiring reproduction of a 1 min interval.
sentences.s37: With respect to temporal foresight as measured in delay discounting tasks, which typically probe much longer time intervals from 1 day up to several years, better performance has been shown in older adolescents relative to children and in adults relative to adolescents (Christakou et al., 2011; Scheres et al., 2006; Steinberg et al., 2009).
sentences.s38: People with impulsive disorders typically show deﬁcits in temporal processing.
sentences.s39: Impulsiveness is deﬁned as a premature, impatient, delay-aversed, non-reﬂected and immediacy-bound response style, where actions are executed before all available information and the future consequences are being considered (Rubia, 2002; Rubia, Halari, Christakou, & Taylor, 2009a).
sentences.s40: As can be observed from the above provided deﬁnition of impulsiveness, temporal processes appear to be underlying many of its features, such as abnormalities in motor timing (response prematurity), in subjective time sense (impatience and delay-aversion, suggesting that the passage of time is subjectively more insufferable and possibly elongated for impulsive than reﬂective personalities) and in temporal foresight (unreﬂected behaviour and not considering future consequences of one’s acts, suggesting temporal myopia).
sentences.s41: In fact, impulsive disorders have typically been associated with deﬁcits in timing functions, including attention deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, and alcohol and substance abuse (Rubia et al., 2009a).
sentences.s42: However, also other psychiatric disorders have been associated with abnormal timing processes (for a review, see Allman & Meck, 2012), such as autism spectrum disorder (Falter & Noreika, 2011; Falter, Noreika, Wearden, & Bailey, in press) or depression (Gil & Droit-Volet, 2009).
sentences.s43: ADHD is considered the disorder of impulsiveness per excel- lence.
sentences.s44: ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental psychiatric disorders, presenting about 5% of the population (Polanczyk et al., 2007) and persisting in about 65% into adult- hood (Biedermann et al., 2006).
sentences.s45: ADHD is deﬁned in the DSM-IV by persistent patterns of age-inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity whereby impulsiveness is considered the core feature (DSM-IV-TR, 2000).
sentences.s46: Based on the predominant primary symptom pattern, three ADHD subtypes are currently being distinguished: the most common inattentive-hyperactive impul- sive combined type, and the lesser occurring predominantly inattentive and predominantly hyperactive-impulsive types.
sentences.s47: Neuropsychological studies have shown that ADHD patients have consistent deﬁcits in executive functions, deﬁned as functions that are necessary for mature adult goal-directed behaviour, such as set-shifting and set maintenance, attention control (sustained and selective attention), interference and motor inhibition, planning, decision making, temporal foresight and working memory (Stuss & Alexander, 2000).
sentences.s48: It should be noted that we use the wider deﬁnition of executive functions that includes attention control functions as well as speciﬁc aspects of temporal processing such as temporal foresight because they are underlying other goal-directed behaviours, such as planning.
sentences.s49: The most prominent deﬁcits in executive functions in ADHD are in tasks of motor response inhibition, working memory and sustained attention (Cubillo, Halari, Smith, Taylor, & Rubia, 2012; Rubia, 2011; Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington, 2005).
sentences.s50: However, there is also consistent evidence that ADHD patients have cognitive deﬁcits in the timing domain, including impairments in motor timing, time perception and temporal foresight (Rubia et al., 2009a; Toplak, Dockstader, & Tannock, 2006).
sentences.s51: Furthermore, there is emerging evidence that ADHD patients have abnormalities in the underlying neurofunctional networks that mediate these timing functions (Rubia et al., 2009a).
sentences.s52: Despite converging evidence for neurocognitive deﬁcits in timing functions in ADHD, this cognitive domain is still relatively neglected and omitted from recent reviews of the cognitive abnormalities in ADHD.
sentences.s53: The aim of this review is therefore (1) to provide a focused summary of the neurocognitive evidence regarding deﬁcits in timing functions in individuals with ADHD, (2) to review the evidence for the neurofunctional basis of such impairments in ADHD from functional neuroimaging studies, and (3) to initiate a closer integration of ADHD studies of timing with the cognitive neuroscience literature on the brain basis of temporal functions.
sentences.s54: An overview of the evidence on the interactions between timing functions and other cognitive functions and behavioural traits will show that timing deﬁcits are independent but associated with behavioural as well as cognitive measures of impulsivity and inattention, supporting the proposal that impaired timing plays a fundamental role in the disorder. 2.
sentences.s55: Timing functions: deﬁnitions and experimental paradigms 2.1.
sentences.s56: Motor timing Motor timing refers to the temporal organisation of motor behaviour, which is typically measured by free tapping, sensorimotor synchronisation, and rhythm reproduction tasks.
sentences.s57: In free tapping experiments, participants are instructed to tap their ﬁnger in a freely chosen regular rhythm.
sentences.s58: Sensorimotor synchronisation (also called cued synchronisation) experiments require participants to tap with their ﬁnger in synchrony with regularly presented sensory stimuli (e.g., ﬂashing visual or auditory stimuli), and thus measure motor timing, sensorimotor synchronisation as well as estimation of the interval that the motor response needs to be adjusted to (see Fig. 1).
sentences.s59: This task is the most commonly used neurocognitive paradigm in studies investigating motor timing abnormalities in ADHD (e.g., Ben-Pazi, Gross-Tsur, Bergman, & Shalev, 2003; Pitcher, Piek, & Barrett, 2002; Rubia, Taylor, Taylor, & Sergeant, 1999a; Rubia, Noorloos, Smith, Gunning, & Sergeant, 2003, see Section 4.1).
sentences.s60: In sensorimotor synchronisation and continuation (also called cued and uncued synchronisation) experiments participants are required to synchronise their motor response to a sensory cue (synchronisation) and to continue tapping at the same rhythm as before after the sensory stimulation discontinues which allows separating percep- tually- and memory-driven timing in ADHD (e.g., Toplak & Tannock, 2005b; Tifﬁn-Richards, Hasselhorn, Richards, Banaschewski, & Rothenberger, 2004; Valera et al., 2010).
sentences.s61: In rhythm reproduction tasks participants have to replicate externally presented sensory rhythm patterns by motor tapping, requiring sensorimotor synchro- nisation and duration reproduction, loading on both motor and perceptual timing functions.
sentences.s62: Unfortunately only one ADHD study used this task (Tifﬁn-Richards et al., 2004).
sentences.s63: The most common dependent variables in all the above described tapping experiments are the average inter-tapping interval (duration of the tapping experi- ment divided by the count of taps) and the intraindividual response variability of tapping (e.g., intraindividual standard deviation, SDintra, Fig. 1.
sentences.s64: Schematic illustration of typical trials in a range of timing tasks: (a) sensorimotor synchronization task in which participants are asked to tap in phase with a visual or auditory pacemaker; (b) duration discrimination task in which participants have to respond according to which of two subsequently presented visual stimuli occurred for a longer period; (c) duration reproduction task which requires participants to reproduce a previously presented duration by pressing a button for an equal interval, and (d) delay discounting task in which participants have to choose between an immediate small reward or a later larger reward. of inter-tapping intervals).
sentences.s65: In sensorimotor anticipation tasks, parti- cipants are instructed to adjust their motor responses prior to the onset of a sensory target stimulus that appears with a predetermined regular delay, thus requiring the estimation of the delay period and its sensorimotor anticipation.
sentences.s66: Notably, the strong dependence of sensor- imotor anticipation on the perceptual estimation of durations and the explicit requirement to attend to the temporal intervals places this task very close to the perceptual timing tasks.
sentences.s67: Nevertheless, sensor- imotor anticipation will be classiﬁed in this review as a motor timing task because of its strong dependence on the accuracy of the temporal adjustment of the motor output (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003). 2.2.
sentences.s68: Perceptual timing Perceptual timing refers to the ability to estimate explicitly attended temporal intervals, which is often measured by tasks of duration discrimination, verbal duration estimation, and duration production or reproduction.
sentences.s69: A large number of ADHD studies of perceptual timing used duration discrimination task, where parti- cipants are instructed to decide which of two presented stimuli last longer, and the intervals can differ by milliseconds or seconds (e.g., Rubia et al., 1999a; Smith, Taylor, Rogers, Newman, & Rubia, 2002; Toplak, Rucklidge, Hetherington, John, & Tannock, 2003, see Section 4.2.1 and Fig. 1).
sentences.s70: The dependent variable of this task can be the time discrimination threshold—the shortest interval required to discriminate two different durations, or the discrimina- tion accuracy if the task consists of standard intervals that need to be discriminated from probe intervals.
sentences.s71: Duration discrimination is perhaps the most perceptual of all interval timing tasks used in ADHD research, given that it requires ﬁne temporal discrimination in the shortest temporal range and has therefore a relatively minimal load on other functions such as working memory or attention to time that are more demanded by time estimation of longer temporal intervals (Rubia & Smith, 2004; Smith et al., 2002).
sentences.s72: In duration reproduction tasks, participants are ﬁrst presented with a stimulus lasting for a speciﬁc duration, typically seconds or minutes, which they then have to ‘‘reproduce’’ e.g., by pressing a button for the same period of time (see Section 4.2.2 and Fig. 1).
sentences.s73: The task, however, has a high load on working memory, since the ﬁrst interval needs to be held on line in order to be able to reproduce the same interval length which is hence an important confound in ADHD studies of timing (e.g., Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003, see Section 5.2).
sentences.s74: In verbal duration estimation tasks, a sensory stimulus is ﬁrst presented for a speciﬁc period of time, typically seconds or minutes, following which participants are asked to report verbally its temporal duration.
sentences.s75: In duration production tasks, parti- cipants are asked to produce a time interval that is verbally or visually indicated (seconds or minutes), typically, by a button press.
sentences.s76: Notably, both estimation and production tasks require the ability to have an abstract representation of the temporal intervals required to estimate/produce.
sentences.s77: It should also be noted that time production and time estimation are typically negatively inter-correlated (Bindra & Waksberg, 1956), i.e., a subjective overestimation of time (e.g., 10 s) would lead to overestimation in the duration estimation task (e.g., 15 s), but to underproduction in the duration production task (e.g., 5 s).
sentences.s78: The common dependent variables of duration estimation, production and reproduction tasks are: an absolute discrepancy score, which shows the error degree irrespective of its direction, the error direction, i.e., over- and underestimation/under- and over(- re)production, and SDintra, which reﬂects trial-to-trial performance variability within each individual. 2.3.
sentences.s79: Temporal foresight Temporal foresight or inter-temporal bridging is the ability to consider the consequences of one’s decisions or actions in the more distant future, which is crucial for decision making, future planning or inter-temporal choice behaviour.
sentences.s80: Unfortunately, it is very complicated to measure temporal foresight directly, and thus it is typically measured indirectly in inter-temporal choice tasks, for example in delay discounting (also called temporal discount- ing) or gambling paradigms.
sentences.s81: In delay discounting tasks, a parti- cipant has to choose between an immediate but smaller reward and a larger but delayed reward (see Fig. 1).
sentences.s82: The subjective choice between the immediate smaller reward and the delayed larger reward depends on both the length of the delay and the magnitude or the difference in magnitude between rewards, i.e., it might be worth waiting one day but not one year for a 10% larger reward, whereas immediate rewards might be preferred if the delayed reward is larger just by 1%.
sentences.s83: Typically these types of task manipulate the delay of the reward in order to measure to what degree a reward is being discounted in proportion of its delay.
sentences.s84: These tasks thus measure the sensitivity of an individual to the varying real or hypothetical delay of time in units of reward and require temporal foresight to understand the future gain of the delayed choice, inter-temporal decision making and inter- temporal bridging, as well as reward evaluation with respect to its delay.
sentences.s85: Most of the studies on temporal foresight in ADHD have used a ‘‘ﬁxed’’ delay discounting paradigm, in which participants have to make a choice between two predetermined different size rewards paired with two predetermined different size delays (e.g., Antrop et al., 2006; Bitsakou, Psychogiou, Thompson, & Sonuga- Barke, 2009; Sonuga-Barke, Taylor, Sembi, & Smith, 1992, see Section 4.3).
sentences.s86: Notably, most of the ﬁxed delay discounting studies in ADHD employed temporal comparisons between relatively short intervals, e.g., 2 s vs. 30 s (e.g., Schweitzer & Sulzer- Azaroff, 1995; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992).
sentences.s87: More detailed informa- tion about the pattern of discounting rewards against delays can be measured using individually adjusted ‘‘graded’’ hypothetical delay discounting paradigms (e.g., Barkley, Edwards, Laneri, Fletcher, & Metevia, 2001b; Hoogman et al., 2011; Richards, Mitchell, de Wit, & Seiden, 1997; Rubia et al., 2009a; Scheres, Tontsch, Thoeny, & Kaczkurkin, 2010).
sentences.s88: In these paradigms an adjusting amount procedure is incorporated into the task, where depending on the individual choice the immediate reward (or the delays) is adjusted using an algorithm based on the previous choices of the participant for different delays.
sentences.s89: This narrows the range of the immediate values offered for each delay trial type, converging towards the value of the participant’s subjective equivalent of the ﬁxed delayed reward (Richards et al., 1997; Richards, Zhang, Mitchell, & de Wit, 1999).
sentences.s90: Based on this informa- tion a delay discounting function can be calculated, which is typically hyperbolical and the steepness of which indicates the individual discounting rate (Richards et al., 1999).
sentences.s91: The steepness of discounting rates (typically indexed with the parameter k) has been associated with impulsivity (e.g., Richards et al., 1999).
sentences.s92: In another type of temporal foresight task, the related inter- temporal choice task or gambling task, participants have to choose between risky choices that provide alluringly large rewards but even larger losses, leading to overall monetary net loss, and safe choices that provide very small rewards but even smaller losses, leading to overall net gain.
sentences.s93: The task instructions are to gain as much money as possible.
sentences.s94: Optimal task performance thus requires temporal foresight to understand the long-term gain of the safe choices in order to reject the alluringly large rewards that are then lost again.
sentences.s95: Poor performance on delay discounting and gambling tasks has been associated with impul- siveness (Bechara & Van der Linden, 2005; Peters & Buechel, 2011) and is thought to reﬂect ‘myopia for the future’ (Bechara, Tranel, & Damasio, 2000), i.e., problems with temporal fore- sight.
sentences.s96: In the delay discounting tasks, impulsive participants, including individuals with ADHD, drug & substance abuse, and other impulsive pathologies, have shown steeper delay discount- ing functions (Peters & Buechel, 2011; Rubia et al., 2009a), suggesting that the subjective value of the reward is dispropor- tionally more devalued in more impulsive participants when the reward is delayed in time.
sentences.s97: This suggests that waiting for the reward is more intolerable for impulsive individuals and hence they show suboptimal choice behaviour.
sentences.s98: In the ADHD literature this has been termed ‘‘delay aversion’’ (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992).
sentences.s99: Likewise, impulsive pathologies, including ADHD, show subopti- mal choice behaviour in gambling tasks, where they are more likely to choose risky choices despite of the long-term loss (Bechara & Van der Linden, 2005; Garon, Moore, & Waschbusch, 2006; Toplak, Jain, & Tannock, 2005).
sentences.s100: In delay discounting tasks the temporal intervals are typically explicitly presented, and the task is more explicitly measuring the sensitivity to temporal delays in units of reward.
sentences.s101: In gambling tasks, the delay of reward is only implicit and several functions other than temporal fore- sight are co-measured such as learning which decks are safe and which are risky, working memory (holding this learned informa- tion online throughout the task), the inhibition of the choice to the alluringly and thrilling large rewards that are then lost again (i.e., motivation control), and reward-related decision making.
sentences.s102: For this reason, the studies using gambling tasks will only be men- tioned brieﬂy in this review while temporal foresight deﬁcits will be discussed in light of the delay discounting literature. 3.
sentences.s103: Brain areas mediating timing functions in typical individuals 3.1.
sentences.s104: Sub-second intervals Regarding neural mechanisms of different timing functions in healthy individuals, sensorimotor synchronisation of sub-second intervals is associated with activation of the dorsolateral pre- frontal cortex (DLPFC) (Jantzen, Oullier, Marshall, Steinberg, & Kelso, 2007; Lewis, Wing, Pope, Praamstra, & Miall, 2004; Rubia et al., 1998; Rubia et al., 2000), the inferior frontal cortex (IFC) (Jantzen et al., 2007; Rao et al., 1997), medial frontal cortex (MFC) (Jantzen, Steinberg, & Kelso, 2004; Jantzen, Steinberg, & Jelso, 2005; Oullier, Jantzen, Steinberg, & Kelso, 2005), and the supple- mentary motor cortex (SMA) (Jantzen et al., 2004, 2005, 2007; Lewis et al., 2004; Rao et al., 1997; Riecker, Wildgruber, Mathiak, Grodd, & Ackermann, 2003; Rubia et al., 1998; Stoodley, Valera, & Schmahmann, 2012).
sentences.s105: The caudal SMA-proper sub-area appears to play a special role in sub-second synchronisation, as revealed by a meta-analytic contrast between functional neuroimaging studies of sensory vs. sensorimotor as well as sub-second vs. supra- second timing tasks (Schwartze, Rothermich, & Kotz, 2012).
sentences.s106: Apart from frontal regions, also subcortical structures are involved in sub-second motor timing functions, in particular the cerebellum (J¨ancke et al., 2000; Mayville, Jantzen, Fuchs, Steinberg, & Kelso, 2002; Oullier et al., 2005; Penhune, Zatorre, & Evans, 1998; Rao et al., 1997; Riecker et al., 2003; Stoodley et al., 2012), the basal ganglia (Jantzen et al., 2004, 2005; Oullier et al., 2005; Penhune et al., 1998; Rao et al., 1997), the thalamus (Rao et al., 1997; Stoodley et al., 2012), and the insula (Oullier et al., 2005; Stoodley et al., 2012).
sentences.s107: Notably, the cerebellum and the basal ganglia have reciprocal connections with the frontal cortices that control the motor output (Middleton & Strick, 1994, 2000), forming a fronto- striato-cerebellar network of motor timing functions (for review see Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004).
sentences.s108: In line with these ﬁndings, a recent voxel-wise meta-analysis of functional magnetic reso- nance imaging (fMRI) studies of sub-second motor timing tasks showed the involvement of predominantly bilateral SMA and DLPFC, right IFC, insula, basal ganglia, inferior parietal cortex (IPC), thalamus and cerebellum (Wiener et al., 2010). 3.1.2.
sentences.s109: Supra-second intervals Sensorimotor synchronisation of supra-second intervals has more prominently been shown to be associated with activation in frontal regions than sub-second motor timing.
sentences.s110: The frontal regions involved include DLPFC (Lejeune et al., 1997; Rubia et al., 1998, 2000), IFC (Lejeune et al., 1997), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) (Lejeune et al., 1997; Rubia et al., 1998; Stevens, Kiehl, Pearlson, & Calhoun, 2007), and SMA (Gountouna et al., 2010; Kawashima et al., 2000; Stevens et al., 2007).
sentences.s111: Internally paced articulation of the same word at a 2 s rhythm was found to activate a fronto-parietal network of the ACC, IFC, right DLPFC and (IPC) (Shergill, Tracy, Seal, Rubia, & McGuire, 2006).
sentences.s112: Similarly to sub-second sensorimotor timing, supra-second sensorimotor synchronisation also activates subcortical regions such as the cerebellum (Gountouna et al., 2010; Kawashima et al., 2000; Lejeune et al., 1997) and the basal ganglia, in particular the putamen (Bengtsson, Ehrsson, Forssberg, & Ullen, 2005; Garraux et al., 2005; Gountouna et al., 2010; Rubia et al., 2000; Stevens et al., 2007), and the insula (Gountouna et al., 2010) (for review see Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004). 3.1.3.
sentences.s113: Comparison of sub-second and supra-second intervals There is a clear overlap in the neural mechanisms of motor timing of sub- and supra-second intervals, further shown in a conjunction of the meta-analyses of a large number of fMRI studies of sub- and supra-second motor timing tasks that found that the key areas of overlap are in bilateral SMA, right IFC and IPC, and left MFG and insula (Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s114: Some studies, however, which tried to differentiate between sub-second and supra-second motor timing tasks, showed that sensorimotor synchronisation of seconds by contrast with sub-second sensorimotor sunchronisa- tion was more mediated by DLPFC and IFC, whereas sensorimotor synchronisation of milliseconds by contrast evoked increased activation in the SMA and ACC (Rubia et al., 2000).
sentences.s115: Furthermore, following the distinction between automatic and perceptual timing (Lewis & Miall, 2003b), DLPFC, IFC and IPC might be more involved in timing of longer cognitively processed intervals, whereas the SMA and subcortical structures may be more required for a ﬁne- temporal adjustment of the pre-cognitive motor output.
sentences.s116: Similar ﬁndings were observed in the meta-analysis of fMRI studies of supra-second motor timing by Wiener et al. (2010) who found bilateral ACC, right SMA, DLPFC and IPC to be more involved in supra-second motor timing, while basal ganglia, cerebellum, and left SMA were more involved during sub-second timing.
sentences.s117: However, it should be noted that the category of supra-second motor timing included duration (re)production studies in this meta-analysis, whereas we regard duration (re)production as a perceptual timing task in the present review. 3.2.
sentences.s118: Sub-second intervals The role of the DLPFC and IFC in perceptual timing of sub-second intervals is well-conﬁrmed by a number of fMRI and PET studies with healthy individuals (Aso, Hanakawa, Aso, & Fukuyama, 2010; Ferrandez et al., 2003; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Livesey et al., 2007; Maquet et al., 1996; Nenadic et al., 2003; Pedersen et al., 2000; Pouthas, Garnero, Ferrandez, & Renault, 2000; Rao, Mayer, & Harrington, 2001; Shih, Kuo, Yeh, Tzeng, & Hsieh, 2009; Smith, Taylor, Lidzba, & Rubia, 2003; Teki, Grube, Kumar, & Grifﬁths, 2011; Tregellas, Davalos, & Rojas, 2006).
sentences.s119: In addition to these lateral frontal regions, medial frontal areas have also been implicated such as the SMA (Aso et al., 2010; Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Dormal, Dormal, Joassin, & Pesenti, 2011; Ferrandez et al., 2003; Rao et al., 2001; Shih et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2003; Tregellas et al., 2006; Teki et al., 2011), and ACC (Jueptner et al., 1995; Lejeune et al., 1997; Maquet et al., 1996; Nenadic et al., 2003; Pouthas et al., 2000; Shih et al., 2009).
sentences.s120: Particularly interesting is the activation of SMA in the non-motor perceptual timing tasks, such as duration discrimination (Rao et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2003; Teki et al., 2011), which is observed for both the visual and auditory modalities (Shih et al., 2009).
sentences.s121: The involvement of the same frontal regions in both motor and perceptual timing suggests a common underlying neural substrate for both of these different timing functions.
sentences.s122: Another cortical site commonly reported to be active during sub-second perceptual timing tasks is the parietal cortex, especially the IPC (Aso et al., 2010; Dormal et al., 2011; Ferrandez et al., 2003; Lejeune et al., 1997; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Maquet et al., 1996; Pedersen et al., 2000; Rao et al., 2001; Shih et al., 2009).
sentences.s123: The IPC has been suggested to have a generic function of perceptual coding of magnitudes (Walsh, 2003).
sentences.s124: In addition, duration dis- crimination tasks have also been found to activate temporal cortices (Aso et al., 2010; Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Nenadic et al., 2003; Shih et al., 2009; Teki et al., 2011; Tregellas et al., 2006).
sentences.s125: Similarly to the motor timing mechanisms, the commonly reported sub-cortical structures which show increased activation during perceptual timing of sub-second intervals, e.g., during duration discrimination, are the insula (Aso et al., 2010; Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Livesey et al., 2007; Tregellas et al., 2006), cerebellum, especially the lateral portions of its hemispheres and vermis (Aso et al., 2010; Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Dormal et al., 2011; Jueptner et al., 1995; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Maquet et al., 1996; Rao et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2003; Teki et al., 2011; Tregellas et al., 2006), the basal ganglia, in particular caudate and putamen (Aso et al., 2010; Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Ferrandez et al., 2003; Jueptner et al., 1995; Livesey et al., 2007; Nenadic et al., 2003; Shih et al., 2009; Teki et al., 2011; Tregellas et al., 2006), and the thalamus (Aso et al., 2010; Jueptner et al., 1995; Nenadic et al., 2003; Teki et al., 2011; Tregellas et al., 2006).
sentences.s126: Bueti, Walsh, Frith and Rees (2008) showed that both the percep- tion and reproduction of 300–1200 ms intervals are associated with increased activity in cerebellum and basal ganglia, whereas duration reproduction in addition involves activation of a larger cortical network including the left MFC, the pre-SMA, and the right IPC.
sentences.s127: The meta-analysis of Wiener et al. (2010) of eight whole brain fMRI studies of perceptual timing tasks identiﬁed the left IFC and SMA, the DLPFC, the IPC, right insula, left putamen, right caudate and cerebellum as the key regions involved in the sub-second perceptual timing (for review see also Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004). 3.2.2.
sentences.s128: Supra-second intervals Frontal cortices, especially the DLPFC, are commonly reported brain regions involved in perceptual timing of relatively long supra- second intervals (Basso, Nichelli, Wharton, Peterson, & Grafman, 2003; Lewis & Miall, 2002, 2003a; Jech, Dusek, Wackermann, & Vymazal, 2005; Macar et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2011).
sentences.s129: Indeed, given the well-established roles of DLPFC in working memory (Curtis & D’Esposito, 2003; Marklund et al., 2007), sustained attention (Adler et al., 2001), and endogenous shift of attention to time (Coull, 2004), it seems that DLPFC becomes more important with increasing load of executive functions that are needed for timing of relatively longer intervals.
sentences.s130: A well-designed study of transcranial magnetic stimulation of right DLPFC and SMA showed that these frontal regions have increasing involvement when longer intervals are tested (Jones, Rosenkranz, Rothwell, & Jahanshahi, 2004).
sentences.s131: Nevertheless, studies showing that DLPFC is activated during perceptual sub-second timing as well (Rao et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2003) suggest that DLPFC might have a more direct role in perceptual timing (Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004).
sentences.s132: Other commonly reported frontal areas of activation during perceptual timing of supra-second intervals are, as mentioned, the SMA (Hinton, Harrington, Binder, Durgerian, & Rao, 2004; Jech et al., 2005; Macar et al., 2002; Macar, Anton, Bonnet, & Vidal, 2004; Wittmann, Simmons, Aron, & Paulus, 2010), but also the premotor cortex (Lewis & Miall, 2003a), and the ACC (Macar et al., 2002).
sentences.s133: In addition to the numerous frontal regions, timing of supra- second intervals activates also parietal (Basso et al., 2003; Brunia, de Jong, van den Berg-Lenssen, & Paans, 2000; Lewis & Miall, 2002, 2003a; Macar et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2011), and inferior temporal cortices (Tracy et al., 2000) as well as the subcortical regions in the insula (Brunia et al., 2000; Lewis & Miall, 2003a; Wittmann et al., 2010), the cerebellum (Lewis & Miall, 2002; Smith et al., 2011; Tracy et al., 2000) and the basal ganglia (Jech et al., 2005; Lewis & Miall, 2002).
sentences.s134: A meta-analysis of supra-second perceptual timing fMRI tasks showed consistently activated clusters in the right IFC, right SMA, ACC and DLPFC, left IPL and putamen (Wiener et al., 2010). 3.2.3.
sentences.s135: Comparison of sub-second and supra-second intervals The review and meta-analyses show that the brain networks of supra-second and sub-second perceptual timing functions are relatively similar, with however, subcortical regions such as the basal ganglia and cerebellum being signiﬁcantly more involved in sub-second timing.
sentences.s136: The involvement of these regions for sub-second timing is interesting in view of the striatal beat frequency model that suggests a putative ‘internal clock’ crucially depending on striatal integration of oscillating cortical activity (Matell & Meck, 2004).
sentences.s137: The cerebellum has long been postulated to be a key area of timing (Braitenberg, 2002; Braitenberg & Onesto, 1962), most prominently mediating temporal predictions (Coull, Cheng, & Meck, 2011), which are important for both motor and perceptual timing tasks.
sentences.s138: There appears also to be a laterality effect with left IFC and left SMA being more involved in sub-second timing and right IFC and right SMA being more involved in supra-second timing, which parallels ﬁndings of the involvement of these regions in sub- and supra-second motor timing (Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s139: More promi- nently right frontal activation for longer versus shorter intervals in perceptual and motor timing may reﬂect the higher load on attentional and working memory mechanisms that are mediated by right lateralised fronto-parietal mechanisms (Baier et al., 2010; Lawrence, Ross, Hoffmann, Garavan, & Stein, 2003).
sentences.s140: Interestingly, a conjunction analysis of all 44 fMRI studies on perceptual and motor timing tasks showed that the key areas underlying both motor and perceptual timing, independently of the temporal frame, are the right IFG and bilateral SMA, which hence may be the key players in both motor and perceptual timing functions (Wiener et al., 2010). 3.3.
sentences.s141: Temporal foresight Over the recent years there has been an exponential emer- gence of fMRI studies of delay discounting.
sentences.s142: Although ﬁndings have not always been consistent, there is some convergent evidence that the immediate choice and reward evaluation per se (whether immediate or distant) is more prominently reliant on the activation of the ventral striatum and the ventro- medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
sentences.s143: Delayed reward choices and reduced steepness of delay discounting, thought to reﬂect tem- poral foresight and inter-temporal bridging, however, appear to rely more on the activation of cognitive control regions including the DLPFC and the IFC, insula and parietal lobes (Bickel et al., 2009; Christakou et al., 2011; McClure, Laibson, Loewenstein, & Cohen, 2004, McClure et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004, 2007).
sentences.s144: More sophisticated analyses using game theory have shown that reward evaluation is mediated by the ventromedial orbitofrontal cortex (vmOFC) and the vmPFC, the ventral striatum and the posterior cingulate (Kable & Glimcher, 2009; Peters & Buechel, 2009, 2011).
sentences.s145: However, there is evidence that these regions do not only evaluate immediate but also distant reward values, suggest- ing they are also involved in the distant choice behaviour.
sentences.s146: In particular the vmOFC appears to be involved in the evaluation of distant rewards and temporal foresight.
sentences.s147: A lesion study showed that lesions of the vmOFC impair delay discounting (Sellitto, Ciaramelli, & di Pellegrino, 2010), which is in line with consistent evidence from lesion and fMRI studies that this region also mediates foresighted choices in the Iowa gambling task (Christakou, Brammer, Giampietro, & Rubia, 2009, for review see Bechara & van der Linden, 2005).
sentences.s148: In a developmental fMRI study of delay discounting, adults showed a less steep discounting behaviour than adolescents.
sentences.s149: The vmOFC was associated with less steep dis- counting and was progressively more activated with increasing age in the development from adolescence to adulthood (Christakou et al., 2011).
sentences.s150: Furthermore, the vmOFC was progressively more intercon- nected to the ventral stiatum activation that was associated with decreasing age and worse discounting behaviour, suggesting that with increased age and better delay discounting, there is progressive top-down control of the vmOFC over the ventral striatum that appears to be associated with the limbic response to the immediate reward choices (Christakou et al., 2011).
sentences.s151: In addition, better delay discounting was associated with better inter-regional connectivity between the vmOFC and the lateral IFC and insula regions, reconciling the view that cognitive control areas in lateral frontal areas mediate temporal foresight (Christakou et al., 2011).
sentences.s152: The ﬁnding of increased connectivity between the lateral frontal and the vmOFC is in line with several other studies that show evidence for the implication in the lateral frontal regions together with the posterior parietal lobes for delayed choices suggesting that these areas subserve temporal fore- sight (Ballard & Knutson, 2009; Bickel, Pitcock, Yi, & Angtuaco, 2009; Hinvest, Elliott, McKie, & Anderson, 2011; McClure et al., 2004, 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004).
sentences.s153: Similar ﬁndings have emerged from fMRI studies of the IOWA gambling task, where vmOFC together with lateral frontal areas appears to mediate more foresighted choice behaviour (Christakou et al., 2009; Lawrence et al., 2009).
sentences.s154: In addition to these fronto-striatal regions, more mature delay discounting has also been associated with activation in the parietal cortex (Ballard & Knutson, 2009; Bickel et al., 2009; Christakou et al., 2011; Hinvest et al., 2011; McClure et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2004; Wittmann et al., 2010), the insula (Bickel et al., 2009; Christakou et al., 2011; Hinvest et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2004, 2007; Wittmann et al., 2010), the dorsal striatum (Hinvest et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2004, 2007), and the cerebellum (Bickel et al., 2009; Christakou et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2004, 2007; Wittmann et al., 2010), perhaps pointing towards a ventrolateral and ventromedial fronto-striato-parieto-cerebellar network of temporal foresight.
sentences.s155: In conclusion, there is consistent evidence suggesting that temporal foresight during inter-temporal choice tasks depends on the inter- play between the lateral prefrontal areas and the ventromedial orbital and medial prefrontal cortex, possibly together with inter- connections to the dorsal striatal and the posterior parietal areas. 4.
sentences.s156: Motor timing Motor timing has been investigated in individuals with ADHD using tasks of free tapping (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Tifﬁn- Richards et al., 2004), cued and uncued sensorimotor synchronisation (Ben-Pazi et al., 2003; Ben-Pazi, Shalev, Gross- Tsur, & Bergman, 2006; Gilden & Marusich, 2009; Pitcher et al., 2002; Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Tifﬁn-Richards et al., 2004; Toplak & Tannock, 2005b; Zelaznik et al., 2012), rhythm reproduction (Tifﬁn-Richards et al., 2004), and sensorimotor anticipation (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Sonuga-Barke, Saxton, & Hall, 1998; Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) tasks (see Table 1).
sentences.s157: Increased intra-individual variability of a freely tapped intervals was found in a community sample of undiagnosed children with hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive behaviours (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003), but not in a clinically diagnosed ADHD sample (Rubia et al., 2003).
sentences.s158: Higher intraindividual tapping variability relative to controls during sen- sorimotor synchronisation to externally given inter-stimulus inter- vals (0.2–2 s) was found in undiagnosed community children with hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive behaviours and in clinically diagnosed ADHD children in the visual domain (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003), in the auditory modality in children (Zelaznik et al., 2012) and adults with ADHD (Gilden & Marusich, 2009), and in cross- modal auditory and visual sensorimotor synchronisation experi- ments in children (Ben-Pazi et al., 2006) and adolescents (Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) with ADHD.
sentences.s159: However, one study found no signiﬁcant group differences in the sensorimotor synchronization task (Tifﬁn-Richards et al., 2004).
sentences.s160: In line with the notion of a faster internal clock in ADHD patients (Rubia et al., 1999a), two studies showed that ADHD children tap faster than controls in an audio–visual sensorimotor synchronisation task (Ben-Pazi et al., 2003, 2006).
sentences.s161: However, several other studies did not ﬁnd group differences in the speed of free tapping (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003) nor in the tapping speed of synchronised intervals (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Zelaznik et al., 2012).
sentences.s162: Contrary to these results, however, Pitcher et al. (2002) reported that children with ADHD-inattentive and ADHD- combined diagnoses had longer inter-tap intervals in the auditory sensorimotor synchronisation task than healthy controls.
sentences.s163: These ﬁndings may point to different types of tapping deﬁcits: Pitcher et al. (2002) used a relatively fast tapping task (300 ms) and the slower tapping speed among participants with ADHD may have been related to the slower reaction times.
sentences.s164: Ben-Pazi et al. (2003, 2006) used a wider range of tapping frequencies (167–1000 ms) and the hastened tapping in the ADHD group was possibly inﬂuenced by premature responding (see Table 1).
sentences.s165: Arguably, a pervasive premature response style in cognitive tasks can be regarded as an indirect measure of poor motor timing (Rubia, Smith, & Taylor, 2007).
sentences.s166: In fact, ADHD children have shown consistently premature responses across a range of execu- tive function tasks, as measured in the Maudsley attention and response suppression battery (MARS), which is thus task- independent (Rubia et al., 2001, 2007).
sentences.s167: Furthermore, among all tasks premature responding across all tasks was one of the most sensitive discriminators between children with ADHD and healthy controls (Rubia et al., 2007).
sentences.s168: A premature response style has more typically been related to the timing aspects of impul- siveness such as a relatively fast cognitive tempo and a speed- accuracy trade-off, favouring speed (Dykman, Ackerman, & Oglesby, 1979; Rubia et al., 2001).
sentences.s169: A context-independent, perva- sive premature response style is consistent with the behavioural deﬁnition of impulsiveness as a premature, rapid and unplanned response style, where acts are executed before all consequences have been fully considered (Moeller, Barratt, Dougherty, Schmitz, & Swann, 2001; Rubia, 2002; Rubia et al., 2009a).
sentences.s170: Several studies investigated sensorimotor anticipation in chil- dren (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1998) and adolescents (Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) with ADHD.

sentences.s175: However, no group differences were found in the mean anticipa- tion times (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003) (see Table 1).
sentences.s176: To conclude, all motor timing studies except for one (Tifﬁn- Richards et al., 2004) reported signiﬁcant differences between ADHD and healthy control groups, conﬁrming a highly consistent pattern of motor timing abnormalities in ADHD.
sentences.s177: Performance differences between participants with ADHD and healthy controls were found using amodal free tapping (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003), and auditory (Gilden & Marusich, 2009; Pitcher et al., 2002; Zelaznik et al., 2012), visual (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) and audio–visual (Ben-Pazi et al., 2003, 2006) timed tapping tasks.
sentences.s178: Regarding age groups, children (Ben-Pazi et al., 2003, 2006; Pitcher et al., 2002; Rubia et al., 2003; Zelaznik et al., 2012), adolescents (Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) and adults (Gilden & Marusich, 2009) with ADHD showed abnormal motor tapping.
sentences.s179: Finally, abnormal motor timing was observed in partici- pants with ADHD both in the sub-second (Ben-Pazi et al., 2003, 2006; Pitcher et al., 2002; Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005b; Zelaznik et al., 2012) and supra-second (Gilden & Marusich, 2009; Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003) interval scales (see Table 1). 4.2.
sentences.s180: Duration discrimination One of the most consistent ﬁndings of perceptual timing abnormalities in ADHD (see Table 2) comes from studies using duration discrimination tasks of millisecond temporal differences, which tap into early perceptual processing and do not depend as much on executive functions like other perceptual timing tasks involving longer intervals, such as duration reproduction or duration estimation.
sentences.s181: Even in the longer supra-second interval range, duration discrimination is less prone to possible motor control problems than duration reproduction tasks.
sentences.s182: Compared to duration estimation paradigms when only one interval is pre- sented within a trial, duration discrimination between two inter- vals is arguably less biased by premature impulsive judgments over a single interval that may lead to duration over- or under- estimation.
sentences.s183: Twelve neurocognitive studies compared duration discrimination in individuals with ADHD and healthy control participants and reported signiﬁcant group differences (Gooch, Snowling, & Hulme, 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003, 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003 (two experiments); Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Valko et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2007).
sentences.s184: Seven of these studies tested for differences in the discrimination thresholds which were in the millisecond range and reported signiﬁcantly higher, i.e., less sensitive duration discrimination thresholds in participants with ADHD than in healthy controls (Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003 (two experiments); Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Yang et al., 2007).
sentences.s185: Three studies did no test for discrimination thresholds but for group differences in the ability to discriminate between several predetermined temporal intervals that differed by seconds (Rubia et al., 2003) or tens to hundreds of milliseconds (Rubia et al., 2007; Valko et al., 2010) and found increased error rates in the ADHD group (see also Gooch et al., 2011).
sentences.s186: One of these studies found that only clinically diagnosed children with ADHD were signiﬁcantly impaired in the discrimination of intervals that differed by seconds, while undiag- nosed community children with high levels of ADHD behaviours only showed a trend of impairment, suggesting that ADHD severity may be related to the deﬁcits (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003).
sentences.s187: An fMRI study on 12 adolescents with ADHD found increased error rates in ADHD patients relative to controls (Smith et al., in press).
sentences.s188: One study found higher discrimination thresholds only in adolescents with ADHD who also had a comorbid reading disorder (Toplak et al., 2003 (Experiment 2)).
sentences.s189: Three studies also reported increased reaction times (RT) varia- bility in the ADHD group during task performance (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2003; Valko et al., 2010), although Valko et al. (2010) found this deﬁcit only in adult but not in pediatric patients.
sentences.s190: Contrary, only children but not adults with ADHD made more duration discrimination errors than age-matched controls (Valko et al., 2010).
sentences.s191: Regarding age groups, impaired duration discrimina- tion was reported in children (Gooch et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Rubia et al., 2003, 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003; Valko et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2007), adolescents (Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a) and adults (Marx et al., 2010; Valko et al., 2010) with ADHD.
sentences.s192: Regarding modality, participants with ADHD showed impaired performance in both auditory (Gooch et al., 2011; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), visual (Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Rubia et al., 2003, 2007; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Valko et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2007), and audio–visual (Smith et al., 2002) duration discrimination tasks.
sentences.s193: Interval scale-wise, impaired discrimination was observed among participants with ADHD both within the sub-second range (Huang et al., 2012; Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Valko et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2007), the second range, where intervals differed by several hundreds of milliseconds (Gooch et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Rubia et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2012; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Yang et al., 2007), and supra-second (Rubia et al., 2003) standard intervals.
sentences.s194: In the same auditory unﬁlled interval discrimination task, Radonovich and Mostofsky (2004) found higher discrimination thresholds among children with ADHD for the 4 s standard, but not for the 550 ms standard conditions (see Table 2).
sentences.s195: In conclusion, this review of the studies on duration discrimi- nation in ADHD indicates that the temporal resolution required to distinguish stimuli of different durations is consistently lower in individuals with ADHD than in typically developing controls.
sentences.s196: This impairment seems to be an intrinsic timing abnormality, and has been shown to remain unaffected by differences in IQ (Rubia et al., 1999a; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), which is frequently lower among individuals with ADHD (Bridgett & Walker, 2006), as well as by verbal and visual working memory deﬁcits (Yang et al., 2007).
sentences.s197: However, two studies found that working memory measures signiﬁcantly predicted the duration discrimination thresholds of ADHD patients (Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a).
sentences.s198: It is thus possible that working memory, which is required for the temporary storage and retrieval of the interval length for stimuli comparison, may at least partly be responsible for the lower duration discrimination thresholds among individuals with ADHD (see Section 5.2).
sentences.s199: Furthermore, duration discrimination errors were found to corre- late positively with the coefﬁcient of variance and premature responding across a battery of computerised executive function tasks (Rubia et al., 2007).
sentences.s200: Increased frequency of premature responding may increase the noise level in the data, resulting in higher discrimination thresholds in the ADHD groups.
sentences.s201: In addition, premature responding itself can be regarded as a timing deﬁcit at the motor level, suggesting that motor and perceptual timing deﬁcits in ADHD are inter-correlated.
sentences.s202: More research is thus required to assess how much variance of the duration discrimina- tion thresholds and errors can be attributed to working memory and inhibition differences between the ADHD and control groups.

sentences.s209: Duration reproduction Since one of the ﬁrst studies of perceptual timing deﬁcits in ADHD used a duration reproduction paradigm (Barkley, Koplowitz, Anderson, & McMurray, 1997), this task became the most commonly replicated timing paradigm in ADHD research (see Table 2).
sentences.s210: Thus, twenty one studies explored group differences in duration reproduction between participants with ADHD and healthy controls (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001b; Barkley, Murphy, & Bush, 2001a; Bauermeister et al., 2005; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Gooch et al., 2011; Hurks and Hendriksen, 2010; Huang et al., 2012; Hwang, Gau, Hsu, & Wu, 2010; Kerns, McInerney, & Wilde, 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003; Mullins, Bellgrove, Gill, & Robertson, 2005; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Rommelse, Oosterlaan, Buitelaar, Faraone, & Sergeant, 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003 (two experiments); Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000).
sentences.s211: The most consistent ﬁnding is that of decreased reproduction accuracy (Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003), higher absolute discrepancy scores (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001a, 2001b; Bauermeister et al., 2005; Gooch et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2010; Kerns et al., 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Rommelse et al., 2007; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000), and increased SDintra of reproduced intervals in ADHD patients relative to controls (Mullins et al., 2005; Toplak et al., 2003; Valko et al., 2010) (see Table 2).
sentences.s212: Abnormal duration reproduction in ADHD was observed in all age groups: in children (Barkley et al., 1997; Bauermeister et al., 2005; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Gooch et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Kerns et al., 2001; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Rommelse et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000), adolescents (Barkley et al., 2001b; Hwang et al., 2010; Marx et al., 2010; Toplak et al., 2003) and adults with ADHD (Barkley et al., 2001a; Marx et al., 2010).
sentences.s213: However, Valko et al. (2010) found higher absolute discrepancy scores among children with ADHD, but no reproduction deﬁcits in the adult ADHD group.
sentences.s214: Most of the studies reporting signiﬁcant group differences used the visual modality (Barkley et al., 1997; Bauermeister et al., 2005; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Gooch et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2010; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Kerns et al., 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Rommelse et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2002; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000), however, group differences were also observed in amodal (i.e., empty intervals with verbal onset and offset) (Barkley et al., 2001a, 2001b), auditory (Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Rommelse et al., 2007; Toplak et al., 2003; West et al., 2000), and audio–visual (Plummer & Humphrey, 2009) versions of the duration reproduction task.
sentences.s215: Participants with ADHD dif- fered from healthy controls in the reproduction of a broad range of intervals, from 500 ms (West et al., 2000) to 90 s (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010).
sentences.s216: However, rather consistently, ﬁve studies found signiﬁcantly higher reproduction errors in the ADHD group only for the relatively longer intervals: 5 s vs. 12–17 s (Hwang et al., 2010), 2–24 s vs. 36–48 s (Marx et al., 2010), 3–12 s vs. 15–90 s (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010), 3 s vs. 5–45 s (Huang et al., 2012), and 2–12 s vs. 15–60 s (Barkley et al., 2001a) (see Table 2).
sentences.s217: Phenomenological observations suggest that subjective time is running faster for individuals with ADHD, and a characteristic response of a child with ADHD after for example a 14 min task might be ‘‘Oh!
sentences.s218: That took 3 hours!’’ (McGee, Brodeur, Symons, Andrade, & Fahie, 2004, p. 488).
sentences.s219: Such reports are consistent with neurocognitive evidence, as the studies reporting duration under-reproduction among participants with ADHD compared to typical controls (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001a; Huang et al., 2012; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Kerns et al., 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2002; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000) considerably outnumber the studies reporting dura- tion over-reproduction in the ADHD group (Barkley et al., 1997; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Toplak et al., 2003; West et al., 2000).
sentences.s220: Other studies, however, did not ﬁnd directional differences or report inconsistent results (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001a; Huang et al., 2012; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Marx et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s221: For example, Barkley et al. (1997) reported that compared to typical controls children with ADHD over-reproduced shorter 12 s and 24 s durations, but under-reproduced longer 48 s and 60 s durations, and were precise in reproduction of the middle 36 s interval.
sentences.s222: Nevertheless, the majority of studies conﬁrm that indi- viduals with ADHD tend to reproduce intervals shorter than the standard durations, described as ‘‘duration underestimation’’ (e.g., Kerns et al., 2001; Mullins et al., 2005; West et al., 2000); however, given that production is negatively correlated with duration estimation (Bindra & Waksberg, 1956), underproduction would be equivalent to overestimation in duration reproduction tasks.
sentences.s223: For example, participants with ADHD may perceive a 10 s standard interval to ﬁnish in 8 s, suggesting they are counting faster, and would hence overestimate a given 8 s interval as 10 s.
sentences.s224: That is, an interval may seem to contain more seconds than it actually has for individuals with ADHD (if they count faster for example), suggesting that internal time runs faster for them than it does for typically developing individuals, which would result in a subjectively elongated time sense (the external passage of time would appear longer to them).
sentences.s225: One could argue that duration under-reproduction can be confounded by diminished general intelligence (Bridgett & Walker, 2006) and decreased working memory capacity in ADHD (Dige, Maahr, & Backenroth-Ohsako, 2010; Westerberg, Hirvikoski, Forssberg, & Klingberg, 2004; Willcutt et al., 2005).
sentences.s226: In fact, several studies showed that the full-scale IQ is a signiﬁcant predictor of the duration reproduction performance among parti- cipants with ADHD (Toplak et al., 2003) and that duration reproduction differences between the ADHD and control groups disappeared after controlling for IQ and working memory scores (Smith et al., 2002) (see Section 5.1).
sentences.s227: However, lower IQ scores alone do not seem to fully explain an abnormal duration repro- duction, as evidenced by two other ADHD studies that found no impact of IQ scores on duration reproduction (Barkeley et al., 2001a; Rommelse et al., 2007).
sentences.s228: Given that a standard interval cannot be reproduced accu- rately if it is not remembered precisely, working memory might be a crucial confound.
sentences.s229: Indeed, several studies of reproduction tasks in ADHD have reported signiﬁcant correlations between working memory measures and duration reproduction perfor- mance (McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Toplak et al., 2003 (Experiment 1)), or showed that working memory scores signiﬁcantly pre- dicted duration reproduction errors (Bauermeister et al., 2005).
sentences.s230: One study found no signiﬁcant correlation between the total time reproduction error and working memory measures when children with ADHD and typical controls were taken together (Kerns et al., 2001); however, it was not reported if a correlation would have been signiﬁcant in a within-group analysis.
sentences.s231: Overall, the available evidence suggests that abnormal duration reproduction might be partially caused by lower IQ and working memory scores, which should be carefully assessed and their inﬂuence statisti- cally analyzed in future studies comparing duration reproduction between ADHD and control groups.
sentences.s232: Duration underreproduction has been also associated with impulsiveness and been suggested to reﬂect an enhanced internal clock leading to faster reproduction (Rubia et al., 1997) (for a detailed discussion and modelling of duration reproduction tasks in the framework of scalar expectancy theory, see Wearden, 2003); however, it might also be partially explained by modulation of perceptual timing by other neurocognitive functions.
sentences.s233: For instance, one reason why participants with ADHD may under-reproduce intervals could be motivation-modulated delay aversion: a shorter reproduction would ﬁnish the task earlier.
sentences.s234: In line with this, Sonuga-Barke et al. (1992) showed that children with ADHD are more concerned how to reduce the delay than how to maximise the reward amount in a delay discounting task (2 s vs. 30 s).
sentences.s235: McInerney and Kerns (2003) used a rewarded duration reproduc- tion task and found that performance of their ADHD group became more accurate when a reward was expected, although the patient group still made larger timing errors than the control group.
sentences.s236: Interestingly, the self-reported motivation scores did not differ between the groups and did not predict duration reproduction errors (McInerney & Kerns, 2003).
sentences.s237: Alternatively, duration under- reproduction in ADHD might depend on the inability to inhibit premature responses, as waiting for the motor response till the temporal interval of several seconds has elapsed may require some degree of self-inhibitory skills, which are well established to be impaired in ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2005).
sentences.s238: The suggested hypotheses of duration under-reproduction being modulated by delay aver- sion, premature responding or working memory should therefore be tested directly in future studies.
sentences.s239: To conclude, it is rather impressive that almost all studies that used duration reproduction tasks found signiﬁcant timing abnorm- alities in the ADHD groups, with the exception of only one study that found a trend only for the longer 12 s interval after controlling for IQ and working memory scores (Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s240: Notably, it is unclear whether deﬁcits in temporal reproduction measure pure temporal abilities.
sentences.s241: Performance in the duration reproduction task depends on several neuro-cognitive functions, not only time estima- tion, but also most prominently working memory to hold the temporal information online for reproduction and sustained atten- tion to the time interval to be reproduced—both of which have been shown to be consistently impaired in ADHD (Cubillo et al., 2012; Rubia, 2011; Toplak et al., 2006; Willcutt et al., 2005).
sentences.s242: It is possible that this combination of several impairments makes the duration reproduction task such a sensitive test for differentiating between ADHD participants and healthy controls (see Table 2). 4.2.3.
sentences.s243: Duration production and estimation Four studies investigated duration production in participants with ADHD (Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; McGee et al., 2004; Rommelse et al., 2008) and three of them reported duration underproduction in ADHD compared to control groups (Huang et al., 2012; Marx et al., 2010; Rommelse et al., 2008).
sentences.s244: Huang et al. (2012) found higher absolute discrepancy scores and lower accuracy coefﬁcients (reﬂecting duration underproduction) for production of 6 s, 12 s and 24 s intervals in children with ADHD when compared to healthy controls, but there were no group differences in the production of 1 s and 3 s intervals.
sentences.s245: Similarly, Marx et al. (2010) reported that compared to the typically developing controls, participants with ADHD underproduced 6–48 s intervals, but once again there were no group differences in the shortest 2 s condition.
sentences.s246: The same ﬁndings applied to children, adolescents and adults.
sentences.s247: It thus seems that individuals with ADHD have impaired production of duration only for inter- vals lasting longer than 3 s.
sentences.s248: However this is not always reported, as for example McGee et al. (2004) found no signiﬁcant group differences in either of the two versions (active and passive) of the 30 s production tasks, whereas Rommelse et al. (2008) reported underproduction of 1 s intervals among participants with ADHD (see Table 2).
sentences.s249: Much less consistent group differences are reported in studies of retrospective verbal duration estimation.
sentences.s250: Three studies found signiﬁcantly higher retrospective overestimation of supra-second (Barkley et al., 2001a; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010) and supra- minute (McGee et al., 2004) intervals among individuals with ADHD compared to typical controls.
sentences.s251: These reports of underproduc- tion in time production and overestimation in time estimation are consistent with studies showing duration under-reproduction (which corresponds to duration overestimation) in participants with ADHD (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001a; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2012; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Kerns et al., 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2002; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000) and are in line with the hypothesis of a faster internal clock or an elongated subjective sense of the passage of time in ADHD patients (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2009a).
sentences.s252: A faster internal clock would be associated with faster counting, leading to overestimation of time intervals that need to be estimated and an under(re)production of intervals that need to be (re)produced.
sentences.s253: However, four other duration estimation studies found no group differences in the retrospective duration estimation in children (Bauermeister et al., 2005; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003; Smith et al., 2002) and adolescents with ADHD (Barkley et al., 2001b), using either amodal (Barkley et al., 2001b; Smith et al., 2002) or visual (Bauermeister et al., 2005; Meaux & Chelonis, 2003) interval presentations (see Table 2).
sentences.s254: To conclude, even though duration estimation studies did not yield consistent ﬁndings, the studies of duration discrimination, reproduction, and production provide consistent evidence for impaired perceptual timing in ADHD.
sentences.s255: Arguably, rather than aiming at a simple replication of duration discrimination or reproduction abnormalities, future studies using duration discrimination and reproduction tasks should focus on more complex underlying questions, such as how these timing impairments interact with other cognitive functions that are impaired in the disorder (e.g., Toplak et al., 2003), whether the timing abnormalities can be regarded as a candidate endophenotype for ADHD (e.g., Rommelse et al., 2007), or the nature of the neural mechanisms underlying abnormal perceptual timing in ADHD (e.g., Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith, Taylor, Brammer, Halari, & Rubia, 2008; Smith et al., 2012). 4.3.

sentences.s264: Age-wise, most of the studies which found group differences tested children (Antrop et al., 2006; Bitsakou et al., 2009; Kuntsi et al., 2001; Marco et al., 2009; Rapport et al., 1986; Sagvolden et al., 1998; Scheres et al., 2010; Schweitzer & Sulzer-Azaroff, 1995; Solanto et al., 2001; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992 (Experiment 2); Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s265: However, Barkley et al. (2001b) reported differences in the steepness of delay discounting function among adolescent participants with ADHD and typical controls.
sentences.s266: Marco et al. (2009) compared ADHD and control groups across three age groups (children, adolescents and adults) in the delay discounting task, and found rather small effects size of the reward bias difference between adolescent groups compared to children and adult groups.
sentences.s267: Finally, Hoogman et al. (2011) conﬁrmed impaired delay discounting in adult participants with ADHD.
sentences.s268: In addition, they investigated possible effects of the NOS1 gene which is known to be linked with impulsivity, and found that participants with ADHD who had the short-short genotype of the NOS1 exon 1f- VNTR chose more immediate rewards than ADHD participants with short-long or long-long genotype.
sentences.s269: The same genetic differ- ence was not found among control participants.
sentences.s270: In conclusion, there is consistent evidence that individuals with ADHD are impaired in delay discounting paradigms, suggesting problems with temporal foresight and inter-temporal bridging and choice behaviour (see Table 3).
