sentences.s281: Interaction between timing and other neurocognitive functions in ADHD 5.1.
sentences.s282: Timing and general intelligence The link between IQ and abnormal timing functions in ADHD, as reviewed in Section 4, is not suprising given that measures of perceptual timing vary with IQ scores (Wearden, Wearden, & Rabbitt, 1997), and that IQ tends to be lower in individuals with ADHD than in the age-matched typical controls (Bridgett & Walker, 2006; Kuntsi et al., 2004).
sentences.s283: Indeed, such a link has been demonstrated in perceptual timing and temporal foresight stu- dies, including duration reproduction (Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003), estimation (Barkeley et al., 2001a), and delay discounting (Marco et al., 2009) tasks.
sentences.s284: In particular, Smith et al. (2002) reported that a signiﬁcant under-reproduction of 12 s intervals in children with ADHD only survived at a trend-level after controlling for working memory and IQ scores.
sentences.s285: Interestingly, IQ did not inﬂuence the increased duration discrimination thresh- olds (lower sensitivity) in the ADHD group (Smith et al., 2002), suggesting that that lower IQ scores in ADHD group might have more impact on perceptual timing in the range of several seconds than sub-seconds.
sentences.s286: However, Toplak et al. (2003) showed that reproduction of 400 ms intervals is also signiﬁcantly associated with the full-scale IQ scores in the group of participants with ADHD.
sentences.s287: Barkeley et al. (2001a) reported that between-group differences in the raw scores of the estimation task lost signiﬁ- cance after controlling for IQ, whereas reproduction of intervals was not inﬂuenced by IQ scores, contradicting other reports from duration reproduction studies (Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s288: Furthermore, a large number of studies did not ﬁnd IQ scores to affect or be associated with timing functions in such tasks as free and synchronised motor tapping (Rubia et al., 1999a), duration discrimination (Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Rubia et al., 1999a; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), duration reproduction (Rommelse et al., 2007), and sensorimotor anticipation (Rubia et al., 1999a).
sentences.s289: Two delay discounting studies reported that differences in delay aversion between ADHD and control groups remained signiﬁcant after controlling for IQ (Bitsakou et al., 2009; Kuntsi et al., 2001).
sentences.s290: Overall, IQ seems to mediate speciﬁc abnormalities of timing functions, in particular reproduction of temporal intervals, but this is not consistently observed.
sentences.s291: Unfortunately, none of the reviewed studies aimed to identify how exactly IQ is linked to abnormal timing functions, such as through misunderstanding of verbal instructions (verbal IQ), performance-related inattention (performance IQ), or some other pathways, such as mathematical thinking or achievement motivation (Gut, Heckmann, Meyer, Schmid, & Grob, 2012). 5.2.
sentences.s292: Timing and working memory Working memory is a necessary basis function for perfor- mance in those perceptual timing tasks where the judgement of one temporal interval depends on another previously presented interval to be held in working memory, which is particularly the case in reproduction tasks but may also apply to duration discrimination tasks.
sentences.s293: The load on working memory is substan- tially higher for longer intervals of several seconds or minutes than for shorter intervals in the millisecond’s range up to 2–3 s that can be perceived immediately, as the latter falls within the so-called subjective ‘now’ (Poeppel, 1978).
sentences.s294: Intervals that last more than 2–3 s need to be remembered and hence load on working memory (Poeppel, 1978).
sentences.s295: Accordingly, the majority of studies that tested this link showed that working memory is associated with duration discrimination and duration reproduc- tion tasks in ADHD (Bauermeister et al., 2005; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Yang et al., 2007, but see Kerns et al., 2001 for a negative ﬁnding for duration reproduction).
sentences.s296: Regarding speciﬁc associa- tions, working memory scores were found to correlate with the thresholds in duration discrimination task (Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Yang et al., 2007), as well as absolute discrepancy scores (Bauermeister et al., 2005) and mean produced intervals (Toplak et al., 2003) in duration reproduction tasks.
sentences.s297: Working memory measures were also found to signiﬁcantly predict duration dis- crimination thresholds (Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a) and absolute discrepancy scores in duration reproduction tasks (McInerney & Kerns, 2003).
sentences.s298: These ﬁndings seem to suggest that duration discrimination and reproduction abnormalities in ADHD may not reﬂect an exclusively timing deﬁcit, but may be confounded by working memory deﬁcits.
sentences.s299: However, the causality of the association is unclear.
sentences.s300: Timing models, such as the scalar expectancy theory, assume that the reference memory of a standard duration and the working memory of a probe duration are an intrinsic part of a neurocognitive clock (e.g., Wearden & Lejeune, 2008; Wearden & Bray, 2001), which would suggest that the association between working memory and perceptual timing in ADHD might reﬂect an impairment of a speciﬁc memory- related part of the internal clock.
sentences.s301: Alternatively, there is evidence that neural mechanisms that mediate timing (see Section 3.2) overlap with neural mechanisms of working memory (Fuster, 2000), which would suggest a shared neurofunctional basis.
sentences.s302: At present, these hypotheses remain speculative and require more research. 5.3.
sentences.s303: Timing and attention Attention to the temporal intervals to be discriminated, estimated or reproduced is another important basis function crucial for performing well on perceptual timing tasks (Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004).
sentences.s304: Three studies have tested the interaction between performance in duration reproduction and attention tasks (Barkley et al., 1997; Kerns et al., 2001; Mullins et al., 2005) and reported signiﬁcant positive ﬁndings.
sentences.s305: Three other studies reported that clinical ADHD symptoms of inattention are signiﬁcantly associated with decreased performance in duration discrimination (Gooch et al., 2011) and reproduction (Bauermeister et al., 2005; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010) tasks.
sentences.s306: Barkley et al. (1997) found that distraction during a duration reproduction task increased the magnitude of performance errors among children with ADHD but not among typical controls, which suggests that the allocation of attentional resources to time is more vulnerable in ADHD.
sentences.s307: Mullins et al. (2005) reported that total errors and response variability in the sustained attention to response task correlated with the SDintra of the error direction in the duration reproduction task.
sentences.s308: Kerns et al. (2001) reported that time reproduction errors correlated positively with omission errors in the Go/NoGo task and with d-prime, a measure of inattentiveness, in Conner’s continuous performance task (CPT) when ADHD and control children were grouped together.
sentences.s309: Con- trary to duration reproduction ﬁndings, no association was found between deﬁcits in the CPT and time discrimination errors (Rubia et al., 2007).
sentences.s310: Regarding behavioural attention as measured in behavioural questionnaires, performance in the relatively long lasting free tapping, synchronised tapping, and sensorimotor anticipation tasks but not in the duration discrimination task with a short individual trial duration correlated with the attention scales of the Teacher Rating Form and the Child Behaviour Checklist (Rubia et al., 1999a).
sentences.s311: These ﬁndings suggest that the inﬂuence of attention to time increases in ADHD with the increasing length of intervals during which attentional resources must be allocated to monitor stimuli and task performance.
sentences.s312: If so, the presumably reduced temporal span of attention in ADHD may be associated with and confound with timing errors when relatively long intervals are being probed. 5.4.
sentences.s313: Timing and inhibition Although these two functions are likely to be uncorrelated in the healthy population, there is some evidence that timing function deﬁcits in ADHD may be associated with inhibitory control deﬁcits that are closely associated with impulsiveness and one of the key impairments in ADHD (Cubillo et al., 2012; Rubia, 2011; Willcutt et al., 2005).
sentences.s314: Poor inhibitory control may in particular impinge upon tasks where the time interval needs to be indicated by a motor response, since a premature and impulsive response style could potentially account for underproduced or underreproduced temporal intervals.
sentences.s315: For example, children with ADHD may have problems with inhibiting their motor response until the correct time interval has elapsed.
sentences.s316: In fact, Kerns et al. (2001) found that duration reproduction errors correlated posi- tively with and were predicted by commission errors in the Go/NoGo task.
sentences.s317: Similarly, the speed of inhibitory control as measured in a stop signal task was found to predict duration reproduction errors in both children with ADHD and typical controls (McInerney & Kerns, 2003) and both the commission errors in the Go/NoGo task and the stop signal RT were correlated with time discrimination errors (Rubia et al., 2007).
sentences.s318: It is thus possible that speciﬁc timing deﬁcits in ADHD, such as in parti- cular duration under-reproduction, are associated with impulsive responding due to a lack of inhibitory control, impinging upon their perceptual judgement of temporal intervals.
sentences.s319: Likewise, pre- mature responding was also correlated with time discrimination errors, suggesting that inhibition-related motor timing deﬁcits impinge upon time estimation in ADHD (Rubia et al., 2007).
sentences.s320: In conclusion, timing deﬁcits in ADHD patients appear to be associated with other deﬁcits in executive functions, in particular with working memory (for temporal discrimination and repro- duction tasks), but also with attention and to a minor degree with their deﬁcits in inhibitory control during a reproduction task.
sentences.s321: However, ﬁndings have not always been consistent and the interrelationship between timing and executive functions in ADHD needs to be further investigated. 5.5.
sentences.s322: Timing and clinical behavioural measures of ADHD Not only ADHD, but also other impulsive disorders, such as bipolar disorder or alcohol and substance abuse, have been reported to show abnormal timing functions, suggesting that there might be a more direct link between timing and behavioural impulsivity (Rubia et al., 2009a; Wittmann & Paulus, 2008).
sentences.s323: In fact, an association between timing impairments in ADHD and their clinical severity measures of hyperactive-impulsive beha- viour traits has been found in studies using duration discrimina- tion (Rubia et al., 2007; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), duration reproduction (Toplak et al., 2003), duration estimation (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010), delay discounting (Scheres et al., 2010; Solanto et al., 2001), and the inter-temporal choice gambling tasks (Toplak et al., 2005).
sentences.s324: Two other reports, however, did not ﬁnd a signiﬁcant association between hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms and performance in duration discrimination (Gooch et al., 2011) and reproduction (Bauermeister et al., 2005) tasks.
sentences.s325: There is furthermore evidence that hyperactivity/impulsivity as well as inattention scores may have a different association with timing functions in ADHD and control groups (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a).
sentences.s326: Thus, duration discrimination thresholds correlated with hyperactive/impulsive ratings only in the adolescent ADHD group, whereas inattention ratings correlated with discrimination thresholds only in the control group (Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), suggesting that percep- tual timing may be mediated by different cognitive functions in individuals with ADHD and typical controls.
sentences.s327: The ﬁndings are in line with the notion that impulsiveness in ADHD might account for their timing deﬁcits, while in the healthy population poor attention appears to be associated with deﬁcits in timing tasks.
sentences.s328: To conclude, of the different ADHD behavioural symptoms, impulsivity in particular seems to be associated with both perceptual timing and temporal foresight functions in ADHD, as evidenced by a wide range of timing tasks, reinforcing the theory that impulsiveness and timing deﬁcits are closely interconnected in ADHD. 6.
sentences.s329: Neural mechanisms of timing abnormalities in ADHD Considering that there is consistent evidence for deﬁcits in ADHD patients in a range of timing processes it is surprising that relatively few fMRI studies in ADHD have focused on these functions (see Table 4 and Fig. 2). 6.1.
sentences.s331: Sensorimotor synchronisation of milliseconds Several fMRI studies have compared ADHD patients and controls during sensorimotor synchronisation of short intervals in the milliseconds range.
sentences.s332: An early study found relatively small differences between seven ADHD patients and nine healthy boys during comparable performance in a sensorimotor synchronisa- tion task of 600 ms in occipital regions, which were enhanced in control boys in lateral parts, while medial parts were increased in ADHD patients (Rubia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s333: A fMRI study requiring free sequential ﬁnger sequencing with the right or left hand in 11 ADHD patients and controls (which resulted on average in an equivalent speed of 600 ms rhythms for both groups) found no performance deﬁcits but reduced activation in ADHD relative to healthy control boys in right inferior and superior parietal lobes in a whole brain analysis (Mostofsky et al., 2006).
sentences.s334: An additional region of interest analysis found reduced activation in the con- tralateral premotor cortex (Mostofsky et al., 2006).
sentences.s335: The right parietal cortex is important for somatotopic imagery and spatial attention to time (Posner & Petersen, 1990) and is also crucial to integrate visual and somatosensory information that is important for timing of movement representations (Danckert et al., 2002).
sentences.s336: The ﬁndings suggest abnormalities in ADHD in basic pre- motor fronto-parietal connections that are integral for visual- spatial timing of patterned sequential movement and rhythm production.
sentences.s337: A later fMRI study by Valera et al. (2010) compared 21 ADHD male and female adults with healthy controls in the cued and uncued sensorimotor synchronisation tasks.
sentences.s338: During both tasks, ADHD adults relative to controls showed enhanced intraindivi- dual response variability and decreased activation in typical areas of sub-second sensorimotor synchronisation including IFC and OFC, precentral gyrus, insula and cerebellum (Wiener et al., 2010), with however laterality differences across conditions (see Table 4).

sentences.s344: Sensorimotor synchronisation of seconds Two fMRI studies have tested for differences between ADHD and control boys in sensorimotor synchronisation tasks of second intervals.
sentences.s345: In our early study we contrasted motor synchronisation to a visual stimulus of a short delay condition of 600 ms with synchronisation to a long delay condition of 5 s (delay task) between seven ADHD patients and nine healthy controls (Rubia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s346: Despite comparable performance, during the long delayed synchronisation condition, ADHD children relative to healthy control boys showed reduced activation in the key areas of motor timing (Rubia & Smith, 2004; Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010) in anterior and posterior cingulate and pre-SMA, but enhanced activation in a more posterior part of the SMA (Rubia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s347: The ﬁndings suggest problems with typical medial frontal neural networks of stimulus anticipation and motor timing in anterior cingulate and SMA, while the reduced activa- tion in medial parietal areas was more likely related to deﬁcits with attention to time.
sentences.s348: In a more recent study, a parametrically modiﬁed sensorimotor vigilance task was used, which contrasted motor responses to series of high-frequent stimuli appearing with a predictable delay of 500 ms, triggering sensorimotor synchro- nisation, with neural responses to stimuli appearing in rare and unpredictable variable delay conditions of either 2 s, 5 s and 8 s, interspersed within the series of the high frequent short delays (Christakou et al., in press).
sentences.s349: Participants had to respond as fast as possible to all stimuli, which in the unpredictable long delays required increasing vigilance for the three progressively longer delay conditions relative to the predictable short delays, thus providing a parametrically increased load of sensorimotor antici- pation and vigilance.
sentences.s350: ADHD patients relative to controls showed reduced activation in left DLPFC, bilateral putamen and thalamus, the left pre- and postcentral gyrus, and the superior parietal regions, which in controls but not ADHD patients were progres- sively more activated with increasing delays and vigilance load (Christakou et al., in press).
sentences.s351: The deﬁcits in left DLPFC furthermore were associated with enhanced intraindividual response varia- bility in patients, thought to reﬂect poor concentration and poor stimulus anticipation (Rubia et al., 2003).
sentences.s352: The ﬁndings thus suggest that ADHD patients have deﬁcits in a contralateral fronto- premotor and striato-thalamic networks of stimulus anticipation and vigilance.
sentences.s353: The contralateral reduced prefrontal activation likely reﬂects problems with motor timing and anticipation of a right handed motor response, while the superior parietal activa- tion is more likely to reﬂect visual-spatial attention to time (Rubia, 2006).
sentences.s354: In addition, ADHD patients relative to controls had problems with deactivation of the default mode network in precuneus, which was progressively more deactivated in healthy controls but not ADHD patients with increasing delay.
sentences.s355: The default mode network is thought to reﬂect task-unrelated thoughts and is progressively deactivated with increasing load of attention (Greicius, Krasnow, Reiss, & Menon, 2003).
sentences.s356: Problem to deactivate the default mode network is characteristic of ADHD, and has been associated with attention lapses and poorer concentration (Broyd et al., 2009; Sonuga-Barke & Castellanos, 2007).

sentences.s363: Duration discrimination of milliseconds Four fMRI studies have tested the neural substrates of duration discrimination in patients with ADHD (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012; Vloet et al., 2010).
sentences.s364: Three studies from our lab tested the ability to discriminate time intervals of 1 s length, that differed by 300 ms, 400 ms or 500 ms (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012).
sentences.s365: In the ﬁrst study we found that 21 medication- naı¨ve ADHD boys showed reduced activation relative to 17 healthy control boys in the two key areas that are most prominently activated during duration discrimination in the seconds range across a meta-analysis of time perception tasks (Wiener et al., 2010), i.e., in right DLPFC and SMA (Smith et al., 2008).
sentences.s366: Further- more both the DLPFC and ACC/SMA activation clusters that were reduced in ADHD patients were also associated with duration discrimination errors, which, however, were only marginally reduced in ADHD patients.
sentences.s367: The second study was conducted in a smaller sample of 12 medication-naı¨ve patients with ADHD.

(2008).
sentences.s373: In addition, we also tested for effects of methylphe- nidate (MPH) in two of these studies and found that this psychos- timulant normalised all brain deﬁcits that were observed in ADHD boys under placebo (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s374: Furthermore, in one of these studies the non-stimulant medication of Atomoxetine was also tested but showed only normalisation effects on right inferior frontal underactivation, (i.e., the under- activation in ADHD relative to controls was no longer observed when they were under Atomoxetine) (Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s375: The ﬁnding of normalisation with psychostimulants of all areas of underactivation in two fMRI studies of time discrimination is relatively unique compared to ﬁndings of only partial normal- isation of typical underactivation in fronto-striatal areas in the context of other, cognitive control tasks (Rubia et al., 2001b, 2009b, 2011a, 2011b).
sentences.s376: The ﬁndings are in line with the strong association between dopamine and perceptual timing (Rammsayer, 1993; Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004) and potentially suggest that psychostimulant medication may have a stronger effect on timing network deﬁcits in ADHD than other network deﬁcits associated with more noradrenergically or serotoninergically innervated func- tions such as attention, inhibition and reward-related processes Fig. 2. fMRI studies showing underactivation in ADHD patients relative to healthy controls during different timing tasks.

sentences.s382: ADHD patients had reduced activation in rostral anterior cingulate and posterior left cerebellum, with an additional superior frontal underactivation in relation to the more difﬁcult duration discrimination condition.
sentences.s383: All ﬁndings survived covariance for performance and working memory, suggesting that the neural differences are truly related to brain abnormalities in ADHD during duration discrimination (Vloet et al., 2010).
sentences.s384: The underactivation ﬁndings in IFC and cerebellum areas are relatively consistent with those observed in the ﬁrst three studies, suggesting that duration discrimination of milliseconds in ADHD is associated with abnor- mally reduced activation in typical brain areas of sub-second time discrimination in the lateral prefrontal cortex, ACC/SMA and cerebellum (Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s385: Furthermore there is evidence that the abnormalities affect neural networks rather than isolated brain regions, as two of these studies found that ADHD patients had reduced functional inter-regional connectivity between the affected areas, i.e., between IFC and cerebellum and between IFC and ACC/SMA, suggesting abnormal fronto-cingulate and fronto-cerebellar neural networks of time perception rather than isolated areas (Vloet et al., 2010) (see Table 4). 6.2.2.
sentences.s386: Mismatch negativity response to duration deviance Several ADHD studies have used a mismatch negativity (MMN) paradigm to investigate pre-attentive sensory timing in the auditory modality (Huttunen, Halonen, Kaartinen, & Lyytinen, 2007; Huttunen-Scott, Kaartinen, Tolvanen, & Lyytinen, 2008).
sentences.s387: MMN is an event-related potential (ERP), indexing the detection of auditory stimuli that deviate in the length of time they are displayed for, such as shorter lasting sounds, in a sequence of standard stimuli of the same temporal length (e.g., N¨a¨at¨anen, Syssoeva, & Takegata, 2004).
sentences.s388: The MMN response, as measured by electroencephalography (EEG), is generated in the early auditory cortex, although its frontal modulation cannot be excluded (Alho, 1995; Opitz, Rinne, Mecklinger, Cramon, & Schr¨oger, 2002).
sentences.s389: Huttunen et al. (2007) investigated MMN responses to shorter deviating sounds (30 ms or 50 ms) in a stream of longer sounds (100 ms), and found no difference in MMN amplitude or latency between healthy children, children with reading disability, and children with attention deﬁcit (AD) as screened by the Conners’ scales (Goyette, Conners, & Ulrich, 1978).
sentences.s390: Reanalysis of the data with a separation of the fourth comorbid group of children with both reading disability and AD revealed that MMN responses peaked earlier in the AD group compared to the control group (Huttunen-Scott et al., 2008), which points to a more efﬁcient rather than impaired sensory timing in individuals with AD.
sentences.s391: These studies suggest that abnormal perceptual timing in ADHD is not due to impaired sensory processing.
sentences.s392: Furthemore, the psychostimulant MPH did not modulate the dipole strength of MMN responses to duration deviance in healthy individuals (Korostenskaja, Kicˇic´, & K¨ahk¨onen, 2008).
sentences.s393: This ﬁnding suggests that MPH which has been shown to improve several timing functions in ADHD (see Section 7), may not inﬂuence auditory timing in the sensory cortex where the MMN is generated, but other brain regions than the sensory cortices. 6.2.3.
sentences.s394: Reproduction of supra-second intervals The duration reproduction task, which is perhaps the most frequently used perceptual timing paradigm in ADHD studies, taps into two distinct phases of neurocognitive timing: duration encoding which takes place when a sensory stimulus is presented, and duration reproduction which depends on the accuracy of time encoding as well as on the working memory maintenance and attention to time.
sentences.s395: When the two phases of time reproduction task were compared in an event-related potential (ERP) study of reproduction of 2.5–5.5 s intervals, abnormal neuronal processing was observed in an ADHD group only during the duration reproduction phase in the 250–450 ms and 650–1000 ms time windows over frontal regions but not the duration estimation phase (Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008).
sentences.s396: The group differences in P300 and late negativity time window suggests that impaired memory of or sustained attention to temporal intervals rather than sensory encoding determines poor ADHD performance in duration reproduction experiments. 6.3.
sentences.s397: Temporal foresight Two recent fMRI studies have tested the neural correlates of delay discounting in ADHD patients.
sentences.s398: Our study was conducted in a relatively small sample of 10 ADHD patients compared to 10 healthy controls during a delay discounting task of temporal intervals of a week, a month, and 1 year.
sentences.s399: ADHD patients showed no differences in the steepness of their delay discounting func- tion, although the steepness of discounting correlated positively with the severity of their behavioural impulsiveness.
sentences.s400: However, ADHD patients deliberated relatively less during delayed choices than controls, who showed relatively longer deliberation times for delayed versus immediate choices, suggesting a decreased use of inter-temporal bridging time and thus presumably less fore- sighted delayed reward choices (Rubia et al., 2009b).
sentences.s401: In the fMRI data, ADHD patients had reduced activation during the delayed choices in regions that have previously been associated with temporal foresight (Christakou et al., 2011; Hariri et al., 2006; McClure et al., 2004; Wittmann, Leland, & Paulus, 2007), such as bilateral IFC, reaching into left OFC, the basal ganglia, inferior and medial parietal regions, and the cerebellum (Rubia et al., 2009b).
sentences.s402: All areas of underactivation correlated with the severity of ADHD symptoms while the underactivation in the cerebellum in parti- cular was associated with the delayed choice reaction time effect that was absent in ADHD patients.
sentences.s403: The OFC has been found to be crucial for reward-related decision making, in particular with respect to comparing future and immediate rewards in this and the related gambling task (Christakou et al., 2009, 2011; McClure et al., 2004).
sentences.s404: The IFC is a key area of sub-second and supra-second timing (Wiener et al., 2010) and is inversely associated with the steepness of delay discounting in adults (Wittmann et al., 2007) and progressively more recruited with more reﬂective perfor- mance in adults relative to adolescents (Christakou et al., 2011).
sentences.s405: The inferior and medial parietal regions are important for allocat- ing attention to time and quantity representations, and may thus contribute to inter-temporal choice in their role as magnitude comparators of both time and reward (McClure et al., 2004; Sandrini, Rossini, & Miniussi, 2004; Tanaka et al., 2004; Wittmann et al., 2007).
sentences.s406: The putamen is important for attention to time, in particular when comparing long with short intervals (Coull, 2004; Rubia et al., 1998).
sentences.s407: Although the cerebellum is considered a key area of sub-second timing in a recent meta- analysis of timing processes (Wiener et al., 2010), the meta- analysis did not include temporal processes beyond seconds such as discounting tasks of longer time periods.
sentences.s408: The cerebellum, however, has been found to be activated during delay discounting tasks (Christakou et al., 2011) and was the only region that correlated with deliberation time to delayed choices in the ADHD study (Rubia et al., 2009a), suggesting a direct role in the temporal perspective of the expected delayed gratiﬁcation.
sentences.s409: The functional interplay between these different brain regions may thus provide the combination of skills that are necessary to compare and then make an informed decision for delayed gratiﬁcation.
sentences.s410: Overall, the ﬁndings of reduced recruitment of this ventrolateral fronto-striato-parieto-cerebellar network in ADHD adolescents during delayed gratiﬁcation choices combined with the reduced use of reﬂection time – a typical impulsiveness feature – may be the neural substrate for the typically observed reduced temporal foresight mechanisms in ADHD.
sentences.s411: The study of Plichta et al. (2009) compared 14 ADHD adults and 12 healthy controls during delay discounting of 1 day, 2 weeks, and 4 weeks.
sentences.s412: The performance ﬁndings were opposite in adult ADHD than in our previous ADHD pediatric sample (Rubia et al., 2009a), in that in this study the deliberation time for delayed versus immediate choices was signiﬁcantly enhanced in ADHD versus controls (Plichta et al., 2009).
sentences.s413: Unfortunately the study was analysed with a region of interest approach in the basal ganglia and limbic regions, with particular focus on immediate choices, which is less relevant to the timing mechanisms of temporal foresight.
sentences.s414: ADHD patients showed reduced ventral stria- tum activation for all choices.
sentences.s415: In the caudate, however, ADHD patients showed reduced activation in the ventral part for immediate delay choices while they showed enhanced activation in the dorsal part for delayed choices, which furthermore corre- lated with symptom severity.
sentences.s416: The same was observed for the amygdala which was enhanced in ADHD patients for the delayed choices only.
sentences.s417: The abnormally enhanced amygdala and caudate response toward delayed rewards correlated with enhanced delay discounting, suggesting that the neural hyperactivity in ADHD most likely relates to a negative emotional response to the delayed reward option.
sentences.s418: The diminished hyporesponsiveness of the ventral striatum likely reﬂects a blunted responsiveness to rewards in ADHD (Scheres, Milham, Knutson, & Castellanos, 2007; Stroehle et al., 2008) (see Table 4). 6.4.
sentences.s419: Conclusions on brain dysfunctions in ADHD during timing performance In conclusion, ADHD patients appear to show brain function abnormalities in key areas for timing (see Table 4 and Fig. 2).
sentences.s420: A key deﬁcit of timing processes in ADHD is the abnormal recruit- ment of IFC and DLPFC, including SMA and ACC, which appears to be present across timing domains, including sub-second and supra-second motor timing, duration discrimination and tem- poral foresight (Christakou et al., in press; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012; Valera et al., 2010; Vloet et al., 2010).
sentences.s421: As mentioned before, the IFC in particular is a key area for both sub-second and supra-second timing processes (Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004; Wiener et al., 2010) and may hence be a key area of dysfunction in ADHD that may explain poor temporal performance in a variety of sub-second and supra- second timing processes.
sentences.s422: The IFC/DLPFC is also a key area of dysfunction in ADHD in the context of other cognitive tasks, in line with the notion that this important brain region subserves several cognitive functions, depending on its interconnections with other cortical and subcortical regions (Cubillo et al., 2012; Rubia, 2011).
sentences.s423: Another consistent ﬁnding across studies appears to be the reduced activation of the ACC reaching into the SMA, in particular during tasks of sub-second duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012; Vloet et al., 2010), although reduced activation in this region was also observed during sub-second motor timing (Rubia et al., 1999b), in line with the role of this region for sub-second motor and perceptual timing functions (Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s424: Other consistently under- activated regions are the posterior and medial parietal lobes, which were underfunctioning in particular during sub-second and supra-second motor timing (Christakou et al., in press; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Valera et al., 2010), in line with the role of the parietal lobe in sensorimotor integration and visual attention to time (Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s425: Parietal areas were also underactivated during temporal foresight, possibly reﬂecting attention to delayed gratiﬁcation (Rubia et al., 2009b).
sentences.s426: The basal ganglia were also implicated in several timing processes, includ- ing sub-second and supra-second motor timing (Christakou et al., in press; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Valera et al., 2010), but also duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012) and temporal foresight (Plichta et al., 2009; Rubia et al., 2009b), presumably reﬂecting reduced attention to time (Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s427: Lastly, the cerebellum was found to be reduced in activation during cued and uncued synchronised tapping (Valera et al., 2010), duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a; Vloet et al., 2010), temporal prediction of seconds (Durston et al., 2007) and in the context of temporal foresight of longer intervals.
sentences.s428: The cerebellum is one of the key areas of structural deﬁcits in ADHD patients (Valera, Faraone, Murray, & Seidman, 2007) and is also a key region for timing functions (Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s429: Although it is thought to be more implicated in sub-second timing processes such as sensorimotor synchronisation, free tapping or duration discrimination of milliseconds (Wiener et al., 2010), there is also evidence for its involvement in duration estimation of longer intervals and for temporal foresight (Christakou et al., 2011), in line with a role of cerebellum in interval timing and temporal prediction (Coull & Nobre, 2008; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s430: The functional brain imaging ﬁndings thus conﬁrm the notion that ADHD patients suffer from deﬁcits in temporal processes by showing that they have difﬁculties in the recruitment of the key areas that mediate these temporal processes.
sentences.s431: The ﬁndings show brain dysfunctions in ADHD patients in key regions of sub-second and supra-second timing, including the IFC, ACC and SMA, basal ganglia, parietal regions, and the cerebellum.
sentences.s432: Some limitations of the studies reviewed, however, need to be highlighted.
sentences.s433: With a few exceptions (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012) the majority of studies were conducted in previously medicated ADHD patients, which, given the strong positive association between dopamine agonists and timing processes, suggest that deﬁcit ﬁndings may perhaps be over- shadowed by long-term stimulant effects on brain function.
sentences.s434: Only two studies were in adult ADHD and so far little can be said about the progression of brain deﬁcits during timing processes in childhood ADHD into adult ADHD.
sentences.s435: Ideally, future studies should investigate medication naı¨ve patients and test for continuity of deﬁcits into adulthood in longitudinal studies.
sentences.s436: Another potential confound is comorbidity with antisocial behaviours such as conduct disorder, which is rarely controlled for in fMRI studies, but is likely to impact upon the deﬁcit ﬁndings (Rubia, 2011).
sentences.s437: Notably, while half of the fMRI studies of timing functions did not observe performance differences in ADHD patients (see Table 4), despite evidence for ofﬂine neurocognitive deﬁcits in these tasks (see Tables 1–3), it should be pointed out that fMRI studies are usually statistically underpowered to detect beha- vioural performance differences between groups, as typically sub- ject numbers are less than 20 in each group.
sentences.s438: In addition, fMRI adaptations of cognitive tasks lose behavioural sensitivity.
sentences.s439: In event-related fMRI task designs, for example, target trials have to be separated sufﬁciently from non-target trials in order to allow for separability of the haemodynamic response.
sentences.s440: This results in higher predictability of target stimuli compared to ofﬂine task versions.
sentences.s441: Also, most neurocognitive studies in children with ADHD are from a relatively young age group of typically 6–13 years.
sentences.s442: The adoles- cent group tested in fMRI studies is usually older between 10 and 17, due to the fact that very young children have scanner anxiety and too many movement artefacts, in particular ADHD children.
sentences.s443: Also, it is known that ADHD children become better in behaviour as well as neurocognitive task performance with age (Biederman et al., 1996; Hart, Lahey, Loeber, Applegate & Frick, 1995).
sentences.s444: In addition, patients with the most severe cases of hyperactivity are not scanneable due to motion artefacts.
sentences.s445: Lastly, it is a common ﬁnding that brain activation is more sensitive to group differences than behavioural performance (e.g., Mostofsky et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 1999b, 2005, 2008, 2009c; Smith, Taylor, Brammer, Toone, & Rubia, 2006; Vloet et al., 2010).
sentences.s446: Nevertheless, despite these limita- tions, several fMRI studies reported not only neuroimaging but also behavioural timing differences between ADHD and control groups (e.g., Christakou et al., in press; Durston et al., 2007; Plichta et al., 2009; Rubia et al., 2009a; Valera et al., 2010). 7.
sentences.s447: Methylphenidate modulation of timing functions in ADHD It is well-established that the basal ganglia have an important role in timing functions (Riecker et al., 2003; Meck, 1996; Nenadic et al., 2003; Rubia, 2006; Rubia & Smith, 2004; Tanaka et al., 2004; Wiener et al., 2010), which are known to be mediated at least in part by dopamine, a neurotransmitter produced in the substantia nigra pars compacta, and the key neurotransmitter innervating the frontal-basal ganglia systems.
sentences.s448: Dopamine and its agonists have been shown to have an important role in timing functions (Meck, 1996; Rammsayer, 1993; Rubia, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s449: Recent meta-analyses and reviews show that ADHD is most prominently associated with structural as well as func- tional deﬁcits in the basal ganglia as well as frontal regions (Cubillo et al., 2012; Dickstein, Bannon, Castellanos, & Milham, 2006; Frodl & Skokauskas, 2012; Nakao, Radua, Rubia, & Mataix- Cols, 2011).
sentences.s450: Furthermore, a recent PET meta-analysis shows that there are abnormalities in the dopamine transporter levels in the basal ganglia in ADHD patients (Fusar-Poli, Rubia, Rossi, Sartori, & Ballotin, 2012).
sentences.s451: Given the association between ADHD and fronto- striatal structural, functional and dopaminergic abnormalities (Cubillo et al., 2012; Frodl & Skokauskas, 2012; Fusar-Poli et al., 2012; Nakao et al., 2011; Rubia, 2011), as well as the association between fronto-striatal networks and timing functions (Meck, 1996), it is hence plausible that dopamine agonists would improve timing functions in ADHD.
sentences.s452: This hypothesis was tested by nine studies that assessed the effects of the dopamine agonist MPH, the most commonly used psychostimulant to treat ADHD symptoms, on performance of different timing tasks using either single-dose placebo-controlled designs (Ben-Pazi et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2003, 2009a), single-dose MPH on/off designs (Baldwin et al., 2004), varying-dose placebo-controlled designs (Barkley et al., 1997; Shiels et al., 2009), chronic MPH adminis- tration (Rubia et al., 2003), or statistical covariance of timing performance for long-term use of MPH (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Hwang et al., 2010; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004).
sentences.s453: Two studies tested MPH effects on motor timing and found reduced motor tapping variability after MPH administration (Ben-Pazi et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2003).
sentences.s454: Rubia et al. (2003) compared performance in the free tapping and the synchronised tapping (0.7–1.8 s) tasks in 13 children with ADHD in the baseline condition without MPH administration, after a placebo drug intake, after a single MPH dose, and after 4 weeks of MPH administration.
sentences.s455: Both a single and multiple MPH administration reduced SDintra in the synchronised tapping task.
sentences.s456: Persistent administration of MPH also accelerated the synchronisation times.
sentences.s457: In contrast, the speed and the variability of free tapping did not differ between the experimental conditions.
sentences.s458: A similar improvement was reported in a placebo-controlled synchronised tapping study that probed timing of shorter sub-second intervals (0.2–1 s) in 38 children with ADHD, who were tested twice, 2 h and 26 h after the last MPH administration (Ben-Pazi et al., 2006).
sentences.s459: Tapping variability was reduced for both adequate and hastened tapping responses by a single MPH dose taken 2 h before the test.
sentences.s460: Rubia et al. (2003) reported that 4 weeks MPH administration reduced variability of anticipation and the amount of impulsive errors in the sensorimotor anticipation task (testing 6 s intervals), whereas the mean anticipation times did not differ between the medication conditions.
sentences.s461: With respect to perceptual timing tasks, ﬁndings have not been consistent.
sentences.s462: Several studies found no effects of MPH on time percep- tion.
sentences.s463: Thus, no signiﬁcant effects were observed for one single dose of MPH on time reproduction performance in 17 ADHD children on the mean estimation, but MPH reduced the intraindividual response variability of produced 10–14 s intervals (Baldwin et al., 2004).
sentences.s464: Similarly, no effect was found for three different MPH doses on reproduction of 12–60 s intervals (Barkley et al., 1997).
sentences.s465: For duration discrimination there have been both positive and negative ﬁndings.
sentences.s466: No signiﬁcant MPH effects were found for a supra-second time discrimination task (Rubia et al., 2003).
sentences.s467: However, a small sampled study on 13 ADHD patients found that a single dose MPH admin- istration yielded a trend for more correct responses than placebo on visual duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a), while a sub- sequent study with the same task on 20 ADHD adolescents showed a signiﬁcant improvement with a single dose of MPH (Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s468: Three studies covaried long-term stimulant medication treatment effects on timing performance, and none of them found a signiﬁcant medication effect (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Hwang et al., 2010; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004).
sentences.s469: The only study on temporal foresight tasks that tested MPH effects in children with ADHD reported reduced delay discounting after administration of a single MPH dose when compared to the placebo condition (Shiels et al., 2009).
sentences.s470: Interestingly, delay discounting was reduced under MPH only in the task when real money was rewarded in the real time conditions (7–28 s), but not during the delayed (1 day to 1 year) hypothetical awards of $100.
sentences.s471: To conclude, the reported results are somewhat inconsistent, as the effects of MPH medication seems to be task-dependent, i.e., MPH administration seems to improve timing in the synchronised tapping (Ben-Pazi et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2003), temporal anticipation (Rubia et al., 2003), and delay discounting (Shiels et al., 2009) tasks, but not in duration reproduction tasks (Barkley et al., 1997; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Hwang et al., 2010) and with mixed results for duration discrimination (Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s472: There is hence still a questionmark of whether perceptual timing is improved by MPH.
sentences.s473: Replication studies are needed with larger sample sizes as several perceptual timing studies showed either an effect (Smith et al., 2012) or tendencies towards an improve- ment of duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a) and produc- tion accuracy (Baldwin et al., 2004), yet possibly due to the small samples the results did not reach statistical signiﬁcance.
sentences.s474: Notably, even though Rubia et al. (2009a) did not ﬁnd signiﬁcant medica- tion effects in the performance on a duration discrimination task in the smaller sample, the same task was improved in a larger sample (Smith et al., 2012), and fMRI analyses showed that a single dose MPH administration normalised the entire neural network of perceptual timing deﬁcits in IFC, DLPFC, ACC, and cerebellum in both studies (Rubia et al., 2009a, Smith et al., 2012). 8.
sentences.s475: Timing and diagnostic subtypes of ADHD Several studies investigated potential differences in timing functions between diagnostic subtypes of ADHD (Barkley et al., 2001a; Huang et al., 2012; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s476: Two of these studies found that only children with the ADHD impulsive-hyperactive and inattentive-combined subtype but not those with inattentive symptoms only were more impaired than controls in their variability of duration reproduction errors (McInerney & Kerns, 2003) or had steeper discounting rates in a delay discounting task (Scheres et al., 2010).
sentences.s477: In addition the area under the curve in the discounting function was modulated by hyperactivity/impulsiv- ity, but not by inattention symptoms.
sentences.s478: Toplak et al. (2005) investigated inter-temporal choice in the gambling task and found that participants with the ADHD-combined subtype more frequently selected cards from disadvantageous decks than parti- cipants with the ADHD-inattentive only subtype.
sentences.s479: However, there have also been negative ﬁndings in seven studies that found no signiﬁcant differences between ADHD subtypes in duration dis- crimination (Huang et al., 2012; Radonovich & Mostofsky, 2004; Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a), reproduction (Huang et al., 2012; Toplak et al., 2003), estimation (Barkley et al., 2001a), and delay discounting (Shiels et al., 2009) tasks.
sentences.s480: In conclusion, the evidence for differential timing deﬁcits according to ADHD subtypes is sparse with some controversial evidence that the combined type ADHD may be more impaired in perceptual timing and temporal foresight than the inattentive subtype.
sentences.s481: No studies have tested for subtype differences during motor timing.
sentences.s482: Future studies on large samples are needed to elucidate the question whether any or which of the ADHD subtypes may be more strongly associated with timing deﬁcits. 9.
sentences.s483: Comorbidities and timing deﬁcits Comorbidities are likely to have an impact on timing functions in ADHD, as they also impact other functions (Rubia, 2011).
sentences.s484: Individuals with ADHD frequently have comorbid disorders, most commonly conduct disorder (CD), oppositional deﬁant disorder (ODD), dyslexia, and anxiety, all of which may have a unique contribution to timing abnormalities.
sentences.s485: Only few studies, however, assessed a possible inﬂuence of comorbidities on timing abnorm- alities in ADHD.
sentences.s486: Several studies tested for differences in ADHD children with and without reading disorders (Gooch et al., 2011; McGee et al., 2004; Toplak et al., 2003 (Experiment 1)).
sentences.s487: Thus, children with ADHD and comorbid reading disorder were reported to perform more variably in a duration discrimination task than ADHD children without reading problems despite shared deﬁcits in accuracy of duration discrimination and repro- duction (Toplak et al., 2003, Experiment (1)), which was however, not observed by McGee et al. (2004).
sentences.s488: A third study found task- dependent effects in the two single disorders, but did not test the comorbid group.
sentences.s489: Thus, children with ADHD-only but not children with dyslexia-only made larger absolute errors in the duration reproduction task when compared to typically developing con- trols, while both groups shared deﬁcits in the duration discrimi- nation task relative to typical controls (Gooch et al., 2011).
sentences.s490: In a motor timing study, no signiﬁcant differences were found between ADHD-only and dyslexia groups in free tapping and synchronised tapping tasks (Tifﬁn-Richards et al., 2004).
sentences.s491: It thus appears that dyslexia is associated in particular with increased deﬁcits in duration discrimination tasks, in line with evidence that ﬁne-temporal discrimination and event timing in the milli- seconds range in dyslexia is associated with their speech impedi- ments, possibly due to poor discrimination of phonemes that last about 40–70 ms (Liberman et al., 1961; Wittmann & Fink, 2004).
sentences.s492: Several studies tested for associations of abnormal timing in ADHD with CD (Kuntsi et al., 2001; Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s493: Kuntsi et al. (2001) reported a signiﬁcantly stronger delay aversion in a delay discounting task in a group of children with ADHD compared to typical controls; however, the group difference was no longer signiﬁcant after controlling for conduct problems.
sentences.s494: Similarly, in a group of adolescents with ADHD, comorbid CD was associated with increased variability in the duration reproduction task (Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s495: However, several other studies found no effect of CD on timing functions (Smith et al., 2002; Solanto et al., 2001; Tripp & Alsop, 2001; Toplak et al., 2003).
sentences.s496: In particular, no signiﬁcant effect of comorbid conduct disorder was observed among children with ADHD in duration reproduction and discrimination tasks (Smith et al., 2002).
sentences.s497: Similarly, aggressive behaviour (Schweitzer & Sulzer- Azaroff, 1995), ODD (Antrop et al., 2006; Bitsakou et al., 2009), or ODD/CD (Solanto et al., 2001; Tripp & Alsop, 2001) were not found to inﬂuence performance in the delay discounting task.
sentences.s498: Likewise, Toplak et al. (2003) found no effect of comorbid disorders ODD, CD, and separation anxiety on a duration discrimination task in a group of children with ADHD.
sentences.s499: Barkley et al. (2001b) found that neither ODD, delinquency, nor anxiety/depression contributed to the time reproduction errors beyond the effects of age, IQ and ADHD.
sentences.s500: However, the level of anxiety inﬂuenced absolute discrepancy scores in a duration estimation task in addition to the effect of ADHD (Barkley et al., 2001a).
sentences.s501: Marco et al. (2009) found a non-signiﬁcant trend of an effect of anxiety but not ODD in a delay discounting task.
sentences.s502: In conclusion, it appears that dyslexia and reading disorder may be associated with duration discrimination deﬁcits in ADHD, while CD and anxiety may affect performance in temporally more extended duration reproduction, estimation, and delay discounting tasks in ADHD.
sentences.s503: There is poor if not negative evidence for ODD, depression or other comorbid disorders to account for the timing deﬁcits in ADHD, although more replication studies are needed to conﬁrm this.
sentences.s504: The ﬁndings suggest that timing deﬁcits may be a key to ADHD itself rather than to its comorbid conditions.
sentences.s505: However, the comorbid manifestation of ADHD, which is also commonly asso- ciated with more severe symptoms, may exacerbate timing deﬁ- cits.
sentences.s506: Currently, more studies with 4 groups-designs (ADHD, ADHD- comorbid, Comorbid, Control) as well as using comparison to other disorders that have been associated with timing deﬁcits such as ASD (e.g., Falter, et al., in press) are needed to assess the exact contribution of these disorders on timing functions in ADHD. 10.
sentences.s507: ADHD familial associations and timing deﬁcits Several studies have indicated that timing functions might be associated with a family history of ADHD, which opens an intri- guing prospect to frame timing abnormalities as an endophenotype of ADHD.
sentences.s508: Two studies showed familial effects in a duration reproduction task with ADHD patients with a family history being more impaired than those without a family history (Huang et al., 2012) and non-affected siblings of individuals with ADHD having lower reproduction accuracy than typical controls (Rommelse et al., 2007).
sentences.s509: In a follow-up study, Rommelse et al. (2008) found enhanced variability of duration production in non-affected sib- lings relative to controls, but reduced relative to affected siblings and probands, conﬁrming that perceptual timing might be related to a familial predisposition for ADHD.
sentences.s510: Similarly, in a ﬁxed delay discounting study (2 s vs. 30 s) not only children with ADHD, but also their unaffected siblings differed signiﬁcantly in the delay aversion measure from typical controls (Bitsakou et al., 2009).
sentences.s511: Further developments of these ADHD research programs may provide unique data on genetic and environmental factors con- tributing to the timing functions in ADHD. 11.
sentences.s512: General discussion The present synthesis of neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies of timing functions in ADHD provides consistent evidence that ADHD is associated with both cognitive as well as neurofunc- tional deﬁcits in a remarkably wide range of timing functions, including motor timing, perceptual timing, and temporal fore- sight.
sentences.s513: Neurocognitively, the most investigated and consistent deﬁcits are in sensorimotor synchronisation, duration discrimina- tion, duration reproduction, and delay discounting tasks.
sentences.s514: Further- more, ADHD patients are impaired in temporal tasks ranging all temporal intervals, from hundreds of milliseconds and one or two seconds (in sensorimotor synchronisation and duration discrimi- nation tasks) to tens of seconds (in duration reproduction and ﬁxed delay discounting tasks) and even temporal foresight into the upcoming years (in individually adjusted graded delay discounting task).
sentences.s515: These ﬁndings of deﬁcits across such a wide range of different timing functions could suggest that timing deﬁcits in ADHD may be inter-related.
sentences.s516: In fact, the presence of timing deﬁcits in different timing functions in ADHD is supported by studies that show signiﬁcant correlations in ADHD patients between measures in different timing tasks.
sentences.s517: For instance, signiﬁcant associations were found between SDintra in sensorimotor synchronisation and sensorimotor anticipation tasks that have a higher load on duration perception (Toplak & Tannock, 2005b), or between duration judgements in verbal estimation and reproduction tasks across a wide range of intervals from 3 s to 90 s (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; but see Smith et al., 2002).
sentences.s518: However, these studies reported signiﬁcant correlations either within motor timing (Toplak & Tannock, 2005b) or within perceptual timing (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010) tasks, and more research is needed to investigate correlations and possible predictive interactions between different timing function domains, i.e., motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight.
sentences.s519: With respect to the direction of timing deﬁcits, the analysis of the error direction in duration estimation (Barkley et al., 2001a; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; McGee et al., 2004) and especially reproduction tasks (Barkley et al., 1997, 2001a; Gonza´lez-Garrido et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2012; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Kerns et al., 2001; Marx et al., 2010; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Mullins et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2002; Valko et al., 2010; West et al., 2000) in their majority indicates that for ADHD participants, time is subjectively elongated, although there have also been a few studies in the opposite direction (Barkley et al., 1997; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Plummer & Humphrey, 2009; Toplak et al., 2003; West et al., 2000).
sentences.s520: A subjectively elongated time sense would mean that the passage of time appears subjectively more insuf- ferable for people with ADHD.
sentences.s521: This subjective experience could provide a possible explanation for increased impulsivity in ADHD behaviours, in particular behavioural problems with waiting, delay aversion, impatience, premature responses, and the preference for present- oriented choices rather than future orientation.
sentences.s522: For example, duration overestimation due to a subjectively elongated time sense could well lead to premature impulsive responding or delay aversion, when tasks require waiting for a certain period of time, which is perceived as particularly insufferable by an ADHD individual.
sentences.s523: Given that individuals with ADHD tend to subjectively overestimate temporal intervals, they may perceive their res- ponses as subjectively timely, despite that their responses or behavioural acts are being judged as premature and impulsively early from an external, objective point of view.
sentences.s524: Several studies support this hypothesis by showing that perceptual timing and temporal foresight are indeed associated with clinical measures of behavioural impulsivity in ADHD (Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Rubia et al., 2007; Scheres et al., 2010; Solanto et al., 2001; Toplak et al., 2003, 2005; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a).
sentences.s525: In fact, in an attempt to adjust the social environment to the needs of ADHD children in the UK, a policy has recently been proposed that ADHD children should receive free passes for fun fair activities, to avoid them (and their parents) having to wait in a cue, which is known to cause problems to ADHD children (according to our review, due to the subjectively elongated time sense).
sentences.s526: It is debatable whether such policies will ultimately help ADHD children, who might be better served with training of their waiting behaviour for a better social adjustment than with adjustment of society to their needs.
sentences.s527: In addition to an association between timing deﬁcits and clinical behavioural traits of impulsivity, there is also an associa- tion with clinical (Bauermeister et al., 2005; Gooch et al., 2011; Hurks & Hendriksen, 2010; Rubia et al., 1999a) and cognitive measures of inattention (Barkley et al., 1997; Kerns et al., 2001; Mullins et al., 2005).
sentences.s528: If abnormal timing functions are associated with inattentive and/or impulsive behaviours and with correlated cognitive functions, i.e., if there is a causal relationship between them, then a cognitive-behavioural training of timing functions could improve ADHD symptoms and other related cognitive functions.
sentences.s529: This has in fact been shown in a study by Shaffer et al. (2001) who showed that ADHD symptoms could be improved through motor timing training.
sentences.s530: Future studies will be needed to investigate the potential and efﬁcacy of training of timing functions in ADHD as a clinical treatment.
sentences.s531: More research is also required to address important incon- sistencies of ﬁndings that were identiﬁed in the present review.
sentences.s532: For instance, the exact role of working memory for timing performance in ADHD should be investigated with studies speci- ﬁcally designed to investigate this question.
sentences.s533: Studies with a well- controlled manipulation of working memory load within a timing task may eventually explain why most (Bauermeister et al., 2005; McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Smith et al., 2002; Toplak et al., 2003; Toplak & Tannock, 2005a; Yang et al., 2007) but not all (e.g., Kerns et al., 2001) studies ﬁnd working memory to be a signiﬁcant factor modulating timing functions.
sentences.s534: Little evidence exists on differentiation between different ADHD subtypes in timing func- tions, with some controversial evidence that the combined type ADHD may be more impaired in perceptual timing and temporal foresight than the inattentive subtype (McInerney & Kerns, 2003; Scheres et al., 2010; Toplak et al., 2005).
sentences.s535: Future studies with larger samples would be useful to elucidate the impact of ADHD diagnostic subtypes on timing deﬁcits.
sentences.s536: Somewhat more evidence exists on the impact of comorbidities on timing functions in ADHD.
sentences.s537: For instance, dyslexia and RD are associated with duration discrimination deﬁcits in ADHD (Gooch et al., 2011; Toplak et al., 2003), although there is little evidence that other comorbidities inﬂuence timing functions in ADHD (Antrop et al., 2006; Bitsakou et al., 2009; Schweitzer & Sulzer-Azaroff, 1995; Smith et al., 2002; Solanto et al., 2001; Tripp & Alsop, 2001).
sentences.s538: Regarding life-span changes in ADHD timing performance, several studies reported that deﬁcits persist into adulthood for motor timing (Gilden & Marusich, 2009), perceptual timing (Barkley et al., 2001a; Marx et al., 2010) and temporal foresight (Hoogman et al., 2011; Marx et al., 2010), although one study observed smaller perceptual timing deﬁcits in adults with ADHD (Valko et al., 2010).
sentences.s539: However, the exact mechanisms of age- dependent changes in timing functions should be investigated further, ideally using longitudinal designs.
sentences.s540: There is also some preliminary evidence for familiality of timing deﬁcits, in particu- lar for perceptual timing (Huang et al., 2012; Rommelse et al., 2007, 2008) and temporal foresight (Bitsakou et al., 2009), which suggests that genetic factors may be implicated in the timing impairments in ADHD.
sentences.s541: Direct evidence for shared underlying neural mechanisms of different timing functions comes from neuroimaging studies, both in healthy individuals as well as in patients with ADHD.
sentences.s542: In healthy adults, for example, the right IFG and bilateral SMA appear to be common underlying neural substrates across different motor and perceptual timing functions in different temporal domains, in addition to basal ganglia, cerebellum, and parietal lobes (Wiener et al., 2010).
sentences.s543: Echoing these meta-analysis ﬁndings of common neural networks for different timing functions in healthy popula- tions, the present review of neuroimaging studies of timing functions in ADHD indicates that abnormal processing in ventro- lateral and medial prefrontal regions including SMA and ACC is a key deﬁcit underlying performance in motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight functions across a wide range of temporal intervals (Christakou et al., in press; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 1999b, 2009a; Smith et al., 2008, 2012; Valera et al., 2010; Vloet et al., 2010).
sentences.s544: Other brain regions commonly associated with abnormal timing in ADHD are the parietal cortex (Christakou et al., in press; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2009a; Valera et al., 2010), the basal ganglia (Christakou et al., in press; Plichta et al., 2009; Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2012; Valera et al., 2010), and the cerebellum (Durston et al., 2007; Rubia et al., 2009a; Valera et al., 2010; Vloet et al., 2010), which suggests that timing deﬁcits in ADHD are related to impaired processing in lateral and medial fronto-parietal net- works subserving attention to time, and in fronto-striato- cerebellar networks that are thought to subserve more intrinsic timing processes.
sentences.s545: The neuroimaging evidence in the present review therefore indicates that the neural substrates underlying timing functions in the healthy population as well as the ADHD-related neural network impairments are implicating dedicated neural timing systems that consist of complex interactions between lateral and medial prefrontal cortical areas (IFC, SMA, ACC), IPC, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum.
sentences.s546: This supports ‘‘dedicated’’ theories of timing (Harrington, Haaland, & Hermanowicz, 1998; Ivry et al., 2002; Lewis & Miall, 2006; Wiener et al., 2010) that assume that there are speciﬁc modality-independent brain regions dedi- cated or specialised in time processing, such as the cerebellum (Ivry, Spencer, Zelaznik, & Diedrichsen, 2002), the basal ganglia (Harrington et al., 1998) or the right prefrontal cortex (Lewis & Miall, 2006) as opposed to intrinsic theories of time processing that propose that timing is an intrinsic property of any neuronal population in the brain, and the involvement of concrete net- works depends on the speciﬁc characteristic of a particular timing task or its modality (Bueti & Macaluso, 2011; Buonomano, 2002; Reutimann, Yakovlev, Fusi, & Senn, 2004; for a review, see Ivry & Schlerf, 2008).
sentences.s547: Further reinforcement of the dedicated theory comes from the fact that individuals with ADHD have normal sensory MMN responses to duration deviants (Huttunen et al., 2007; Huttunen-Scott et al., 2008), and do not show sensory deﬁcits in fMRI studies of motor timing (e.g., Valera et al., 2010; but see Rubia et al., 2001), perceptual timing (e.g., Smith et al., 2008), or temporal foresight (e.g., Rubia et al., 2009a).
sentences.s548: These ﬁndings suggest that timing deﬁcits in ADHD are not due to modality-speciﬁc sensory abnormalities, as some of the intrinsic theories would predict, but instead impaired timing is related to neuronal abnormalities in more generic timing networks (see Section 6).
sentences.s549: Furthermore, in line with the notion that fronto-striatal net- works are crucially implicated in timing deﬁcits in ADHD, the psychostimulant MPH, the gold-standard treatment of ADHD, has been shown to improve and even normalise both the cognitive performance in several timing tasks (Baldwin et al., 2004; Ben- Pazi et al., 2006; Rubia et al., 2003) as well as the poor recruit- ment of the underlying fronto-striato-cerebellar networks in ADHD during duration discrimination (Rubia et al., 2009a; Smith et al., 2012).
sentences.s550: However, more studies are needed to investigate the effects of other ADHD treatments, such as Atomoxetine or Dexamphetamines, on different timing functions and their under- lying substrates in ADHD.
sentences.s551: In conclusion, there is consistent evidence that individuals with ADHD have neurocognitive deﬁcits in a wide range of timing tasks, underpinned by abnormal functioning in the fronto-parietal and fronto-striato-cerebellar networks that mediate these func- tions.
sentences.s552: Furthermore, the association between these neurocognitive timing deﬁcits and clinical behavioural measures of impulsivity and inattention suggest that timing impairments are integral to ADHD, demonstrating that ADHD is at least in part a disorder of abnormal temporal processing.
sentences.s553: Future studies will have to eluci- date the relatively unknown impact of genetic factors, comorbid- ities, and ADHD subtypes on these timing deﬁcits.
sentences.s554: Also, studies are necessary that evaluate pharmacological and behavioural treatment avenues for timing impairments in ADHD and their impact on co-improving other behavioural and cognitive deﬁcits.
sentences.s555: While MPH has shown positive effects on performance deﬁcits and underlying neural networks, the effects of other pharmaco- logical treatments of ADHD such as Atomoxetine, Guanfacine, or Dexamphetamines remain to be studied.
sentences.s556: Non-pharmacological treatments such as cognitive-behavioural training of timing functions may also be fruitful, as shown by evidence for a positive impact on reducing ADHD symptom through behavioural treat- ment that included time management skills and waiting beha- viour (Solanto, Marks, Mitchell, Wasserstein, & Kofman, 2008; Solanto et al., 2010).
sentences.s557: Lastly, neurotherapy in the form of Neuro- feedback using EEG (Arns, de Ridder, Strehl, Breteler, & Coenen, 2009) or fMRI could also potentially be used to upregulate the key regions that are underfunctioning in ADHD children during timing tasks and test their effects upon cognition and behaviour.
sentences.s558: Given that timing functions appear to be closely associated with impulsiveness, treatment of timing deﬁcits via either pharmaco- logical or non-pharmacological interventions such as behavioural therapy, cognitive training or neurotherapy is likely to impact upon the behavioural manifestation of the disorder.

sentences.s16: As mentioned by Brown, O'Leary and Barlow (1993), changes in the conceptualization of GAD over the last few years have provided new directions in research on worry (see Barlow, 1988; Borkovec, Metzger & Pruzinsky, 1986; Dugas, Gagnon, Ladouceur & Freeston, 1998; Macleod, Williams & Bekerian, 1991).
sentences.s17: Our research team has recently proposed a theoretical model of GAD and excessive worry that includes four cognitive variables: intolerance of uncertainty, poor problem orientation, cognitive avoidance and erroneous beliefs about the usefulness of worry (Dugas et al., 1998).
sentences.s18: Among these four cognitive variables, intolerance of uncertainty is viewed as the most important and is believed to play a key role in the acquisition and maintenance of excessive worries.
sentences.s19: The preliminary results of a cognitive-behavioral treatment based on this model demonstrate good treatment e cacy (Dugas & Ladouceur, in press).
sentences.s20: Although many authors have included the notion of uncertainty in their model of GAD (Andrews & Borkovec, 1988) and anxiety (Garber, Miller & Abramson, 1980), Krohne (1989, 1993) was the ®rst author to include the construct of intolerance of uncertainty in his general model of anxiety.
sentences.s21: According to this model, intolerance of uncertainty and intolerance of emotional arousal are the main variables underlying anxiety disorders.
sentences.s22: He suggested that an elevated level of intolerance of uncertainty provokes reactions of hypervigilance when individuals are faced with uncertain or ambiguous problems, while an elevated level of intolerance to emotional arousal stimulates cognitive avoidance reactions.
sentences.s23: Excessive anxiety would then result from the constant shifting from a hypervigilant state (linked to the uncertainty of the situation) to a state of avoidance (linked to the anxious reactions felt by the individual).
sentences.s24: Even though the components included in Krohne's model (1993) open interesting avenues for research, they need to be more precisely de®ned.
sentences.s25: Our previous work in the ®eld of anxiety lead us to de®ne intolerance of uncertainty as a predisposition to react negatively to an uncertain event or situation, independent of its probability of occurrence and of its associated consequences.
sentences.s26: In other words, for the same uncertain situation, two individuals with identical perceptions of both its probability of occurrence and consequences may di er in their threshold of tolerance towards the situation.
sentences.s27: An individual who is intolerant of uncertainty would evaluate the situation as being disturbing, even unacceptable, whereas another individual who is tolerant of uncertainty would assess the situation as being less disturbing.
sentences.s28: Thus, the ®rst person's threshold of tolerance is lower than that of the second individual.
sentences.s29: This de®nition emphasizes the subjective appraisal of uncertainty by the individual and represents the reality expressed by individuals during therapy.
sentences.s30: Considering that everyday life necessarily involves uncertain and/or ambiguous situations, individuals who are intolerant of uncertainty will perceive many sources of danger in their daily life.
sentences.s31: Numerous worries will thus follow, as well as negative emotions, such as anxiety and depression (Dugas, Freeston, Blais & Ladouceur, 1994; Macleod & Mathews, 1988).
sentences.s32: This con®rms the results of previous studies indicating that worry is characterized by (1) a tendency to de®ne ambiguous situations as threatening (Butler & Mathews, 1983, 1987; Russel & Davey, 1993), (2) an elevated estimation of risk (Butler & Mathews, 1983, 1987; Vasey & Borkovec, 1992) and (3) a tendency to generate negative scenarios in uncertain situations (Macleod et al., 1991; Tallis, Eysenck & Mathews, 1991a; Vasey & Borkovec, 1992).
sentences.s33: This could also explain why high worriers are slower to make a decision when confronted with ambiguous stimuli (Ladouceur, Talbot & Dugas, 1997; Metzger, Miller, Cohen, Softka & Borkovec, 1990; Tallis, 1989; Tallis, Eysenck & Mathews, 1991b).

sentences.s37: In this study, a computerized roulette game was developed in order to increase and decreased intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s38: While taking into consideration the current de®nition of intolerance of uncertainty, we developed a task whereby the uncertainty of the situation was acceptable for one group, and unacceptable for a second group, without changing either the objective probability of winning (probability of occurrence) or the consequences associated with the situation.
sentences.s39: The main hypothesis of this study was that, following manipulation of intolerance of uncertainty, participants in the increased intolerance group would report a higher level of worry compared to participants in the decreased intolerance group. 2.

sentences.s41: The sample included 30 women with a mean age of 23.8 years (S.D.=7.07) and twelve men with a mean age of 21.7 years (S.D.=1.92).

sentences.s45: Material and procedure A multimedia IBM computer with a color screen was used in this study.
sentences.s46: The computer was equipped with a computerized roulette game that simulates those found in casinos.
sentences.s47: Student were invited to an individual meeting lasting approximately 1 hour with the aim of studying people's thoughts about gambling.
sentences.s48: None of the participants were informed beforehand as to the real goal of the study, which consisted of the manipulation of intolerance of uncertainty.
sentences.s49: The experimenter presented himself as part of a research team studying beliefs associated with gambling.
sentences.s50: After brie¯y explaining the experimental task (roulette game), the experimenter asked the participants to sign a consent form.
sentences.s51: Once the task was completed, the participants ®lled out two questionnaires; a manipulation check measure, and a measure of worry. 2.3.
sentences.s52: Experimental task The task consisted of a computerized roulette game in which the player must bet on 15 consecutive trials.
sentences.s53: Each participant was allowed to bet on one of three columns of 12 numbers.
sentences.s54: For each trial, a betting amount of $2 was set.
sentences.s55: Each participant began the task with a $20 bankroll.
sentences.s56: The roulette game was programmed so that the ®nal amount for each participant, after all betting was ®nished, was $14.
sentences.s57: The experimenter ®rst explained the rules of the roulette game.
sentences.s58: Emphasis was placed on the probability associated with the three di erent types of bets; (i.e. one chance in two if the bet was on colors, one chance in 36 if the bet was on a single number, one chance in three if the bet was placed on one column).
sentences.s59: After having veri®ed that the participant understood the various probabilities associated with the game, the experimenter indicated that for this study s/he must bet on columns, thereby setting a one in three chance of winning on each trial.
sentences.s60: The experimenter then explained that to create a situation that most resembles a real game with stakes, an amount of $100 would be donated to a Foundation (®ctitious).
sentences.s61: However, the experimenter stipulated that the money would be donated to the Foundation only if the ®nal amount for each participant, after 15 trials, was equal or superior to $20 (equal or superior to the initial amount).
sentences.s62: If the ®nal amount was inferior to $20, nothing would be donated to the Foundation. 2.4.
