sentences.s97: In the context of these strong and conflicting emotional demands on them, young children tend to be vigilant and attentive to their mother’s emotional state (Zahn-Waxler & Kochanska, 1990).
sentences.s98: In addition, there is evidence for enhanced empathy and greater prosocial initiatives by the young children of chronically depressed mothers, perhaps as a means of providing helpful assistance to reduce the mother’s affective distress, but with the cost of children becoming further enmeshed in the mother’s emotional difficulties (Radke-Yarrow, Zahn-Waxler, Richardson, Susman, & Martinez, 1994).
sentences.s99: There are also indications that this style of interaction extends to others outside the family, including peers, leading researchers to con- clude that young children with a depressed parent have “learned to treat others carefully” (Zahn-Waxler & Kochanska, 1990, p. 227).
sentences.s100: In addition to maintaining ongoing vigilance of the mother’s affective state, therefore, young children also have the goal of managing the mother’s emotions as a means of managing their own, albeit with limited success, and thus at risk to their own continuing emotional well-being.
sentences.s101: Even in more “typical” family circumstances, there is consider- able evidence that children are motivated to pursue goals that may provide immediate coping at a cost of long-term risk for affective psychopathology.
sentences.s102: The extensive research on the responses of young children to marital conflict show that aversive encounters between parents are upsetting to children and undermine their emotional security in the family and their emotion regulation, contributing to enhanced risk of behavioral difficulties and inter- nalizing problems (see review by Cummings & Davies, 2010).
sentences.s103: Considerable research shows that exposure to chronic marital conflict causes children to develop heightened sensitivity to parental distress and anger, strive to manage parental conflicts by becoming overinvolved in parental disputes, and regulate their exposure to intrafamilial conflict.
sentences.s104: Although this may provide some management of their own emotional arousal when parents are arguing, the double-edged sword of their coping is reflected not only in children’s heightened risk for affective psychopathol- ogy but also in the development of insecure representations of relationships that extend outside the family.
sentences.s105: These are perhaps inevitable consequences of the immediate goal of managing parental conflict coupled with their continued sensitivity to par- ents’ emotional and relational well-being.
sentences.s106: Interim conclusions There are other examples of how children who are emotionally dysregulated and at heightened risk of affective psychopathology may be motivated to achieve goals for emotion management that are atypical, and which provide some immediate coping at the cost of longer term dysfunction.
sentences.s107: For example, young children at heightened genetic risk for anxiety disorders show hypervigi- lance to threat in situations previously associated with fearful events.
sentences.s108: They also exhibit attentional orienting toward anxiety- provoking stimuli, and a tendency to construe benign situations as disproportionately negative or threatening.
sentences.s109: They do so, often with parental enablement and support, in order to manage expo- sure to anxiety-provoking situations, even though this has dys- functional longer term consequences (Thompson, 2001).
sentences.s110: As this and the preceding examples illustrate, biological processes— including altered stress neurobiology, heightened inflammation, and heritable traits—interact with characteristics of challenging family environments to potentiate their influence and strengthen motivation toward immediate emotional coping and heightened risk of emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s111: Taken together, this research offers several conclusions.
sentences.s112: First, emotion dysregulation is based not only on inappropriate or dys- functional strategies of reacting emotionally to events but also— perhaps primarily—on antecedent strategies in anticipation of those events.
sentences.s113: Considering again the model of emotion regulation outlined by Gross and Thompson (2007), several kinds of emo- tion regulation strategies are antecedent to the response to an emotionally evocative event, including situation selection (choos- ing actions or settings that change the probability of encountering an emotion elicitor), situation modification (changing the circum- stances to alter their emotional impact), and attentional deploy- ment (directing attention within a situation to modify its emotional influence).
sentences.s114: The preceding discussion of children at risk for affective psychopathology in difficult family environments illustrates the functioning of these antecedent strategies, including situation selection (e.g., the avoidance of anxiety-provoking stim- uli or of marital conflict), situation modification (e.g., providing comfort to a depressed mother or intervening into parental argu- ments), and attentional deployment (e.g., sensitivity to anticipa- tory cues of adult anger, sadness, or distress, and vigilance for emerging domestic conflict or a parent’s depressive episode).
sentences.s115: In typical circumstances, these antecedent strategies might contrib- ute to emotional well-being in children as they do for adults, but the preceding discussion shows how enlisting these strategies in difficult family contexts is motivated by the need for immediate coping but often also heightens young children’s immediate vul- nerability and their longer term risk for affective psychopathology.
sentences.s116: Understanding that many challenges leading to the development of emotion dysregulation concern strategies that are antecedent to (and in anticipation of) emotion-eliciting events can be helpful in considering potentially helpful intervention avenues.
sentences.s117: Second, manifestly dysregulated emotional responding may derive from coping strategies that are among the few options per- mitted in difficult home environments.
sentences.s118: A young child whose engagement with social or learning tasks is impaired by threat vigilance is not only emotionally dysregulated but also responding adaptively, behaviorally and biologically, to a history of physical abuse, domestic conflict, or anxiety.
sentences.s119: Not only vigilance to poten- tial danger but also heightened sensitivity to adult sadness and emotional lability in family conflict can simultaneously reflect emotion dysregulation and also reflect efforts to cope emotionally with challenging situations, especially when more adaptive strate- gies are impossible.
sentences.s120: Viewed in this light, it seems apparent that to describe children in these circumstances as emotionally dysregu- lated offers a useful but limited perspective on their behavior.
sentences.s121: In addition, it is necessary to inquire into the goals they may be motivated to achieve, and the means for achieving those goals in the circumstances in which they live, to better understand their behavior.
sentences.s122: Third, many situations involve multiple goals, and emotion regulation often requires trade-offs among them.
sentences.s123: There can be multiple goals in immediate circumstances, such as determining how to respond to a depressed mother with respect to managing one’s own feelings, helping the parent, defending oneself from criticism, soliciting assistance from the other parent, or escaping the situation.
sentences.s124: These goals cannot all be accomplished at the same time, and choosing among them requires an assessment of current circumstances and the consequences they potentially entail, including the trade-offs in their emotional outcomes (e.g., escaping the situation may provide immediate relief but unknown and potentially hazardous consequences upon return).
sentences.s125: There can also be multiple emotional goals relevant to longer term outcomes, as many of the foregoing examples illustrate.
sentences.s126: In challenging circumstances, immediate coping in the context of limited options comes at a price of longer term vulnerability.
sentences.s127: It is thus often true that, in these situations, emotional behavior can be both adaptive and maladaptive within different time frames and in relation to different goals.
sentences.s128: Emotion dysregulation is especially likely when multiple goals are impeded or impaired in a particular context, or when essential goals are accomplished at very high cost.
sentences.s129: Fourth, it follows that strategies of emotion regulation are not inherently adaptive or maladaptive, rather, it depends on the con- text.
sentences.s130: Studies of adult emotion regulation have concluded that strategies of cognitive reappraisal, problem solving, and accep- tance are adaptive for emotion management, while strategies such as suppression, avoidance, and rumination are not (e.g., Gross & John, 2003).
sentences.s131: However, as Aldao (2013) notes, context is an important determinant of the efficacy of these emotion reg- ulation strategies for adults, and context is especially important for conditions posing risk for psychopathology, especially for chil- dren.
sentences.s132: Cognitive reappraisal is unlikely to be an effective strategy for emotion self-regulation for children living in violent families, for example, whereas in the studies described above, threat vigi- lance (analogous perhaps to rumination) promotes immediate coping although at a cost of longer term vulnerability.
sentences.s133: Stated dif- ferently, apart from consideration of context, goals, and the time frame, judgments of emotion dysregulation based on strategy alone should be made cautiously.
sentences.s134: Fifth and finally, this discussion underscores that the develop- ment of emotion dysregulation, like the development of emotion regulation, is inherently relational.
sentences.s135: This is also consistent with a functionalist approach to emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s136: In particular, the family environment shapes the emotional demands with which children must cope, the models of emotionally regulated or dysregulated behavior that they observe, the emotional climate in which skills of emotion management evolve, the strategies that are effective or ineffective, the emotional goals that are para- mount, the manner in which children’s emotions are evaluated by others, and a broad variety of other interpersonal influences.
sentences.s137: Because emotion dysregulation is a transdiagnostic feature of most forms of psychopathology, it has been natural to view emo- tion dysregulation as a transcontextual characteristic of the person to be addressed through individual therapy.
sentences.s138: However, in its devel- opment, especially early in life, relational influences are para- mount in shaping the behavioral and biological qualities that contribute to emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s139: This issue is considered fur- ther in the next section.
sentences.s140: Developing Relationships and Developing Biology in Emotion Dysregulation Although it is primarily concerned with the development of emo- tion regulation, the research on family influences in emotional development evocatively highlights at least four ways that family processes contribute to the development of emotionally dysregu- lated behavior (Morris, Silk, Steinberg, Myers, & Robinson, 2007; Thompson, 2013).
sentences.s141: First is the general emotional climate of the family: the relative amounts of positive or negative emotion expressed by family members, together with the predictability of these emotional expressions.
sentences.s142: The developmental profiles of children at risk for emergent psychopathology discussed above are consistent in por- traying family environments as emotionally insurmountable in ways that overwhelm developmentally appropriate emotion regu- lation skills and motivate children to pursue atypical goals that promote their emotion management in the context of immediate coping.
sentences.s143: The emotional climate of the family not only shapes goals for emotion management but also defines the kinds of strategies that are likely to provide relief for the child.
sentences.s144: Second, young children acquire modes of emotional respond- ing and management from their observations of parents.
sentences.s145: In many cases, observational learning complements and potentiates the influence of shared genes.
sentences.s146: Thus it is not surprising that, for exam- ple, the 4- to 7-year-old daughters of depressed mothers tended to emulate the more passive, less competent styles of emotion man- agement of their mothers (Silk, Shaw, Skuban, Oland, & Kovacs, 2006).
sentences.s147: In a similar manner, young children with anxiety disorders learn anxious appraisals and avoidance of fear-provoking situa- tions from their parents, who may share the child’s genetic risk for anxious symptomatology (Dadds, Barrett, Rapee, & Ryan, 1996).
sentences.s148: Third, parenting practices directly related to the socialization of emotion also influence the development of emotionally dysre- gulated behavior.
sentences.s149: In a meta-analysis, for example, Johnson, Hawes, Eisenberg, Kohlhoff, and Dudeney (2017) showed that child conduct problems are predicted by parents’ nonsupportive emotion socialization practices, especially those directed toward children’s negative emotions, and that this influence is greater with younger children.
sentences.s150: Nonsupportive practices include minimiz- ing or punishing children’s emotional expressions, refusing to talk about the meaning or significance of the child’s feelings, and fre- quent expression of negative emotion, especially toward children.
sentences.s151: They noted that over time, child conduct problems and parents’ nonsupportive emotion socialization practices became mutually influential, and thus emotion socialization had compounding effects.
sentences.s152: Parents’ emotion socialization has also been found to be influential in the development of children’s internalizing prob- lems (Schwartz, Sheeber, Dudgeon, & Allen, 2012).
sentences.s153: Fourth and finally, the general security and affective tone of specific parent–child relationships influence emotional develop- ment and the growth of emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s154: Secure attach- ments to parents, for example, promote the growth of constructive forms of emotion self-regulation, and conversely, insecure attachments contribute to emotion dysregulation because of the adult’s lack of responsiveness to the child’s feelings, psycho- logical unavailability when children are distressed, and the unpre- dictability of their support (Brumariu, 2015).
sentences.s155: Some attachment researchers argue that patterns of emotion dysregulation that result, including the intense distress of insecure–resistant children and the disoriented, dissociation-like responding of insecure– disorganized children, are adaptations to patterns of parental care by which young children manage themselves in the context of expectations of parental responsiveness (Cassidy, 1994).
sentences.s156: That these patterns of emotion dysregulation confer longer term risk for affective symptomatology has been demonstrated empirically (e.g., Bosquet & Egeland, 2006) and is based, in part, on the devel- opment of internal “working models” by which children general- ize their expectations for emotional responsiveness from the parent–child relationship to other relationships.
sentences.s157: In difficult family environments, of course, these multiple influences on the development of emotion dysregulation tend to overlap and amplify their effects.
sentences.s158: An example is when parents have borderline personality disorder (BPD).
sentences.s159: Parenting by adults with BPD is characterized by pervasive emotion dysregulation along with hostility and impulsivity, controlling behavior, harsh reactions to children, and erratic, mood-dependent responsiveness.
sentences.s160: Linehan (1993) and Musser, Zalewski, Stepp, and Lewis (2018) have further described the emotionally “invalidating environment” created by BPD parents who misattribute children’s emotions, minimize children’s emotional problems, respond only to extreme emotional expressions, and contribute to children doubting and “self-invalidating” their own emotional experiences.
sentences.s161: These circum- stances encompass a harsh family emotional climate, poor paren- tal modeling of emotion regulation, a variety of nonsupportive emotion socialization practices, and quite likely, insecure attach- ment relationships.
sentences.s162: In a recent study, children’s emotion dysregu- lation mediated the association between maternal borderline and antisocial symptomatology and children’s internalizing and exter- nalizing symptoms a year later (Kaufman et al., 2017).
sentences.s163: Parenting practices are important not just as direct influences on the development of emotion dysregulation, especially early in life, but for their interaction with developing biological systems that are also potent influences on emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s164: The fol- lowing sections profile examples of this interactive process, and illustrate parenting practices as catalysts and moderators of indi- vidual differences in these biological processes.
sentences.s165: Neurobiological consequences of stress and its social buffering In the examples of emergent psychopathology discussed above, young children exhibited biological as well as behavioral dysregu- lation.
sentences.s166: Complex patterns of dysregulation of stress neurobiology were especially apparent in studies of maltreated children, but the extremity of maltreatment is not required to dysregulate activ- ity of the limbic–hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenocortical (L-HPA) axis and other neurobiological stress systems.
sentences.s167: Studies of children living in the context of chronic maternal depression, foster care placement, interparental violence, and poverty have documented that as early as the first year, young children exhibit alterations in basal and/or acute cortisol responding that can cause, as in the case of maltreatment, hyperreactivity (reflecting sensitization) or hyporeactivity (thought to reflect systemic exhaustion) of stress responding (see Thompson, 2014, for a review).
sentences.s168: That biological dysregulatory effects derive primarily from the consequences of relational influences in these contexts, rather than from resource depletion or other causes, comes from studies, discussed below, showing that positive relational influences can buffer these neuro- biological outcomes.
sentences.s169: There are three additional observations about the neurobiological effects of stress and its social buffering meriting note.
sentences.s170: One is that these influences begin prenatally.
sentences.s171: Experimental animal studies and correlational research with humans indicate that prenatal maternal anxiety and stress, and prenatal maternal cortisol levels, predict newborn stress reactivity and fearful and difficult temperament in the first 2 years and beyond (Blair, Glynn, Sandman, & Davis, 2011; Davis, Glynn, Waffarn, & Sandman, 2011).
sentences.s172: These and other studies in the expanding research literature on fetal programming are consistent with evi- dence for fetal exposure to maternal stress hormones and their influence on developing behavioral and biological functioning (see Davis & Thompson, 2014, for a review).
sentences.s173: These origins of individual differences in emotion dysregulation thus begin before birth and are a foundation for the infant’s response to environ- mental experiences.
sentences.s174: The biological dysregulation deriving from chronic stress also extends beyond the L-HPA axis to other systems because gluco- corticoid receptors are widely distributed throughout the brain and because L-HPA dysregulation has downstream effects on other systems.
sentences.s175: These include impairment to major neurotransmit- ter systems relevant to the development of internalizing and exter- nalizing disorders as well as neurodegenerative effects on sensitive brain regions, including the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex, which have behavioral consequences for memory, execu- tive function, and emotion regulation (Arnsten, 2009; Mead, Beauchaine, & Shannon, 2010).
sentences.s176: Neural networks important to emotion regulation are also affected, including abnormal amyg- dala–prefrontal cortical connectivity as a consequence of early life stress (Chen & Baram, 2016).
sentences.s177: Structural and functional dysre- gulation of this circuit has been related to the development of anxiety disorders in children (Swartz & Monk, 2014), and this dysregulation can be found as early as the newborn period in infants born to prenatally depressed mothers (Posner et al., 2016).
sentences.s178: In addition to these, early life stress disrupts the interaction between neurological and immune systems, contributing to enhanced risk for physical and mental health problems, including depression (Hostinar et al., 2017).
sentences.s179: Taken together, early chronic stress provokes a cascade of neurobiological changes that together increase risk for diminished self-regulatory capabilities and increased emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s180: Early life stress has complex origins, but the primary and most potent stressors are social and relational in nature: maternal depression or anxiety, domestic conflict or interparental violence, and disengaged and emotionally inaccessible parenting (e.g., Sturge-Apple, Davies, Cicchetti, & Manning, 2012).
sentences.s181: However, relational influences can also buffer the effects of stress on early neurobiological functioning (Hostinar, Sullivan, & Gunnar, 2014).
sentences.s182: In a study of families living in rural poverty, for example, researchers found that infants’ chronic exposure to domestic vio- lence was associated with elevated stress reactivity by age 2 years.
sentences.s183: When mothers in these families were observed behaving sensi- tively with their children in earlier home observations, however, repeated exposure to domestic violence was not associated with heightened stress reactivity in the children (Hibel, Granger, Blair, Cox, & Family life Project Key Investigators, 2011).
sentences.s184: Based in part on findings such as these, several evidence-based interven- tions have been developed for infants and children with maltreat- ment histories that are designed to improve the sensitivity, warmth, and responsiveness of their care providers in foster care (Dozier, Peloso, Lewis, Laurenceau, & Levine, 2008; Fisher, Van Ryzin, & Gunnar, 2011).
sentences.s185: Each program succeeded in normal- izing the heightened levels of cortisol reactivity that children showed when they entered the program, and there were also con- current behavioral changes, including the development of more secure attachments to foster parents.
sentences.s186: Not enough is currently known about whether the biological processes involved in social support primarily buffer the influence of stress-reactive systems or also strengthen systems relevant to coping and emotional well- being.
sentences.s187: Candidates for the latter include changes in the oxytocinergic system and improvements in prefrontal cortical functioning (Hostinar et al., 2014).
sentences.s188: Early physiological attunement The research on fetal programming indicates that before birth, fetal biological and behavioral development is affected by maternal stress and its transmission to the fetus through maternal cortisol levels.
sentences.s189: When mothers are stressed prenatally, the constel- lation of characteristics that develop in the fetus increase risk for emotional dysregulation after birth (e.g., fearful and difficulty temperament in newborns) but are consistent with the view that fetal development is being prepared for coping with an extra- uterine environment of challenge and stress (e.g., the newborn’s heightened stress reactivity).
sentences.s190: Another kind of early biological/behavioral transmission can be observed in the research on mother–infant physiological attunement.
sentences.s191: This research focuses on the biological and behavio- ral coordination of infant and mother to provide physiological support for the infant’s self-regulatory development and the growth of affiliative bonds between them (Feldman, 2012).
sentences.s192: For a young infant whose capacities for physiological and emotion regulation are limited, the mother’s ability to respond sensitively promotes the attunement of her physiological state (such as car- diac rate) with the infant’s and helps regulate the baby’s state.
sentences.s193: This attunement also provides a foundation for a positive, secure parent–child relationship.
sentences.s194: This research shows, however, that individual differences in attunement are predicted by maternal stress and affective symptomatology and predict infant risk for emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s195: In one study, for example, mothers with depression and anxiety disorders had greater difficulty establish- ing affective attunement with their 9-month-olds who, in turn, showed greater stress reactivity and poorer fear management than control children (Feldman et al., 2009).
sentences.s196: Physiological attunement between mother and child can pro- mote early biobehavioral organization but can also set the stage for developing problems in emotion dysregulation when mothers are chronically stressed, even in the absence of symptomatology.
sentences.s197: In an experimental study, mothers experienced a modified Trier stress test involving extemporaneous speaking before judges who either negatively or positively responded to them, and then moth- ers were reunited with their 1-year-olds.
sentences.s198: The mother’s physiolog- ical arousal deriving from each condition was mirrored in the infant’s increased cardiac activity after reunion, but this was greater for mothers in the negative evaluation condition.
sentences.s199: Moreover, only when mothers were in the negative evaluation condition did infants’ physiological synchrony with her arousal increase over time (Waters, West, & Mendes, 2014).
sentences.s200: Waters et al. argued that this physiological attunement can contribute to affective contagion in shared circumstances.
sentences.s201: In another study, mothers were random- ized to have either a positive or a conflictual discussion with their marital partners, and then were reunited with their 6-month-olds, after which the infants were observed during mild challenge tasks.
sentences.s202: Mothers’ cortisol reactivity during conflictual discussions, but not positive discussions, predicted infants’ cortisol reactivity to the challenge tasks after their reunion (Hibel & Mercado, 2019).
sentences.s203: Considerably more research is needed to examine further the significance of the transmission of physiological states to what is implied by these studies, especially the means by which this transmission occurs and why emotionally negative arousal is more likely to be conveyed than positive.
sentences.s204: Together with the research on fetal programming, however, these studies suggest that the early years may be a period of unusual susceptibility of the infant to the mother’s physiological and emotional states.
sentences.s205: This susceptibility derives from the prenatal entraining of the infant’s biobehavioral development to signals from the mother’s physiological state, and after birth this susceptibility contributes to organizing and regulating early biological and behavioral func- tioning until the infant can become more independently self- regulating.
sentences.s206: These findings indicate, however, that vulnerability to the mother’s stress and affective difficulties inhere in these developmental processes, and underscore how early the transmis- sion of risk for emotion dysregulation may emerge.
sentences.s207: Differential susceptibility The discussion thus far has emphasized risk factors for the devel- opment of emotion dysregulation arising from the interaction of challenging family environments and biological characteristics of children.
sentences.s208: The approach is consistent with a diathesis-stress ori- entation that has historically been dominant in developmental psychopathology, in part because of its direct applications to interventions to prevent or remediate conditions that enhance vulnerability for at-risk children.
sentences.s209: However, it is not the only ori- entation that can be taken to the interaction of biology and envi- ronment in the development of emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s210: From the perspective of differential susceptibility, individuals vary not only in risk factors but also in their general susceptibility to environmental influences (Belsky & Pluess, 2009).
sentences.s211: According to this view, some people are more readily influenced by their environments than others.
sentences.s212: For more susceptible individuals, the environment has the potential of affecting them “for better and for worse” such that they experience greater negative outcomes when environments are stressful (consistent with the diathesis- stress model), but also exhibit greater positive outcomes when environments are supportive.
sentences.s213: For less susceptible individuals, out- comes are less significantly moderated by environmental quality.
sentences.s214: Groups that are more susceptible are often viewed as being more vulnerable because research studies (until recently) have typically only focused on their responses to adversity, not on how they function in both adverse and supportive circumstances.
sentences.s215: Once they are studied in both contexts, positive and negative outcomes associated with their susceptibility factors can be better identified.
sentences.s216: Many of the risk factors for emotion dysregulation discussed thus far, including negative emotionality, physiological reactivity, and difficult temperament, have been identified in other studies as susceptibility factors that increase vulnerability in challenging environments (consistent with the foregoing review) but fore- shadow more positive outcomes in supportive environments.
sentences.s217: Additional susceptibility factors identified in other studies consist of specific genetic alleles (e.g., 5-HTTPLR and DRD4 7-repeat), temperamental qualities (including high impulsivity and high fearfulness), and other biomarkers such as high respiratory sinus arrhythmia or skin conductance (Belsky & Pluess, 2009).
sentences.s218: Although many of these variables appear self-evidently to confer enhanced risk for emotion dysregulation, the view that they would yield more positive outcomes for emotional behavior under more supportive environmental conditions suggests that the vulnerabil- ity they confer is not biologically determined but rather in inter- action with the environment.
sentences.s219: Furthermore, the differential susceptibility literature suggests that if those environmental con- ditions were improved, biological characteristics conventionally interpreted as conferring vulnerability to emotion dysregulation might instead prove more beneficial.
sentences.s220: Considerable research indicates that insen- sitive and harsh parenting increases risk for the development of externalizing disorders.
sentences.s221: There is also evidence that the DRD4 7-repeat polymorphism causes poor dopamine reception and is linked to aggression, oppositional behavior, and other forms of externalizing behavior.
sentences.s222: To study the interaction of these factors, Bakermans-Kranenburg and van IJzendoorn (2006) observed 10-month-old infants with their mothers to assess the quality of parenting and also genotyped cheek cells obtained from the child; later, maternal ratings of the child’s behavior were obtained.
sentences.s223: Children with mothers deemed insensitive later were rated higher in externalizing behavior but only when they had the DRD4 7-repeat allele; for children without this genotype, insensitivity was unpredictive of externalizing.
sentences.s224: Similar results were found for ratings of aggressive and oppositional behavior.
sentences.s225: This is an exam- ple of gene–environment interaction.
sentences.s226: Based in part on these findings, this research group subse- quently recruited a sample of families with 1- to 3-year-olds who were high in externalizing behavior and invited the parents to participate in a parenting program designed to enhance sensi- tivity and positive discipline.
sentences.s227: For children with the DRD4 7-repeat allele, the intervention was effective in decreasing externalizing behavior on the follow-up assessment, whereas for children with- out the allele, the intervention was ineffective.
sentences.s228: Significantly, the program showed greatest influence on children’s externalizing behavior when parents showed the greatest increases in sensitivity (Bakermans-Kranenburg, van Ijzendoorn, Pijlman, Mesman, & Juffer, 2008).
sentences.s229: Taken together, this is an example of differential susceptibility, with the young children with the DRD4 7-repeat showing greater vulnerability to externalizing behavior in the con- text of insensitive parenting, but showing greater benefits result- ing from an intervention designed to increase parental sensitivity.
sentences.s230: The importance of differential susceptibility is both the chal- lenge it presents to diathesis-stress formulations that have long been conventional to thinking in developmental psychopathology, and the emphasis it places on the environmental context in appraising the influence of intrinsic characteristics of the child that have traditionally been viewed as enhancing risk for affective disorders.
sentences.s231: One of the most important contributions of this liter- ature is that in alerting developmental researchers to their failure to examine the influence of these characteristics outside of typical contexts of environmental adversity, it suggests that changing environmental conditions for the positive has significant potential for altering the developmental consequences of these characteris- tics for emotion regulation and dysregulation.
sentences.s232: Interim conclusion Biological and experiential influences, especially in the family, contribute interactively to the development of emotion dysregula- tion, and these research literatures illustrate emergent views con- cerning the nature of this interaction (see Thompson & Waters, in press).
sentences.s233: In particular, it increasingly appears that multiple levels of “under the skin” influences operate not as fixed but as dynamic processes for which experiential influences are catalysts and mod- erators.
sentences.s234: Whether considering the “programming” of fetal and infant stress neurobiology by maternal behavioral and physiolog- ical influences, the social buffering of stress reactivity and its correlates, or the manner in which the influence of susceptibility factors can be altered by experimental interventions with caregivers, these studies underscore that the multilevel processes contributing to the development of emotion dysregulation are biologically dynamic and experience based (Thompson, 2015).
sentences.s235: Such a view of biology × environment interaction is emerging in other fields as well, such as behavioral epigenetics.
sentences.s236: Epigenetics describes how elements of the chemical environment surrounding DNA can alter gene expression without changes to DNA sequence.
sentences.s237: There are several ways that the chemical environ- ment can be altered through DNA methylation, histone modifica- tions, and other processes (see Champagne, 2016).
sentences.s238: Research on behavioral epigenetics underscores two kinds of experiential influ- ences in the early years that are significantly associated with epi- genetic changes in gene expression: environmental adversity and parental nurturance (Thompson, 2015).
sentences.s239: Yang et al. (2013) reported, for example, a higher rate of methylation in a sample of children with histories of maltreatment who had been removed from their parents compared to a demographically matched con- trol group.
sentences.s240: Meaney (2010), in a series of studies, has shown how variations in maternal nurturance of rat pups induced epigenetic changes in gene expression in offspring that had multigenera- tional consequences for behavior, coping, and subsequent paren- tal behavior.
sentences.s241: Taken together, emerging work in behavioral epigenetics with animals and humans indicates that gene activity in behavior and development is not static but dynamic, and that central aspects of experience regulate gene expression.
sentences.s242: It would not be surprising that experiences of adversity and nurturance, especially early in life, would be central epigenetic regulators in light of the significance of these experiences for guiding modifica- tions of gene expression to adapt to critical aspects of the environment.
sentences.s243: These considerations are especially important in light of the conclusion that emotion dysregulation is one of the less heritable risk factors for psychopathology (Beauchaine, 2015).
sentences.s244: This makes understanding of the experiential—and most important, rela- tional—influences on gene expression and other biological con- tributors to emotion dysregulation a central research priority, with implications for clinical intervention as well as developmen- tal theory.
sentences.s245: Conclusion: What Does the Concept of Emotion Dysregulation Contribute to the Study of Emergent Psychopathology?
sentences.s246: Emotion dysregulation is a transdiagnostic element of affective psychopathology.
sentences.s247: Furthermore, research reviewed above indicates that dysregulation has temporal precedence and likely causal influence on the development of externalizing and internalizing disorders in childhood.
sentences.s248: These associations are strong, in part because emotion dysregulation is part of the diagnostic criteria for many disorders.
sentences.s249: Affective disorders are clearly much, much more than simply pathology of emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s250: However, the concept of emotion dysregulation has the potential of contributing significantly to the study of emergent psychopa- thology, especially if a developmental perspective contributes a conceptualization of emotion dysregulation that underscores the multiple goals that can underlie manifestly dysregulated emotion, the settings and relationships that help to define those goals, and the complex influence of experience in shaping (and being shaped by) biological processes.
sentences.s251: Although researchers and clinicians recognize that compe- tency at the management of emotion varies continuously, the manner in which emotion dysregulation is contrasted with “opti- mal” emotion regulation in the literature establishes misleading anchors for thinking about the complex processes involved in regulating emotion.
sentences.s252: It is not just children in emotionally insur- mountable environments who struggle to juggle multiple immedi- ate and long-term goals related to coping in those environments, but most people, in the complex social circumstances in which they live, are managing their emotions with complex, sometimes irreconciliable, goals. “Optimal” emotion regulation may be accomplished less commonly than ordinary emotion regulation that achieves some desirable outcomes, but not all (the research literature on family relationships illustrates these outcomes).
sentences.s253: Viewed in this light, it is also possible to see variations in emotion dysregulation on a continuum in which immediate and longer term costs and benefits of dysregulated responses are considered in relation to the environments in which those responses func- tion.
sentences.s254: Some forms of dysregulation are better than others.
sentences.s255: In this manner, better understanding of the origins of dysregulated behavior might be achieved with better understanding of the sec- ondary gain, reinforcement processes, and other means by which this behavior is maintained despite its otherwise dysfunctional consequences.
sentences.s256: The development of emotion dysregulation also focuses atten- tion on the bottom-up processes that contribute to dysregulated responses that derive from experiential shaping of stress neurobi- ology and its correlates, the emotional dynamics of the family, heritable characteristics, early physiological synchrony between mother and infant, epigenetic modification of gene expression, and other processes.
sentences.s257: These are in contrast with the emphasis in the study of emotion regulation on top-down processes, such as prefrontal control over limbic structures and rational use of self- generated strategies of emotion regulation.
sentences.s258: Viewing emotion reg- ulation and dysregulation on a continuum suggests that the emphasis of each field reveals potential oversight in the other.
sentences.s259: Emotion regulation significantly involves the influence of bottom-up processes and their interaction with cognitive and pre- frontal control mechanisms (Thompson, 2011; Thompson, Lewis, & Calkins, 2008).
sentences.s260: Likewise, greater attention to the cognitive pro- cesses involved in the development of emotion dysregulation would also be warranted.
sentences.s261: These might include studying how the situations evoking emotion are appraised, how internal cues of emotional arousal are interpreted, how emotional self-monitoring occurs (or not), deficiencies in emotional self-efficacy, and other top-down cognitive processes that are also likely to contribute to individual differences in emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s262: Research on abnormal prefrontal–amygdala cortical connectivity as a risk fac- tor for affective psychopathology (Swartz & Monk, 2014) offers another model for considering how the interaction of top-down and bottom-up processes affects emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s263: One advantage of a developmental perspective to these issues is that emergent processes contributing to the development of emotion dysregulation can be identified and studied before they have become consolidated and characterological.
sentences.s264: This perspective is one of the reasons that this discussion has emphasized how emotionally dysregulated responses function in the contexts in which they develop.
sentences.s265: More broadly, the emphasis on adaptation to these contexts, particularly in developmentally critical environ- ments like the family, is also consistent with an evolutionary- developmental approach to behavioral and biological develop- ment (Ellis, Bianchi, Griskevicius, & Frankenhuis, 2017).
sentences.s266: This approach focuses especially on chronic childhood adversity and the developmental adaptations children require in which apparent impairments in emotionality, learning, and behavior may actually be strengths in the contexts in which children live.
sentences.s267: Such a devel- opmental orientation may not consistently fit the evidence on emotion dysregulation and emergent psychopathology, but it sets forth a perspective meriting consideration of how, before they have become consolidated to become characterological, patterns of emotional dysregulation emerge early in life as part of a child × context adaptation.
sentences.s268: Finally, a developmental perspective emphasizes the critical influence of early relationships, a perspective that is easily lost in the focus on individual psychopathology of the adult literature.
sentences.s269: The centrality of early relationships is part of the meaning of Donald Winnicott’s (1957/1947, p. 137) famous aphorism, “[t]here is no such thing as a baby… you are describing a baby and someone.” In the literatures surveyed above, relational experience is the most critical element of the environmental con- ditions shaping the growth of emotion regulation and dysregula- tion, and several studies reviewed earlier further attest to the influence of change in relational experience for normalizing dis- ordered patterns of emotional responding in children.
sentences.s270: Similar influences may be true for adults as well, despite the consolidation of these disordered patterns, and therapy can sometimes serve as an alternative relational experience that promotes greater emo- tional well-being.
sentences.s271: Across the developmental spectrum, however, understanding how atypical patterns of emotional experience and expression function in the relational contexts in which indi- viduals live can provide significant perspective on how those pat- terns may have developed and continue to be maintained, as well as how they might be changed.
sentences.s272: Defining emotion dysregulation as patterns of emotional expe- rience and expression that interfere with goal-directed activity is only the beginning to a fuller conceptualization of what those goals are, the functional purposes that may underlie some forms of emotion dysregulation, the influence of relationships in the contexts in which these goals develop, and the complex interaction of experience and biology in how processes of emotion dysregulation emerge.
sentences.s273: As this definitional conceptualization unfolds, it will also potentially contribute to greater insight into the emergence of developmental psychopathology.

10.1023/a:1021980002473.printed_title: The ADHD Response-Inhibition Deficit as Measured by the Stop Task: Replication with DSM–IV Combined Type, Extension, and Qualification

sentences.s1: Nigg1 Received November 24, 1998; revision received March 30, 1999; accepted April 29, 1999 Although response inhibition has been proposed as a core element of child attention-deficit hyperactiv- ity disorder (ADHD), the literature is heavily reliant on studies using DSM-III-R diagnostic criteria, older methods of measuring response inhibition, samples of boys, and failing to control thoroughly for comorbid problems—both as diagnoses and as subclinical variation.
sentences.s2: The present study replicated a deficit in response inhibition in the ADHD combined type (DSM-IV, American Psychiatric Associa- tion, 1994) using samples matched on age and sex.
sentences.s3: The study replicated an effect size of approximately d = .6 in boys with ADHD, and observed an even larger effect size for girls, although the Sex x Group interaction was nonsignificant.
sentences.s4: Children with ADHD also had problems with response output, shown by variable responding.
sentences.s5: Excluding comorbid conduct disorder, reading disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder, major depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder from the sample did not alter the results.
sentences.s6: Correlations indicated that response inhibition was associated with both attentional problems and reading level.
sentences.s7: Covarying for reading problems did not eliminate the ADHD group effect, but the association of response inhibition with reading clearly requires fur- ther examination.
sentences.s8: Overall, the study supported the role of response inhibition in the DSM-IV ADHD combined type, but with key qualifications as to degree of specificity in reference both to comorbid problems and other executive functions.
sentences.s9: Child attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains a major concern for etiological and phe- nomenological studies due to its prevalence and associ- ated risk for poor long-term outcome (Farrington, Loeber, & Van Kammen, 1990; Hinshaw et al., 1997).
sentences.s10: Efforts to isolate a specific psychological dysfunction that might underly child ADHD have increasingly scrutinized the domain of neuropsychological executive functions (Pennington & Ozonoff, 1996) and within that domain, be- havioral or response inhibition (Chelune, Ferguson, Koon, & Dickey, 1986 ;Schachar& Logan, 1990).
sentences.s11: Effective mea- surement of an ADHD deficit in behavioral inhibition is therefore crucial to several current theories of the disor- der (Barkley, 1997; Tannock, 1998; Quay, 1988).
sentences.s12: Efforts 1Address all correspondence to Joel T.
sentences.s13: Nigg, Psychology Department, Michigan State University, 153 Snyder Hall, Bast Lansing, MI 48824- 1117.
sentences.s14: Electronic mail may be sent to nigg@pilot.msu.edu. to operationalize behavioral inhibition in the laboratory for purposes of experimental study have had important shortcomings historically (Milich & Kramer, 1984), al- though much has been learned from use of the Go-No-Go task (Casey et al., 1997) and other measures.
sentences.s15: In particular, work in this area has benefited from use of a measurement approach borrowed from cognitive psychology—the stop signal paradigm (Logan & Cowan, 1984).
sentences.s16: The stop task is a straightforward dual-task com- puter paradigm.
sentences.s17: The child faces the computer monitor and presses the appropriate choice key (e.g., X or O) depending on whether an X or an O appears on the screen.
sentences.s18: However, when a tone sounds, the child does not press the key (stop signal trial).
sentences.s19: This paradigm has the substantial measure- ment advantage of a well-worked out mathematical model that explains performance on the task, known as the "race model" (Logan, 1994; Logan & Cowan, 1984).
sentences.s20: In brief, this model posits that two processes operate independently 393 009l-(X>27/99/1000-0393$16.00/0© 1999 Plenum Publishing Corporation KEY WORDS: ADHD; response inhibition; stop task. of one another in responding to the task—a "go" process and a "stop" process.
sentences.s21: These two processes "race" to de- termine the behavioral response.
sentences.s22: By varying the timing of the inhibition (stop) signal tone, the model allows es- timation of the speed of the "stop" process and the "go" process.
sentences.s23: The use of the stop signal paradigm has appeared promising in understanding child ADHD.
sentences.s24: Beginning with Schachar and Logan (1990), several studies have shown that children with ADHD have slower stop signal reaction times than normal comparison children (Aman, Roberts, & Pennington, 1998; Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996; Pliszka, Borcherding, Sprattey, Leon, & Irick, 1997; Schachar, Tannock, Marriott, & Logan, 1995; for a thorough review see Oosterlaan, Logan, & Sergeant, 1998).
sentences.s25: These findings have supported the idea that behavioral inhibition (with an unspecified or speculated underlying neural process) may be a core deficit in the development of child ADHD (Barkley, 1997; Quay, 1997; Tannock, 1998).
sentences.s26: Prior data have also suggested that the reason children with ADHD exhibit behavioral impulsivity is not due to a fast "go" pro- cess, but to a slow "stop" process.
sentences.s27: However, meta-analytic results (Oosterlaan et al., 1998) have indicated potential milder problems in the "go" process as well, indicating that problems in response organization, arousal, or effort (Sergeant, Oosterlaan, & van der Meere, 1999) may also play a part in the disorder.
sentences.s28: Despite this paradigm's mathematical elegance and replications of an ADHD deficit on the task, several con- siderations mandate further modified replications of this potentially critical ADHD deficit. (a) Studies published to date in ADHD used an older version of the task, in which stop signal reaction time was estimated from a se- ries of predetermined delays.
sentences.s29: Recently, a new tracking method has been introduced that dynamically varies stop signal delay depending on participant response, presum- ably enabling a more accurate estimate of stop signal reaction time (Logan, Schachar, & Tannock, 1997).
sentences.s30: Do ADHD effects replicate using this new method? (b) The existing literature relies on samples that were diagnosed with DSM-III-R or other non-DSM-IV specific criteria (e.g., Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996; Pliszka et al., 1997; Schachar et al., 1995) or had both combined and inatten- tive subtypes in their samples (e.g., Aman et al., 1998).
sentences.s31: Will the effect replicate and be similar in magnitude (i.e., d ~ .6; Oosterlaan et al., 1998) using a sample restricted to the DSM-IV combined type? (c) Many key studies re- lied on samples that were either entirely male (Aman et al., 1998; Schachar & Logan, 1990; Schachar et al., 1995) or had groups that were not matched on sex (Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996; Pliszka et al., 1997) and did not ex- amine sex by group interactions.
sentences.s32: Do findings replicate in samples that include proportionate numbers of girls with ADHD, and do effects interact with child sex?
sentences.s33: This ques- tion is germane in view of questions about whether the nature and severity of cognitive mechanisms and brain substrates of ADHD are similar in boys and girls (Ernst et al., 1994; James & Taylor, 1990) and in light of the general lack of research on girls with ADHD (Arnold, 1996). (d) Last, but far from least, questions remain about the specificity of this task in relation to ADHD symptoms versus comorbid symptoms, particularly conduct disorder (CD) and reading problems.
sentences.s34: Oosterlaan et al. (1998) re- ported that children with conduct disorder also exhibited a significant, though smaller, deficit in stop signal reaction time.
sentences.s35: Emerging data also raise questions about the role of reading disorder in the ADHD symptoms observed in the laboratory (Nigg, Hinshaw, Carte, & Treuting, 1998; Tannock 1998; Tannock & Marriott, 1992).
sentences.s36: In addressing comorbidity, removing children with comorbid diagnoses is only a partial solution, because the remaining ADHD children are still likely to have higher, subclinical levels of comorbid problems than the control group.
sentences.s37: Therefore, covarying of behavioral and reading levels is also needed (Nigg et al., 1998), but has been lacking for stop data.
sentences.s38: In addition, most studies have relied on between-group comparisons only.
sentences.s39: However, Pliszka et al. (1997) reported that stop signal response time correlated with teacher rat- ings of hyperactivity and inattention but not aggression, whereas Oosterlaan & Sergeant (1996) reported that stop signal response time correlated with ratings of attention problems as well as aggressive and delinquent behavior.
sentences.s40: Therefore, correlations of stop task responses with dimen- sional behavior ratings were also examined to assess the replicability of those reports with DSM-IV and the new procedure.
sentences.s41: The present article thus reported a replication of in- hibitory deficits in DSM-IV ADHD-combined type chil- dren in groups matched on age and sex, using the tracking method of assessing stop signal response time, with vari- ous controls for comorbid conduct and reading problems, METHOD Participants Child participants with possible ADHD ranging from first through sixth grade were recruited from a local pedi- atric clinic specializing in ADHD referrals, from a local support group for parents of children with ADHD, and from invitation letters sent to randomly selected parents of children in the local school districts.
sentences.s42: Normal compari- son children were matched on recruitment source, sex, and age as much as possible (thus, they were recruited from either a general pediatric clinic in the same medical com- plex as the ADHD-specialty clinic or from the same lo- cal school districts).
sentences.s43: Children were excluded if they were mentally retarded, autistic, had a history of seizure dis- order or other known frank neurological condition, had Tourette syndrome, did not live with at least one biological parent (due to ancillary studies of parents now underway), or had valid Full Scale IQ < 70.
sentences.s44: Children were considered as possible ADHD "combined type" if they either (a) ex- ceeded screening cut-offs on at least one parent and one teacher rating scale, from the Child Behavior Checklist (Achenbach, 1991) attention problems T > 60 (Chen, Faraone, Biederman, & Tsuang, 1994), Conners Rating Scale hyperactivity index T > 65, or at least four symp- toms of inattention or hyperactivity endorsed (with a rat- ing of "2" or "3") on the DSM-IV SNAP rating scale [Swanson, 1992]; or (b) were diagnosed as ADHD by a physician or psychologist in the community who used both parent and teacher ratings as part of the diagnostic decision.
sentences.s45: Diagnosis was then confirmed by the Diagnostic In- terview Schedule (DISC) for DSM-IV (Schaffer, Fisher, & Lucas, 1997).
sentences.s46: The DISC-IV is an NIMH structured diagnostic interview.
sentences.s47: It implements a stringent diagnos- tic algorithm requiring onset before age 7, persistence of symptoms greater than 6 months, and symptom-specific impairment in at least two settings.
sentences.s48: Prior versions of the DISC have exhibited acceptable reliability and validity (Schwab-Stone et al., 1996).
sentences.s49: The computer-assisted inter- view was administered to the child's primary caregiver by trained interviewers.
sentences.s50: Interview and trainer training was ob- tained from Prudence Fisher of the Columbia DISC work group and then provided by the author to graduate students in clinical psychology, who administered the interviews.
sentences.s51: Interview quality was checked by videotaping the inter- views and viewing a randomly selected 20% of the tapes to confirm appropriateness of interview methods.
sentences.s52: To con- firm interrater reliability, 40% of the tapes were viewed by a second rater; as expected with the computer-assisted interview, agreement reached kappa = 1.0 for ADHD, op- positional defiant disorder (ODD), and CD.
sentences.s53: To implement a modified best estimate diagnostic procedure (Kosten & Rounsaville, 1992), if the DISC-IV was one or two symp- toms shy of threshold (and cross-setting impairment was affirmed on the DISC), then the ADHD diagnosis could still be assigned if sufficient additional symptoms were endorsed by the child's teacher as indicated by a rating of 2 (quite a bit) or 3 (very much) on the SNAP-IV (see Hinshaw et al., 1997 for a similar procedure in the multi- site multimodal NIMH treatment study of ADHD).
sentences.s54: Four children in the ADHD group required this process to reach the ADHD diagnosis.
sentences.s55: Removing these four children did not alter the findings.
sentences.s56: Children with the inattentive or hy- peractive subtype of ADHD, as well as children with sit- uational ADHD, were excluded from both groups.
sentences.s57: Com- parison children were negative for ADHD based on the criteria given and could not have CD or reading disorder.
sentences.s58: One comparison child had an ADHD sibling (the sibling did not participate in the study).
sentences.s59: Reading disorder was assessed as follows.
sentences.s60: First, Full Scale IQ was estimated for the ADHD children with a Five-test short form of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, 3rd edition (WISC-III) (WISC-III; Wechsler, 1991) consisting of Vocabulary, Block Design, Informa- tion, Object Assembly, and Picture Completion, with re- liability = .95, and validity = .90 (Sattler, 1992).
sentences.s61: Due to resource constraints, several comparison children and a handful of ADHD children completed a two-subtest short form (Vocabulary and Block Design, with reliability = .91 and validity = .86).
sentences.s62: A valid IQ estimate could not be obtained for 1 ADHD child due to time and behavioral constraints; he was reading at grade level so the sample mean was substituted for his IQ.
sentences.s63: Reading and spelling were assessed with the Wechsler Individual Achievement Test Screener (Wechsler, 1992).
sentences.s64: These reliable and valid tests have a norm group linked to the WISC-III stan- dardization sample, making direct comparison of reading and IQ levels dependable.
sentences.s65: Following DSM-IV criteria, to be diagnosed with reading disorder children had to have (a) average reading and spelling <85 (standard score) and (b) Full Scale IQ minus reading/spelling average of at least 15 points.
sentences.s66: Finally, CD and additional comorbid diagnoses were carefully screened using the CBCL, the SNAP-IV, and the Conners ratings scales.
sentences.s67: If any symptoms of other disorders were endorsed on these ratings scales, that disorder was evaluated with the DISC-IV.
sentences.s68: Children with current major depressive disorder or evidence of bipolar disorder were excluded (n = 2).
sentences.s69: The other disorders assessed but not excluded are detailed in the Results.
sentences.s70: Procedure Stop task practice and instructions.
sentences.s71: Children com- pleted the stop task in a single session lasting about 20 min.
sentences.s72: They sat facing the computer screen accompanied by a trained examiner who gave verbal instructions from a prac- ticed script.
sentences.s73: The examiners were blind to child diagnosis and study hypotheses.
sentences.s74: The procedures were taken from Logan, Schachar, and Tannock (1997) as follows.
sentences.s75: The computer screen displayed an X or an O on a black and white 14" computer monitor in random sequence.
sentences.s76: Chil- dren first were given two sets of 32 practice trials, during which they practiced pressing the designated key on the keyboard for the X or the O as quickly as possible, us- ing two fingers on their dominant hand.
sentences.s77: In the second set of 32 practice trials they again pressed the appropri- ate key, but this time tried not to hit any key when they heard the tone.
sentences.s78: Following Logan (1994; Logan et al., 1997; Tannock, personal communication, May 1997), children were instructed to respond as quickly as possible without making errors on the X/0 discrimination, that they would be unable to stop every time, and that they should not wait for the beep.
sentences.s79: The experimenter remained with each child throughout the task.
sentences.s80: Stop task experimental procedure.
sentences.s81: In the experimen- tal procedure, a fixation point appeared at the center of the screen for 500 ms at the beginning of each trial.
sentences.s82: It was then replaced by an X or O for 1,000 ms.
sentences.s83: The child re- sponded with a key press, and the screen was then blank for 1,000 ms.
sentences.s84: Four blocks of 64 trials were administered, with a rest in between each block, for a total of 256 trials.
sentences.s85: On 25% of the trials, the stop tone sounded for 100 ms.
sentences.s86: Thus, a total of 64 trials (16 per block) included the stop signal tone.
sentences.s87: The timing of the stop tone was varied to implement the tracking procedure as follows.
sentences.s88: The stop signal delay was initially set at 250 ms.
sentences.s89: If the child failed to inhibit their response when the tone sounded, on the subsequent trial the stop signal delay was decreased by 50 ms (making it easier to stop next time); if they inhibited successfully, stop signal delay was increased by 50 ms on the next trial (making it harder to stop next time).
sentences.s90: Probability of stop- ping successfully was thus maintained at approximately 50%.
sentences.s91: In this procedure, stop signal reaction time is es- timated simply by subtracting mean stop signal latency from mean go response time (see Logan, 1994).
sentences.s92: Because past experience (Logan, personal communication, May 1997) and our own pilot data indicated that the first block was often the most unreliable, for most children the final three blocks were av- eraged to obtain their experimental data.
sentences.s93: Exceptions were when accuracy was below 70% or probability of stopping was outside the range of 20% to 80% on only one block other than the first block (indicating either waiting for or ignoring the tone on that block).
sentences.s94: That block was deemed invalid and discarded prior to analyzing the data.
sentences.s95: These decisions were made blind to child diagnosis or stop sig- nal response time.
sentences.s96: In addition, children were dropped from the study if their overall accuracy fell below 75% (n = 1, indicating either failure to attend to the task or administra- tion error), probability of stopping fell outside the range of 20% to 80% (n = 0), or stop signal reaction time was <0 ms (n = 1, indicating failure to comply with the task).
sentences.s97: Hypotheses, Power, Effect Size, and Data Analytic Plan Hypotheses.
sentences.s98: The hypotheses were that ADHD is characterized by (1) deficient inhibition process (slow stop signal response time), with d ~ .6; and/or (2) deficient re- sponse organization, indicated by slower response time; and/or (3) deficient arousal, indicated by greater response variability (Parasuraman, Warm, & See, 1998, provide ra- tionale for using variability as an index of arousal).
sentences.s99: Sec- ondary hypotheses were that (4) as predicted by a primary inhibition model, the stop deficit was larger than the go deficit (task by group interaction), and (5) that effects were similar in boys and girls with ADHD (no Sex x Group in- teraction).
sentences.s100: Finally, (6) the hypothesis that comorbid read- ing or conduct problems would account for any effects was checked with analyses of covariance (ANCOVAS) to control subclinical variation and with reanalysis removing children with selected comorbid diagnoses.
sentences.s101: As part of the final hypothesis, stop task variables were correlated with dimensional behavior ratings.
sentences.s102: The first three hypotheses were tested with a between-group ANCOVA of stop signal reaction time, go reaction time, and within-subject standard devi- ation with age covaried (preceded by a multivariate anal- ysis of covariance [MANCOVA]).
sentences.s103: The interactions were tested in a 2 x 2 x 2 analysis of variance (ANOVA) de- sign, with two between-subjects factors of group (ADHD, control) and sex (boy, girl) and one within-subjects fac- tor, task (go, stop).
sentences.s104: Levene's test revealed unequal vari- ances across the ADHD and control groups in stop signal reaction time (p = .01).
sentences.s105: To address possible effects of unequal variances, all ANOVA's were recomputed with log-transformed variables with no change in results un- less noted.
sentences.s106: Assumptions of regression were examined by extensive scrutiny of both raw data and residuals plots, which supported the validity of the regression and covari- ance analysis.
sentences.s107: As a further check, correlations were recom- puted using log transformed dependent variables with no change in results unless otherwise noted.
sentences.s108: Raw data results are thus reported to ease interpretability.
sentences.s109: The meta-analysis by Oosterlaan et al. (1998) suggested a population effect size for ADHD versus control children of d = .64 for stop signal reaction time and d = .94 for slope of the inhibition function.
sentences.s110: The available sample in the current study had power >.80 to detect effects of this magnitude in a factorial design.
sentences.s111: Power was >.80 to detect an effect size of / = .3 (d = .6) for the Task x Group interaction (Hypothesis 4).
sentences.s112: However, the Sex x Group interaction would have inadequate power with a = .05 to detect any but the largest effect.
sentences.s113: Given that the Sex x Group interaction was one for which a Type II error would potentially lead to erroneous data analysis, alpha was adjusted to .10 to bring power to >.80 to detect an interaction of magnitude / = .36 (d ~ .7; Cohen, 1988).
sentences.s114: Although a change to a = . 10 to improve power is well-supported logically and statistically (Cohen, 1988), it had no effect on the conclusions.
sentences.s115: Overall, power was equal to or greater than most prior studies of the stop task.
sentences.s116: For key comparisons, effect sizes are reported with both "d" and with eta-squared (interpreted in a similar manner to R-squared; Cohen, 1988).
sentences.s117: RESULTS Sample Demographics The comparison and ADHD groups each had 25 chil- dren.
sentences.s118: Table I indicates the demographic and behavioral features of the two groups.
sentences.s119: As the table indicates, the groups were reasonably well-matched by age and sex.
sentences.s120: The ADHD group had a nonsignificantly lower full-scale IQ.
sentences.s121: Reading level was lower in the ADHD group; 3 out of the 25 ADHD children met criteria for learning disability (LD; reading disorder), versus 0 out of the 27 comparison children.
sentences.s122: In addition, 4 of the 25 of the ADHD children met criteria for CD (including 1 child with both CD and LD, 1 child with CD + generalized anxiety disorder + post- traumatic stress disorder, and 1 child with CD + general- ized anxiety disorder + obsessive–compulsive disorder).
sentences.s123: One other ADHD child met criteria for generalized anx- iety disorder.
sentences.s124: In the ADHD group, 10 of the 25 children met criteria for ODD, versus 0 of the 25 in the compar- ison group.
sentences.s125: Overall, 8 of the 25 ADHD children had no comorbid diagnosis; 18 of the 25 had no comorbid diag- nosis or only comorbid ODD.
sentences.s126: These rates are comparable to others in the literature (Biederman, Newcorn, & Sprich, 1991; Hinshaw, 1987).
sentences.s127: With regard to ethnicity, the control group included African American (12%), Hispanic/Latino (11%) and Asian American (4%) children, whereas the ADHD group was 8% African American.
sentences.s128: Ethnicity was unrelated to the dependent variables.
sentences.s129: Preliminary Checks on Data The stop signal task appeared to work as intended.
sentences.s130: For the sample as a whole, probability of stopping was .53, and accuracy was 91%.
sentences.s131: Reliability over three blocks was a = .88 for stop signal reaction time, a = .96 for go response time, and a = .87 for response vari- ability.
sentences.s132: Age was significantly correlated with go response time (r = -.36, p = .01) and with response variability (r = —.29, p < .05), so age was covaried in the anal- yses.
sentences.s133: Stopping probability and accuracy are summarized in Table II along with the raw cell means and standard deviations for the three study variables of stop signal re- action time, go reaction time, and response variability (within-subject standard deviation).

sentences.s172: The ADHD response inhibition problem was independent of age, IQ, reading, and other disruptive behaviors.
sentences.s173: Regarding the issue of clinical utility, exploratory analysis was conducted.
