sentences.s177: DISCUSSION Diagnostic criteria for ADHD changed substantively with the transition from DSM-III-R to DSM-IV, making replication of previous findings with the new diagnostic criteria crucial to accumulating theory and knowledge in the field.
sentences.s178: The DSM-IV combined subtype is the focus of current theories of a behavioral inhibition deficit in ADHD.
sentences.s179: With regard to the DSM-IV ADHD combined type, the results show that the new tracking procedure yields the same findings for response inhibition as in prior studies that relied on DSM-III-R criteria.
sentences.s180: ADHD was as- sociated with slower stop signal response time.
sentences.s181: The re- sponse inhibition effect appeared to be similar in boys and girls with ADHD combined type, although effects were nonsignificantly larger in the girls.
sentences.s182: The latter is pre- liminary due to the smal numbers of boys or girls in each group separately.
sentences.s183: Nevertheless, it is an important piece of information, indicating that girls with the combined type of ADHD have equally clear deficits in response in- hibition.
sentences.s184: When data were examined dimensionally, the present study replicated significant correlations of stop signal reaction time with ratings of attention problems (cf.
sentences.s185: Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996; Pliszka et al., 1997).
sentences.s186: Taken as a whole, these results bolster the idea that deficits in mo- tor inhibition processes are associated with the DSM-IV ADHD combined type (Barkley, 1997; Tannock, 1998).
sentences.s187: Further support for an inhibition deficit in ADHD was that the effect was independent of age, IQ, read- ing, or associated disruptive behavior problems.
sentences.s188: A crit- ical problem in neuropsychological and cognitive stud- ies of ADHD has been insufficient control of comorbid problems.
sentences.s189: Many studies simply do not assess or report the extent of comorbid conditions in the ADHD group (Oosterlaan et al., 1998).
sentences.s190: Thus, it has been difficult to know whether various findings of ADHD deficit are spe- cific to ADHD or explained by associated conditions.
sentences.s191: Re- cent reviews (Pennington & Ozonoff, 1996) and empirical reports (Nigg et al., 1998) have supported the idea that ex- ecutive neuropsychological deficits are specific to ADHD at least in part, and not wholly explainable by associated conditions.
sentences.s192: Yet this question has had limited investiga- tion with the stop task and response inhibition per se.
sentences.s193: Aman et al. (1998) undertook perhaps the most careful control to date by screening out children with CD, read- ing disorder, and other conditions.
sentences.s194: However, like other investigators, they reported that despite these controls, the ADHD group exhibited higher levels of subthreshold antisocial and aggressive behavior problems than the con- trol group.
sentences.s195: Given this state of affairs, control of subclinical problems by statistical covariance is needed to demon- strate that cognitive effects are truly independent of these associated problems (see Nigg et al., 1998).
sentences.s196: The present study demonstrated that even with these problems covar- ied (using several instruments across several data sources), a deficit in response inhibition is linked to the ADHD com- bined type.
sentences.s197: Despite these substantial supports for behavioral in- hibition models of ADHD, some important caveats bear noting.
sentences.s198: Conceptually, the "race" model, which describes the stop task, is not a process model.
sentences.s199: It does not specify what inhibition process is impaired or how it works.
sentences.s200: Thus, whether this is a frontal, behavioral inhibition system or some other inhibition process remains to be worked out.
sentences.s201: Nevertheless, it is presumed to reflect an executive control process (Logan, 1994).
sentences.s202: Thus, the relation of behavioral inhibition to (a) other kinds of inhibition (Mezzacappa, Kindlon, Saul, & Earls, 1998) and (b) other executive func- tions needs further multivariate study (e.g., Aman et al., 1998).
sentences.s203: Further, with regard to the data reported here, the chil- dren with ADHD also had greater within-child response variability.
sentences.s204: This secondary finding could be interpreted as indicating problems in arousal (Parasuraman et al., 1998) or effort under the cognitive-energetic model (Sergeant et al., 1999) and suggests that the ADHD deficit is not limited to inhibition processes per se.
sentences.s205: A less crucial point concerns the wide variability in response in the ADHD group.
sentences.s206: Nearly all models that were checked sustained the ADHD effect for stop signal reac- tion time.
sentences.s207: The one exception was using log transformed data with reading covaried.
sentences.s208: That model reached signifi- cance for go reaction time but not stop signal reaction time.
sentences.s209: However, given the preponderance of evidence across all models and the lack of justification for favoring the trans- formed over the raw data (e.g., group variabilities did not differ signficantly for go reaction time), the primary model results are seen as most trustworthy.
sentences.s210: The go response deficit in the meta-analysis by Oosterlaan et al. (1998) was d = .49.
sentences.s211: At first glance, this appears quite a bit larger than the nonsignificant d = .21 reported in the current study.
sentences.s212: However, this is not a surpris- ing finding when the data are considered more carefully.
sentences.s213: Prior studies of the stop task have yielded ADHD versus normal Go RT d- values from d = .00 (Schachar & Logan, 1990) to d = 1.2 (Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996).
sentences.s214: Thus, there is wide variability in the effects observed in this pa- rameter across studies.
sentences.s215: Also, the effect size in the present study is with age covaried, which reduced the effect (prior to age correction it was nonsignificant at d = .38).
sentences.s216: The effect size reported by Oosterlaan et al. (1998) did not in- clude age adjustment.
sentences.s217: However, from the point of view of differential deficit (Chapman & Chapman, 1978), it was not possible to show that the deficit in response inhibition was greater than a (subthreshold) deficit in response or- ganization (because the interaction was not significant).
sentences.s218: Thus, isolating response inhibition, rather than response organization, as the primary deficit specific to ADHD re- mains unclear when the data are considered as a whole.
sentences.s219: Given the above issues, and in particular the finding of both an inhibition deficit and an arousal (or variability) effect in the ADHD group, further theoretical integration of response inhibition (e.g., Barkley, 1997) and response output or arousal (effort/energy) models of ADHD (e.g. Sergeant et al., 1999) may be needed.
sentences.s220: It is interesting to consider whether the older suggestions by Eysenck (e.g., Eysenck & Eysenck, 1985) regarding individual differ- ences in cortical hypoarousal would contribute to such integration (but see Barkley, 1997).
sentences.s221: Another caveat in these data was that the correlation of response inhibition with reading was substantial and comparable in magnitude to its correlation with attention problems.
sentences.s222: Although the ADHD effect survived control for reading problems in this sample selected for ADHD, it raises the question of what would happen in a sample selected for reading disorder.
sentences.s223: Again, the specificity of this measure to symptoms of ADHD apart from reading prob- lems appeared less than fully convincing based on these qualitative aspects of the data.
sentences.s224: It may be that reading dis- order is a more important confound than CD in isolating an inhibitory deficit in ADHD.
sentences.s225: A final issue for the inhibition theory concerns clin- ical utility.
sentences.s226: Little data are available regarding the degree to which stop signal response time, for example, can ac- curately identify children with ADHD.
sentences.s227: The limited data on this point presented in the current article suggest that the measure can improve on chance prediction but fails to achieve extremely high classification rates.
sentences.s228: Thus, further efforts to examine clinical utility are needed in larger sam- ples to determine whether this measure has the potential to be useful in case identification.
sentences.s229: In short, the research agenda to show that inhibitory problems are central in ADHD remains long.
sentences.s230: Limitations In addition to the considerations just noted, limita- tions of this study were the heavy reliance on a clinical sample of ADHD children, which can raise potential refer- ral artifacts in seeking correlates of the disorder (Goodman et al., 1997) and the extensive representation of opposi- tional defiant children in the ADHD group.
sentences.s231: However, these characteristics probably support the generalizability of the results to clinical samples.
sentences.s232: Moreover, studies that have drawn population samples reported results for inhibition similar to those herein (e.g., Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 1996).
sentences.s233: Summary Overall, the study shows that using the newer and presumably more robust method of estimating stop signal response time, the ADHD deficit was confirmed.
sentences.s234: The ef- fect size for boys was about the same as in the prior lit- erature (about d = .6) and comparable (larger but non- significantly so) for girls.
sentences.s235: Effects were not accounted for by age, IQ, reading ability, or comorbid behavioral prob- lems.
sentences.s236: The prior findings in the literature were not due to reliance on DSM-lIl-R criteria, exclusion of girls, or use of older methods of measuring stop signal delay.

10.1023/b:joba.0000007455.08539.94.printed_title: Multidimensional Assessment of Emotion Regulation and Dysregulation: Development, Factor Structure, and Initial Validation of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale

sentences.s1: Gratz and Lizabeth Roemer University of Massachusetts Boston In press, Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment Abstract Given recent attention to emotion regulation as a potentially unifying function of diverse symptom presentations, there is a need for comprehensive measures that adequately assess difficulties in emotion regulation among adults.
sentences.s2: This paper (a) proposes an integrative conceptualization of emotion regulation as involving not just the modulation of emotional arousal, but also the awareness, understanding, and acceptance of emotions, and the ability to act in desired ways regardless of emotional state; and (b) begins to explore the factor structure and psychometric properties of a new measure, the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS).
sentences.s3: Two samples of undergraduate students completed questionnaire packets.
sentences.s4: Preliminary findings suggest that the DERS has high internal consistency, good test-retest reliability, and adequate construct and predictive validity.
sentences.s5: Keywords: emotion regulation; emotion dysregulation; assessment; experiential avoidance; deliberate self-harm Multidimensional Assessment of Emotion Regulation and Dysregulation: Development, Factor Structure, and Initial Validation of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale Consistent with behavioral theories of psychopathology that highlight the importance of the function of problem behaviors rather than symptom picture (Hayes, Wilson, Gifford, Follette, & Strosahl, 1996), increasing attention has been paid to emotion regulation as a potentially unifying function of diverse symptom presentations and maladaptive behaviors (Gross & Munoz, 1995).
sentences.s6: Although there is some preliminary literature on the role of emotion regulation deficits in a range of clinical disorders, including substance abuse (Hayes et al., 1996), generalized anxiety disorder (Mennin, Heimberg, Turk, & Fresco, 2002), and complex post-traumatic stress disorder (Cloitre, 1998), the most comprehensive work highlighting the role of emotion dysregulation in a clinical disorder has been Linehan’s (1993) theoretical work on the development of borderline personality disorder.
sentences.s7: Linehan proposes that emotion dysregulation is one of the central features of borderline personality disorder and underlies many of the associated behaviors of this disorder, including deliberate self-harm (a behavior thought to serve an emotion-regulating function).
sentences.s8: Her conceptualization of self-harm as an emotion regulation strategy is supported by both empirical and theoretical literature on the function of this behavior (see Briere & Gil, 1998; Gratz, 2003).
sentences.s9: It has been similarly suggested that the perpetration of violence toward others (e.g., intimate partners) may function to regulate emotions (Jakupcak, Lisak, & Roemer, 2002) – consistent with findings from experimental studies that aggressive behavior can serve an affect regulatory function (Bushman, Baumeister, & Phillips, 2001).
sentences.s10: Despite its clinical significance, however, the role of emotion regulation deficits in the development and maintenance of clinical difficulties has not been adequately researched in adults.
sentences.s11: Likely contributing to the lack of research in this area is the absence of both consistent, agreed-upon conceptualizations of emotion regulation and comprehensive measures that adequately assess the complexity of this construct among adults.
sentences.s12: The purpose of the present study was to develop and validate a measure of clinically-relevant difficulties in emotion regulation that is based on a comprehensive, integrative conceptualization of emotion regulation.
sentences.s13: This paper (a) reviews the extant literature on the conceptualization and measurement of emotion regulation (and dysregulation); (b) provides an integrative conceptualization of emotion regulation that may be used in future research in this area; and (c) begins to explore the factor structure and psychometric properties of a new measure of difficulties in emotion regulation, the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS).
sentences.s14: Some conceptualizations of emotion regulation emphasize the control of emotional experience and expression (especially the expressive control of negative emotions) and the reduction of emotional arousal (see Cortez & Bugental, 1994; Garner & Spears, 2000; Kopp, 1989; Zeman & Garber, 1996).
sentences.s15: In contrast, others emphasize the functional nature of emotions in conceptualizing emotion regulation, suggesting that emotion regulation is not synonymous with emotional control and, as such, does not necessarily involve immediately diminishing negative affect (Cole, Michel, & Teti, 1994; Thompson, 1994).
sentences.s16: These latter approaches suggest that deficiencies in the capacity to experience (and differentiate) the full range of emotions and respond spontaneously may be just as maladaptive as deficiencies in the ability to attenuate and modulate strong negative emotions (Cole et al., 1994; Gross & Munoz, 1995; Paivio & Greenberg, 1998).
sentences.s17: Similarly, some researchers have suggested that adaptive emotion regulation involves monitoring and evaluating emotional experience in addition to modifying it, highlighting the importance of the awareness and understanding of emotions (Thompson & Calkins, 1996).
sentences.s18: The emphasis on the functionality of emotions is consistent with theory and research highlighting the potentially paradoxical, dysregulating effects of attempts to control emotional experience and expression (despite the fact that such emotional control has often been equated with emotion regulation, e.g., Garner & Spears, 2000; Zeman & Garber, 1996).
sentences.s19: Hayes and colleagues (1996) have suggested that efforts to avoid internal experiences (e.g., unwanted thoughts and feelings) underlie many psychological disorders – a theory with growing empirical support (see Stewart, Zvolensky, & Eifert, 2002).
sentences.s20: Further, both the general tendency to constrict emotional expression and experimental instructions to conceal one’s emotional expressions have been associated with increased physiological arousal (Notarius & Levenson, 1979; Gross & Levenson, 1997), suggesting that attempts to control emotional expression may increase risk for emotion dysregulation (given that high levels of arousal are more difficult to regulate; see Eisenberg, Cumberland, & Spinrad, 1998; Flett, Blankstein, & Obertynski, 1996).
sentences.s21: This literature suggests that an emphasis on the control, rather than the acceptance, of emotional responses may confound processes that undermine regulation with those that are regulatory.
sentences.s22: Therefore, some conceptualizations of emotion regulation emphasize the importance of accepting and valuing emotional responses (Cole et al., 1994; Linehan, 1993).
sentences.s23: Consistent with these approaches, researchers have suggested that the tendency to experience negative emotions in response to one’s own emotional reactions (indicative of a lack of emotional acceptance) is maladaptive, and associated with greater difficulties in emotion regulation (Cole et al., 1994; Hayes, Strosahl, & Wilson, 1999; Paivio & Greenberg, 1998).
sentences.s24: Researchers have suggested the necessity of considering the demands of the situation and goals of the individual when evaluating emotion regulation (Thompson, 1994; Thompson & Calkins, 1996), as emotion regulation can only be understood and evaluated within a specific context (Cole et al., 1994; Thompson, 1994).
sentences.s25: Knowledge of the specific emotion regulation strategies used by an individual, in the absence of information on the context in which they are used, may provide little information about the individual’s ability to regulate her or his emotions effectively.
sentences.s26: Adaptive emotion regulation instead involves flexibility in the use of emotion regulation strategies (Cole et al., 1994; Thompson, 1994).
sentences.s27: Researchers have also suggested that adaptive emotion regulation involves altering the intensity or duration of an emotion rather than changing the discrete emotion that is experienced (Thompson, 1994; Thompson & Calkins, 1996).
sentences.s28: In other words, adaptive regulation involves modulating the experience of emotions rather than eliminating certain emotions.
sentences.s29: This modulation of arousal is thought to be in the service of reducing the urgency associated with the emotion so that the individual is able to control her or his behavior (as opposed to controlling emotions themselves).
sentences.s30: These conceptualizations of emotion regulation emphasize the ability to inhibit inappropriate or impulsive behaviors, and behave in accordance with desired goals, when experiencing negative emotions (see Linehan, 1993; Melnick & Hinshaw, 2000).
sentences.s31: Based on the above conceptual and empirical work, emotion regulation may be conceptualized as involving the (a) awareness and understanding of emotions, (b) acceptance of emotions, (c) ability to control impulsive behaviors and behave in accordance with desired goals when experiencing negative emotions, and (d) ability to use situationally-appropriate emotion regulation strategies flexibly to modulate emotional responses as desired in order to meet individual goals and situational demands.1 The relative absence of any or all of these abilities would indicate the presence of difficulties in emotion regulation, or emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s32: Despite the clinical utility of assessing difficulties in emotion regulation, there are few measures of emotion regulation or dysregulation in adults.
sentences.s33: Most of the measures used to assess emotion regulation deficits are actually measures of closely-related constructs, leading some researchers to use multiple measures in an attempt to capture the construct of emotion regulation (see, e.g., Mennin et al., 2002).
sentences.s34: The most commonly used measure of emotion regulation is Catanzaro and Mearns’ (1990) Generalized Expectancy for Negative Mood Regulation Scale (NMR).
sentences.s35: The NMR measures beliefs that some “behavior or cognition will alleviate a negative state or induce a positive one” (p. 547), emphasizing the elimination and avoidance of negative emotions (as opposed to the ability to act in desired ways in the presence of these emotions).
sentences.s36: Many items on the NMR refer to particular emotion regulation strategies that people may use to modulate emotional arousal.
sentences.s37: This practice implies that emotion regulation strategies are adaptive regardless of context and that certain strategies are more adaptive than others universally – an implication that is inconsistent with conceptualizations of emotion regulation that emphasize the contextually-dependent nature of adaptive regulation strategies (see Cole et al., 1994; Thompson, 1994; Thompson & Calkins, 1996).
sentences.s38: Moreover, many of the strategies listed in the NMR seem to equate emotion regulation with emotional avoidance (e.g., “When I’m upset, I believe that I won’t be able to put it out of my mind” (negatively scored); or “When I’m upset, I believe that I can forget about what’s upsetting me pretty easily”).
sentences.s39: While the NMR does not assess some potentially important aspects of emotion regulation (such as the awareness, understanding, and acceptance of emotions), it does measure one important aspect of emotion regulation as conceptualized here: access to emotion regulation strategies perceived as effective.
sentences.s40: Another measure occasionally used to capture the construct of emotion regulation is the Trait Meta-Mood Scale (TMMS; Salovey, Mayer, Goldman, Turvey, & Palfai, 1995), which assesses “individual differences in the ability to reflect upon and manage one’s emotions” (Salovey et al., 1995, p. 126).
sentences.s41: Participants rate the degree to which they endorse a series of statements regarding their attitudes toward, and experience of, their emotions.
sentences.s42: Factor analyses have yielded three subscales (attention to feelings, clarity of feelings, and mood repair), each of which demonstrates good internal consistency and convergent validity.
sentences.s43: While the TMMS assesses some aspects of emotion regulation that are absent from the NMR (e.g., emotional awareness and understanding), the repair subscale is similar to the NMR in its emphasis on emotional avoidance (e.g., “I try to think good thoughts no matter how badly I feel”).
sentences.s44: The TMMS also does not include an assessment of the ability to engage in desired behaviors when experiencing negative emotions – the absence of which may be particularly important in the clinical realm.
sentences.s45: The Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) was developed to assess emotion dysregulation more comprehensively than existing measures.
sentences.s46: The DERS items were chosen to reflect difficulties within the following dimensions of emotion regulation: (a) awareness and understanding of emotions; (b) acceptance of emotions; (c) the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior, and refrain from impulsive behavior, when experiencing negative emotions; and (d) access to emotion regulation strategies perceived as effective.
sentences.s47: The final dimension reflects an attempt to measure the flexible use of situationally-appropriate strategies to modulate emotional responses.
sentences.s48: Given the aforementioned limitations associated with the practice of delineating specific regulation strategies when attempting to measure emotion regulation (in particular, the implication that certain strategies are more adaptive than others regardless of context), the subjective appraisal of effectiveness was assessed instead, with the hope that this would take into account the contextually-dependent nature of adaptive regulation strategies.
sentences.s49: The primary purpose of the two studies reported below was to begin to explore the factor structure and psychometric properties of the DERS, thereby aiding in the development of a theoretically-based, comprehensive, empirically validated measure of emotion dysregulation.
sentences.s50: The first study examined the factor structure, internal consistency, and construct and predictive validity of the DERS, and a second study examined the measure’s test-retest reliability.
sentences.s51: Study 1 Method Participants Questionnaire packets were distributed to 479 students from undergraduate psychology courses offered at the University of Massachusetts Boston.
sentences.s52: Of these, 373 packets were returned, resulting in a response rate of 78%.
sentences.s53: There were no significant differences in age, racial background, or gender between participants who returned the packets and those who did not.
sentences.s54: As they were missing data on one or more of the variables of interest, 16 participants were excluded from the following analyses.
sentences.s55: The final sample of 357 participants ranged in age from 18 to 55, with a mean age of 23.10 (SD = 5.67).
sentences.s56: Seventy-three percent (n = 260) of these participants were female.
sentences.s57: Sixty-five percent of participants self-identified as White, 17% as Asian, 8% as Black/African-American, 4% as Hispanic, and 6% reported another or unspecified racial background.
sentences.s58: Participants were predominantly single (89%) and heterosexual (90%).
sentences.s59: There was little difference, demographically, between participants who completed all of the measures and those who did not.
sentences.s60: The initial Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) was a 41-item, self-report measure developed to assess clinically-relevant difficulties in emotion regulation.
sentences.s61: The DERS items were developed and selected on the basis of numerous conversations with colleagues well-versed in the emotion regulation literature.
sentences.s62: The NMR (Catanzaro & Mearns, 1990; see below) was used as a template and helped to structure the format of some of the items (although not the content of the items).
sentences.s63: Specifically, in order to assess difficulties regulating emotions during times of distress (when regulation strategies are most needed), many items begin with “When I’m upset,” similar to the NMR.
sentences.s64: The content of the items differ, however, as DERS items were chosen to reflect difficulties within the following dimensions of emotion regulation: (a) awareness and understanding of emotions; (b) acceptance of emotions; (c) the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior, and refrain from impulsive behavior, when experiencing negative emotions; and (d) access to emotion regulation strategies perceived as effective.
sentences.s65: Participants are asked to indicate how often the items apply to themselves, with responses ranging from 1 to 5, where 1 is “almost never (0-10%),” 2 is “sometimes (11-35%),” 3 is “about half the time (36-65%),” 4 is “most of the time (66-90%),” and 5 is “almost always (91-100%).” For the purposes of this study, DERS items were recoded so that higher scores in every case indicated greater difficulties in emotion regulation (i.e., greater emotion dysregulation).
sentences.s66: Generalized Expectancy for Negative Mood Regulation Scale.
sentences.s67: The Generalized Expectancy for Negative Mood Regulation Scale (NMR; Catanzaro & Mearns, 1990) is a 30- item, self-report questionnaire used to measure expectancies for the self-regulation of negative moods.
sentences.s68: The NMR asks participants to indicate the extent to which they believe that their attempts to alter their negative moods will work.
sentences.s69: The NMR has high internal consistency, and adequate construct and discriminant validity (Catanzaro & Mearns, 1990).
sentences.s70: The NMR also has adequate test-retest reliability over periods of three to four weeks (r = .74 for women; r = .76 for men) and six to eight weeks (r = .78 for women; r = .67 for men; Catanzaro & Mearns, 1990).
sentences.s71: Items were recoded so that higher scores in every case indicated higher expectancies for negative mood regulation (or greater emotion regulation), and a sum was calculated.
sentences.s72: Given that the NMR is the most commonly used, empirically-supported measure of emotion regulation, it was included in the present study to assess the construct validity of the DERS.
sentences.s73: Acceptance and Action Questionnaire.
sentences.s74: The Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ; Hayes et al., 2003), is a 9-item, self-report measure of experiential avoidance (i.e., the tendency to avoid unwanted internal experiences, such as emotions and thoughts).
sentences.s75: Items assess experiential avoidance and control, negative evaluations of internal experience, psychological acceptance (or lack thereof), and the extent to which an individual acts regardless of emotional distress or, conversely, allows distress to prompt behavioral avoidance (Hayes et al., 2003).
sentences.s76: Sample items include “I rarely worry about getting my anxieties, worries, and feelings under control (reverse scored)” and “If I could magically remove all the painful experiences I’ve had in my life, I would do so.” The AAQ is significantly correlated with the tendency to engage in the suppression of thoughts in both clinical and non-clinical populations (rs = .44 to .50; Hayes et al., 2003), providing preliminary evidence of its construct validity.
sentences.s77: There is also evidence that the AAQ assesses a unique, clinically-relevant construct, as it remains significantly correlated with measures assessing a wide range of psychopathology when controlling for social desirability and the tendency to suppress thoughts (Hayes et al., 2003).
sentences.s78: Items on the AAQ were recoded so that higher scores in every case indicated greater experiential avoidance, and a sum was calculated.
sentences.s79: The AAQ was included to assess the construct validity of the DERS, and was expected to be positively associated with DERS scores (see Cole et al., 1994; Hayes et al., 1999; Hayes et al., 1996; Linehan, 1993; Paivio & Greenberg, 1998).
sentences.s80: Emotional Expressivity Scale.
sentences.s81: The Emotional Expressivity Scale (EES; Kring, Smith, & Neale, 1994) is a 17-item, self-report questionnaire that assesses general emotional expressivity.
sentences.s82: The EES is based on the conceptual definition of emotional expressiveness as “the extent to which people outwardly display their emotions” (p. 936, Kring et al., 1994), regardless of the valence of the emotion (i.e., positive or negative) or the manner in which it is expressed (i.e., facially, vocally, or gesturally).
sentences.s83: The EES has high internal consistency, and adequate convergent, discriminant, and construct validity (Kring et al., 1994).
sentences.s84: The EES is significantly correlated with spontaneous emotional expressiveness in the laboratory (as assessed by observer ratings of general expressivity in response to emotionally-evocative film clips) among both college students (r = .38) and community residents (r = .43; Kring et al., 1994).
sentences.s85: The EES also has good test-retest reliability over a 4-week period (r = .90; Kring et al., 1994).
sentences.s86: Items on the EES were recoded so that higher scores in every case indicated greater emotional expressivity, and a sum was calculated.
sentences.s87: The EES was included to assess the construct validity of the DERS.
sentences.s88: Contrary to some definitions of emotion regulation (see e.g., Garner & Spears, 2000; Zeman & Garber, 1996), the conceptualization of emotion regulation on which the DERS is based does not equate emotion regulation with expressive control.
sentences.s89: On the contrary, emotional expressiveness is expected to facilitate emotion regulation (see Linehan, 1993).
sentences.s90: Thus, the DERS was expected to be negatively correlated with EES scores of emotional expressivity.
sentences.s91: Deliberate Self-Harm Inventory.
sentences.s92: The Deliberate Self-Harm Inventory (DSHI; Gratz, 2001) is a behaviorally-based, self-report questionnaire that assesses deliberate self-harm (the deliberate, direct destruction or alteration of body tissue without conscious suicidal intent, but resulting in injury severe enough for tissue damage to occur).
sentences.s93: This measure is composed of 17 items and assesses various aspects of deliberate self-harm, including frequency, severity, duration, and type of self-harming behavior.
sentences.s94: The DSHI has high internal consistency ( = .82), adequate construct, convergent, and discriminant validity, and adequate test-retest reliability over a period ranging from 2 to 4 weeks, with a mean of 3.3 weeks ( = .68, p < .001; Gratz, 2001).
sentences.s95: For the present study, a continuous variable was created to measure frequency of reported self-harm behavior.
sentences.s96: Participants’ scores on the frequency questions for each of the 17 items were summed to create a variable of the total frequency of self-harm behavior.
sentences.s97: Given the growing body of literature on the emotion regulating function of self-harm behavior (see Gratz, 2003; Linehan, 1993), the DSHI was included in the present study to provide some preliminary data on the predictive validity of the DERS.
sentences.s98: The DERS was expected to be positively associated with frequency of self-harm behavior.
sentences.s99: Abuse and Perpetration Inventory.
sentences.s100: The Abuse-Perpetration Inventory (API; Lisak, Conklin, Hopper, Miller, Altschuler, & Smith, 2000) is a self-report, behaviorally-based instrument that assesses childhood physical and sexual abuse as well as four types of perpetration.
sentences.s101: The API has been shown to have adequate criterion and construct validity (Lisak et al., 2000).
sentences.s102: The section of the API assessing perpetration behavior, the Perpetration History (PH) questionnaire, was used to assess the extent to which an individual had engaged in intimate partner abuse.
sentences.s103: The PH is comprised of 28 items assessing four types of perpetration, including physical and sexual abuse of children and adults.
sentences.s104: Seven of these items describe specific experiences of intimate partner abuse, ranging from slapping one’s partner to attempting to kill one’s partner with a knife or gun.
sentences.s105: For each question answered “yes,” participants answer several follow-up questions regarding their age at the time, the age of their victim, and the frequency of the behavior.
sentences.s106: For the present study, participants’ scores on the frequency questions for each of the seven items pertaining to intimate partner abuse were summed to create a variable of the total frequency of partner abuse.
sentences.s107: Given recent suggestions that the abusive behavior of men toward an intimate partner may function as an attempt to regulate emotions (e.g., by reducing distressing arousal; Jakupcak et al., 2002), the PH was included in the present study to provide preliminary data on the predictive validity of the DERS.
sentences.s108: Although the emotion regulating function of partner abuse has been suggested only for men, this relationship was examined among women as well.
sentences.s109: Procedure Participants were informed fully, both verbally and in writing, about the purpose of the study prior to participation, and signed a consent form describing the purpose of the study, the potentially distressing subject matter, and the confidential nature of the data (i.e., a code number was assigned to each questionnaire before the data were examined, the data were stored in a secure area, and access to the data was limited to the research team).
sentences.s110: Students who chose to participate in the study completed questionnaire packets consisting of the measures described above (see Measures) and other measures unrelated to the current study.
sentences.s111: Participants received research credits in exchange for their participation.
sentences.s112: Results Factor Structure Exploratory factor analysis was used to provide preliminary data on the factor structure of the DERS and identify the underlying dimensions of emotion regulation as assessed by this scale.
sentences.s113: As the conceptualization of emotion regulation on which the DERS was based is multi- faceted, it was expected that this measure would be composed of different (albeit associated) factors, each reflecting a dimension of emotion regulation wherein difficulties may occur.
sentences.s114: Prior to conducting the factor analyses, the response distributions of all individual DERS items were examined.
sentences.s115: As none of these variables were excessively skewed or kurtotic (Kendall & Stuart, 1958), no items were excluded from the analyses on the basis of their response distributions.
sentences.s116: However, upon inspection of the correlation matrix for all items, item 13 (“When I’m upset, I allow myself to feel that way”) was excluded from future analyses on the basis of its low correlations with the overall scale score (r = .06, ns), as well as the other scale items (mean r with other items = .01; 36 of 40 rs below .20).
sentences.s117: The decision to omit this item on the basis of its minimal association with the other variables was supported by the fact that, in a preliminary factor analysis of all items, the communality of item 13 upon extraction was below .30 (the only item for which this was the case).
sentences.s118: Responses to the remaining 40 items were subjected to a common factor analysis (see Floyd & Widaman, 1995), using the principal axis factoring method of extraction and promax oblique rotation to allow for correlations among factors.
sentences.s119: Given Floyd and Widaman’s (1995) suggestion that the scree test is a more accurate method for retaining factors than the more commonly used criterion of eigenvalues > 1.00 (the Kaiser-Guttman criterion), the scree test was used in the present study.
sentences.s120: The scree test suggested retaining 6 or 7 factors, and thus analyses were conducted to examine the interpretability and utility of both 6- and 7-factor solutions.
sentences.s121: As the 6-factor solution was more interpretable (and the 7-factor solution contained a factor on which only 2 variables had primary loadings), 6 factors were retained in the final analyses.
sentences.s122: In regard to item selection for the 6 factors, factor loadings of .40 and higher were considered meaningful.
sentences.s123: Items with loadings below .40 on all factors were excluded from further analyses.
sentences.s124: In addition, variables that appeared to have double loadings on two factors (i.e., loadings of greater than .40 and of comparable size) were excluded.
sentences.s125: Based on these criteria, four items were deleted following the first factor analysis.
sentences.s126: Items 2 (“I feel at ease with my emotions”), 11 (“My emotions make me uncomfortable”), and 18 (“When I’m upset, I become scared and fearful of those feelings”) had loadings of less than .40 on all factors, and item 36 (“When I’m upset, I know there are things I can do to manage my emotions”) had a double loading on two factors (with loadings of .46 and .50 on factors 4 and 6, respectively).
sentences.s127: After excluding these four items, the factor analysis was recomputed on the remaining 36 items to ensure that all had factor loadings of .40 or higher (see Table 1 for the final factor loadings).2 Upon extraction, the six factors accounted for 55.68% of the total variance of the measured variables (see Table 2 for the eigenvalues and percentage of variance accounted for by the six factors initially and upon extraction).
sentences.s128: The six factors comprising the DERS are highly-interpretable and reflect the multi- faceted definition of emotion regulation on which the scale was based (see Table 3).
sentences.s129: Factor 1 can be labeled Non-Acceptance of Emotional Responses (NON-ACCEPTANCE).
sentences.s130: It is composed of items reflecting a tendency to have negative secondary emotional responses to one’s negative emotions, or non-accepting reactions to one’s distress.
sentences.s131: Factor 2 can be labeled Difficulties Engaging in Goal-Directed Behavior (GOALS).
sentences.s132: It is composed of items reflecting difficulties concentrating and accomplishing tasks when experiencing negative emotions.
sentences.s133: Factor 3 can be labeled Impulse Control Difficulties (IMPULSE) and is composed primarily of items reflecting difficulties remaining in control of one’s behavior when experiencing negative emotions.
sentences.s134: Factor 4 can be labeled Lack of Emotional Awareness (AWARENESS) and consists of items reflecting the tendency to attend to and acknowledge emotions.
sentences.s135: When these items are appropriately reverse-scored, this factor reflects an inattention to, and lack of awareness of, emotional responses.
sentences.s136: Factor 5 can be labeled Limited Access to Emotion Regulation Strategies (STRATEGIES) and consists of items reflecting the belief that there is little that can be done to regulate emotions effectively, once an individual is upset.
sentences.s137: Factor 6 can be labeled Lack of Emotional Clarity (CLARITY) and is composed of items reflecting the extent to which individuals know (and are clear about) the emotions they are experiencing.
sentences.s138: As expected, the six factors were correlated with one another (see Table 4).
sentences.s139: Results suggest that the four proposed dimensions of emotion regulation on which the DERS is based may be more accurately conceptualized as six distinct (albeit related) dimensions.
sentences.s140: Although the NON-ACCEPTANCE and STRATEGIES factors mapped directly onto the proposed dimensions of emotional acceptance and access to effective emotion regulation strategies, respectively, results suggest that the two other proposed dimensions of emotion regulation are themselves multi-dimensional.
sentences.s141: Items thought to reflect difficulties in the proposed dimension of awareness and understanding of emotions loaded onto two separate factors, AWARENESS and CLARITY, suggesting that there may be a difference between being aware of emotional responses and having a clear understanding of the nature of these responses.
sentences.s142: Similarly, items representing difficulties in the proposed dimension involving the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior and refrain from impulsive behavior when experiencing negative emotions were split into two separate factors, IMPULSE and GOALS, suggesting that there may be a difference between being able to inhibit undesired behavior and engage in desired behavior.
sentences.s143: Mean scores for women and men on the overall DERS as well as each subscale are shown in Table 5.
sentences.s144: Gender differences were found for only the AWARENESS subscale, on which men had significantly higher scores than women (t = 3.5, p < .01; for all other scales, ts < 1.37, ps > .10), suggesting that men reported lower emotional awareness than women.
sentences.s145: Reliability Internal consistency.
sentences.s146: Cronbach’s  was calculated to determine the internal consistency of the DERS items.
sentences.s147: Results indicate that the DERS had high internal consistency ( = .93).
sentences.s148: Item- total correlations ranged from r = .16 to r = .69.
sentences.s149: Thirty-four of the items had item-total correlations above r = .30.
sentences.s150: All of the DERS subscales (computed from the 6 factors obtained in the factor analysis) also had adequate internal consistency, with Cronbach’s  > .80 for each subscale.
sentences.s151: See Table 6 for additional information on the internal consistency of each subscale.
sentences.s152: Validity Construct validity.
sentences.s153: To provide preliminary data on the construct validity of the DERS, correlations between the DERS scores (the overall score as well as the individual subscale scores) and a commonly used measure of emotion regulation, the NMR, were computed.
sentences.s154: Correlations were also computed between the DERS scores and measures of experiential avoidance and emotional expressivity.
sentences.s155: Since the DERS is based on a conceptualization of emotion regulation that distinguishes adaptive emotion regulation from emotional avoidance and expressive control, evidence for the construct validity of this measure of emotion dysregulation would be provided by positive correlations with experiential avoidance and negative (rather than positive) correlations with emotional expressivity.
sentences.s156: As shown in Table 7, all correlations between the overall DERS score and the constructs of interest were in the expected directions and statistically significant.
sentences.s157: Each of the DERS subscales was also significantly correlated (in the expected direction) with the NMR and the measure of experiential avoidance; however, only three of the subscales were significantly correlated with the measure of emotional expressivity.
sentences.s158: Supporting the validity of the factor solution, the DERS subscales showed a differential pattern of association with the constructs of interest.
sentences.s159: Consistent with the expectation that the STRATEGIES subscale would capture difficulties in the aspect of emotion regulation most commonly assessed in the literature, the correlation between the STRATEGIES subscale and the extant measure of emotion regulation (the NMR) was significantly higher than the correlations between the NMR and any of the other DERS subscales (all ts > 4.78, ps < .001; see Cohen & Cohen, 1983, for the test of the significance of the difference between dependent rs).
sentences.s160: In addition, the correlation between the GOALS subscale and the NMR was significantly higher than the correlations between the NMR and the NON-ACCEPTANCE, AWARENESS, and CLARITY subscales (all ts > 2.18, ps < .05).
sentences.s161: The STRATEGIES subscale was also significantly more highly associated with the measure of experiential avoidance (the AAQ) than were the other DERS subscales (all ts > 3.15, ps < .01).
sentences.s162: As for the pattern of associations between the DERS subscales and the measure of emotional expressivity (the EES), only three of the subscales (AWARENESS, CLARITY, and NON- ACCEPTANCE) were significantly correlated with the EES.
sentences.s163: The AWARENESS subscale was significantly more highly correlated with EES scores than were any of the other subscales (all ts > 4.28, ps < 001.), and the CLARITY subscale was significantly more highly correlated with the EES than were the NON-ACCEPTANCE, GOALS, IMPULSE, and STRATEGIES subscales (all ts > 2.02, ps < .05).
sentences.s164: To explore whether the DERS adds to the literature on the assessment of difficulties in emotion regulation by accounting for additional variance in constructs of interest above and beyond that accounted for by an extant measure of emotion regulation, partial correlations between the DERS overall and subscale scores and the constructs of interest were computed, controlling for the NMR.
sentences.s165: As shown in Table 7, all of the DERS variables accounted for a significant amount of additional variance in experiential avoidance, above and beyond that accounted for by the NMR.
sentences.s166: In addition, the AWARENESS, CLARITY, GOALS, and STRATEGIES subscales accounted for a significant amount of additional variance in emotional expressivity (although for the latter two subscales, the magnitude of the relationship was quite modest and the direction was reversed).
sentences.s167: In order to begin to explore the predictive validity of the DERS (i.e., the extent to which it is associated with clinically-relevant behavioral outcomes), correlations between the DERS scores and two clinically-important behavioral outcomes thought to be associated with emotion dysregulation (frequency of deliberate self-harm and frequency of intimate partner abuse) were computed.
sentences.s168: Given gender differences in the severity and proposed function of partner abuse (see Saunders, 1986; Stets & Straus, 1990), as well as increasing evidence of gender differences in the risk factors for self-harm (see Gratz, 2003; Gratz, Conrad, & Roemer, 2002), the relationships between difficulties in emotion regulation and these outcome variables were examined separately for women and men.
sentences.s169: A history of at least one incident of self-harm was reported by 35% of the women and 44% of the men (with more than 10 incidents reported by 15% of the women and 14% of the men).
sentences.s170: A history of at least one act of intimate partner abuse was reported by 24% of the women and 17% of the men (with 12% of the women and 8% of the men reporting more than three acts of abuse in the past).
sentences.s171: These rates are consistent with past studies on these behaviors among other samples from this urban university (see Gratz et al., 2002; Lisak, Hopper, & Song, 1996).
sentences.s172: Rates of self-harm and partner abuse did not differ significantly across gender (2 = 2.62 for self-harm and 2 = 2.10 for partner abuse; ps > .10).
sentences.s173: Before conducting analyses, logarithms were used to transform the DSHI and PH frequency scores, as the raw frequency scores of both measures were highly positively skewed (as would be expected when assessing these constructs).
sentences.s174: Following transformations, both variables approximated normal distributions among female participants.
sentences.s175: While the transformed DSHI scores approximated a normal distribution among male participants, their PH scores remained positively skewed and kurtotic (skewness = 2.73, kurtosis = 7.63).
sentences.s176: However, Kline (1998) reviewed Monte Carlo studies that indicate that non-normality is not problematic unless skewness > 3 and kurtosis > 10; therefore, analyses were conducted using these transformed variables for women and men.
sentences.s177: As shown in Table 8, the correlations between the overall DERS score and self-harm were significant (and in the expected direction) among both women and men, and the correlation between the overall DERS score and intimate partner abuse (also in the expected direction) was significant among men.
sentences.s178: The overall DERS score was significantly more highly correlated with frequency of partner abuse among men than among women (z = 2.26, p < .05; see Cohen & Cohen, 1983, for a test of the significance of the difference between independent rs), consistent with the emphasis in the literature on the emotion regulatory function of partner abuse among men in particular.
sentences.s179: Providing support for the validity of the factor solution, the DERS subscales showed a differential pattern of association with self-harm and intimate partner abuse, within and across gender.
sentences.s180: Frequency of self-harm was significantly associated with the NON-ACCEPTANCE and IMPULSE subscales among men, but not among women (for whom correlations with the other four subscales were significant).
sentences.s181: However, none of the correlations between frequency of self- harm behavior and the DERS subscales differed significantly from one another among women or men, and none differed significantly across gender.
sentences.s182: As for the relationships between different aspects of emotion regulation and intimate partner abuse, frequency of partner abuse was significantly associated with only the IMPULSE subscale among women, and with the GOALS, IMPULSE, and STRATEGIES subscales among men.
sentences.s183: For women, the correlation between the IMPULSE subscale and frequency of partner abuse was significantly higher than the correlations between the NON-ACCEPTANCE, GOALS, AWARENESS, and STRATEGIES subscales and frequency of partner abuse (ts > 2.16, ps < .05).
sentences.s184: Among men, the correlation between the GOALS subscale and frequency of partner abuse was significantly higher than the correlations between the AWARENESS and CLARITY subscales and frequency of partner abuse (ts > 2.00, ps < .05).
sentences.s185: The GOALS subscale also was significantly more highly correlated with frequency of partner abuse among men than among women (z = 2.96, p < .01).
sentences.s186: These findings support the proposed association between difficulties in emotion regulation and partner abuse among men, and suggest that for women this relationship may exist only for the specific dimension of difficulties controlling one’s behavior when distressed.
sentences.s187: To explore whether the DERS explains additional variance in these clinical outcomes above and beyond that accounted for by an extant measure of emotion regulation, partial correlations between the DERS overall and subscale scores and these behavioral outcome measures were computed, controlling for the NMR.
sentences.s188: As shown in Table 8, there is some evidence that the DERS accounts for unique variance in clinically-relevant behaviors, when controlling for that accounted for by the NMR.
sentences.s189: Specifically, the NON-ACCEPTANCE subscale accounted for a significant amount of additional variance in frequency of self-harm among men, whereas the GOALS subscale accounted for a significant amount of additional variance in frequency of partner abuse among men.
sentences.s190: In addition, the IMPULSE subscale explained a significant amount of additional variance in frequency of partner abuse among women.
sentences.s191: When controlling for the NMR, the overall DERS score explained a significant amount of the variance in frequency of partner abuse among men.
sentences.s192: Study 2 Method Participants and Procedure In order to assess the test-retest reliability of the DERS, a second sample was obtained.
sentences.s193: As part of a larger, unrelated study, 194 participants were recruited from tables located in public areas on the University of Massachusetts Boston campus to complete a questionnaire packet that included the DERS (in addition to other measures for the unrelated study).
sentences.s194: Of these participants, 21 agreed to complete the DERS again four to eight weeks later, in exchange for a small monetary compensation.
sentences.s195: This subset of participants ranged in age from 18 to 48, with a mean age of 25.95 (SD = 8.94).
sentences.s196: Sixty-two percent of these participants were female.
sentences.s197: In regard to the racial/ethnic background of these participants, 67% were White, 24% were Black/African- American, 5% were Asian/Pacific Islander, and 5% were of an unspecified racial/ethnic background.
sentences.s198: This sample completed only the DERS, and not the other measures described above.
sentences.s199: Results For the 21 participants in the test-retest sample, intraclass correlation coefficients were computed for scores on the first and second administration of the DERS in order to determine the test-retest reliability of the DERS scores.
sentences.s200: Results indicate that the overall DERS score had good test-retest reliability over a period ranging from 4 to 8 weeks (ρI = .88, p < .01).
sentences.s201: The test-retest reliability of the DERS subscales was adequate (ρI s = .69 for NON-ACCEPTANCE, .69 for GOALS, .57 for IMPULSE, .68 for AWARENESS, .89 for STRATEGIES, and .80 for CLARITY; all ps < .01).
sentences.s202: General Discussion The results of these studies contribute to and expand upon literature on the conceptualization of emotion regulation and provide preliminary support for the DERS as a measure of difficulties in emotion regulation.
sentences.s203: Results suggest the presence of six separate (albeit related) dimensions of emotion regulation wherein difficulties may occur, including (a) lack of awareness of emotional responses, (b) lack of clarity of emotional responses, (c) non-acceptance of emotional responses, (d) limited access to emotion regulation strategies perceived as effective, (e) difficulties controlling impulses when experiencing negative emotions, and (f) difficulties engaging in goal-directed behaviors when experiencing negative emotions.
sentences.s204: These findings suggest the importance of distinguishing between the awareness and understanding of emotional responses, as well as between the ability to act in desired ways and refrain from acting in undesired ways when experiencing negative emotions.
sentences.s205: Findings provide empirical support for a multi-dimensional conceptualization of emotion regulation.
sentences.s206: Correlations of the DERS variables with several clinically-relevant constructs revealed a differential pattern of associations amongst the different DERS subscales, with certain subscales showing stronger relationships with particular constructs and/or behavioral outcomes than others.
sentences.s207: Significant associations between DERS subscales assessing deficits in awareness, understanding, and acceptance of emotions and the clinically-relevant constructs of emotional avoidance and expressivity support the comprehensive conceptualization of emotion regulation on which the DERS is based.
sentences.s208: Furthermore, the significant relationships between these subscales and the behavioral outcome of self-harm among both women and men (specifically, the AWARENESS and CLARITY subscales among women and the NON-ACCEPTANCE subscale among men) suggest their clinical relevance.
sentences.s209: Findings that the subscales focusing on difficulties controlling behavior when emotion is present (i.e., GOALS and IMPULSE), rather than on difficulties controlling emotion, were significantly related to clinical outcomes suggest the usefulness of considering the impact of these particular dimensions within the clinical realm.
sentences.s210: Although the DERS and its subscales accounted for additional variance in clinical constructs and behavioral outcomes above and beyond that accounted for by the NMR, many of the relationships between the DERS scales and the behavioral outcomes did not remain statistically significant after controlling for the NMR.
sentences.s211: This is likely due to the rather high correlations between the NMR and some of the DERS subscales, suggesting that despite the NMR’s theoretical emphasis on emotional avoidance and inclusion of emotional control items, there is some overlap between the DERS and NMR.
sentences.s212: Nevertheless, the fact that some unique relationships remained between the DERS and behavioral outcomes after controlling for the NMR suggests that the NMR does not capture all clinically-relevant aspects of emotion regulation.
sentences.s213: It will be important to continue to investigate the clinical utility of the DERS in explaining a broad range of behavioral outcomes.
sentences.s214: Despite preliminary findings that the DERS has high internal consistency, good test-retest reliability, and adequate construct and predictive validity, the present studies have limitations that should be addressed in future research.
sentences.s215: One limitation is that the test-retest reliability results are based on a small sample size (N=21), thus requiring replication with a larger sample.
sentences.s216: Another limitation is the reliance on a few select self-report measures of emotional responding to provide data on the construct validity of the DERS.
sentences.s217: As a result, the relationships between the DERS and other aspects of emotional responding remain to be determined.
sentences.s218: Moreover, the reliance on only self-reported emotional responding is limiting, as it is likely that some individuals do not have full awareness of their emotional responses, thereby reducing the extent to which they can accurately report on those responses.
sentences.s219: Despite the comprehensive nature of the DERS, omitted constructs should be noted.
sentences.s220: DERS items focus primarily on the regulation of negative emotional states (i.e., many items begin with the phrase “When I’m upset”), as difficulties in this domain are likely to have the most clinical relevance.
sentences.s221: Future research may want to incorporate items assessing difficulties with the regulation of positive emotional states as well.
sentences.s222: Also, although results support the clinical utility of the NON-ACCEPTANCE subscale, it is important to note that the items included in this subscale assess only one aspect of the non-acceptance of emotional responses, secondary emotional reactions to one’s negative emotions.
sentences.s223: This form of emotional non-acceptance was emphasized due to its clinical relevance and proposed association with negative emotional and behavioral consequences (see Greenberg & Paivio, 1997); however, future research on scale development should include items assessing other aspects of emotional non-acceptance.
sentences.s224: The extent to which the results of this study can be generalized to men or individuals from diverse ethnic/racial backgrounds remains an empirical question.
sentences.s225: Although the sample comes from a diverse urban university that draws heavily from the community and attracts a large number of older, nontraditional college students, the majority of the participants were White women.
sentences.s226: Given evidence of the role of gender socialization and culture in emotional appraisal and expression (see Kitayama & Markus, 1997; Manstead, 1992), it is possible that the factor structure of emotion regulation and/or the relationships of these factors to clinical constructs differs as a function of gender or cultural background.
sentences.s227: It is also important to note that the validity of the DERS for a clinical population has yet to be determined (see Haynes, Richard, & Kubany, 1995).
sentences.s228: Given the preliminary nature of this study, replication of the results with different samples, under different circumstances (e.g., different assessment procedures), and across different functions is necessary to ensure the robustness and generalizability of the findings (Haynes et al., 1995).
sentences.s229: Examination of the psychometric properties and factor structure of the DERS among diverse non-clinical populations, as well as relevant clinical populations (such as individuals with borderline personality disorder; see Linehan, 1993), is necessary.
sentences.s230: Future research on the validity of the DERS should examine its relationships with a broader range of self-report measures of emotional responding (such as the TMMS and other measures of emotional awareness and understanding), as well as assessments of emotional responding in other domains (e.g., physiological responding, the coding of facial expressivity).
sentences.s231: Further research is also needed to examine the discriminant validity of the DERS, especially with respect to other measures of general distress or psychopathology, such as anxiety and depression.
sentences.s232: Further research is needed on the predictive validity of the DERS as well.
sentences.s233: The behavioral outcomes of self-harm and intimate partner abuse were chosen to provide preliminary data in this area in part because of the theoretical support for the role of emotion dysregulation in both behaviors, and in part because of their interest to these authors.
sentences.s234: There are many other clinically- relevant behaviors and constructs that are also thought to be associated with deficits in emotion regulation, including post-traumatic stress disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, and future research on the relationships between the DERS subscales and these clinical outcomes is needed.
sentences.s235: Research exploring the differential role of the various dimensions of emotion dysregulation in clinical problems will be especially important, as it may suggest specific targets for intervention.

sentences.s23: In five studies we evaluated the hypothesis that the self- esteem system functions as a sociometer that monitors the de- gree to which the individual is being included versus excluded by other people and that motivates the person to behave in ways that minimize the probability of rejection or exclusion.
sentences.s24: Explanations of the Self-Esteem Motive Although few efforts have been made to systematically ad- dress the functions of the self-esteem motive, at least three gen- eral explanations of the motive can be gleaned from the literature.
sentences.s25: The most widely acknowledged explanation is that people strive for self-esteem because high self-esteem promotes posi- tive affect by buffering the person against stress and other nega- tive emotions and by enhancing personal adjustment, whereas low self-esteem is associated with depression, anxiety, and mal- adjustment.
sentences.s26: Research findings attest that people with low self- esteem experience virtually every negative emotion more com- monly than those with high self-esteem (e.g., Cutrona, 1982; Goswick & Jones, 1981; Leary, 1983; Taylor & Brown, 1988; White, 1981).
sentences.s27: Furthermore, high self-esteem appears to buffer people against feelings of anxiety, enhance coping, and promote physical health (Baumeister, 1993; Greenberg et al., 1992; Tay- lor & Brown, 1988).
sentences.s28: Although the link between self-esteem, affect, adjustment, and health is undisputed, it is less clear why self-esteem should produce these effects.
sentences.s29: One possibility is that, because self-es- teem is associated with confidence and high expectations of suc- cess, high self-esteem is associated with optimism and lowered anxiety.
sentences.s30: In a variation on this theme, Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and Solomon (1986) suggested that high self-esteem serves as a buffer against the existential anxiety people experience when they contemplate their own fragility and mortality.
sentences.s31: However, it 518 SELF-ESTEEM FEELINGS 519 is unclear why such a psychological system for buffering people against anxiety and uncertainty should have developed.
sentences.s32: Indeed, from an evolutionary perspective, we might expect that people who worried about possible misfortunes (including death) would have been more likely to survive and reproduce.
sentences.s33: A second set of explanations emphasizes the role of high self- esteem in promoting goal achievement.
sentences.s34: The motive to seek self- esteem may have developed because high self-esteem enhances people's willingness to strive toward desired goals and to persist in the face of obstacles and setbacks (Bandura, 1977; Greenwald, 1980; Kernis, 1995).
sentences.s35: In a related vein, Tedeschi and Norman (1985) suggested that people seek self-esteem be- cause self-esteem is associated with feelings of control over one's environment.
sentences.s36: In support of explanations that implicate goal accomplish- ment, people with high self-esteem often work harder and per- form better after an initial failure than people with low self- esteem (Perez, 1973; Shrauger & Sorman, 1977).
sentences.s37: However, it is also true that high self-esteem may lead to nonproductive per- sistence when tasks prove to be insurmountable (McFarlin, Baumeister, & Blascovich, 1984).
sentences.s38: Although self-efficacious cog- nitions can undoubtedly facilitate achievement, this explana- tion cannot explain why self-esteem is inherently affectively laden (Brown, 1993).
sentences.s39: Although we concur that it may often be useful for people to think that they possess certain favorable attributes or abilities (i.e., to have high self-efficacy), this does not explain why self-esteem is intimately linked to strong self- relevant emotions.
sentences.s40: A third set of explanations of the self-esteem motive involves the possibility that people seek self-esteem for its own sake.
sentences.s41: Many writers have implicitly assumed the existence of a self- system that maintains a sense of integrity or adequacy (e.g., Epstein, 1973; James, 1890;Steele, 1988).
sentences.s42: One difficulty with this assumption is that it fails to explain why a motive to behave in ways that promote self-esteem should exist at all.
sentences.s43: It also does not adequately explain why certain events pose threats to self- integrity and others do not.
sentences.s44: In fact, to the extent that, over the long run, rewarding encounters and the attainment of one's goals depends on accurate knowledge of oneself, a self-system that functioned purely to elevate one's sense of self may actually be less adaptive than one that sought accurate self-knowledge (Heatherton & Ambady, 1993).
sentences.s45: Properties of the Self-Esteem System Although each of these explanations can explain why people prefer to evaluate themselves positively under certain circum- stances, none clearly and fully explains why people appear gen- erally to need self-esteem and regularly behave in ways to main- tain and enhance it.
sentences.s46: Before offering an alternative explanation of the self-esteem motive that we believe parsimoniously ex- plains the properties of the self-esteem system, we must clarify precisely what we mean by the term self-esteem.
sentences.s47: Self-esteem has often been described as an attitude, specifi- cally an attitude toward oneself (Coopersmith, 1967; Rosen- berg, 1965).
sentences.s48: Like all attitudes, self-esteem has cognitive and affective components.
sentences.s49: A distinction can be drawn between the self-concept (beliefs about the self) and self-esteem (evaluation of oneself in light of those beliefs).
sentences.s50: Although self-esteem is often based on self-relevant cognitions, not all cognitions about the self, even evaluatively laden ones, are relevant to a person's self- esteem.
sentences.s51: Each person has many self-beliefs that have no affective quality.
sentences.s52: People may believe firmly that they are very good or very bad at certain mundane tasks, for example, yet experience no corresponding increase or decrease in their self-esteem.
sentences.s53: Self-esteem includes an essential affective quality that "cold" cognitions about the self do not.

sentences.s56: Further- more, they fiercely desire to feel good rather than bad.

sentences.s58: We return to this point shortly.
