sentences.s438: Specifically, gender and ethnicity effects may be found to be considerably more complex; for example, men may be more likely to suppress sadness but less likely to suppress anger than women.
sentences.s439: Our data from self and peers served to illustrate that the effects of these emotion regulation strategies are evident across indepen- dent data sources.
sentences.s440: However, these methods do not permit us to directly assess an individual’s use of suppression and reappraisal strategies in the context of specific emotion regulation episodes.
sentences.s441: In future research, diary and experience sampling methods might be used to examine when and where individual differences in reap- praisal and suppression use are most evident, and to map in detail the specific behaviors individuals use in their attempts to use these two strategies.
sentences.s442: Although we have studied emotion regulation with experimental approaches and now also with individual differences, we have not yet put the two approaches together.
sentences.s443: Equipped with our new individual-differences measures, we can now test how individual differences in the use of reappraisal and suppression interact with experimental instructions to reappraise and suppress.
sentences.s444: The practice- effects model suggests that individuals who frequently use a par- ticular emotion regulation strategy would accrue a practice advan- tage that would make it easier for them to use that strategy when asked to do so.
sentences.s445: However, this model applies most obviously to newly acquired behaviors, whereas suppression and reappraisal may represent commonly used and thus highly overlearned behav- iors, similar to driving skills among adults who own cars.
sentences.s446: This overlearned-behavior model suggests that differences due to prac- tice effects should be small and that main effects (rather than interactions) would be evident in most situations.
sentences.s447: At this point, there is one relevant finding, and it favors the overlearned- behavior model: Despite the gender difference in the use of sup- pression documented here (men generally higher than women), we found no gender differences either in the ease with which partic- ipants suppressed on command or in any of the behavioral, sub- jective, or autonomic consequences of suppression in a negative emotion context (Gross, 1998).
sentences.s448: Finally, our focus on two specific, well-defined processes is predicated on the belief that our understanding of complex emo- tion regulatory processes is best advanced if we focus intensively on one or two processes at a time.
sentences.s449: So far, we have found that across the board, reappraisal—with its emphasis on controlling the personal meaning that events have for the individual—has more to recommend it than suppression—with its emphasis on controlling one’s behavioral responses to these events.
sentences.s450: Clearly, there are times when suppression is the best or even the only option.
sentences.s451: Occasionally, there may not be time to cognitively reevaluate a rapidly devel- oping situation, making reappraisal an unworkable choice.
sentences.s452: How- ever, in terms of what we do every day to regulate our emotions, reappraisal has more adaptive consequences for affect, relation- ships, and well-being.
sentences.s453: We also wish to emphasize that our findings refer only to the regulation of emotions, not the regulation of aggressive, sexual, or other impulses: As shown in Table 3, our emotion regulation scales were not correlated with impulse con- trol.
sentences.s454: In future research, it will be important to consider other kinds of emotion regulation processes as well.
sentences.s455: As shown in Figure 1, our own process model proposes three other families of regulatory processes, each with many members.
sentences.s456: Broadening the research agenda will enable us to determine which differences among emotion regulatory processes are responsible for outcomes, and will help us relate these strategies to other important forms of self-regulation such as coping.
sentences.s457: An exciting era of research activity lies ahead that will sharpen our understanding of the relative costs and benefits of different forms of self-regulation for different kinds of emotions.

10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65.printed_title: The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure.

sentences.s1: The Nature of Procrastination: A Meta-Analytic and Theoretical Review of Quintessential Self-Regulatory Failure Piers Steel University of Calgary Procrastination is a prevalent and pernicious form of self-regulatory failure that is not entirely understood.
sentences.s2: Hence, the relevant conceptual, theoretical, and empirical work is reviewed, drawing upon correlational, experimental, and qualitative findings.
sentences.s3: A meta-analysis of procrastination’s possible causes and effects, based on 691 correlations, reveals that neuroticism, rebelliousness, and sensation seeking show only a weak connection.
sentences.s4: Strong and consistent predictors of procrastination were task aversiveness, task delay, self- efficacy, and impulsiveness, as well as conscientiousness and its facets of self-control, distractibility, orga- nization, and achievement motivation.
sentences.s5: These effects prove consistent with temporal motivation theory, an integrative hybrid of expectancy theory and hyperbolic discounting.
sentences.s6: Continued research into procrastination should not be delayed, especially because its prevalence appears to be growing.
sentences.s7: Keywords: procrastination, irrational delay, pathological decision making, meta-analysis Procrastination is extremely prevalent.
sentences.s8: Although virtually all of us have at least dallied with dallying, some have made it a way of life.
sentences.s9: Estimates indicate that 80%–95% of college students engage in pro- crastination (Ellis & Knaus, 1977; O’Brien, 2002), approximately 75% consider themselves procrastinators (Potts, 1987), and almost 50% procrastinate consistently and problematically (Day, Mensink, & O’Sullivan, 2000; Haycock, 1993; Micek, 1982; Onwuegbuzie, 2000a; Solomon & Rothblum, 1984).
sentences.s10: The absolute amount of pro- crastination is considerable, with students reporting that it typically occupies over one third of their daily activities, often enacted through sleeping, playing, or TV watching (Pychyl, Lee, Thibodeau, & Blunt, 2000).
sentences.s11: Furthermore, these percentages appear to be on the rise (Kach- gal, Hansen, & Nutter, 2001).
sentences.s12: In addition to being endemic during college, procrastination is also widespread in the general population, chronically affecting some 15%–20% of adults (J.
sentences.s13: Harriott & Ferrari, 1996; “Haven’t Filed Yet,” 2003).
sentences.s14: Procrastination also appears to be a troubling phenomenon.
sentences.s15: People most strongly characterize it as being bad, harmful, and foolish (Briody, 1980), and over 95% of procrastinators wish to reduce it (O’Brien, 2002).
sentences.s16: Justifying this viewpoint, several studies have linked procrastination to individual performance, with the procrastinator performing more poorly overall (Beswick, Roth- blum, & Mann, 1988; Steel, Brothen, & Wambach, 2001; Wesley, 1994), and to individual well-being, with the procrastinator being more miserable in the long term (Knaus, 1973; Lay & Schouwen- burg, 1993; Tice & Baumeister, 1997).
sentences.s17: For example, a survey by H&R Block indicated that procrastinating on taxes costs people on average $400 because of rushing and consequent errors, resulting in over $473 million in overpayments in 2002 (Kasper, 2004).
sentences.s18: Similarly, the medical field reported that procrastination on the part of patients is a major problem (e.g., Morris, Menashe, Ander- son, Malinow, & Illingworth, 1990; White, Wearing, & Hill, 1994); this is also reflected in the meta-analytic work of Bogg and Roberts (2004).
sentences.s19: A variety of other fields repeat this theme, that procrastination is dangerous.
sentences.s20: In economics, Akerlof (1991) and O’Donoghue and Rabin (1999) considered the relative lack of retirement savings behavior as a form of procrastination, in which many start prepar- ing for their later years far too late.
sentences.s21: In the political arena, procras- tination has been used to describe both presidential decisions (Farnham, 1997; Kegley, 1989) and the banking practices of nations (Holland, 2001), in which important decisions are disas- trously delayed.
sentences.s22: At larger levels of analysis, Gersick (1989) de- scribed how teams consistently delay the bulk of their work until deadlines approach.
sentences.s23: Unfortunately for such an extensive and potentially harmful phenomenon, much has yet to be learned about the causes of procrastination, although there have been some notable reviews.
sentences.s24: Ferrari, Johnson, and McCown’s (1995) book on the topic is extensive but focused primarily on measurement and theory, with less emphasis on empirical findings.
sentences.s25: On the other hand, Van Eerde (2003) did conduct a meta-analysis on procrastina- tion; although statistically solid, it was also limited in scope.
sentences.s26: Based on 88 articles, it did not incorporate environmental variables (e.g., task effects) or noncorrelational findings (e.g., experimental or survey results), did not consider several per- sonality facets (e.g., extraversion or impulsiveness) or theoret- ical foundations, and did not include a moderator search or account for attenuation effects.
sentences.s27: Finally, a book by Schouwen- burg, Lay, Pychyl, and Ferrari (2004) reviewed the topic but focused primarily on technical expositions of procrastination treatment programs for academic counselors.
sentences.s28: Consequently, there is a need for a comprehensive and detailed examination of the research on procrastination.
sentences.s29: With such a review, I would like to sincerely thank Henri Schouwenburg for his enthusiasm in this endeavor as well as his willingness to share and translate his considerable research on procrastination.
sentences.s30: The goal of this article, then, is threefold.
sentences.s31: The first goal is to establish the nature of procrastination conceptually.
sentences.s32: Exactly what is it that is being ex- amined?
sentences.s33: This step involves integrating the many different descrip- tions of procrastination into a single coherent definition, showing that this definition is consistent with the history of procrastination, and then placing procrastination among related concepts.
sentences.s34: With this conceptual foundation, the second goal is to explore broadly the causes and correlates of procrastination, that is, to establish its nomological web.
sentences.s35: These relationships are subse- quently tested through meta-analytic review and consideration of relevant descriptive and experimental studies.
sentences.s36: Finally, these nec- essarily wide-ranging results need to be integrated.
sentences.s37: The findings are evaluated with respect to temporal motivation theory (TMT; Steel & Ko¨nig, 2006), a recent integrative motivational model that seeks to explain self-regulatory behavior in a way that is consistent with a wide variety of theoretical perspectives (e.g., economics, personality, expectancy theory, goal setting).
sentences.s38: Definition of Procrastination Procrastination is occasionally used in a positive sense.
sentences.s39: Several writers have mentioned it as a functional delay or as avoiding rush (e.g., Bernstein, 1998; Chu & Choi, 2005; Ferrari, 1993b).
sentences.s40: For ex- ample, Bernstein (1998) explained, “Once we act, we forfeit the option of waiting until new information comes along.
sentences.s41: As a result, no-acting has value.
sentences.s42: The more uncertain the outcome, the greater may be the value of procrastination [italics added]” (p. 15).
sentences.s43: However, the positive form of procrastination, as the subsequent historical analysis indicates, is secondary in usage.
sentences.s44: The focus of this article is on the primary negative form of procrastination.
sentences.s45: Like many common-language terms drafted into scientific study, definitions for procrastination tend to be almost as plentiful as the people researching this topic (see Ferrari, Johnson, & McCown, 1995).
sentences.s46: Initially, such definitional variation may seem to obscure the nature of procrastination, but it may also serve par- tially to illuminate it.
sentences.s47: Different attempts by researchers to refine understanding can be complementary rather than contradictory.

sentences.s49: It is evident that all conceptualizations of procrastination recognize that there must be a postponing, delaying, or putting off of a task or decision, in keeping with the term’s Latin origins of pro, meaning “forward, forth, or in favor of,” and crastinus, meaning “of tomorrow” (Klein, 1971).

sentences.s4: Further, working memory deficits are suspected in ADHD, yet their distinction from cognitive inhibition is unclear.

sentences.s8: Keywords ADHD; syntactic ambiguity resolution; cognitive inhibition; working memory; interference control Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is now recognized as persisting into adolescence and adulthood in a substantial percentage of cases (Barkley, Fischer, Smallish, & Fletcher, 2002), with some 4% of adults affected in the United States (Kessler et al., 2006).

sentences.s20: With regard to cognitive control mechanisms, extensive research in children suggests that at least one mechanism involved in ADHD is a breakdown in strategic behavior, or a deliberate alteration of behavior, particularly suppressing a triggered motor or oculomotor response (Barkley, 1997; Carr, Nigg, & Henderson, 2006; Nigg, 2001; Nigg, 2006 Pennington & Ozonoff, 1996; Schachar, Tannock, Marriott, & Logan, 1995; Willcutt et al., 2001).
sentences.s21: Yet, several further issues remain when one considers adolescents and adults.
sentences.s22: It remains in debate whether inhibitory control is a unitary construct across cognitive and behavioral domains (Logan & Cowan, 1984; MacLeod & Gorfein, 2007).
sentences.s23: Thus, it is sometimes assumed that ADHD is associated with difficulty in suppressing or inhibiting mental information in addition to motor responses.
sentences.s24: But, these abilities may be distinct, and cognitive suppression is little studied in ADHD.
sentences.s25: Harnishfeger and Bjorkland (1993) defined cognitive inhibition as the active suppression of some previously activated cognitive representation, such as the ability to clear incorrect inferences from memory (see also Dempster, 1993).
sentences.s26: Nigg (2000), in contrast, suggested that interference control as it applies to protecting working memory should be distinguished from cognitive inhibition in analyzing ADHD, similar to Barkley (1997).
sentences.s27: This distinction seems to have merit because tasks purported to measure working memory tend to show an ADHD weakness (Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock, 2005; Willcutt et al., 2001).
sentences.s28: However, data in which these distinctions are used to narrow down the cognitive control problems in ADHD are quite limited.
sentences.s29: First, virtually no working memory studies of ADHD used a competing dual-task paradigm in which items must be held in mind while other cognitive operations are carried out (Engle, Tuholski, Laughlin, & Conway, 1999).
sentences.s30: Instead, most studies used reverse span tasks that were heavily confounded with short-term storage (Martinussen et al., 2005).
sentences.s31: Second, studies purporting to measure cognitive inhibition as a separate ability have generally failed to find ADHD effects, albeit in fairly small samples and in younger children who may not have developed sufficient cognitive control to exhibit a clear ADHD weakness, if such a weakness exists.
sentences.s32: Barkley (1997) tested children on the Matching Familiar Figures task and concluded that cognitive inhibition is not impaired in ADHD.
sentences.s33: Gaultney, Kipp, Weinstein, and McNeill (1999) tested ADHD children with a directed forgetting paradigm and also found no ADHD-related weakness in cognitive inhibition.
sentences.s34: Thus, very few studies have attempted to assess cognitive suppression in ADHD, either as the ability to suppress prior information for new information or conceptualized as the ability to protect working memory contents while carrying out other mental operations.
sentences.s35: More data are needed on these points to evaluate key theories about ADHD (Barkley, 1997; Nigg, 2000, 2001; Martinussen et al., 2005).

sentences.s276: Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Summary The sentence processing task showed no support for a cognitive inhibition deficit in ADHD after controlling for differences in reading ability.
sentences.s277: Garden path sentences require a reader to actively suppress an incorrect interpretation, but we found no inhibition deficits, as ADHD participants were no worse than were control participants with garden path sentences.
sentences.s278: However, we did find that ADHD participants performed more poorly with non–garden path sentences.
sentences.s279: We interpret this result as showing that the ADHD group relies on the plausibility of events in the real world rather than on the actual content of the sentence when evaluating its meaning.
sentences.s280: For example, with a sentence such as The deer ran through the woods while the man hunted, real-world knowledge makes it highly plausible that the man was hunting deer, but crucially this interpretation is not specified by the sentence.
sentences.s281: No effects in sentence processing were moderated by age or gender.
sentences.s282: The working memory task showed an ADHD weakness in working memory related to the ability to protect working memory from interference, as the ADHD group had significantly worse performance for incongruent color words when compared with the control group.
sentences.s283: General Discussion Aside from limitations noted below, the current data suggest two conclusions concerning cognitive control and working memory in ADHD.
sentences.s284: The first is that suppression of a temporary incorrect interpretation in language is not impaired in ADHD (see also Christianson et al., 2006; for a similar result in an aging study).
sentences.s285: Thus, we found no evidence to support a distinction between behavioral and cognitive inhibition as hypothesized by Harnishfeger (1995).
sentences.s286: The second conclusion is that ADHD involves a weakness in controlling interference in working memory.
sentences.s287: Our working memory task indicated that ADHD participants were worse across all conditions, but crucially, the ADHD group showed larger differences between congruent and incongruent color words when compared with the control group.
sentences.s288: This is the first study to assess cognitive inhibition with language processing in adolescents and adults with ADHD, and one of the first to use a dual-task approach to assess working memory.
sentences.s289: We suspected that language functioning in ADHD may be a locus of cognitive control problems, in view of theoretical assertions concerning internalized speech on self- regulation (Barkley, 1997) and also because of ADHD’s overlap with learning and reading disability (Purvis & Tannock, 1997).
sentences.s290: Indeed, some effects in the current study were accounted for by reading ability, but others were not.
sentences.s291: The primary purpose of the current study was to examine the revision of temporary, incorrect interpretations in language processing.
sentences.s292: These types of misinterpretations occur often in natural language and are virtually impossible to avoid; confirming this, the ADHD and control groups had significantly more errors in the garden path than in the non–garden path conditions.
sentences.s293: Thus, the task manipulation was valid.
sentences.s294: Yet the critical result showed that ADHD participants were no worse at revising misinterpretations than were control participants, when reading ability was controlled.
sentences.s295: On this basis, we conclude that ADHD does not involve weakness with cognitive suppression.
sentences.s296: Thus, these results support models of ADHD, which assume deficits in behavioral inhibition (i.e., suppressing a triggered motor Engelhardt et al.
sentences.s298: Author manuscript; available in PMC 2017 January 09.
sentences.s299: Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript responses) rather than weaknesses inhibiting mental representations (i.e., cognitive inhibition) or a global inhibitory control problem.
sentences.s300: The lack of a convincing ADHD deficit in cognitive suppression is consistent with other reports in the literature, all of which failed to show cognitive inhibition deficits in children with other paradigms (Gaultney et al., 1999; Harnishfeger, & Pope, 1996; Kipp & Pope, 1997; cf.
sentences.s302: In the current study, we used a question-answering paradigm to assess cognitive inhibition, but because this task is offline, the possibility exists that some intervening process, such as memory limitations, could affect the results.
sentences.s303: We think this possibility is unlikely because a recent study from our lab did show a relationship between online processing, as measured by pupil dilation, and comprehension accuracy (Engelhardt, Patsenko, & Ferreira, 2007).
sentences.s304: In that study, there was a marginal correlation (r = .434, p = .072) between increases in pupil diameter and accuracy on the comprehension questions.
sentences.s305: In that study, we tested spoken garden path sentences, and there were no know cases of ADHD in the sample.
sentences.s306: We take this result as evidence suggesting that performance on the comprehension questions does reflect processing that took place as the sentence was read.
sentences.s307: At this time, however, we cannot conclusively rule out an intervening process hypothesis, which could limit the ability of the task to detect group differences.
sentences.s308: In future work, we would like to investigate the online processing of garden path sentences in ADHD, using either reading time measures or pupil response.
sentences.s309: The other difference we observed between groups was that ADHD participants were worse than were control participants in the non– garden path conditions, and these effects were not explained by variations in working memory or reading ability.
sentences.s310: We hypothesized that worse performance with the nonambiguous sentences is likely due to a greater reliance on general- world knowledge or, more specifically, on a plausibility heuristic rather than on the actual content of the sentence.
sentences.s311: The good-enough approach to language processing assumes that the language comprehension system does not use an algorithmic mechanism when determining sentence meaning (see Ferreira, Bailey, & Ferraro, 2002, for a review of good-enough processing in language comprehension).
sentences.s312: Such effects have been observed with both garden path and passive sentences.
sentences.s313: For example, Ferreira (2003) found that participants rated a sentence, such as The dog was bitten by the man, as plausible over 25% of the time.
sentences.s314: Thus, when people process a passive sentence, it seems that they use real-world knowledge to determine who did what to whom.
sentences.s315: (2002) have interpreted this pattern of results as showing that people use fast and frugal heuristics when evaluating the meaning of a sentence (Gigerenzer, & Goldstein, 1996).
sentences.s317: (2006) argued that these types of heuristics are more likely in patient groups to compensate for deficits in other domains, such as working memory.
sentences.s318: One possibility is that the ADHD group relies on this type of strategy when processing the non– garden path sentences.
sentences.s319: Alternatively, some other mechanism or process could be responsible for these differences, such as state or energetic factors (Seargeant, Oosterlann, & Van Der Meere, 1999).

sentences.s321: (1999), required the simultaneous storage and processing of information.
sentences.s322: Moreover, the processing component of this task was based on a well-validated neuropsychological task designed to measure interference control (i.e., the Stroop task; see Kane & Engle, 2003 for a review of Engelhardt et al.

sentences.s326: The results from our task showed that ADHD participants made more errors when recalling incongruent Stroop trials from working memory.
sentences.s327: This finding suggests that the ADHD group was more susceptible to interference.
sentences.s328: However, the data did not show an increase in errors as a function of memory load because group did not interact with memory span size.
sentences.s329: Thus, these results support conceptions of working memory deficits in ADHD as an inability to effectively allocate controlled attention under conditions of interference rather than as a limitation in the number of items that can be held in memory (Unsworth & Engle, 2005).
sentences.s330: When we removed the variance due to working memory from the sentence processing results, we found that it only affected the relationship between group and garden path condition with reflexive verbs, suggesting that the ability to control interference in working memory is partially related to overcoming the temporary misinterpretation, at least with this particular class of verbs.
sentences.s331: Even though the current study used a very large sample of community recruited participants, it was not without limitation.
sentences.s332: The first is that the sentences tested in the garden path task were somewhat long and complex.
sentences.s333: These sentences result in a large number of misinterpretations for typically developing, healthy college students.
sentences.s334: It is possible that the difficulty level of these stimuli might have masked some differences in our adolescent participants, as they do not likely have as much experience with complex syntactic structures.
sentences.s335: The second limitation is that we were only able to collect a single measure of working memory.
sentences.s336: It is often the norm to collect several different measures of working memory (e.g., reading span, operation span, or spatial span), and our study in particular could have benefited from a measure of reading span.
sentences.s337: This is especially true considering the ongoing theoretical debate about whether there are domain-specific or domain-general pools of working memory resources.
sentences.s338: The third potential limitation is related to the relationship between working memory deficits and anxiety (Eysenck, 1992; Eysenck, Payne, & Derakshan, 2005).
sentences.s339: Deficits for those with anxiety disorders are thought to include a decrease in the ability of the central executive to control attention within the two slave systems.
sentences.s340: In the current sample, participants were not excluded on the basis of current anxiety disorder, thus, it is possible that some of the differences between groups on the working memory task could be due to the inclusion of participants with anxiety problems.
sentences.s341: In conclusion, our data suggest that ADHD does not involve deficits in cognitive inhibition but does involve deficits in working memory, not merely in short-term storage (Martinussen et al., 2005).
sentences.s342: Further, we showed some language comprehension deficits that are independent of reading ability and working memory.
sentences.s343: That result suggested a greater reliance on good-enough processing or, more specifically, on plausibility of events in the real world.
sentences.s344: The working memory findings are theoretically important in their own right because most prior studies of working memory in ADHD did not include tasks that required the simultaneous storage and processing of information.
sentences.s345: Thus, cognitive control problems in ADHD do not extend to the cognitive suppression domain but do involve interference control in working memory.

10.1037/h0043158.printed_title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information.

sentences.s1: Miller (1956) Harvard University First published in Psychological Review, 63, 81-97.
sentences.s2: My problem is that I have been persecuted by an integer.
sentences.s3: For seven years this number has followed me around, has intruded in my most private data, and has assaulted me from the pages of our most public journals.
sentences.s4: This number assumes a variety of disguises, being sometimes a little larger and sometimes a little smaller than usual, but never changing so much as to be unrecognizable.
sentences.s5: The persistence with which this number plagues me is far more than a random accident.
sentences.s6: There is, to quote a famous senator, a design behind it, some pattern governing its appearances.
sentences.s7: Either there really is something unusual about the number or else I am suffering from delusions of persecution.
sentences.s8: I shall begin my case history by telling you about some experiments that tested how accurately people can assign numbers to the magnitudes of various aspects of a stimulus.
sentences.s9: In the traditional language of psychology these would be called experiments in absolute judgment.
sentences.s10: Historical accident, however, has decreed that they should have another name.
sentences.s11: We now call them experiments on the capacity of people to transmit information.
sentences.s12: Since these experiments would not have been done without the appearance of information theory on the psychological scene, and since the results are analyzed in terms of the concepts of information theory, I shall have to preface my discussion with a few remarks about this theory.
sentences.s13: Information Measurement The "amount of information" is exactly the same concept that we have talked about for years under the name of "variance." The equations are different, but if we hold tight to the idea that anything that increases the variance also increases the amount of information we cannot go far astray.
sentences.s14: The advantages of this new way of talking about variance are simple enough.
sentences.s15: Variance is always stated in terms of the unit of measurement - inches, pounds, volts, etc. - whereas the amount of information is a dimensionless quantity.
sentences.s16: Since the information in a discrete statistical distribution does not depend upon the unit of measurement, we can extend the concept to situations where we have no metric and we would not ordinarily think of using [p. 82] the variance.
sentences.s17: And it also enables us to compare results obtained in quite different experimental situations where it would be meaningless to compare variances based on different metrics.
sentences.s18: So there are some good reasons for adopting the newer concept.
sentences.s19: The similarity of variance and amount of information might be explained this way: When we have a large variance, we are very ignorant about what is going to happen.
sentences.s20: If we are very ignorant, then when we make the observation it gives us a lot of information.
sentences.s21: On the other hand, if the variance is very small, we know in advance how our observation must come out, so we get little information from making the observation.
sentences.s22: If you will now imagine a communication system, you will realize that there is a great deal of variability about what goes into the system and also a great deal of variability about what comes out.
sentences.s23: The input and the output can therefore be described in terms of their variance (or their information).
sentences.s24: If it is a good communication system, however, there must be some systematic relation between what goes in and what comes out.
sentences.s25: That is to say, the output will depend upon the input, or will be correlated with the input.
sentences.s26: If we measure this correlation, then we can say how much of the output variance is attributable to the input and how much is due to random fluctuations or "noise" introduced by the system during transmission.
sentences.s27: So we see that the measure of transmitted information is simply a measure of the input-output correlation.
sentences.s28: There are two simple rules to follow.
sentences.s29: Whenever I refer to "amount of information," you will understand "variance." And whenever I refer to "amount of transmitted information," you will understand "covariance" or "correlation." The situation can be described graphically by two partially overlapping circles.
sentences.s30: Then the left circle can be taken to represent the variance of the input, the right circle the variance of the output, and the overlap the covariance of input and output.
sentences.s31: I shall speak of the left circle as the amount of input information, the right circle as the amount of output information, and the overlap as the amount of transmitted information.
sentences.s32: In the experiments on absolute judgment, the observer is considered to be a communication channel.
sentences.s33: Then the left circle would represent the amount of information in the stimuli, the right circle the amount of information in his responses, and the overlap the stimulus-response correlation as measured by the amount of transmitted information.
sentences.s34: The experimental problem is to increase the amount of input information and to measure the amount of transmitted information.
sentences.s35: If the observer's absolute judgments are quite accurate, then nearly all of the input information will be transmitted and will be recoverable from his responses.
sentences.s36: If he makes errors, then the transmitted information may be considerably less than the input.
sentences.s37: We expect that, as we increase the amount of input information, the observer will begin to make more and more errors; we can test the limits of accuracy of his absolute judgments.
sentences.s38: If the human observer is a reasonable kind of communication system, then when we increase the amount of input information the transmitted information will increase at first and will eventually level off at some asymptotic value.
sentences.s39: This asymptotic value we take to be the channel capacity of the observer: it represents the greatest amount of information that he can give us about the stimulus on the basis of an absolute judgment.
sentences.s40: The channel capacity is the upper limit on the extent to which the observer can match his responses to the stimuli we give him.
sentences.s41: Now just a brief word about the bit [p. 83] and we can begin to look at some data.
sentences.s42: One bit of information is the amount of information that we need to make a decision between two equally likely alternatives.
sentences.s43: If we must decide whether a man is less than six feet tall or more than six feet tall and if we know that the chances are 50-50, then we need one bit of information.
sentences.s44: Notice that this unit of information does not refer in any way to the unit of length that we use - feet, inches, centimeters, etc.
sentences.s45: However you measure the man's height, we still need just one bit of information.
sentences.s46: Two bits of information enables us to decide among four equally likely alternatives.
sentences.s47: Three bits of information enable us to decide among eight equally likely alternatives.
sentences.s48: Four bits of information decide among 16 alternatives, five among 32, and so on.
sentences.s49: That is to say, if there are 32 equally likely alternatives, we must make five successive binary decisions, worth one bit each, before we know which alternative is correct.
sentences.s50: So the general rule is simple: every time the number of alternatives is increased by a factor of two, one bit of information is added.
sentences.s51: There are two ways we might increase the amount of input information.
sentences.s52: We could increase the rate at which we give information to the observer, so that the amount of information per unit time would increase.
sentences.s53: Or we could ignore the time variable completely and increase the amount of input information by increasing the number of alternative stimuli.
sentences.s54: In the absolute judgment experiment we are interested in the second alternative.
sentences.s55: We give the observer as much time as he wants to make his response; we simply increase the number of alternative stimuli among which he must discriminate and look to see where confusions begin to occur.
sentences.s56: Confusions will appear near the point that we are calling his "channel capacity." Absolute Judgments of Unidimensional Stimuli Now let us consider what happens when we make absolute judgments of tones.
sentences.s57: Pollack (17) asked listeners to identify tones by assigning numerals to them.
sentences.s58: The tones were different with respect to frequency, and covered the range from 100 to 8000 cps in equal logarithmic steps.
sentences.s59: A tone was sounded and the listener responded by giving a numeral.
sentences.s60: After the listener had made his response he was told the correct identification of the tone.
sentences.s61: When only two or three tones were used the listeners never confused them.
sentences.s62: With four different tones confusions were quite rare, but with five or more tones confusions were frequent.
sentences.s63: With fourteen different tones the listeners made many mistakes.
sentences.s64: These data are plotted in Fig. 1.
sentences.s65: Along the bottom is the amount of input information in bits per stimulus.
sentences.s66: As the number of alternative tones was increased from 2 to 14, the input information increased from 1 to 3.8 bits.
sentences.s67: On the ordinate is plotted the amount of [p. 84] transmitted information.
sentences.s68: The amount of transmitted information behaves in much the way we would expect a communication channel to behave; the transmitted information increases linearly up to about 2 bits and then bends off toward an asymptote at about 2.5 bits.
sentences.s69: This value, 2.5 bits, therefore, is what we are calling the channel capacity of the listener for absolute judgments of pitch.
sentences.s70: So now we have the number 2.5 bits.
sentences.s71: First, note that 2.5 bits corresponds to about six equally likely alternatives.
sentences.s72: The result means that we cannot pick more than six different pitches that the listener will never confuse.
sentences.s73: Or, stated slightly differently, no matter how many alternative tones we ask him to judge, the best we can expect him to do is to assign them to about six different classes without error.
sentences.s74: Or, again, if we know that there were N alternative stimuli, then his judgment enables us to narrow down the particular stimulus to one out of N / 6.
sentences.s75: Most people are surprised that the number is as small as six.
sentences.s76: Of course, there is evidence that a musically sophisticated person with absolute pitch can identify accurately any one of 50 or 60 different pitches.
sentences.s77: Fortunately, I do not have time to discuss these remarkable exceptions.
sentences.s78: I say it is fortunate because I do not know how to explain their superior performance.
sentences.s79: So I shall stick to the more pedestrian fact that most of us can identify about one out of only five or six pitches before we begin to get confused.
sentences.s80: It is interesting to consider that psychologists have been using seven-point rating scales for a long time, on the intuitive basis that trying to rate into finer categories does not really add much to the usefulness of the ratings.
sentences.s81: Pollack's results indicate that, at least for pitches, this intuition is fairly sound.
sentences.s82: Next you can ask how reproducible this result is.
sentences.s83: Does it depend on the spacing of the tones or the various conditions of judgment?
sentences.s84: Pollack varied these conditions in a number of ways.
sentences.s85: The range of frequencies can be changed by a factor of about 20 without changing the amount of information transmitted more than a small percentage.
sentences.s86: Different groupings of the pitches decreased the transmission, but the loss was small.
sentences.s87: For example, if you can discriminate five high-pitched tones in one series and five low-pitched tones in another series, it is reasonable to expect that you could combine all ten into a single series and still tell them all apart without error.
sentences.s88: When you try it, however, it does not work.
sentences.s89: The channel capacity for pitch seems to be about six and that is the best you can do.
sentences.s90: While we are on tones, let us look next at Garner's (7) work on loudness.
sentences.s91: Garner's data for loudness are summarized in Fig. 2.
sentences.s92: Garner went to some trouble to get the best possible spacing of his tones over the intensity range from 15 to 110 db.
sentences.s93: He used 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, and 20 different stimulus intensities.
sentences.s94: The results shown in Fig. 2 take into account the differences among subjects and the sequential influence of the immediately preceding judgment.
sentences.s95: Again we find that there seems to be a limit. [p. 85] The channel capacity for absolute judgments of loudness is 2.3 bits, or about five perfectly discriminable alternatives.
sentences.s96: Since these two studies were done in different laboratories with slightly different techniques and methods of analysis, we are not in a good position to argue whether five loudnesses is significantly different from six pitches.
sentences.s97: Probably the difference is in the right direction, and absolute judgments of pitch are slightly more accurate than absolute judgments of loudness.
sentences.s98: The important point, however, is that the two answers are of the same order of magnitude.
sentences.s99: The experiment has also been done for taste intensities.
sentences.s100: In Fig. 3 are the results obtained by Beebe-Center, Rogers, and O'Connell (1) for absolute judgments of the concentration of salt solutions.
sentences.s101: The concentrations ranged from 0.3 to 34.7 gm.
sentences.s102: NaCl per 100 cc. tap water in equal subjective steps.
sentences.s103: They used 3, 5, 9, and 17 different concentrations.
sentences.s104: The channel capacity is 1.9 bits, which is about four distinct concentrations.
sentences.s105: Thus taste intensities seem a little less distinctive than auditory stimuli, but again the order of magnitude is not far off.
sentences.s106: On the other hand, the channel capacity for judgments of visual position seems to be significantly larger.
sentences.s107: Hake and Garner (8) asked observers to interpolate visually between two scale markers.
sentences.s108: Their results are shown in Fig. 4.
sentences.s109: They did the experiment in two ways.
sentences.s110: In one version they let the observer use any number between zero and 100 to describe the position, although they presented stimuli at only 5, 10, 20, or 50 different positions.
sentences.s111: The results with this unlimited response technique are shown by the filled circles on the graph.
sentences.s112: In the other version the observers were limited in their responses to reporting just those stimulus values that were possible.
sentences.s113: That is to say, in the second version the number of different responses that the observer could make was exactly the same as the number of different stimuli that the experimenter might present.
sentences.s114: The results with this limited response technique are shown by the open circles on the graph.
sentences.s115: The two functions are so similar that is seems fair to conclude that the number of responses available to the observer had nothing to do with the channel capacity of 3.25 bits.
sentences.s116: The Hake-Garner experiment has been repeated by Coonan and Klemmer.
sentences.s117: Although they have not yet published their results, they have given me permission to say that they obtained channel capacities ranging from 3.2 bits for [p. 86] very short exposures of the pointer position to 3.9 bits for longer exposures.
sentences.s118: These values are slightly higher than Hake and Garner's, so we must conclude that there are between 10 and 15 distinct positions along a linear interval.
sentences.s119: This is the largest channel capacity that has been measured for any unidimensional variable.
sentences.s120: At the present time these four experiments on absolute judgments of simple, unidimensional stimuli are all that have appeared in the psychological journals.
sentences.s121: However, a great deal of work on other stimulus variables has not yet appeared in the journals.
sentences.s122: For example, Eriksen and Hake (6) have found that the channel capacity for judging the sizes of squares is 2.2 bits, or about five categories, under a wide range of experimental conditions.
sentences.s123: In a separate experiment Eriksen (5) found 2.8 bits for size, 3.1 bits for hue, and 2.3 bits for brightness.
sentences.s124: Geldard has measured the channel capacity for the skin by placing vibrators on the chest region.
sentences.s125: A good observer can identify about four intensities, about five durations, and about seven locations.
sentences.s126: One of the most active groups in this area has been the Air Force Operational Applications Laboratory.
sentences.s127: Pollack has been kind enough to furnish me with the results of their measurements for several aspects of visual displays.
sentences.s128: They made measurements for area and for the curvature, length, and direction of lines.
sentences.s129: In one set of experiments they used a very short exposure of the stimulus - 1 / 40 second - and then they repeated the measurements with a 5-second exposure.
sentences.s130: For area they got 2.6 bits with the short exposure and 2.7 bits with the long exposure.
sentences.s131: For the length of a line they got about 2.6 bits with the short exposure and about 3.0 bits with the long exposure.
sentences.s132: Direction, or angle of inclination, gave 2.8 bits for the short exposure and 3.3 bits for the long exposure.
sentences.s133: Curvature was apparently harder to judge.
sentences.s134: When the length of the arc was constant, the result at the short exposure duration was 2.2 bits, but when the length of the chord was constant, the result was only 1.6 bits.
sentences.s135: This last value is the lowest that anyone has measured to date.
sentences.s136: I should add, however, that these values are apt to be slightly too low because the data from all subjects were pooled before the transmitted information was computed.
sentences.s137: Now let us see where we are.
sentences.s138: First, the channel capacity does seem to be a valid notion for describing human observers.
sentences.s139: Second, the channel capacities measured for these unidimensional variables range from 1.6 bits for curvature to 3.9 bits for positions in an interval.
sentences.s140: Although there is no question that the differences among the variables are real and meaningful, the more impressive fact to me is their considerable similarity.
sentences.s141: If I take the best estimates I can get of the channel capacities for all the stimulus variables I have mentioned, the mean is 2.6 bits and the standard deviation is only 0.6 bit.
sentences.s142: In terms of distinguishable alternatives, this mean corresponds to about 6.5 categories, one standard deviation includes from 4 to 10 categories, and the total range is from 3 to 15 categories.
sentences.s143: Considering the wide variety of different variables that have been studied, I find this to be a remarkably narrow range.
sentences.s144: There seems to be some limitation built into us either by learning or by the design of our nervous systems, a limit that keeps our channel capacities in this general range.
sentences.s145: On the basis of the present evidence it seems safe to say that we possess a finite and rather small capacity for making such unidimensional judgments and that this capacity does not vary a great deal from one simple sensory attribute to another.
sentences.s146: You may have noticed that I have been careful to say that this magical number seven applies to one- dimensional judgments.

sentences.s178: Under these conditions the transmitted information was 7.2 bits, which corresponds to about 150 different categories that could be absolutely identified without error.

sentences.s191: If a compromise was necessary, the one we seem to have made is clearly the more adaptive.
sentences.s192: Pollack and Ficks's results are very strongly suggestive of an argument that linguists and phoneticians have been making for some time (11).
sentences.s193: According to the linguistic analysis of the sounds of human speech, there are about eight or ten dimensions - the linguists call them distinctive features - that distinguish one phoneme from another.
sentences.s194: These distinctive features are usually binary, or at most ternary, in nature.
sentences.s195: For example, a binary distinction is made between vowels and consonants, a binary decision is made between oral and nasal consonants, a ternary decision is made among front, middle, and back phonemes, etc.
sentences.s196: This approach gives us quite a different picture of speech perception than we might otherwise obtain from our studies of the speech spectrum and of the ear's ability to discriminate relative differences among pure tones.

sentences.s198: It was probably with this linguistic theory in mind that Pollack and Ficks conducted a test on a set of tonal stimuli that varied in eight dimensions, but required only a binary decision on each dimension.
sentences.s199: With these tones they measured the transmitted information at 6.9 bits, or about 120 recognizable kinds of sounds.

sentences.s203: Somebody will have to do the experiment to find out.
sentences.s204: There is a limit, however, at about eight or nine distinctive features in every language that has been studied, and so when we talk we must resort to still another trick for increasing our channel capacity.
sentences.s205: Language uses sequences of phonemes, so we make several judgments successively when we listen to words and sentences.
sentences.s206: That is to say, we use both simultaneous and successive discriminations in order to expand the rather rigid limits imposed by the inaccuracy of our absolute judgments of simple magnitudes.
sentences.s207: These multidimensional judgments are strongly reminiscent of the abstraction experiment of Külpe (14).
sentences.s208: As you may remember, Külpe showed that observers report more accurately on an attribute for which they are set than on attributes for which they are not set.
sentences.s209: For example, Chapman (4) used three different attributes and compared the results obtained when the observers were instructed before the tachistoschopic presentation with the results obtained when they were not told until after the presentation which one of the three attributes was to be reported.
sentences.s210: When the instruction was given in advance, the judgments were more accurate.
sentences.s211: When the instruction was given afterwards, the subjects presumably had to judge all three attributes in order to report on any one of them and the accuracy was correspondingly lower.
sentences.s212: This is in complete accord with the results we have just been considering, where the accuracy of judgment on each attribute decreased as more dimensions were added.

[p. 90] Subitizing I cannot leave this general area without mentioning, however briefly, the experiments conducted at Mount Holyoke College on the discrimination of number (12).
sentences.s215: In experiments by Kaufman, Lord, Reese, and Volkmann random patterns of dots were flashed on a screen for 1 / 5 of a second.
sentences.s216: Anywhere from 1 to more than 200 dots could appear in the pattern.
sentences.s217: The subject's task was to report how many dots there were.
sentences.s218: The first point to note is that on patterns containing up to five or six dots the subjects simply did not make errors.
sentences.s219: The performance on these small numbers of dots was so different from the performance with more dots that is was given a special name.

sentences.s221: This is, as you will recognize, what we once optimistically called "the span of attention." This discontinuity at seven is, of course, suggestive.

sentences.s234: And yet when we examine the matter more closely, there seems to be a reasonable suspicion that it is nothing more than a coincidence.
sentences.s235: The Span of Immediate Memory Let me summarize the situation in this way.
sentences.s236: There is a clear and definite limit to the accuracy with which we can identify absolutely the magnitude of a unidimensional stimulus variable.
sentences.s237: I would propose to call this limit the span of absolute judgment, and I maintain that for unidimensional judgments this span is usually somewhere in the neighborhood of seven.
sentences.s238: We are not completely at the mercy of this limited span, however, because we have a variety of techniques for getting around it and increasing the accuracy of our judgments.
sentences.s239: The three most important of these devices are (a) to make relative rather than absolute judgments.; or, if that is not possible, (b) to increase the number of dimensions along which the stimuli can differ; or (c) to arrange the task in such a way that we make a sequence of several absolute judgments in a row.
sentences.s240: The study of relative judgments is one of the oldest topics in experimental psychology, and I will not pause to review it now.
sentences.s241: The second device, increasing the dimensionality, we have just considered.
sentences.s242: It seems that by adding [p. 91] more dimensions and requiring crude, binary, yes-no judgments on each attribute we can extend the span of absolute judgment from seven to at least 150.
sentences.s243: Judging from our everyday behavior, the limit is probably in the thousands, if indeed there is a limit.
sentences.s244: In my opinion, we cannot go on compounding dimensions indefinitely.
sentences.s245: I suspect that there is also a span of perceptual dimensionality and that this span is somewhere in the neighborhood of ten, but I must add at once that there is no objective evidence to support this suspicion.
sentences.s246: This is a question sadly needing experimental exploration.
sentences.s247: Concerning the third device, the use of successive judgments, I have quite a bit to say because this device introduces memory as the handmaiden of discrimination.
sentences.s248: And, since mnemonic processes are at least as complex as are perceptual processes, we can anticipate that their interactions will not be easily disentangled.
sentences.s249: Suppose that we start by simply extending slightly the experimental procedure that we have been using.
sentences.s250: Up to this point we have presented a single stimulus and asked the observer to name it immediately thereafter.
sentences.s251: We can extend this procedure by requiring the observer to withhold his response until we have given him several stimuli in succession.
sentences.s252: At the end of the sequence of stimuli he then makes his response.
sentences.s253: We still have the same sort of input-output situation that is required for the measurement of transmitted information.
sentences.s254: But now we have passed from an experiment on absolute judgment to what is traditionally called an experiment on immediate memory.
sentences.s255: Before we look at any data on this topic I feel I must give you a word of warning to help you avoid some obvious associations that can be confusing.
sentences.s256: Everybody knows that there is a finite span of immediate memory and that for a lot of different kinds of test materials this span is about seven items in length.
sentences.s257: I have just shown you that there is a span of absolute judgment that can distinguish about seven categories and that there is a span of attention that will encompass about six objects at a glance.
sentences.s258: What is more natural than to think that all three of these spans are different aspects of a single underlying process?
sentences.s259: And that is a fundamental mistake, as I shall be at some pains to demonstrate.
sentences.s260: This mistake is one of the malicious persecutions that the magical number seven has subjected me to.
sentences.s261: My mistake went something like this.
sentences.s262: We have seen that the invariant feature in the span of absolute judgment is the amount of information that the observer can transmit.
sentences.s263: There is a real operational similarity between the absolute judgment experiment and the immediate memory experiment.
sentences.s264: If immediate memory is like absolute judgment, then it should follow that the invariant feature in the span of immediate memory is also the amount of information that an observer can retain.
sentences.s265: If the amount of information in the span of immediate memory is a constant, then the span should be short when the individual items contain a lot of information and the span should be long when the items contain little information.
sentences.s266: For example, decimal digits are worth 3.3 bits apiece.
sentences.s267: We can recall about seven of them, for a total of 23 bits of information.
sentences.s268: Isolated English words are worth about 10 bits apiece.
sentences.s269: If the total amount of information is to remain constant at 23 bits, then we should be able to remember only two or three words chosen at random.
sentences.s270: In this way I generated a theory about how the span of immediate memory should vary as a function of the amount of information per item in the test materials.
sentences.s271: The measurements of memory span in the literature are suggestive on this [p. 92] question, but not definitive.
sentences.s272: And so it was necessary to do the experiment to see.

sentences.s274: The lists were read aloud at the rate of one item per second and the subjects had as much time as they needed to give their responses.
sentences.s275: A procedure described by Woodworth (20) was used to score the responses.

sentences.s278: The solid curves represent the data.
sentences.s279: Hayes repeated the experiment using test vocabularies of different sizes but all containing only English monosyllables (open circles in Fig. 7).
sentences.s280: This more homogeneous test material did not change the picture significantly.
sentences.s281: With binary items the span is about nine and, although it drops to about five with monosyllabic English words, the difference is far less than the hypothesis of constant information would require.
sentences.s282: There is nothing wrong with Hayes's experiment, because Pollack (16) repeated it much more elaborately and got essentially the same result.

sentences.s284: His results are plotted in Fig. 8.

sentences.s286: And so the outcome is perfectly clear.
sentences.s287: In spite of the coincidence that the magical number seven appears in both places, the span of absolute judgment and the span of immediate memory are quite different kinds of limitations that are imposed on our ability to process information.
sentences.s288: Absolute judgment is limited by the amount of information.
sentences.s289: Immediate memory is limited by the number of items.
sentences.s290: In order to capture this distinction in somewhat picturesque terms, I have fallen into the custom of distinguishing between bits of information and chunks of information.
sentences.s291: Then I can say that the number of bits of information is constant for absolute judgment and the number of chunks of informa- [p. 93] tion is constant for immediate memory.
sentences.s292: The span of immediate memory seems to be almost independent of the number of bits per chunk, at least over the range that has been examined to date.
sentences.s293: The contrast of the terms bit and chunk also serves to highlight the fact that we are not very definite about what constitutes a chunk of information.
sentences.s294: For example, the memory span of five words that Hayes obtained when each word was drawn at random from a set of 1000 English monosyllables might just as appropriately have been called a memory span of 15 phonemes, since each word had about three phonemes in it.
sentences.s295: Intuitively, it is clear that the subjects were recalling five words, not 15 phonemes, but the logical distinction is not immediately apparent.
sentences.s296: We are dealing here with a process of organizing or grouping the input into familiar units or chunks, and a great deal of learning has gone into the formation of these familiar units.
sentences.s297: Recoding In order to speak more precisely, therefore, we must recognize the importance of grouping or organizing the input sequence into units or chunks.
sentences.s298: Since the memory span is a fixed number of chunks, we can increase the number of bits of information that it contains simply by building larger and larger chunks, each chunk containing more information than before.
sentences.s299: A man just beginning to learn radiotelegraphic code hears each dit and dah as a separate chunk.
sentences.s300: Soon he is able to organize these sounds into letters and then he can deal with the letters as chunks.
sentences.s301: Then the letters organize themselves as words, which are still larger chunks, and he begins to hear whole phrases.
sentences.s302: I do not mean that each step is a discrete process, or that plateaus must appear in his learning curve, for surely the levels of organization are achieved at different rates and overlap each other during the learning process.
sentences.s303: I am simply pointing to the obvious fact that the dits and dahs are organized by learning into patterns and that as these larger chunks emerge the amount of message that the operator can remember increases correspondingly.
sentences.s304: In the terms I am proposing to use, the operator learns to increase the bits per chunk.
sentences.s305: In the jargon of communication theory, this process would be called recoding.
sentences.s306: The input is given in a code that contains many chunks with few bits per chunk.
sentences.s307: The operator recodes the input into another code that contains fewer chunks with more bits per chunk.
sentences.s308: There are many ways to do this recoding, but probably the simplest is to group the input events, apply a new name to the group, and then remember the new name rather than the original input events.
sentences.s309: Since I am convinced that this process is a very general and important one for psychology, I want to tell you about a demonstration experiment that should make perfectly explicit what I am talking about.
sentences.s310: This experiment was conducted by Sidney Smith and was reported by him before the Eastern Psychological Association in 1954.
sentences.s311: Begin with the observed fact that people can repeat back eight decimal digits, but only nine binary digits.
sentences.s312: Since there is a large discrepancy in the amount of information recalled in these two cases, we suspect at once that a recoding procedure could be used to increase the span of immediate memory for binary digits.
sentences.s313: In Table 1 a method for grouping and renaming is illustrated.
sentences.s314: Along the top is a sequence of 18 binary digits, far more than any subject was able to recall after a single presentation.
sentences.s315: In the next line these same binary digits are grouped by pairs.
sentences.s316: Four possible pairs can occur: 00 is renamed 0, 01 is renamed 1, 10 is renamed 2, and 11 is [p. 94] renamed 3.
sentences.s317: That is to say, we recode from a base-two arithmetic to a base-four arithmetic.
sentences.s318: In the recoded sequence there are now just nine digits to remember, and this is almost within the span of immediate memory.
sentences.s319: In the next line the same sequence of binary digits is regrouped into chunks of three.
sentences.s320: There are eight possible sequences of three, so we give each sequence a new name between 0 and 7.
sentences.s321: Now we have recoded from a sequence of 18 binary digits into a sequence of 6 octal digits, and this is well within the span of immediate memory.
sentences.s322: In the last two lines the binary digits are grouped by fours and by fives and are given decimal-digit names from 0 to 15 and from 0 to 31.
sentences.s323: It is reasonably obvious that this kind of recoding increases the bits per chunk, and packages the binary sequence into a form that can be retained within the span of immediate memory.
sentences.s324: So Smith assembled 20 subjects and measured their spans for binary and octal digits.
sentences.s325: The spans were 9 for binaries and 7 for octals.
sentences.s326: Then he gave each recoding scheme to five of the subjects.
sentences.s327: They studied the recoding until they said they understood it - for about 5 or 10 minutes.
sentences.s328: Then he tested their span for binary digits again while they tried to use the recoding schemes they had studied.
sentences.s329: The recoding schemes increased their span for binary digits in every case.
sentences.s330: But the increase was not as large as we had expected on the basis of their span for octal digits.
sentences.s331: Since the discrepancy increased as the recoding ratio increased, we reasoned that the few minutes the subjects had spent learning the recoding schemes had not been sufficient.
sentences.s332: Apparently the translation from one code to the other must be almost automatic or the subject will lose part of the next group while he is trying to remember the translation of the last group.
sentences.s333: Since the 4:1 and 5:1 ratios require considerable study, Smith decided to imitate Ebbinghaus and do the experiment on himself.
sentences.s334: With Germanic patience he drilled himself on each recoding successively, and obtained the results shown in Fig. 9.
sentences.s335: Here the data follow along rather nicely with the results you would predict on the basis of his span for octal digits.
sentences.s337: With the 2:1 recoding, these 12 chunks were worth 24 binary digits.
sentences.s338: With the 3:1 recoding they were worth 36 binary digits.
sentences.s339: With the 4:1 and 5:1 recodings, they were worth about 40 binary digits.
sentences.s340: It is a little dramatic to watch a person get 40 binary digits in a row and then repeat them back without error.
sentences.s341: However, if you think of this merely as [p. 95] a mnemonic trick for extending the memory span, you will miss the more important point that is implicit in nearly all such mnemonic devices.
sentences.s342: The point is that recoding is an extremely powerful weapon for increasing the amount of information that we can deal with.
sentences.s343: In one form or another we use recoding constantly in our daily behavior.
sentences.s344: In my opinion the most customary kind of recoding that we do all the time is to translate into a verbal code.
sentences.s345: When there is a story or an argument or an idea that we want to remember, we usually try to rephrase it "in our own words." When we witness some event we want to remember, we make a verbal description of the event and then remember our verbalization.
sentences.s346: Upon recall we recreate by secondary elaboration the details that seem consistent with the particular verbal recoding we happen to have made.
sentences.s347: The well-known experiment by Carmichael, Hogan, and Walter (3) on the influence that names have on the recall of visual figures is one demonstration of the process.
sentences.s348: The inaccuracy of the testimony of eyewitnesses is well known in legal psychology, but the distortions of testimony are not random - they follow naturally from the particular recoding that the witness used, and the particular recoding he used depends upon his whole life history.
sentences.s349: Our language is tremendously useful for repackaging material into a few chunks rich in information.
sentences.s350: I suspect that imagery is a form of recoding, too, but images seem much harder to get at operationally and to study experimentally than the more symbolic kinds of recoding.
sentences.s351: It seems probable that even memorization can be studied in these terms.
sentences.s352: The process of memorizing may be simply the formation of chunks, or groups of items that go together, until there are few enough chunks so that we can recall all the items.
sentences.s353: The work by Bousfield and Cohen (2) on the occurrence of clustering in the recall of words is especially interesting in this respect.
sentences.s354: Summary I have come to the end of the data that I wanted to present, so I would like now to make some summarizing remarks.
sentences.s355: First, the span of absolute judgment and the span of immediate memory impose severe limitations on the amount of information that we are able to receive, process, and remember.
sentences.s356: By organizing the stimulus input simultaneously into several dimensions and successively into a sequence of chunks, we manage to break (or at least stretch) this informational bottleneck.
sentences.s357: Second, the process of recoding is a very important one in human psychology and deserves much more explicit attention than it has received.
sentences.s358: In particular, the kind of linguistic recoding that people do seems to me to be the very lifeblood of the thought processes.
sentences.s359: Recoding procedures are a constant concern to clinicians, social psycholo- [p. 96] gists, linguists, and anthropologists and yet, probably because recoding is less accessible to experimental manipulation than nonsense syllables or T mazes, the traditional experimental psychologist has contributed little or nothing to their analysis.
sentences.s360: Nevertheless, experimental techniques can be used, methods of recoding can be specified, behavioral indicants can be found.
sentences.s361: And I anticipate that we will find a very orderly set of relations describing what now seems an uncharted wilderness of individual differences.
sentences.s362: Third, the concepts and measures provided by the theory of information provide a quantitative way of getting at some of these questions.
sentences.s363: The theory provides us with a yardstick for calibrating our stimulus materials and for measuring the performance of our subjects.
sentences.s364: In the interests of communication I have suppressed the technical details of information measurement and have tried to express the ideas in more familiar terms; I hope this paraphrase will not lead you to think they are not useful in research.
sentences.s365: Informational concepts have already proved valuable in the study of discrimination and of language; they promise a great deal in the study of learning and memory; and it has even been proposed that they can be useful in the study of concept formation.
sentences.s366: A lot of questions that seemed fruitless twenty or thirty years ago may now be worth another look.
sentences.s367: In fact, I feel that my story here must stop just as it begins to get really interesting.
sentences.s368: And finally, what about the magical number seven?
sentences.s369: What about the seven wonders of the world, the seven seas, the seven deadly sins, the seven daughters of Atlas in the Pleiades, the seven ages of man, the seven levels of hell, the seven primary colors, the seven notes of the musical scale, and the seven days of the week?
sentences.s370: What about the seven-point rating scale, the seven categories for absolute judgment, the seven objects in the span of attention, and the seven digits in the span of immediate memory?
sentences.s371: For the present I propose to withhold judgment.
sentences.s372: Perhaps there is something deep and profound behind all these sevens, something just calling out for us to discover it.
sentences.s373: But I suspect that it is only a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence.

sentences.s10: Wiersemab and Anouk Scheresa aBehavioural Science Institute, Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands; bDepartment of Experimental Clinical and Health Psychology, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium ABSTRACT Adolescents with attention-deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are known to have stronger preferences for smaller immediate rewards over larger delayed rewards in delay discounting tasks than their peers, which has been argued to reﬂect delay aversion.
sentences.s11: Here, participants performed a delay discounting task with gains and losses.
sentences.s12: In this latter condition, participants were asked whether they were willing to wait in order to lose less money.
sentences.s13: Following the core assumption of the delay aversion model that individuals with ADHD have a general aversion to delay, one would predict adolescents with ADHD to avoid waiting in both conditions.
sentences.s14: Adolescents (12–17 years) with ADHD (n = 29) and controls (n = 28) made choices between smaller immediate and larger delayed gains, and between larger immediate and smaller delayed losses.
sentences.s15: All delays (5–25 s) and gains/losses (2–10 cents) were experienced.
sentences.s16: In addition to an area under the curve approach, a mixed-model analysis was conducted to disentangle the contributions of delay duration and immediate gain/delayed loss amount to choice.
sentences.s17: The ADHD group chose the immediate option more often than controls in the gain condition, but not in the loss condition.
sentences.s18: The contribution of delay duration to immedi- ate choices was stronger for the ADHD group than the control group in the gain condition only.
sentences.s19: In addition, the ADHD group scored higher on self-reported delay aversion, and delay aversion was associated with delay sensitivity in the gain condition, but not in the loss condition.
sentences.s20: In sum, we found no clear evidence for a general aversion to delay in adolescents with ADHD.
sentences.s21: ARTICLE HISTORY Received 15 September 2017 Accepted 16 July 2018 KEYWORDS ADHD; delay discounting; reward; loss; delay aversion The delay aversion model proposes that children with attention-deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) develop an aversion to delay due to negative emotions associated with waiting, as a result of disturbances in the brain’s reward circuits (Sonuga-Barke, Dalen, & Remington, 2003; Sonuga-Barke, Taylor, Sembi, & Smith, 1992).
sentences.s22: This can explain their impulsive behavior in daily life.
sentences.s23: In the laboratory, impulsive choice is often measured by the use of delay discounting tasks in which participants are repeatedly asked to choose between smaller immediate rewards (e.g., 5 dollars now) and larger delayed rewards (e.g., 10 dollars next week) (e.g., Scheres, de Water, & Mies, 2013).
sentences.s24: Mies g.w.mies@amc.nl Department of Psychiatry, Academic Medical Center Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands Supplemental data for this article can be accessed here.
sentences.s25: Published by Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.
