sentences.s30: Such views, however, were not widely adopted, nor did they serve as an impetus to much new research.
sentences.s31: Zentall (1985) set forth an optimal stimulation theory of ADHD, arguing that the hyperac- tivity arises from low levels of arousal and serves to maintain an optimal arousal level; the hyperactivity, in a sense, is a form of self-stimulation.
sentences.s32: More recently, researchers theorizing on ADHD have emphasized poor behavioral inhibition as the central im- pairment of the disorder (Barkley, 1990, 1994; Quay, 1988a; Schachar, Tannock, & Logan, 1993; Schachar, Tannock, Marri- ott, & Logan, 1995).
sentences.s33: In keeping with this trend, in this article I attempt to provide a unifying model of ADHD that is founded on prior theories of the neuropsychological functions of the brain's prefrontal lobes.
sentences.s34: Poor behavioral inhibition is specified as the central deficiency in ADHD.
sentences.s35: The model then sets forth a linkage between response inhibition and four executive functions that depend on such inhibition for their own effective performance.
sentences.s36: These four func- tions serve to bring behavior under the control of internally represented information and self-directed actions.
sentences.s37: By doing so, the four functions permit greater goal-directed action and task persistence.
sentences.s38: The model provides a more comprehensive account of research findings on the cognitive deficits associated with ADHD than does the current clinical view, which sees ADHD as primarily an attention deficit.
sentences.s39: The model also predicts many additional deficits likely to be associated with ADHD that have received little or no testing in research.
sentences.s40: Such predictions provide avenues for attempts at falsification of the model and point to new areas for scientific investigation.
sentences.s41: The goal here is admittedly ambitious, perhaps overly so, because the model I propose may be potentially misconstrued as a "theory of everything." Yet its boundaries are generally circumscribed to the domain of self-regulation in developmental psychology or executive functions in neuropsychology.
sentences.s42: Albeit a broad domain, it is not unlimited.
sentences.s43: It can be readily distinguished from other major domains of neuropsychological functioning such as sensation and perception, memory, language, and the spatial, sequential, emotional, and motivational domains, among others.
sentences.s44: The model may overlap with these other domains, how- ever, to the extent that self-regulation may affect them.
sentences.s45: Before I proceed to discuss the origins of the model, its components, and its extension to ADHD, the ambitiousness of this undertak- ing demands a justification for why a new model of ADHD is even necessary at this time.
sentences.s46: The Need for a New Model of ADHD A new theory of ADHD is needed for a number of reasons.
sentences.s47: First, current research on ADHD is nearly atheoretical, at least in regards to its basic nature.
sentences.s48: That research is mainly exploratory and descriptive, with two exceptions.
sentences.s49: One is Quay's (1988a, 1988b, 1996) use of Gray's (1982) neuropsychological model of anxiety to explain the origin of the poor inhibition seen in ADHD.
sentences.s50: This Quay-Gray model states that the impulsiveness arises from an underfunctioning of the brain's behavioral inhibi- tion system.
sentences.s51: That system is said to be sensitive to signals of conditioned punishment, and the model predicts that those with ADHD should prove less sensitive to such signals, particularly in passive avoidance paradigms (Milich, Hartung, Martin, & Haigler, 1994; Quay, 1988b).
sentences.s52: The second exception is the work of Sergeant and van der Meere (1988; Sergeant, 1995a, 1995b, 1996; van der Meere, in press; van der Meere, van Baal, & Sergeant, 1989), who successfully used information-processing theory and its associated energetic model (arousal, activation, and effort) for isolating the central deficit(s) in ADHD within that paradigm (Sergeant, 1995b).
sentences.s53: However, this approach does not set forth a theory of ADHD; like the Quay-Gray theory, it makes no effort at large-scale theory construction so as to pro- vide a unifying account of the various cognitive deficits associ- ated with ADHD.
sentences.s54: Apart from these exceptions, the current clini- cal view of ADHD (i.e., that of the DSM-IV) and the vast majority of current research being conducted on its nature are not theory driven (Taylor, 1996).
sentences.s55: One sign of advancement in a scientific field is that its research becomes so driven.
sentences.s56: This synthesis is an attempt to move research on ADHD further along in that direction.
sentences.s57: Douglas's (1980) earlier model of ADHD is not actually a theory; it is mainly descriptive and was arrived at inductively from a review of the extant research findings on ADHD in which Douglas (1980, 1983; Douglas & Peters, 1979) discerned a pattern among the findings consistently noted in this field.
sentences.s58: That pattern comprised the four deficiencies noted earlier.
sentences.s59: Although it was tremendously helpful at the time, such pattern discernment remains at a descriptive level, albeit one more synthetic than prior efforts at conceptualizing ADHD.
sentences.s60: But it is neither explana- tory nor, more important, predictive of new hypotheses that are testable.
sentences.s61: It still begs the question of just how the pattern itself is to be explained.
sentences.s62: Appealing to the construct of self-regulation (Douglas, 1988) is a step in the right direction but is of only modest help unless self-regulation itself is defined and the man- ner in which it leads to the four impairments is explained.
sentences.s63: Both the pattern and the later use of self-regulation as an explanatory construct by Douglas fit well within the model developed below.
sentences.s64: This theory, however, goes much further by providing the needed definition of self-regulation, articulating the cognitive compo- nents that contribute to it, specifying the primacy of behavioral inhibition within the theory, and setting forth a motor control component to ADHD.
sentences.s65: Most important, the model reveals a diver- sity of new, untested, yet testable predictions about cognitive and behavioral deficits deserving of study.
sentences.s66: A second reason why a theory of ADHD is sorely needed is that the current clinical view of ADHD (i.e., that of the DSM- IV ), being purely descriptive of two behavioral deficits (inatten- tion and hyperactivity-impulsivity), also cannot readily account for the many cognitive and behavioral deficits associated with ADHD that are reviewed later in this article.
sentences.s67: To account for such findings, any model must fulfill at least five key require- ments: (a) It must explain why an actual deficit in attention in children with ADHD has not been found (Schachar et al., 1993, 1995; Sergeant, 1995a, 1995b; van der Meere, in press; van der Meere & Sergeant, 1988a, 1988b, 1988c), even though research on parent and teacher ratings of ADHD repeatedly identifies a This document is copyrighted by the American Psychological Association or one of its allied publishers.

sentences.s70: INHIBITION AND ADHD 67 factor of "inattention"; (b) it must explain the link between poor behavioral inhibition (hyperactivity-impulsivity) and this sister impairment of inattention, or whatever this symptom turns out to be; (c) it also must link these two constructs with execu- tive or metacognitive functions because most, if not all, of the cognitive deficits associated with ADHD seem to fall within the realm of self-regulation or executive functions (Barkley, 1995; Denckla, 1994, 1995; Douglas, 1988; Grodzinsky & Diamond, 1992; Pennington & Ozonoff, 1996; Pennington, Grossier, & Welsh, 1993; Seidman et al., 1995; Torgesen, 1994; Welsh, Pen- nington, & Grossier, 1991; Weyandt & Willis, 1994); (d) it must ultimately connect the literature on ADHD with the larger literatures of developmental psychology and developmental neu- ropsychology as they pertain to self-regulation and executive functions if it is to argue that ADHD arises from a disruption in developmental processes; and (e) it must be useful as a scien- tific tool and must make explicit predictions about new phenom- ena that will both drive research initiatives and provide a means of falsifying the theory.
sentences.s71: A third reason for a new model of ADHD is that the current view treats the subtypes of ADHD as sharing qualitatively identi- cal deficits in attention while differing only in the presence of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms.
sentences.s72: As noted above, it is doubtful that the problems with inattention associated with hyperactive- impulsive behavior lie in the realm of attention, whereas those seen in the predominantly inattentive type of ADHD appear to do so.
sentences.s73: A digression is necessary here.
sentences.s74: The predominantly hyperactive—impulsive type actually seems to be a develop- mental precursor to the combined type.
sentences.s75: In the field trial for ADHD in the DSM-IV, this hyperactive-impulsive type was chiefly found among preschool children (Applegate et al., 1995).
sentences.s76: In contrast, the combined type was far more represented in school-aged children, as was nearly the entire sample of the inattentive type.
sentences.s77: This relationship of ADHD type to the ages associated with it likely arises from a simple observation made in prior studies.
sentences.s78: The hyperactive—impulsive behavior pattern seems to emerge first in development, during the preschool years, whereas the symptoms of inattention associated with it appear to have their onset several years later, at least according to parental reports (Hart, Lahey, Loeber, Applegate, & Frick, 1995; Loeber, Green, Lahey, Christ, & Frick, 1992).
sentences.s79: Moreover, the types of problems with inattention seen in the predominantly inattentive type appear to have their onset even later than those that would eventually be associated with hyperactive-impulsive behavior (Applegate et al., 1995).
sentences.s80: Returning, then, to the start of this digression, it appears that the predominantly inattentive type may not, in fact, have its impairment in the same form of attention as that found in the other two types (see Barkley, 1990; Barkley, Grodzinsky, & DuPaul, 1992; Goodyear & Hynd, 1992; Hinshaw, 1994; and Lahey & Carlson, 1992, for reviews).
sentences.s81: Research on the inatten- tive subtype suggests that symptoms of daydreaming, "spacing out,'' being "in a fog," being easily confused, staring frequently, and being lethargic, hypoactive, and passive are more common (Barkley, DuPaul, & McMurray, 1990; Lahey & Carlson, 1992).
sentences.s82: This type of ADHD has a deficit in speed of information processing, generally, and in focused or selective attention, spe- cifically (Goodyear & Hynd, 1992; Lahey & Carlson, 1992).
sentences.s83: The deficit in the combined type of ADHD has been character- ized as being in the realm of sustained attention (persistence) and distractibility.
sentences.s84: If this distinction is valid, the present clinical view of ADHD may be clustering into a single set of disorders what are, in reality, two qualitatively different disorders.
sentences.s85: Such a distinction would also argue that children with ADHD combined type who may develop the inattentive type as they get older (because of reductions in hyperactive behavior) are not actually changing types of ADHD at all.
sentences.s86: The type of inattention that they continue to manifest (lack of persistence and distractibility) is still qualitatively different from the inattention manifested by children classified as the inattentive type.
sentences.s87: Any new theory of ADHD needs to address this emerging distinction.
sentences.s88: The model presented here provides a means of testing this dissociation between types of inattention by using functional neuroimaging methods along with measures of the executive functions whose deficiencies are linked in this model to the hyperactive-impul- sive types of ADHD.
sentences.s89: Clarification of Terms and Assumptions The term ADHD is used here to refer only to that subgroup of this population previously identified as hyperactive (Chess, 1960), hyperkinetic (APA, 1968), attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity (APA, 1980), ADHD (APA, 1987), or, more re- cently, ADHD-combined type and hyperactive-impulsive type (APA, 1994).
sentences.s90: In this article, ADHD and the model of it devel- oped here do not refer to that subgroup whose chief problem is inattention alone (predominantly inattentive type).
sentences.s91: The model set forth below presumes that the essential impair- ment in ADHD is a deficit involving response inhibition.
sentences.s92: This deficit leads to secondary impairments in the four neuropsycho- logical abilities that are partially dependent on inhibition for their effective execution.
sentences.s93: These secondary impairments then lead to decreased control of motor behavior by internally represented information and self-directed action.
sentences.s94: One consequence of this hierarchical relationship is that improvement or amelioration of the inhibitory deficit should result in improvement or normaliza- tion in the four executive functions that depend on it and also in improved motor control.

sentences.s117: Four of these abilities are critical for self-regulation and goal- directed persistence, so they are called executive functions here.

sentences.s123: These four executive func- tions, therefore, should be viewed as neuropsychological sys- tems separate from the behavioral inhibition system yet hierar- chically (or pyramidally) perched on it to assist in self- regulation.
sentences.s124: Self-regulation is any response, or chain of responses, by the individual that serves to alter the probability of the individual's subsequent response to an event and, in so doing, functions to alter the probability of a later consequence related to that event (Kanfer & Karoly, 1972; Skinner, 1953).

sentences.s129: The term executive Junc- tion refers to these mainly private (cognitive) self-directed ac- tions that contribute to self-regulation.
sentences.s130: So defined, the term incorporates most of the attributes often ascribed to it by others (Denckla, 1994; Stuss & Benson, 1986; Torgesen, 1994; Welsh &Pennington, 1988), including (a) self-directed actions; (b) the organization of behavioral contingencies across time; (c) the use of self-directed speech, rules, or plans; (d) deferred gratification; and (e) goal-directed, future-oriented, purposive, or intentional actions.

sentences.s150: The immediate purpose of the four executive functions de- scribed below seems to be the achievement of greater prediction and control over the individual's own behavior and environment, but their ultimate purpose seems to be an alteration in the future consequences a response is likely to produce (Bronowski, 1977; Fuster, 1989; Skinner, 1953).
sentences.s151: Such executive functions likely arise from (a) the development of neural networks within the prefrontal lobes, which underly these neuropsychological abili- ties and permit the acquisition of more specific skills used for self-control (Bronowski, 1977; Fuster, 1989); (b) the success these actions have had in the past for maximizing the net conse- quences of behavior, both immediate and delayed, when consid- ered across long time periods (Kanfer & Karoly, 1972); (c) the socialization of the child; and (d) the ongoing reinforcement of the individual for using self-regulatory actions (Hayes, 1989; Kopp, 1982; Skinner, 1953).

sentences.s153: Origins of the Model Much of the present model linking inhibition to four executive functions was set forth by Bronowski (1967) 30 years ago.
sentences.s154: Bronowski's theory has been discussed in more detail elsewhere as it pertains to ADHD (Barkley, 1994).
sentences.s155: The present explication differs substantially from the initial application of Bronowski's ideas to ADHD (Barkley, 1994,1995) in the following respects: (a) the incorporation of portions of Fuster's (1989,1995) theory and the views of others (Knights, Grabowecky, & Scabini, 1995; Milner, 1995) on the neuropsychological functions subserved by the prefrontal cortex into a new hybrid model; (b) the inclu- sion of more precise definitions of behavioral inhibition and self-regulation; (c) the addition of a motor control-fluency- syntax component to the model; (d) the inclusion of the self- regulation of drive and motivation as well as that of emotion in the model; (e) the reconfiguration of the model components more logically than before (Barkley, 1994); (f) the addition of numerous recent findings bearing on the linkages among these components and their applicability to ADHD; and (g) additional predictions about ADHD.
sentences.s156: In some sense, the evidence reviewed in this article in support of the hypothesized link between inhibition and executive func- tions, and even the extension of Bronowski's (1967, 1977) the- ory to ADHD, would have been anticipated by his theory and could be viewed as subsequent validation of it.
sentences.s157: The model devel- oped here also includes the later theory of Fuster (1989, 1995) on the neuropsychological functions of the prefrontal cortex, which was drawn from his extensive review of the animal and human neuropsychological literatures pertaining to these func- tions.
sentences.s158: Though developed independently, and for somewhat differ- ent purposes, Bronowski's and Fuster's models have a substan- tial number of similarities, so their combination into a hybrid model of behavioral inhibition and executive functions makes sense.
sentences.s159: Space permits only a brief summary of these two earlier theories to illustrate their many points of overlap.
sentences.s160: Bronowski's Theory on the Uniqueness of Human Language Bronowski (1977) identified four unique properties of human language that distinguish it from the languages of animals.
sentences.s161: He argued that human language is distinctive because it is not sim- ply a means of communication but of reflection, during which plans of action are proposed, played out, and tested.
sentences.s162: Reflection can only happen if there is a delay between the arrival of a stimulus or event and the response to that event.
sentences.s163: Bronowski treated this capacity to inhibit and delay responses as the central and formative feature in the evolution of the unique features of human language.
sentences.s164: It is not just the response that is being delayed but the decision to respond (Bronowski, 1976).
sentences.s165: Four conse- quences flow from the evolution of this ability to inhibit and delay responses; prolongation, separation of affect, internaliza- tion, and reconstitution.
sentences.s166: The capacity to delay responses as well as the four consequent mental functions flowing from it are attributed to the brain's prefrontal cortex.
sentences.s167: Prolongation is the ability to refer backward and forward in time and to exchange messages with others that propose action in the future.
sentences.s168: This prolongation of reference, or the relation of past events to future actions, requires a special form of memory.
sentences.s169: During the delay in responding, the features of the signal, situa- tion, or event must be briefly prolonged, fixed, and held in some symbolic form, so they can be retained for later recall when they will serve to revive the responses associated with them in the future.

sentences.s174: This form of memory is, in a sense, remembering so as to do.

sentences.s176: For instance, Goldman-Rakic (1995) denned working memory as "the ability to keep an item of information in mind in the absence of an external cue and utilize that information to direct an impending response" (p. 57).
sentences.s177: This form of memory and the prolongation of reference it affords are said to permit both imagination and the concept of time.
sentences.s178: The recall of the past surely is of the self-past, and the holding in mind of present events is the self-present, both of which should contribute to self-awareness.
sentences.s179: Thus are the functions of working memory, hindsight, fore- thought, anticipatory set, sense of time, and self-awareness de- pendent on inhibition.
sentences.s180: A second, subsidiary consequence of inhibition and response delay is the separation of affect.
sentences.s181: This refers to the separation of the emotional charge from the content of a message or event and, as a result, the separation of the emotional valence from the content of the response to the event.
sentences.s182: This involves the self- regulation of emotion apart from motor behavior, and it affords the generation of neutral responses despite emotionally provoca- tive events that may elicit highly charged feelings within the individual.
sentences.s183: Examples include remaining silent or speaking calmly when angered.
sentences.s184: The delay between event and response also permits time for the event to be referred to more than one center in the brain and gives rise to an inner discussion of alternatives before a response is formed.
sentences.s185: This internalizatiott of language gives a unique form to human thought and speech.
sentences.s186: During the delay in responding, language comes to be turned on the self.
sentences.s187: It thereby moves from being primarily a means for communication with others to one of communication with the self, a means of reflec- tion and exploration that permits the construction of hypothetical messages or responses before one is chosen to utter or perform.
sentences.s188: It also permits the creation of self-directed instructions and thereby becomes a fundamental tool for self-control.
sentences.s189: In support- ing his assertions, Bronowski (1967, 1977) referenced the views of Vygotsky (1978, 1987), so they are briefly discussed here.
sentences.s190: Vygotsky's (1978, 1987) theory on the development of pri- vate speech remains the most accepted view on the topic at this time (Berk, 1994).
sentences.s191: Such speech starts out as "speech uttered aloud by children that is addressed either to the self or to no one in particular" (Berk & Potts, 1991, p. 358).
sentences.s192: In its earliest stages, it is thought spoken out loud that accompanies ongoing action.
sentences.s193: As it matures, it functions as a form of self-guidance and direction by assisting with the formulation of a plan that will eventually assist the child in controlling his or her own actions (Berk & Potts, 1991).
sentences.s194: Gradually, speech becomes pro- gressively more private or internalized, and behavior comes in- creasingly under its control; private speech thus becomes inter- nal verbal thought that can exert a substantial controlling influ- ence over behavior.
sentences.s195: This internalization of speech proceeds in an orderly fashion.
sentences.s196: It seems to evolve from more conversational, task-irrelevant, and possibly self-stimulating forms of speech to more descriptive, task-relevant forms and then on to more prescriptive and self-guiding speech.
sentences.s197: It then progresses to more private, inaudible speech and finally to fully private, subvocal speech (Berk, 1986, 1994; Berk & Garvin, 1984; Berk & Potts, 1991; Bivens & Berk, 1990; Frauenglas & Diaz, 1985; Kohlberg, Yaeger, & Hjertholm, 1968).
sentences.s198: The internalization of language brings with it the fourth con- sequence of inhibition, which Bronowski (1977) called recon- stitution.
sentences.s199: It comprises two processes.
sentences.s200: The first is analysis, which is the decomposition of sequences of events or messages into their parts.
sentences.s201: This allows the progressive redistribution of the event or message to other parallel information-processing systems within the brain so that its cognitive content becomes more particularized, and its hortative content more generalized . . ..
sentences.s202: The physical world is pic- tured as made up of units that can be matched in language, and human language itself thereby shifts its vocabulary from command to description or predication. (Bronowski, 1977, p. 121) The second process is synthesis, wherein these parts can be manipulated and used to construct or reconstitute entirely new messages or responses to others.
sentences.s203: In addition, because the units in such messages can represent and initiate units of behavior, those behavioral units also can be reconstituted into entirely novel behavioral structures.
sentences.s204: This gives a synthetic and increas- ingly hierarchical structure to both human language and behav- ior.
sentences.s205: Increasingly complex, novel units come to be formed out of more elemental ones, and thus a layered structure to behavior is created.
sentences.s206: Reconstitution, it is argued, creates the potential for original productivity in human language and hence in the human actions controlled by that language (Bronowski, 1977).
sentences.s207: The rules or syntax for the sequencing of these verbal and behavioral productions are an inherent part of the process of reconstitution.
sentences.s208: Reconstitution is quite evident in verbal fluency and discourse because they represent the capacity to rapidly access and recon- stitute parts of speech into complete messages for others.
sentences.s209: The speed, accuracy, fluency, syntax, and general efficiency with which cognitive content is translated into units of speech and then into whole messages to others reflect the synthetic function of reconstitution.
sentences.s210: Verbal reconstitution should be most evident in confrontational language tasks or in goal-directed speech or writing, where ideas must be rapidly conveyed to achieve the goal of the task.
sentences.s211: However, it should also be evident in goal- directed behavioral creativity in general because this reflects the capacity to generate a variety of novel, complex sequences of behavior directed toward goals.
sentences.s212: Various hypothetical futures and the potential responses to them can now be internally simulated and tested before one is executed.

sentences.s225: On the other hand, time being inserted between the elements of the contingency (i.e., event, responses, and consequences) would be sufficient to do so.

sentences.s227: It is this synthesis of novel, cross-temporal behavioral struc- tures mediating cross-temporal contingencies that requires the involvement of prefrontal functions.
sentences.s228: It is also the goal they subserve that defines these behaviors and gives them cohesion and direction.
sentences.s229: Smaller sequences of behavior linked over shorter time periods can be used to create longer, more complex units of behavior with increasing durations and complexities and longer term objectives.
sentences.s230: This pyramiding of simpler units of be- havior into more complex ones produces a hierarchical structure to goal-directed behavior and bridges the temporal delays.
sentences.s231: This function is quite similar to Bronowski's (1977) concept of reconstitution.
sentences.s232: Several functions must occur for behavioral structures to be linked across time.
sentences.s233: Two of these are temporally symmetrical and are called retrospective and prospective functions.
sentences.s234: The retro- spective function entails the retention of information about past events that are held in their temporal sequence as they pertain to a goal.
sentences.s235: Such memory is provisional, having timeliness and term, and permits the referring of current events to previous events in a sequence as well as the retention of action-related information derived from that analysis.
sentences.s236: The retrospective func- tion gives rise to formulation and retention of a goal-directed behavioral structure.
sentences.s237: This forms the prospective function, and it leads to a preparation to act in anticipation of events or an anticipatory set.
sentences.s238: The behavioral scheme and its relevant events are temporarily represented, deployed in the preparation to act and the execution of those actions, and retained until the goal has been accomplished.
sentences.s239: These functions are identical to Bro- nowski's (1977) concepts of prolongation, hindsight, and fore- thought, as well as to the neuropsychological concept of working memory (Fuster, 1989, 1995).
sentences.s240: Fuster (1989, 1995) argued that the proficiency of working memory is dependent on response inhibition and interference control, just as Bronowski (1977) had done.
sentences.s241: It is in working memory that goals and intentions to act are retained and that action plans are formulated and used to guide the performance of the goal-directed responses.

sentences.s713: Conclusion The present theory holds that the satisfactory development of inhibition is essential for the normal performance of five other neuropsychological abilities: working memory, internalization of speech, self-regulation of affect-motivation—arousal, recon- stitution, and motor control—fluency—syntax.
sentences.s714: The first four of these are considered executive in nature because they permit self-regulation, the control of behavior by internally represented information, and the cross-temporal organization of behavior.
sentences.s715: Such self-regulation gives rise to the direction and persistence of behavior toward future goals and the ability to re-engage that behavior if disrupted.
sentences.s716: This intentional, purposive form of goal- directed behavior apparently functions to maximize future con- sequences over immediate ones for the individual.
sentences.s717: So behavioral inhibition is linked to working memory and sense of time, inter- nalization, self-motivation, behavioral creativity, and self-con- trol more generally.
sentences.s718: Besides its immediate application here to the understanding of ADHD, the hybrid model shown in Figure 1 would seem to have significant explanatory power within both neuropsychology and developmental psychology, perhaps helping to bridge these literatures with respect to the concepts of executive functions and self-regulation.
sentences.s719: Substantial evidence points to an impairment in three pro- cesses involving behavioral inhibition in ADHD: inhibition of prepotent responses, stopping of ongoing responses given feed- back on errors, and interference control.
sentences.s720: When the hybrid model of executive functions discussed above is extended to ADHD, impairments are predicted in the four executive functions in those having this disorder.
sentences.s721: These executive deficits then create deficiencies in motor control-fluency-syntax or the control of motor behavior by internally represented information.
sentences.s722: Research findings on ADHD, to varying degrees, seem to be consistent with deficits in the components of the model.
sentences.s723: The most consis- tent evidence to date appears to support the components of behavioral inhibition, working memory, poor self-regulation of motivation, and motor control and sequencing.
sentences.s724: It is not so much that the remaining components (internalized speech and recon- stitution) have gone unsupported but that they have been less studied in ADHD.
sentences.s725: The few researchers who have ventured to examine them have produced suggestive evidence that these components may also be impaired in ADHD.
sentences.s726: Much of the literature that does exist on the cognitive or neuropsychological deficits in ADHD suffers from numerous methodological problems.
sentences.s727: Most significant among these would have to be (a) the use of such small sample sizes that there is inadequate statistical power for detecting the small to moderate effect sizes that are probably associated with deficits in these executive functions; (h) the use of inconsistent selection criteria across studies in defining ADHD; (c) the failure to control for potentially confounding comorbid disorders; (d) the lack of attention to maturational and gender effects; and (e) the lack of regard for the effects of family history of ADHD on the deficits associated with ADHD in children.
sentences.s728: Such procedural compro- mises make much of the extant research inadequate for testing and potentially falsifying the predictions of the present model.
sentences.s729: Better designed research should help to resolve these inconsis- tencies and will undoubtedly lead to modifications of the model presented here.
sentences.s730: The hybrid model of executive functions developed here and the impairments it predicts in those with ADHD point to a large number of additional avenues for future investigation.
sentences.s731: These may yield new and important information on both the nature of executive functions and self-regulation as well as on the nature of ADHD itself.
sentences.s732: Such theory-driven research is to be welcomed into the science of ADHD and should offer much promise for improving the understanding and treatment of those with the disorder.

sentences.s1: Evidence fora pure timeperception deficit in children with ADHD Anna Smith, Eric Taylor, Jody Warner Rogers, Stuart Newman, and Katya Rubia Kings College, London, UK Background: Deﬁcits have been found previously in children with ADHD on tasks of time reproduction, time production and motor timing, implicating a deﬁcit in temporal processing abilities, which has been interpreted as either secondary or primary to core executive dysfunctions.
sentences.s2: The aim of this study was to explore further the abilities of hyperactive children in skills of time estimation, using a range of time perception tasks in different temporal domains.
sentences.s3: Method: Time estimation was tested in a verbal estimation task of 10 seconds.
sentences.s4: Time reproduction was also acquired for two time intervals of 5 and 12 seconds.
sentences.s5: A temporal discrimination task aimed to determine the idiosyncratic threshold of minimum time interval (in milliseconds) necessary to distinguish two intervals differing by approximately 300 milliseconds.
sentences.s6: Twenty-two children diagnosed with ADHD were compared to 22 healthy children, matched for age, handedness and working memory skills.
sentences.s7: Results: Children with ADHD were signiﬁcantly impaired in their time discrimination threshold: on average, time intervals had to be 50 ms longer for the hyperactive children in order to be discriminated when compared with controls.
sentences.s8: Children with ADHD also responded earlier on a 12-second reproduction task, which however only approached signiﬁcance after controlling for IQ and short-term memory.
sentences.s9: No group differences were found for the 5-second time reproduction or verbal time estimation tasks.
sentences.s10: Conclusions: The ﬁndings suggest that children with ADHD perform poorly on time reproduction tasks which load heavily on impulsiveness and attentional processes and they also suggest that these children may have a perceptual deﬁcit of time discrimination, which may only be detectable in brief durations which differ by several hundred milliseconds.
sentences.s11: A temporal perception deﬁcit in the range of milliseconds in ADHD may impact upon other functions such as perceptual language skills and motor timing.
sentences.s12: Keywords: ADD/ ADHD, attention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, time perception.
sentences.s13: Neuropsychological research over the last 30 years has addressed the question of the speciﬁc deﬁcits associated with ADHD, ﬁnding primarily frontal-lobe mediated executive dysfunctions, including deﬁcits in motor response inhibition, executive attentional control and working memory (Barkley, 1997).
sentences.s14: Sev- eral studies in the eighties and a few more recent studies have investigated skills associated with the temporal dimension of behaviour in ADHD (Stevens, Stover, & Backus, 1970; Cappella, Gentile, & Juli- ano, 1977; Senior, Towne, & Huessy, 1979; Barratt, 1981; Brown, 1982; Walker, 1982; Barkley, Koplo- witz, Anderson, & McMurray, 1997; Sonuga-Barke, Saxton, & Hall, 1998; Rubia, Taylor, Taylor, & Sergeant, 1999b; Rubia et al., 2001).
sentences.s15: Temporal pro- cessing skills include time perception and motor timing.
sentences.s16: Time perception has been measured in the form of verbal time estimation, temporal production, time reproduction and time discrimination.
sentences.s17: Motor timing has been measured by the ability to tempor- ally adjust a motor response to sensory stimulation.
sentences.s18: Temporal processing skills may play an important role in the deﬁcits observed in ADHD.
sentences.s19: Impulsivity can be deﬁned as a temporally inadequate and pre- mature behavioural style, where responses are made early, inaccurately and without consideration of future consequences.
sentences.s20: Deﬁcits in time estimation or an altered sense of time could underlie several problems of impulsiveness, such as problems with waiting behaviour (Barkley, 1997), delaying re- sponses (Sonuga-Barke, Taylor, Sembi, & Smith, 1992b), and with delaying gratiﬁcation (Gorenstein & Newman, 1980; Douglas & Parry, 1983).
sentences.s21: It is also possible that time estimation deﬁcits play a role in the observed deﬁcits in motor output control or impulsive executive cognitive style.
sentences.s22: Indeed, deﬁcits have been found in temporal reproduction and production estimations in hyper- active children (Cappella et al., 1977; Brown, 1982; Barkley et al., 1997; Sonuga-Barke et al., 1998), male delinquents (Barratt, 1981), impulsive boys (Walker, 1982) and impulsive adults (Van den Broek, Bradshaw, & Szabadi, 1992; Rubia, Schuri, van Cramon, & Poeppel, 1997).
sentences.s23: Production or reproduc- tion of time requires subjects to produce a time in- terval given in clock units or to reproduce a previously demonstrated time interval.
sentences.s24: In some of these studies, impulsivity appears to lead to an un- derestimation of time, which manifests in shorter production or reproduction of time intervals.
sentences.s25: (1997) found that children with ADHD were signiﬁcantly more inﬂuenced by distraction com- pared to control children in their reproduction esti- mates of 12s to 60s which were more inaccurate.
sentences.s26: Differences in temporal processing are deﬁned by Barkley as secondary, resulting from a primary Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 43:4 (2002), pp 529–542  Association for Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 2002.
sentences.s27: Published by Blackwell Publishers, 108 Cowley Road, Oxford OX4 1JF, UK and 350 Main Street, Malden, MA 02148, USA deﬁcit of behavioural inhibition, which prevents the proper development of working memory, or the ability to hold information online, which, in turn, disrupts the sense of time (Barkley, 1997).
sentences.s28: However, the authors also considered the possibility of a pri- mary deﬁcit of time estimation in children with ADHD.
sentences.s29: Sonuga Barke and his colleagues found sig- niﬁcant underestimates in temporal reproductions by children with ADHD using 5- and 15-second in- tervals.
sentences.s30: These underestimates were thought to be evidence of a relatively fast internal clock in children with ADHD during waiting periods, leading to an aversion to delay (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1998).
sentences.s31: (1999b) used an anticipation task, where sub- jects had to predict the onset of a target appearing every 6 seconds by anticipating the motor response to target appearance.
sentences.s32: Children with hyperactive beha- viour made more impulsive errors and had more variable anticipation times than healthy controls, but were not more inaccurate in time estimation, which was interpreted by the authors as a motor timing rather than a time estimation deﬁcit (Rubia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s33: This was further supported by additional ﬁndings in the same study of no temporal discrim- ination deﬁcit in the same hyperactive children between two intervals which differed by 2 seconds.
sentences.s34: While there is evidence that hyperactive children demonstrate differences in production and repro- duction tasks, responses in these timing tasks might not entirely be due to a perceptive time estimation deﬁcit, but can be confounded by other cognitive deﬁcits present in ADHD, such as the inability to withhold an ongoing response (Schachar, Tannock, & Logan, 1993), a prepotent impulsive response style (Schachar, Tannock, Marriot, & Logan, 1995), the preference not to wait, described as delay aversion (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992b), or even working memory deﬁcits in the case of reproduction, where the interval to be reproduced has to be held ‘online’ (Pennington & Ozonoff, 1996).
sentences.s35: The reproduction task used by Sonuga-Barke et al.
sentences.s36: (1998) was designed to incorporate a control task for potential deﬁcits in motor response inhibi- tion.
sentences.s37: The control task requires the subject to respond to a clearly deﬁned signal marking the end of the standard duration, providing a measure of response control.
sentences.s38: In the reproduction task the same duration as the standard interval has to be produced, but now the previously deﬁned signal is masked and no lon- ger visible to the subject.
sentences.s39: The required response to the standard interval in the ﬁrst part of the task provides a measure of potential premature response deﬁcits, controlling for confounding inhibitory deﬁ- cits in the temporal reproduction of the second part of the task.
sentences.s40: However, according to the authors, the observed underestimates of hyperactive children in the second part of the task may still have been con- founded by the differences in visual structure be- tween the standard and the reproduction intervals, whereby the less structured visual masking might have precipitated premature responses rather than true temporal underestimations (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1998).
sentences.s41: As time intervals increase, a greater load is placed upon working memory (Fraisse, 1984), motor per- sistence, sustained attention to time and inhibition of distraction (Barkley et al., 1997), all of which may lead to greater inaccuracy in normal sample groups (Fraisse, 1984; Marmaras, Vassilakis, & Dounias, 1995; Koivula, 1996).
sentences.s42: While the studies described above have focused upon temporal skills involving the duration estima- tion of several seconds, other studies have focused on timing at the motor output level, so-called motor timing functions.
sentences.s43: (1970) found faster tapping by hyperkinetic children compared with controls on a free tapping task.
sentences.s44: (1999b) found no differences in speed, but greater inconsis- tencies in sensorimotor synchronisation or timed tapping in children with hyperactive behaviour using time intervals of 400 ms to 1800 ms.
sentences.s45: Since the same sample of children showed no differences in time discrimination of several seconds, the deﬁcits in the motor timing tasks were attributed to inconsistency of motor adjustment and impulsive style of per- formance at the output level, rather than a percep- tive time estimation deﬁcit.
sentences.s46: However, this ﬁnding of greater inconsistencies in motor timing was not replicated in a later study using a clinical sample (Rubia et al., 2001).
sentences.s47: The length at which duration judgement becomes possible is thought to share a similar scale with units of fast-paced motor activity (Keele, Polorny, Corcos, & Ivry, 1985), and it is possible that sensorimotor or motor tasks may share a common mechanism with temporal perception.
sentences.s48: Therefore, inaccuracies of time perception in ADHD may lie in a shorter temporal window and may only be perceivable in the sub- second range.
sentences.s49: Potential time perceptual deﬁcits may therefore be better detected by tasks that measure the estimation of brief intervals that differ by only several hundred milliseconds rather than tasks using longer intervals of several seconds.
sentences.s50: The studies used so far have used production, reproduction, time estimation and time discrimin- ation of longer time intervals exceeding 2 seconds to investigate time estimation skills in children with ADHD.
sentences.s51: Evidence exists that longer durations of several seconds are processed differently from smaller durations in the range of sub-seconds and both processes may be considered to be distinct.
sentences.s52: Intervals of less than 3 seconds are thought to lie within the range of the ‘perceived present’ (Fraisse, 1984).
sentences.s53: This is supported by psychophysiological evidence suggesting that the threshold of a duration to be deﬁned as the psychological present, which can be perceived as a unit, and therefore is not inﬂu- enced by working memory, lies between 1 and 3 seconds (Mates, Mueller, Radil, & Poeppel, 1994; Poppel, 1997).

sentences.s56: Such a task would help to establish whether a true perceptual timing deﬁcit exists in children with ADHD.
sentences.s57: The purpose of this study was thus to investigate ‘pure’ time perception in a sample of children with ADHD by use of a temporal discrimination task, which determines the idiosyncratic threshold at which intervals differing by several milliseconds can be perceived as different.
sentences.s58: In addition, we wanted to compare this measurement of time discrimination in the shorter time range with measurements of time estimation of longer durations of several seconds.
sentences.s59: A verbal time estimation task of 10 seconds and two time reproduction tasks of 5 and 12 seconds were used to determine the ability of longer time estima- tions.
sentences.s60: If differences in time estimation can be ex- plained by other aspects of executive or attentional dysfunctions in ADHD that are not pure time esti- mation deﬁcits, such as delay aversion, prepotent response style or difﬁculties with inhibiting distrac- tion, then we predict that there will be an increased deﬁcit on the 12-second reproduction task for chil- dren with ADHD compared to the 5-second repro- duction task.
sentences.s61: Verbal estimates of a 10-second interval will be unaffected by confounding elements response related deﬁcits in ADHD, since this task does not require the executive function needed in a production or reproduction task.
sentences.s62: However, deﬁcits in sustained attention or freedom of distraction could still interfere with the pure time estimation compo- nent of the task.
sentences.s63: Due to the shortness of the temporal discrimination tasks, confounding neuropsycholo- gical functions such as working memory, sustained attention, delay aversion and inhibitory control are kept to a minimum.
sentences.s64: For this reason time discrimina- tion tasks have been considered more suitable tests of pure time estimation than other temporal tasks (Ru- bia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s65: Time perception in this short range has never been investigated in children with ADHD.
sentences.s66: If children with ADHD are impaired in the temporal discrimination of milliseconds, we woulddetect a pure time estimation deﬁcit, not confounded by other executive or attentional dysfunctions.
sentences.s67: Finally, it is interesting to note that ﬁne temporal discrimination has been found to be deﬁcient in dyslexic children (Nicolson, Fawcett, & Dean, 1995) and dyslexic adults (Hari & Kiesila, 1996) and has even been suggested as the cause of their language problems (Hari & Kiesila, 1996; von Steinbuchel, Wittman, Strasburger, & Szelag, 2000).
sentences.s68: Given the comorbidity between dyslexia and ADHD (Gilger, Pennington, & Defries, 1992), we thought the in- vestigation of ﬁne time perception in children with ADHD would be revealing.
sentences.s69: Method Subjects The clinical group comprised 19 boys and 3 girls, in the age range of 7 to 14 years (mean age ¼ 11.3, SD ¼ 2.3).
sentences.s70: The clinical diagnosis of ADHD (impulsive or combined subtype) or hyperkinetic disorder was made by a trained psychiatrist following DSM-IV (DSM IV, Ameri- can Psychiatric Association, 1995) or ICD-10 (ICD-10; World Health Organisation, 1994) diagnostic criteria.
sentences.s71: All subjects had received a systematic assessment at a research clinic including full parental and child inter- views to yield the information for the HYPESCHEME system (Curran, Newman, Taylor, & Asherson, 2000).
sentences.s72: In addition, subjects had to score above cut-off for hyperactive symptoms on the Rutter A (2) Parental Questionnaire (Rutter, Tizard, & Whitmore, 1970) and Conners Abbreviated Questionnaire for parents (Loney & Milich, 1982).
sentences.s73: Of these children, nine were also diagnosed with comorbid conduct disorder, which has shown to correlate highly with ADHD (Fergusson, Horwood, & Lloyd, 1991).
sentences.s74: All children were given a thorough assessment by a trained clinical psychologist to determine whether other comorbid diagnoses were present, including learning disabilities, using the Brit- ish Ability Scales (BAS).
sentences.s75: Children with these disorders were excluded from the sample.
sentences.s76: All children were free of medication for 24 hours prior to testing.
sentences.s77: A group of 20 male and 2 female referred control children, aged 8 to 14 (mean age ¼ 11.2, SD ¼ 1.7), was recruited from King’s College Dental Hospital with parental consent.
sentences.s78: Control children scored below cut- off for hyperactive symptoms or any other symptoms on Rutter A (2) and Rutter B (2) questionnaires, completed by parents and teachers.
sentences.s79: Exclusion criteria for all children were history of brain damage, epilepsy, emotional problems, learning disability or an IQ deviation score below 50, as estima- ted from the two WISC III sub-tests of vocabulary and block design (Sattler, 1988).
sentences.s80: All children were also tested for short-term and working memory using the digit span sub-test (forwards and backwards).
sentences.s81: The whole testing session lasted approximately 45 min.
sentences.s82: Time discrimination task A green circle was presented ﬁrst, consistently placed on the left side of the screen, followed by a red circle on the right side of the screen.

sentences.s84: One of the circles had a ﬁxed standard duration of 1000 msecs and the other circle was shown for a comparison duration, which was initially set at 1300 msecs.
sentences.s85: The experimental status attributed to each colour circle (i.e., standard or comparison) was randomised.
sentences.s86: After the presentation of the two circles, a question appeared on the screen, together with a diagram indicating which key represented which colour circle, asking ‘which circle lasted the longest, the green one, or the red one?’ The subjects then responded accordingly, by pressing the left (green) or right (red) key.
sentences.s87: Each time an error in judgement was made, the comparison duration was increased, thus increasing the difference between the two durations to be compared.

sentences.s173: Furthermore, no signiﬁcant correlations were found between the four dependent variables of the four tasks, suggesting that all of them are loading on different processes of time perception.

sentences.s192: Our ﬁndings support a motivational account of delay aversion (Sonuga-Barke et al., 1992b) as the main reason for deﬁcient time under- reproductions, rather than an intrinsic time per- ceptual problem, which should have been apparent in the shorter interval as much as in the verbal es- timation task.
sentences.s193: Motivational delay aversion is more likely to inﬂuence longer intervals, particularly when they have to be reproduced rather than verbally es- timated, since it is tempting to press the button prematurely to shorten the temporal delay.
sentences.s194: This was particularly the case in this study design where the duration of the 12-second task could be shortened by premature responding, whereas the 5-second re- production task included trials with a ﬁxed length which could not be shortened by premature re- sponding.
sentences.s195: In addition, poor performance on the long but not the short reproduction task could also be explained by other cognitive deﬁcits such as in- creased sensitivity to distraction or a failure to sus- tain attention, although no differential time-on-task effect was found.
sentences.s196: In sum, the ﬁndings presented here on time reproductions of 5 s and 12 s demonstrate that children with ADHD made earlier rather than later responses, but only on the longer of the two tasks.
sentences.s197: We suggest that the deﬁcits revealed by chil- dren with ADHD in these circumstances can be at- tributable to both impulsivity and other cognitive processes which load more heavily on longer time intervals, rather than a pure temporal deﬁcit.
sentences.s198: The deﬁcit found in the ability of children with ADHD to discriminate between very brief durations differing by about 300 msecs is very interesting in view of ﬁndings of the literature of predominantly executive, output-related deﬁcits in ADHD.
sentences.s199: These ﬁndings demonstrate deﬁcits at a ﬁne-perceptual level in ADHD.
sentences.s200: Signiﬁcant differences could not be explained by differences in trial number for each group since, while they varied for each subject on this task, there were no group differences in trial numbers.
sentences.s201: The overall short duration of the time discrimination task makes it unlikely that perform- ance differences in children with ADHD can be ac- counted for by deﬁcits in working and short-term memory, and when digit span scores are divided into backwards and forwards scores no signiﬁcant rela- tionships are seen between these measures and temporal threshold.
sentences.s202: This is further supported by the lack of group differences on the digit span sub-test of the WISC III, a reliable test of short-term memory, as well as the use of this variable as a covariate.
sentences.s203: The brief length of the durations also makes it unlikely that differences could be attributed to problems with motivation, delay aversion or sustained attention.
sentences.s204: This study therefore demonstrates for the ﬁrst time a real time perception deﬁcit in hyperactive children.
sentences.s205: Perceptual deﬁcits have been suggested to account for the deﬁcits hyperactive children have on the CPT in a meta-analysis on Methylphenidate-CPT studies on children with ADHD (Losier et al., 1996).
sentences.s206: The meta-analysis uses signal detection theory to show that the positive effects of Methylphenidate on CPT-performance were sensitive to stimulus dura- tion, number of trials and target probability, and, consequently, suggest an input/encoding locus of operation for Methylphenidate.
sentences.s207: The meta-analysis therefore hypothesises that a deﬁcit in encoding/ perceptual sensitivity accounts for omission and commission errors on the CPT, rather than a re- sponse bias, which would have supported a tradi- tional view of a primary output deﬁcit in ADHD.
sentences.s208: The ﬁndings presented here, showing a pure time per- ception deﬁcit in children with ADHD, support this hypothesis of a perceptual deﬁcit in ADHD using direct experimental methodology as recommended by Losier et al.
sentences.s209: This ﬁnding of a pure time perception deﬁcit in children with ADHD challenges the view that the deﬁcits in ADHD are exclusively to be found at the output level of performance (Van der Meere, 1996).
sentences.s210: The ﬁnding that children with ADHD may have an alteration in their ability to discriminate time inter- vals differs from the ﬁndings of Rubia et al.
sentences.s211: (1999b), who found no group differences in a time discrim- ination task.
sentences.s212: However, the intervals to be compared in that study differed by 2 seconds and the task may not been sensitive enough to elicit group differences.
sentences.s213: The present ﬁndings suggest that sequential time discrimination tasks with small step sizes are more suitable than methods using constants differing by several seconds to detect deﬁcits in children with ADHD.
sentences.s214: If two consistent durations are utilised for a discrimination task, but the threshold at which dif- ferences can no longer be perceived for both groups lies somewhere between zero and the value of the difference between those two chosen durations, then no differences will be observable.
sentences.s215: A sequential ex- periment, such as the one used here, means that the course of the experiment is dependent upon the performance of individual subjects.
sentences.s216: This kind of task is able to locate the point of subjective equality for each subject, which then enables the detection of group differences in threshold, unobservable with a method of constants.
sentences.s217: The ﬁndings regarding temporal perception are interesting in view of ﬁndings of similar time per- ception deﬁcits in other psychiatric groups, particu- larly those with language and speech disorder.

sentences.s220: Poor readers have also been shown to be impaired in a task of temporal order judgement (May, Williams, & Dunlap, 1988).
sentences.s221: Differences in temporal perception have been found in patients with dysphasia (Needham & Black, 1970) and dyslexic children (Nicolson et al., 1995).
sentences.s222: Inter- estingly, dyslexic children also demonstrate deﬁcits of speed, rhythm and precision upon speeded motor tasks (Denckla & Rudel, 1976), supporting a pro- posed association between time perception and mo- tor timing (Keele et al., 1985).
sentences.s223: Several characteristics of ADHD are shared by dyslexia, such as late language development and reading problems.
sentences.s224: Children with ADHD have more speech and language problems than can be ex- plained by chance alone (Semrud-Clikeman et al., Richards, 1998) and signiﬁcant language deﬁcits have been reported in a sample of boys with ADHD (Carte, Nigg, & Hinshaw, 1996).
sentences.s225: Given that dys- lexia is frequently comorbid with ADHD and that the two disorders may share aetiology (Gilger et al., 1992), it is possible that a shared deﬁcit which interferes with temporal perception of very brief intervals may interfere with language and reading skills.
sentences.s226: Phonemes last about 50 msecs and the present ﬁndings show that for children with ADHD to perceive differences in duration, intervals need to differ by about 50 msecs more than they do for controls, which may impact on their reading and perceptual language abilities.
sentences.s227: Improvement of temporal discrimination threshold by training has shown to improve the perceptive language prob- lems in aphasic patients (von Steinbuchel, 2000), further supporting the link between ﬁne temporal perception and language functions.
sentences.s228: In this study, children with comorbid dyslexia were excluded, supporting the view that a shared deﬁcit of tem- poral perception may be underlying common lan- guage difﬁculties.
sentences.s229: As well as with speech and language difﬁculties, a deﬁcit of ﬁne temporal perception may possibly im- pact upon motor timing abilities.
sentences.s230: Poor and variable sensori-motor coordination has been observed in both dyslexic children (Denckla & Rudel, 1976) and children with ADHD (Carte et al., 1996; Rubia et al., 1999b).
sentences.s231: Children with ADHD have been found to have slow reaction times during most cognitive and motor tasks (Firestone & Martin, 1979; Douglas & Parry, 1983; Temporowski, Tinsley, & Hager, 1994; Van der Meere, Shalev, Boerger, & Gross-Tsur, 1995; Leth-Steensen, King-Elbaz, & Douglas, 2000).
sentences.s232: Differences have also been found between children with ADHD and controls on tasks requiring speed modulation (Stevens et al., 1970; Van der Meere, 1996; Carte et al., 1996) or with certain manipula- tion of the preparatory interval (Zahn, Kruesi, & Rapoport, 1991).
sentences.s233: Cognitive performance in the hy- peractive child has been found either to beneﬁt from a fast event rate (Kappauf & Powe, 1959; Dalby, Kinsbourne, Swanson, & Sobol, 1977; Dalby, Kins- bourne, & Swanson, 1989; Van der Meere, Vreeling, & Sergeant, 1992), or to fail to be optimised by a slow event rate (Sykes, Douglas, Weiss, & Minde, 1971; Conte, Kinsbourne, Swanson, Zirk, & Samu- els, 1986) and even to decline with a slow pre- sentation rate (Swanson, Kinsbourne, Roberts, & Zucker, 1978; Chee et al., 1989; Temporowski et al., 1994; van der Meere et al., 1995).
sentences.s234: Hyperactive chil- dren prefer shorter stimulus presentation rates than controls in memory tasks (Sonuga-Barke, Taylor, & Heptinstall, 1992a).
sentences.s235: To summarise, it is possible that speed preference and motor timing variability in hyperactive children is related to their problems with time perception.
sentences.s236: However, it may also be rela- ted to their attentional deﬁcits.

sentences.s240: The variability of response style was interpreted by the authors as an indicator of poor attentional control or poor attention allocation.
sentences.s241: While we do not exclude the possibility that poor motor timing may be caused by poor motor atten- tion, it is conceivable that the ﬁndings of a differ- ential effect of external temporal structures on the performance of hyperactive children is at least partly related to deﬁcits in ﬁne temporal perception, as observed here.
sentences.s242: Timing has been described as ‘the essence of motor skill’ (Thelen, 1991) and it is possible that a deﬁcit of time perception can impact upon motor timing and consequently upon motor skills.
sentences.s243: How- ever, an association between time perception and motor timing may only be detectable if intervals used in both paradigms are comparable themselves.
sentences.s244: Associations have been found between temporal discrimination and motor timing in the range of 400 msecs (Keele et al., 1985).
sentences.s245: For this reason, a dis- crimination task comparing durations with differ- ences of milliseconds such as the one used in the current study may be more suitable to relate ﬁne temporal perception with motor timing.
sentences.s246: A common neural basis for both reaction time and time per- ception has also been suggested (Rammsayer, 1989).
sentences.s247: There is evidence that the same timing mechanism underlies the performance on both motor timing tasks and perceptual tasks of time discrimination.
sentences.s248: Motor variability has been found to be related to the accuracy of perceptual timing (Smith, 1957; Keele et al., 1985; Pastor, Artieda, Jahanshahi, & Obeso, 1992).

sentences.s250: The same prefrontal, striatal and cerebellar brain regions have been associated with both time per- ception (Ivry & Keele, 1989; Jueptner et al., 1995; Pedersen et al., 1997; Rubia et al., 1997; Rubia et al., 1998; Harrington, Haaland, & Hermanowicz, 1998; Mangels, Ivry, & Shimizu, 1998; Schubotz, Friederici, & Yves von Cramon, 2000; Maquet et al., 1996; Harrington et al., 1998; Harrington, Mead, Mayer, Haaland, & Rao, 2000) and motor timing (Ivry & Keele, 1989; Jueptner et al., 1995; Ivry, 1996; Penhune, Zatorre, & Evans, 1997; Penhune, Zatorre, & Evans, 1998; Harrington et al., 1998; Rubia et al., 2000, 2001).
sentences.s251: Interestingly, the brain regions that have been associated with time perception, namely prefrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia and the cerebellum, are key brain regions found to be impaired in ADHD.
sentences.s252: The vermis of the cerebel- lum, a region of the brain associated with percep- tual timing skills (Ivry & Keele, 1989; Nichelli, Alway, & Grafman, 1996; Mangels et al., 1998; Ivry, 1996; Jueptner et al., 1995; Penhune, Zatorre, & Evans, 1997, 1998), has been shown to be reduced in size in children with ADHD (Berquin et al., 1998; Mostofsky, Reiss, Lockhart, & Denckla, 1998).

sentences.s254: These two regions have been found to be underactivated during a time estimation task in adolescents with ADHD (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2000, 2001) and form part of grey matter areas that have been found to be morphologically reduced in pa- tients with ADHD (Castellanos et al., 1996).
sentences.s255: Besides cortical brain regions, sub-cortical structures such as the basal ganglia have also shown to be involved in time perception and to be dysfunctional and dysmorphological in children with ADHD.
sentences.s256: The basal ganglia are in fact key regions of morphological abnormality in ADHD (Hynd, Hern, Novey, & Elio- pulos, 1993; Castellanos et al., 1994; Aylward, Reiss, Reader, & Singer, 1996; Filipek, Semrud- Clikeman, & Steingard, 1997; Casey et al., 1997; Mataro, Garcia-Sanchez, Junque, Estevez-Gonz- alez, & Pujol 1997).
sentences.s257: They have also been found to be dysfunctional during cognitive testing and dur- ing rest in adolescents and adults with ADHD (Rubia et al., 1999a, 2000, 2001; Vaidya et al., 1998; Teicher et al., 2000).
sentences.s258: Children with thalamus and basal ganglia injury are signiﬁcantly more likely to develop secondary ADHD than children with other brain injuries (Gerring et al., 2000).
sentences.s259: The basal ganglia have been identiﬁed as strongly in- volved with timekeeping and time perception pro- cesses (Harrington et al., 2000; Schubotz et al., 2000; Rubia et al., 2000; Ivry, 1996; Harrington, Haaland, & Hermawicz, 1998; Nose et al., 2001).
sentences.s260: Patients with Parkinson’s disease and subsequent damage to the basal ganglia show do not perform well on time discrimination of brief intervals, while their processing of longer intervals is intact (Riesen & Schnider, 2001).
sentences.s261: An fMRI study using a time discrimination task nearly identical to the one used here, where subjects had to discriminate between time durations differing by several hundreds of milliseconds, found brain activation in caudate and putamen, the vermis of the cerebellum, and dorso- lateral prefrontal cortex (Rao, Mayer, & Harrington, 2001), all brain regions found to be compromised in children with ADHD (see above).
sentences.s262: In conclusion, brain regions found to be compromised in children with ADHD in both functional and structural brain imaging studies are implicated in time perception processes and in particular in a time discrimination task similar to the one used here.
sentences.s263: We therefore conclude that poor activation in these brain regions in ADHD may have been the cause for the poor performance on the temporal discrimination task.
